# Setup guide

The tasks that the labs share, in one place. Do each one once: every lab lists the ones it needs under **Before you
begin** and links back here, so the labs themselves stay short. On the labs site, set **Your values** first, and the
commands below fill in your subscription, tenant, and region. The site also opens this guide in a panel from any lab,
and you can mark each task **Done**: the labs then stop listing it. Your browser keeps the marks.

| Task | When you need it |
| :-- | :-- |
| [Check your subscription and permissions](#check-your-subscription-and-permissions) | Before your first lab |
| [Choose where to run commands](#choose-where-to-run-commands) | Every track except the portal |
| [Sign in to Azure](#sign-in-to-azure) | On your own machine. Cloud Shell is already signed in. |
| [Install the `aigateway` extension](#install-the-aigateway-extension) | The Azure CLI tracks and the **Verify** steps |
| [Register the resource providers](#register-the-resource-providers) | Once per subscription, before you create a gateway with the Azure CLI |
| [Find the available regions](#find-the-available-regions) | Before you choose a location |
| [Clone the labs repo](#clone-the-labs-repo) | The Bicep + azd tracks, the notebooks, and the code samples |
| [Deploy a lab with azd](#deploy-a-lab-with-azd) | The Bicep + azd tracks |

## Check your subscription and permissions

You need an Azure subscription where you can create resources. For the gateway's pricing, see the
[AI Gateway documentation](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs). Connected services, such as Foundry inference and
Application Insights, are billed normally.

| To | You need, for example |
| :-- | :-- |
| Create a gateway in the portal or with the Azure CLI | **Contributor** on the resource group, or on the subscription if you create a new resource group. Creating a gateway needs write access to both API Management and connector gateways. |
| Change a gateway that already exists | **Contributor** on its resource group |
| Give the gateway a role on a Foundry account, as most Bicep + azd tracks do | **Owner**, or **Contributor** plus **Role Based Access Control Administrator**, on the subscription. The templates create a resource group and role assignments, so that the gateway can call your models with its own identity. |

Each lab lists any other role that it needs under **Before you begin**. In the portal, a subscription where you
can't create gateways shows as disabled in the subscription picker.

## Choose where to run commands

[Azure Cloud Shell](https://shell.azure.com) is the quickest way. Open it in Bash or PowerShell: it's already signed
in, and it has the Azure CLI, the Azure Developer CLI (`azd`), Git, `jq`, `curl`, Python, Node.js, and .NET. Add
the [`aigateway` extension](#install-the-aigateway-extension), and you're ready for every track.

To work on your own machine, install the tools for the tracks you plan to follow:

| Tool | Used by |
| :-- | :-- |
| [Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli) 2.75 or later | The Azure CLI tracks, the **Verify** steps, and `azd env new` in the Bicep + azd tracks |
| The [`aigateway` extension](#install-the-aigateway-extension) | The `az aigateway` commands |
| [Azure Developer CLI (`azd`)](https://aka.ms/azd-install) | The Bicep + azd tracks. It installs Bicep the first time it needs it. |
| [Git](https://git-scm.com/downloads) | Cloning the labs repo |
| [`jq`](https://jqlang.org/download/) | The Bash snippets that build or read JSON. The PowerShell snippets don't need it. |
| Python, Node.js, or the .NET 8 SDK | The code samples, depending on the language. Each lab lists the versions it needs. |

Every command comes in a Bash and a PowerShell variant, unless it's the same in both shells. The PowerShell commands
need PowerShell 7 or later, as Cloud Shell has; Windows PowerShell 5.1 doesn't run them.

## Sign in to Azure

Cloud Shell is already signed in, so skip this step there. On your own machine, sign in to the Azure CLI, select the
subscription for the labs, and sign in to `azd` for the Bicep + azd tracks:

```bash title="Bash or PowerShell"
# Sign in to the Azure CLI in your browser, with the account that has access to your subscription
az login &&
  echo "🪪 Signed in to the Azure CLI"

# Select the subscription for the labs, so that every later command creates resources in it
az account set --subscription "<subscription-id>" &&
  echo "🆔 Subscription <subscription-id> is selected"

# Sign in to the Azure Developer CLI (azd) too, for the Bicep + azd tracks
azd auth login &&
  echo "🪪 Signed in to azd"
```

If your account belongs to more than one tenant, sign in to the tenant that has the subscription instead:

```bash title="Bash or PowerShell"
# Sign in to the Azure CLI in the tenant that has your subscription
az login --tenant "<tenant-id>" &&
  echo "🪪 Signed in to the Azure CLI in tenant <tenant-id>"

# Sign in to azd in the same tenant
azd auth login --tenant-id "<tenant-id>" &&
  echo "🪪 Signed in to azd in tenant <tenant-id>"
```

> **Checkpoint**
> `az account show --query name -o tsv` prints the name of the subscription you selected.

## Install the `aigateway` extension

The labs manage gateways with the `aigateway` extension of the Azure CLI. Install or upgrade it, then check that the
CLI loads it. The installer downloads the published release, verifies it, and needs no Azure sign-in.

```bash title="Bash"
# Install or upgrade the aigateway extension of the Azure CLI: the installer downloads and verifies the release
curl -fsSL https://aka.ms/aigateway-cli-install | sh &&
  echo "🧩 aigateway extension $(az extension show --name aigateway --query version --output tsv) is installed"

# Check that the Azure CLI loads the extension: it prints the extension version and the API version it calls
echo "🧩 The aigateway extension reports:"
az aigateway version
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Install or upgrade the aigateway extension of the Azure CLI: the installer downloads and verifies the release
irm https://aka.ms/aigateway-cli-install-ps | iex
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧩 aigateway extension $(az extension show --name aigateway --query version --output tsv) is installed" }

# Check that the Azure CLI loads the extension: it prints the extension version and the API version it calls
Write-Host "🧩 The aigateway extension reports:"
az aigateway version
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The installer printed `🧩 aigateway extension … is installed`, and `az aigateway version` prints the extension
> version and the API version it calls, `2025-09-01-preview`. The labs need version `1.0.0b14` or later; run the
> installer again to upgrade an older one.

> [!NOTE]
> The labs use `az aigateway` commands wherever the extension covers an operation. A few operations, such as
> gateway-wide policies, telemetry exporters, and the connector gateway, aren't in the extension yet. For those,
> the labs call the Azure Resource Manager REST API with `az rest` and say why.

## Register the resource providers

The gateway lives in the `Microsoft.ApiManagement` resource provider and its companion connector gateway in
`Microsoft.Web`. Most labs also create a Foundry account, in `Microsoft.CognitiveServices`. Register them once per
subscription. Registering returns quickly when a provider is already registered.

```bash title="Bash"
# Register the resource providers for AI Gateway, its connector gateway, and Foundry (once per subscription)
# --wait returns when each provider is registered, and right away if it already is
for ns in Microsoft.ApiManagement Microsoft.Web Microsoft.CognitiveServices; do
  az provider register --namespace "$ns" --wait && echo "🧩 $ns is registered"
done
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Register the resource providers for AI Gateway, its connector gateway, and Foundry (once per subscription)
# --wait returns when each provider is registered, and right away if it already is
foreach ($ns in "Microsoft.ApiManagement", "Microsoft.Web", "Microsoft.CognitiveServices") {
  az provider register --namespace $ns --wait
  if ($?) { Write-Host "🧩 $ns is registered" }
}
```

A few labs use more providers. Register them the same way before you start those labs:

| Provider | Used by |
| :-- | :-- |
| `Microsoft.Insights` and `Microsoft.OperationalInsights` | [13 · Monitoring](13-monitoring/README.md) and [21 · Enterprise reference](21-enterprise-reference/README.md) |
| `Microsoft.Network` | [18 · Private networking](18-private-networking/README.md) |

> **Checkpoint**
> The loop printed a line such as `🧩 Microsoft.ApiManagement is registered` for each provider, and
> `az provider show --namespace Microsoft.ApiManagement --query registrationState -o tsv` prints `Registered`.

Registering a provider needs a role such as **Contributor** on the subscription. If you don't have it, ask your
subscription administrator to register the providers.

## Find the available regions

AI Gateway keeps adding regions. List the current ones: the first command reads the regions of the
`Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways` resource type, and the second matches them to the region names that
`--location` takes.

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the regions of the aigateways resource type, where you can create a gateway
regions=$(az provider show --namespace Microsoft.ApiManagement \
  --query "resourceTypes[?resourceType=='aigateways'].locations | [0]" -o json)

# Match them to the region names that --location takes, and print both as a table
echo "📍 Regions where you can create a gateway:"
az account list-locations -o json |
  jq -r --argjson regions "$regions" '
    ["Display Name", "Name"],
    (.[] | select(.displayName as $d | $regions | index($d)) | [.displayName, .name])
    | @tsv
  ' | column -t -s $'\t'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the regions of the aigateways resource type, where you can create a gateway
$regions = az provider show --namespace Microsoft.ApiManagement `
  --query "resourceTypes[?resourceType=='aigateways'].locations | [0]" -o json | ConvertFrom-Json

# Match them to the region names that --location takes, and print both as a table
Write-Host "📍 Regions where you can create a gateway:"
az account list-locations -o json | ConvertFrom-Json |
  Where-Object { $regions -contains $_.displayName } |
  Format-Table @{ Label = 'Display Name'; Expression = { $_.displayName } }, @{ Label = 'Name'; Expression = { $_.name } }
```

Expected output: the `📍 Regions where you can create a gateway:` line, then one row per region, such as
`East US 2   eastus2`. Use a value from the **Name** column wherever a lab asks for a location. The portal lists the
regions where it can create gateways, which can be fewer. To use a region that it doesn't list, create the gateway
with the Azure CLI or Bicep + azd track.

Most labs also deploy Foundry models, and their templates put the Foundry account in the gateway's region, so pick a
region where those models are available too. Each lab names its models. For example, this command prints the
deployment types of `gpt-6-luna` in a region, and prints nothing if the model isn't available there:

```bash title="Bash"
# List the deployment types of gpt-6-luna in a region, such as GlobalStandard: no output means it isn't there
echo "🧠 Deployment types of gpt-6-luna in <location>:"
az cognitiveservices model list --location "<location>" \
  --query "[?model.name=='gpt-6-luna'].model.skus[].name" -o tsv
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# List the deployment types of gpt-6-luna in a region, such as GlobalStandard: no output means it isn't there
Write-Host "🧠 Deployment types of gpt-6-luna in <location>:"
az cognitiveservices model list --location "<location>" `
  --query "[?model.name=='gpt-6-luna'].model.skus[].name" -o tsv
```

## Clone the labs repo

The Bicep + azd tracks, the notebooks, and the code samples run from the
[labs repo](https://github.com/Azure/ai-gateway/tree/main/labs). Clone it once into your home folder:

```bash title="Bash or PowerShell"
# Clone the labs repo into your home folder, as ~/ai-gateway, where every lab expects it
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/Azure/ai-gateway.git &&
  echo "📂 The labs are in ~/ai-gateway/labs"
```

Each lab then moves into its own folder, for example `cd ~/ai-gateway/labs/06-token-limits`. If you cloned the repo
before, get the latest labs with `git -C ~/ai-gateway pull` instead. If you cloned it somewhere else, use that path
instead of `~/ai-gateway`.

## Deploy a lab with azd

Each Bicep + azd track is a small azd project in its lab's folder: an `azure.yaml` file and an `infra/` folder with
the Bicep templates. It creates its own resource group, gateway, and whatever else the lab needs, so it doesn't
depend on other labs or on **Your values**. Every track follows the same steps:

1. Move into the lab's folder.
2. Create an azd environment. Its name also names the resource group, `rg-<environment name>`. `--location` sets the
   region of every resource, and `--subscription` selects the Azure CLI's current subscription, so azd doesn't
   prompt you.
3. Run `azd up` to deploy the templates. It ends with `SUCCESS`.
4. Read the outputs that the next steps use with `azd env get-value <NAME>`, or list them all with
   `azd env get-values`.

For example, for [lab 06](06-token-limits/README.md):

```bash title="Bash"
# Move into the lab's folder, which holds its azure.yaml file and its infra/ templates
cd ~/ai-gateway/labs/06-token-limits &&
  echo "📂 Lab folder: $(pwd)"

# Create an azd environment in your current subscription and region, so that azd doesn't prompt you
azd env new aigw-lab06 --location "<location>" --subscription "$(az account show --query id --output tsv)" &&
  echo "📝 azd environment aigw-lab06 deploys to <location>"

# Deploy the templates: the resource group rg-aigw-lab06, the gateway, and whatever else the lab needs
azd up &&
  echo "🚀 Lab deployed to rg-aigw-lab06"

# Read one of the outputs that the next steps use: the gateway's runtime URL
echo "🌐 Runtime URL:"
azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Move into the lab's folder, which holds its azure.yaml file and its infra/ templates
cd ~/ai-gateway/labs/06-token-limits
if ($?) { Write-Host "📂 Lab folder: $(Get-Location)" }

# Create an azd environment in your current subscription and region, so that azd doesn't prompt you
azd env new aigw-lab06 --location "<location>" --subscription (az account show --query id --output tsv)
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 azd environment aigw-lab06 deploys to <location>" }

# Deploy the templates: the resource group rg-aigw-lab06, the gateway, and whatever else the lab needs
azd up
if ($?) { Write-Host "🚀 Lab deployed to rg-aigw-lab06" }

# Read one of the outputs that the next steps use: the gateway's runtime URL
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL:"
azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL
```

Each lab gives its environment name, such as `aigw-lab06`, and a region that its models support, usually `eastus2`.
For another region, use a name from [Find the available regions](#find-the-available-regions) where the lab's models
are available. To change a template parameter later, run `azd env set <NAME> <value>`, then `azd provision`.

### Delete what azd created

When you finish a lab, run this from its folder. It deletes the environment's resource group and everything in it,
usually within ten minutes:

```bash title="Bash or PowerShell"
# Delete everything that azd up created, purge the soft-deleted Foundry account, and skip the confirmation prompt
azd down --purge --force &&
  echo "🧹 Everything that azd up created is deleted"
```

`--purge` also purges soft-deleted resources such as the Foundry account, which would otherwise stay soft-deleted
for 48 hours and keep counting against your quota. `--force` skips the confirmation prompt.

## Troubleshooting

For sign-in, extension, resource provider, region, and azd errors, with their likely causes and fixes, see
[Troubleshooting](TROUBLESHOOTING.md#setup-and-deployment).

# Your first model call in 5 minutes

Azure AI Gateway gives your apps and agents one governed endpoint for models and tools. In five minutes you create a
gateway, put a Microsoft Foundry model behind it, and call that model the way an app does: with the gateway's URL, an
alias in the `model` field, and a runtime API key. Click through the AI Gateway portal, paste a few Azure CLI
commands into Azure Cloud Shell, or clone a Bicep template and deploy it with one `azd up`.

![Create the gateway, a Foundry model, a provider, an alias, and a runtime key in the AI Gateway portal, with the Azure CLI in Cloud Shell, or with a Bicep template and azd up. Then your app calls the alias with the key, and the gateway routes the call to Foundry with its managed identity](../assets/diagrams/quickstart.svg "Set up once, in the portal, in Cloud Shell, or with azd up. Then every call goes through the gateway: it checks the key, routes the alias, and signs in to Foundry with its own identity.")

## Before you begin

You need an Azure subscription where you can create resources and role assignments, for example **Owner**, or
**Contributor** plus **Role Based Access Control Administrator**. The gateway gets a role on your Foundry account, so
that it can call the model with its own identity. Each track lists the tools that it needs at its start.

The Azure CLI and Bicep + azd tracks take a location: `eastus2`, or another region from
[Find the available regions](../SETUP.md#find-the-available-regions). They also create the Foundry account in that
region, so pick one where `gpt-6-luna` is available too. Each track includes every setup step that it needs, so you
can paste it into Cloud Shell as it is. The [Setup guide](../SETUP.md) explains these steps, and the later labs
link to it.

## How it works

Every call that goes through AI Gateway uses the same building blocks. In this quick start you create one of each.

| Building block | What it does | In this quick start |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| **Gateway** | The Azure resource (`Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways`) that gives your apps one runtime URL for models and tools | Your gateway, at `https://<gateway>.<location>-01.ai.gateway.azure.com` |
| **Model provider** | A connection to a backend. The gateway signs in to it with its own managed identity, so your apps never hold a backend key | Your Foundry account. The Azure CLI and Bicep tracks name the provider `foundry-models` |
| **Model** | A backend deployment that the gateway can route to | The Foundry deployment `gpt-6-luna` |
| **Alias** | The name that apps send in the `model` field. The gateway routes the alias to one or more models | `<foundry-account-name>/gpt-6-luna` in the portal, `gpt-6-luna` in the Azure CLI and Bicep tracks |
| **Runtime API key** | Identifies the app that calls the gateway, for limits, cost, and monitoring. Azure RBAC with Microsoft Entra ID tokens is the keyless alternative | `app-first-call` |

Your app calls the OpenAI-compatible base URL `<gateway URL>/default/models/openai/v1`, so any OpenAI SDK works with
a different base URL and the runtime key. For the full tour, watch the 3-minute video in
[How Azure AI Gateway works](../00-how-ai-gateway-works/README.md).

## Create a gateway and make your first call

Pick one track. Each one creates the same building blocks, makes your first call through the gateway, and ends with
how to clean up.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

**What you need:** a browser, and a model deployment in a Microsoft Foundry account, for example `gpt-6-luna`.

<details>
<summary>No Foundry deployment yet? Create one in Cloud Shell.</summary>

Open [Azure Cloud Shell](https://shell.azure.com) in Bash and paste these commands. They create a Foundry account with
a `gpt-6-luna` deployment in a new resource group, in a minute or two. Then create the gateway in the same resource
group, so that you can clean up with one command. Model inference is billed per use.

```bash title="Bash"
# Name the resource group, and give the Foundry account a random, globally unique name
RG="rg-aigw-quickstart"; FOUNDRY="aigw$(openssl rand -hex 3)"

# Create the resource group that holds the Foundry account and, later, the gateway
az group create --name "$RG" --location eastus2 --output none &&
  echo "📦 Resource group $RG is ready in eastus2"

# Create the Foundry account, with a custom subdomain so that the gateway can sign in with Microsoft Entra ID
az cognitiveservices account create --resource-group "$RG" --name "$FOUNDRY" --location eastus2 \
  --kind AIServices --sku S0 --custom-domain "$FOUNDRY" --yes --output none &&
  echo "🏭 Foundry account $FOUNDRY is ready"

# Deploy gpt-6-luna with 10,000 tokens per minute of Global Standard capacity
az cognitiveservices account deployment create --resource-group "$RG" --name "$FOUNDRY" \
  --deployment-name gpt-6-luna --model-name gpt-6-luna --model-version 2026-09-22 --model-format OpenAI \
  --sku-name GlobalStandard --sku-capacity 10 --output none &&
  echo "🧠 Model deployment gpt-6-luna is ready"
echo "✅ Create the gateway in $RG, and import gpt-6-luna from $FOUNDRY"
```

</details>

### Create the gateway

1. Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and sign in. For your first gateway, the portal opens
   **Create AI gateway** right away. Otherwise, open the gateway switcher in the top bar and select
   **Create new gateway**.

   ![The gateway switcher open in the top bar, with Recent gateways, View all gateways, and Create new gateway](../assets/screens/quickstart-01-switcher.webp "The gateway switcher lists your recent gateways. Create new gateway opens the Create AI gateway dialog.")

2. Enter a **Name**, or select **Generate a new name**. Then choose your **Subscription**, a **Resource group**, and
   a **Region**. For the resource group, select **New**, or select **Existing** and pick the resource group of your
   Foundry account, so that you can clean up both with one command.

   ![The Create AI gateway dialog with a name, the Existing resource group rg-aigw-quickstart, and the East US 2 region](../assets/screens/quickstart-02-create.webp "Create AI gateway: a generated name, the existing resource group of the Foundry account, and East US 2.")

3. Keep the **Advanced** defaults and select **Create gateway**. **All gateways** opens and shows the provisioning
   status, which moves from **Activating** to **Succeeded** in a few minutes. Then the portal selects your new
   gateway.

   ![All gateways with the banner Gateway creation is in progress and the new gateway in the Activating state](../assets/screens/quickstart-03-provisioning.webp "All gateways while the gateway provisions. You can keep using other gateways in the meantime.")

### Import the model from Foundry

1. **Home** opens with the **Set up your gateway** guide. Under **Add a model**, select
   **Add from Microsoft Foundry**.

   ![Home with the new gateway in the switcher and the Set up your gateway guide, with Add from Microsoft Foundry highlighted](../assets/screens/quickstart-04-home.webp "Set up your gateway walks you through three steps: add a model, test a model, and apply policies.")

   You can also start from **Models** › **Add** › **Models from Microsoft Foundry**.

   ![The Models page with the Add menu open on Models from Microsoft Foundry](../assets/screens/quickstart-05-add-menu.webp "Models › Add imports models from Microsoft Foundry or a custom provider, or creates an alias for a model that you already added.")

2. **Add models from Microsoft Foundry** discovers the model deployments in your subscriptions and selects all of
   them. In **Resource groups**, select only the resource group of your Foundry account. Then check that **Models**
   selects only your Foundry account with `gpt-6-luna`.
3. Keep **Managed identity** as the **Authentication method**, with the system-assigned managed identity, and keep
   **Create an alias for each model** selected. Then select **Add models**.

   ![Add models from Microsoft Foundry, filtered to one resource group, with Managed identity, Create an alias for each model, one selected Foundry account with gpt-6-luna, and the Add models button highlighted](../assets/screens/quickstart-06-import.webp "Filter by resource group, so that you import only the deployment that you need. The gateway calls Foundry with its managed identity.")

4. **Models** opens. The **Backend models** tab lists `gpt-6-luna`, and the **Aliases** tab shows the alias that
   apps call: `<foundry-account-name>/gpt-6-luna`. Note the alias.

   ![The Aliases tab of Models with the alias aigwb92bd1/gpt-6-luna, its backend model gpt-6-luna, and its provider](../assets/screens/quickstart-07-alias.webp "Each alias is named after the Foundry account and the deployment, and routes to the backend model gpt-6-luna.")

### Create a runtime API key

A key is the quickest way to start. Azure RBAC is the keyless alternative: grant the app the
**AI Gateway Models User** role in **Access** › **Entra ID**, and it sends a Microsoft Entra ID token instead of a
key. [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md) shows how.

1. Select **Access**, then the **Keys** tab, then **Create API key**.

   ![Access with the Keys tab, the Create API key button, and the new key app-first-call in the list](../assets/screens/quickstart-08-keys.webp "Access › Keys lists the built-in all-access subscription and your keys. After the next step, app-first-call appears here.")

2. Enter `app-first-call` as the **Key name**, then select **Create**.

   ![The Create API key dialog with the key name app-first-call and the Create button](../assets/screens/quickstart-09-key-create.webp "Give the key a name that identifies the app. Limits, cost, and monitoring use it.")

3. In **API key created successfully**, select **Copy & done** to copy the key. Keep it somewhere safe: you paste it
   in the next steps. You can view, rotate, or delete it later in **Access** › **Keys**.

   ![The API key created successfully dialog with a masked key, the key name, and the Copy & done button](../assets/screens/quickstart-10-key-done.webp "The key stays masked until you select Show. Copy & done copies it and closes the dialog.")

### Make your first call

Call the model through the gateway in the playground, with your new key, the way an app does.

1. Select **Catalog**, then select your model.

   ![The Catalog with the model card aigwb92bd1/gpt-6-luna](../assets/screens/quickstart-11-catalog.webp "The Catalog lists the models and MCP servers that apps can call through this gateway.")

2. Under **Authentication**, choose `app-first-call` as the **API key**, so that the playground calls the gateway
   with your new key. Then send a prompt, for example `In one sentence, what does an AI gateway do?`.

   ![The model page with the API key app-first-call, the prompt, and the model's reply](../assets/screens/quickstart-12-playground.webp "The playground calls the gateway's endpoint with the key that you choose, and shows the reply, the latency, and the tokens.")

3. Optional: to make the same call from code, select **Continue in code**. It shows the endpoint URL and snippets
   for cURL, the OpenAI SDK, LangChain, Vercel AI, the GitHub Copilot SDK, and Microsoft Agent Framework, plus a
   prompt that installs the AI Gateway plugin in your coding agent.

   ![Continue in code with the cURL snippet selected, which calls the alias with the api-key header](../assets/screens/quickstart-13-code.webp "The cURL snippet has your gateway's URL and alias, and reads the key from the AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY environment variable.")

To run the cURL snippet, open [Azure Cloud Shell](https://shell.azure.com) in Bash, paste your key at this prompt so
that it never shows on screen, and then paste the snippet:

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the key without showing it, and export it for the snippet
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

> **Checkpoint:** the playground answered with the key `app-first-call`. Your gateway is live, and your app never
> needs a Foundry key: only the gateway's managed identity calls Foundry.

### Clean up

To keep exploring, skip this step: [lab 03](../03-multi-provider-aliases/README.md) and the labs after it work on this
gateway. On the labs site, save the resource group and the gateway name in **Your values**. Otherwise, delete the
gateway.

1. Open the gateway switcher in the top bar and select **View all gateways**.

2. On your gateway's row, select **More actions** (**⋮**), and then select **Delete**.

   ![All gateways filtered to lucky-brook, with the More actions menu open on its row and Delete marked](../assets/screens/quickstart-14-delete.webp "The More actions menu on a gateway's row: open the gateway in the Azure portal, copy its resource ID, or delete it.")

3. To confirm, select **Delete** in the dialog. The row shows **Deleting** until Azure removes the gateway, in about
   five minutes.

   ![The dialog Delete "lucky-brook-5340"? with the Cancel and Delete buttons, and Delete marked](../assets/screens/quickstart-15-delete-confirm.webp "Deleting a gateway removes its models, aliases, keys, and policies. It can't be undone.")

Deleting the gateway keeps its resource group and your Foundry account. If you created them in Cloud Shell for this
quick start, delete the resource group and purge the Foundry account there too: deleted Foundry accounts stay
soft-deleted for 48 hours and keep counting against your quota until you purge them.

```bash title="Bash"
# Find the Foundry account in the resource group, so that you can purge it after the delete
FOUNDRY="$(az cognitiveservices account list --resource-group rg-aigw-quickstart --query "[0].name" --output tsv)"
echo "🏭 Foundry account: $FOUNDRY"

# Delete the resource group, with everything in it
az group delete --name rg-aigw-quickstart --yes &&
  echo "🧹 Resource group rg-aigw-quickstart is deleted"

# Purge the deleted Foundry account, so that it stops counting against your quota
az cognitiveservices account purge --name "$FOUNDRY" --resource-group rg-aigw-quickstart --location eastus2 &&
  echo "🧹 Foundry account $FOUNDRY is purged"
```

> **Checkpoint:** after you refresh the page, **All gateways** no longer lists your gateway.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

**What you need:** [Azure Cloud Shell](https://shell.azure.com), in Bash or PowerShell. It's already signed in and has
the Azure CLI, `curl`, and `jq`. A local Azure CLI 2.75 or later, signed in with `az login`, works too. The track
installs the `aigateway` CLI extension and creates the Foundry deployment for you.

### Set your variables

<!-- setup-done: tools sign-in extension -->

Paste the block for your shell. It installs or upgrades the `aigateway` extension, then sets the names. A random
suffix keeps the gateway and Foundry account names globally unique.

```bash title="Bash"
# Install or upgrade the aigateway extension of the Azure CLI
curl -fsSL https://aka.ms/aigateway-cli-install | sh &&
  echo "🧩 aigateway extension $(az extension show --name aigateway --query version --output tsv) is installed"

# Name the resources: the random suffix keeps the gateway and Foundry account names globally unique
export RG="rg-aigw-quickstart"
export LOCATION="eastus2"                     # or another region from Find the available regions
SUFFIX="$(openssl rand -hex 3)"
export GATEWAY="aigw-$SUFFIX"                 # part of the runtime URL
export FOUNDRY="aigw$SUFFIX"                  # the Foundry account and its subdomain
export DEPLOYMENT="gpt-6-luna"
export PROVIDER="foundry-models"

# Read your subscription ID, and build the gateway's resource ID that later commands use
export SUBSCRIPTION_ID="$(az account show --query id --output tsv)"
export GATEWAY_ID="/subscriptions/$SUBSCRIPTION_ID/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY"
echo "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY and Foundry account $FOUNDRY, in $RG ($LOCATION)"
echo "🆔 Subscription: $SUBSCRIPTION_ID"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Install or upgrade the aigateway extension of the Azure CLI
irm https://aka.ms/aigateway-cli-install-ps | iex
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧩 aigateway extension $(az extension show --name aigateway --query version --output tsv) is installed" }

# Name the resources: the random suffix keeps the gateway and Foundry account names globally unique
$RG         = "rg-aigw-quickstart"
$LOCATION   = "eastus2"                       # or another region from Find the available regions
$SUFFIX     = [guid]::NewGuid().ToString("N").Substring(0, 6)
$GATEWAY    = "aigw-$SUFFIX"                  # part of the runtime URL
$FOUNDRY    = "aigw$SUFFIX"                   # the Foundry account and its subdomain
$DEPLOYMENT = "gpt-6-luna"
$PROVIDER   = "foundry-models"

# Read your subscription ID, and build the gateway's resource ID that later commands use
$SUBSCRIPTION_ID = az account show --query id --output tsv
$GATEWAY_ID      = "/subscriptions/$SUBSCRIPTION_ID/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY"
Write-Host "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY and Foundry account $FOUNDRY, in $RG ($LOCATION)"
Write-Host "🆔 Subscription: $SUBSCRIPTION_ID"
```

### Start creating the gateway

<!-- setup-done: providers -->

Register the resource providers, which is a one-time step for each subscription, create a resource group, and start
creating the gateway. With `--no-wait`, Azure keeps provisioning the gateway in the background, so you can move on
right away. The portal and the Bicep template also create a companion connector gateway for connector-based MCP
tools. The quick start doesn't use connectors, so this track skips it.

```bash title="Bash"
# Register the resource providers for AI Gateway and Foundry (once per subscription)
for ns in Microsoft.ApiManagement Microsoft.CognitiveServices; do az provider register --namespace "$ns" --wait && echo "🧩 $ns is registered"; done

# Create the resource group that holds the gateway and the Foundry account
az group create --name "$RG" --location "$LOCATION" --output none &&
  echo "📦 Resource group $RG is ready in $LOCATION"

# Start creating the gateway, with a system-assigned managed identity; --no-wait returns right away
az aigateway create --resource-group "$RG" --name "$GATEWAY" --location "$LOCATION" --system-assigned true --no-wait &&
  echo "⏳ Gateway $GATEWAY is provisioning in the background"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Register the resource providers for AI Gateway and Foundry (once per subscription)
foreach ($ns in "Microsoft.ApiManagement", "Microsoft.CognitiveServices") { az provider register --namespace $ns --wait; if ($?) { Write-Host "🧩 $ns is registered" } }

# Create the resource group that holds the gateway and the Foundry account
az group create --name $RG --location $LOCATION --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "📦 Resource group $RG is ready in $LOCATION" }

# Start creating the gateway, with a system-assigned managed identity; --no-wait returns right away
az aigateway create --resource-group $RG --name $GATEWAY --location $LOCATION --system-assigned true --no-wait
if ($?) { Write-Host "⏳ Gateway $GATEWAY is provisioning in the background" }
```

### Deploy the model in Foundry

While the gateway provisions, create a Foundry account with a `gpt-6-luna` deployment. Then give the gateway's
managed identity the **Foundry User** role on the account. The gateway calls the model with this identity, so your
apps never hold a Foundry key.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create the Foundry account, with a custom subdomain so that the gateway can sign in with Microsoft Entra ID
az cognitiveservices account create --resource-group "$RG" --name "$FOUNDRY" --location "$LOCATION" \
  --kind AIServices --sku S0 --custom-domain "$FOUNDRY" --yes --output none &&
  echo "🏭 Foundry account $FOUNDRY is ready"

# Deploy gpt-6-luna with 10,000 tokens per minute of Global Standard capacity
az cognitiveservices account deployment create --resource-group "$RG" --name "$FOUNDRY" \
  --deployment-name "$DEPLOYMENT" --model-name gpt-6-luna --model-version 2026-09-22 --model-format OpenAI \
  --sku-name GlobalStandard --sku-capacity 10 --output none &&
  echo "🧠 Model deployment $DEPLOYMENT is ready"

# Read the Foundry account's resource ID and the principal ID of the gateway's managed identity
export FOUNDRY_ID="$(az cognitiveservices account show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$FOUNDRY" --query id --output tsv)"
PRINCIPAL_ID="$(az aigateway show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$GATEWAY" --query identity.principalId --output tsv)"
echo "🪪 Gateway identity: $PRINCIPAL_ID"

# Give the gateway's identity the Foundry User role on the account, so that it can call the model
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d" --scope "$FOUNDRY_ID" --output none &&
  echo "🛡️ The gateway's identity has the Foundry User role on $FOUNDRY"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Create the Foundry account, with a custom subdomain so that the gateway can sign in with Microsoft Entra ID
az cognitiveservices account create --resource-group $RG --name $FOUNDRY --location $LOCATION `
  --kind AIServices --sku S0 --custom-domain $FOUNDRY --yes --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🏭 Foundry account $FOUNDRY is ready" }

# Deploy gpt-6-luna with 10,000 tokens per minute of Global Standard capacity
az cognitiveservices account deployment create --resource-group $RG --name $FOUNDRY `
  --deployment-name $DEPLOYMENT --model-name gpt-6-luna --model-version 2026-09-22 --model-format OpenAI `
  --sku-name GlobalStandard --sku-capacity 10 --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧠 Model deployment $DEPLOYMENT is ready" }

# Read the Foundry account's resource ID and the principal ID of the gateway's managed identity
$FOUNDRY_ID   = az cognitiveservices account show --resource-group $RG --name $FOUNDRY --query id --output tsv
$PRINCIPAL_ID = az aigateway show --resource-group $RG --name $GATEWAY --query identity.principalId --output tsv
Write-Host "🪪 Gateway identity: $PRINCIPAL_ID"

# Give the gateway's identity the Foundry User role on the account, so that it can call the model
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id $PRINCIPAL_ID --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal `
  --role "53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d" --scope $FOUNDRY_ID --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ The gateway's identity has the Foundry User role on $FOUNDRY" }
```

### Publish the model

Wait for the gateway, then publish the deployment in three steps: a provider that points at the Foundry account and
signs in with the managed identity, a model for the deployment, and an alias that apps send in the `model` field.

```bash title="Bash"
# Wait until the gateway finishes provisioning
az aigateway wait --resource-group "$RG" --name "$GATEWAY" --created &&
  echo "🚀 Gateway $GATEWAY is ready"

# Add a model provider that points at the Foundry account and signs in with the gateway's managed identity
az aigateway model-provider create --resource-group "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --name "$PROVIDER" --output none \
  --kind Foundry --display-name "Foundry models" \
  --foundry "$(jq -cn --arg e "https://$FOUNDRY.cognitiveservices.azure.com/" --arg id "$FOUNDRY_ID" '{endpoint: $e,
      resourceIds: [$id], authentication: {kind: "ManagedIdentity", managedIdentity: {resource: "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/"}}}')" &&
  echo "🔌 Model provider $PROVIDER points at $FOUNDRY"

# Add a model for the deployment, with the endpoints that apps can call
az aigateway model create --resource-group "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" --name "$DEPLOYMENT" \
  --api-format OpenAIChatCompletions --supported-endpoints /openai/v1/chat/completions /openai/v1/responses \
  --deployment-config "{resourceId:$FOUNDRY_ID/deployments/$DEPLOYMENT,modelName:$DEPLOYMENT}" --output none &&
  echo "🧠 Model $DEPLOYMENT is published through $PROVIDER"

# Add the alias that apps send in the model field
ALIAS="$(az aigateway model-alias create --resource-group "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --name "$DEPLOYMENT" --only-show-errors \
  --backend-model resource-id="$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$DEPLOYMENT" \
  --query properties.aliasName --output tsv)" &&
  echo "🏷️ Alias $ALIAS is ready"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Wait until the gateway finishes provisioning
az aigateway wait --resource-group $RG --name $GATEWAY --created
if ($?) { Write-Host "🚀 Gateway $GATEWAY is ready" }

# Add a model provider that points at the Foundry account and signs in with the gateway's managed identity
@{ endpoint       = "https://$FOUNDRY.cognitiveservices.azure.com/"
   resourceIds    = @($FOUNDRY_ID)
   authentication = @{ kind = "ManagedIdentity"; managedIdentity = @{ resource = "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/" } } } |
  ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content foundry.json
az aigateway model-provider create --resource-group $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --name $PROVIDER --output none `
  --kind Foundry --display-name "Foundry models" --foundry "@foundry.json"
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔌 Model provider $PROVIDER points at $FOUNDRY" }

# Add a model for the deployment, with the endpoints that apps can call
az aigateway model create --resource-group $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER --name $DEPLOYMENT `
  --api-format OpenAIChatCompletions --supported-endpoints /openai/v1/chat/completions /openai/v1/responses `
  --deployment-config "{resourceId:$FOUNDRY_ID/deployments/$DEPLOYMENT,modelName:$DEPLOYMENT}" --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧠 Model $DEPLOYMENT is published through $PROVIDER" }

# Add the alias that apps send in the model field
$ALIAS = az aigateway model-alias create --resource-group $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --name $DEPLOYMENT --only-show-errors `
  --backend-model resource-id="$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$DEPLOYMENT" `
  --query properties.aliasName --output tsv
if ($?) { Write-Host "🏷️ Alias $ALIAS is ready" }
Remove-Item foundry.json
```

### Create a runtime API key

Create a key for your app. Then read the key, the gateway URL, and the alias into environment variables, so that
the key never shows on screen. Azure RBAC is the keyless alternative: grant the app the **AI Gateway Models User**
role, and it sends a Microsoft Entra ID token instead of a key, as
[Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md) shows.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create a runtime API key for your app
az aigateway api-key create --resource-group "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --name app-first-call \
  --display-name app-first-call --output none &&
  echo "🔑 API key app-first-call is ready"

# Read the key, the gateway's runtime URL, and the alias into environment variables
export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets --resource-group "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" \
  --name app-first-call --query primaryKey --output tsv)"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az aigateway show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$GATEWAY" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname --output tsv)"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$DEPLOYMENT"
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"
echo "🏷️ Model alias: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Create a runtime API key for your app
az aigateway api-key create --resource-group $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --name app-first-call `
  --display-name app-first-call --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔑 API key app-first-call is ready" }

# Read the key, the gateway's runtime URL, and the alias into environment variables
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az aigateway api-key list-secrets --resource-group $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY `
  --name app-first-call --query primaryKey --output tsv
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL     = "https://" + (az aigateway show --resource-group $RG --name $GATEWAY --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname --output tsv)
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL   = $DEPLOYMENT
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"
Write-Host "🏷️ Model alias: $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

> **Checkpoint:** the commands printed `🏷️ Alias gpt-6-luna is ready` and your gateway's runtime URL, for example
> `🌐 Runtime URL: https://aigw-abc123.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com`.

### Make your first call

Send a Chat Completions request to the gateway's OpenAI-compatible base URL, the way an app does: the alias in the
`model` field and the key in the `api-key` header.

```bash title="Bash"
# Call the model through the gateway, the way an app does: the alias in model, and the key in the api-key header
curl -sS "$AI_GATEWAY_URL/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"In one sentence, what does an AI gateway do?\"}]}" \
  | jq -r 'if .choices then "🤖 \(.choices[0].message.content)" else "⚠️ \(.error.message // .)" end'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Build the request: the alias in model, and one user message
$body = @{
  model    = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL
  messages = @(@{ role = "user"; content = "In one sentence, what does an AI gateway do?" })
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5

# Call the model through the gateway, the way an app does: with the key in the api-key header
$reply = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri "$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
  -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body
if ($?) { Write-Host "🤖 $($reply.choices[0].message.content)" }
```

> **Checkpoint:** the model answers in one sentence. Your gateway is live, and your app never needed a Foundry key:
> only the gateway's managed identity calls Foundry. If you get `403` or `404` in the first minute, the gateway's new
> role on the Foundry account is still taking effect. Wait a minute and run the call again.

To see what you created, open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway in the top
bar: **Models**, **Access** › **Keys**, and the **Catalog** playground.

### Deploy with azd up

Create an azd environment named `aigw-quickstart` in your current subscription, so that azd doesn't prompt you. Then
provision everything with one command. It takes about three minutes.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create an azd environment in your current subscription, so that azd doesn't prompt you
azd env new aigw-quickstart --location eastus2 --subscription "$(az account show --query id --output tsv)" &&
  echo "📝 azd environment aigw-quickstart deploys to eastus2"

# Provision the gateway, the Foundry deployment, the provider, the model, the alias, and the key
azd up &&
  echo "🚀 Gateway deployed: $(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Create an azd environment in your current subscription, so that azd doesn't prompt you
azd env new aigw-quickstart --location eastus2 --subscription (az account show --query id --output tsv)

```

For another region, use its name from [Find the available regions](../SETUP.md#find-the-available-regions).
azd saves the template's outputs, like the gateway URL and the alias, as environment values. The API key isn't an

### Read the URL, the alias, and the key

<!-- setup-done: extension -->

Install the `aigateway` CLI extension, read the outputs, and read the key from the gateway into an environment
variable, so that it never shows on screen.
Azure RBAC is the keyless alternative to the key: grant the app the **AI Gateway Models User** role, and it sends a
Microsoft Entra ID token instead, as [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md) shows.

```bash title="Bash"
# Install or upgrade the aigateway extension of the Azure CLI, which reads the key
curl -fsSL https://aka.ms/aigateway-cli-install | sh &&
  echo "🧩 aigateway extension $(az extension show --name aigateway --query version --output tsv) is installed"

# Read the template's outputs: the gateway's runtime URL and the alias
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL)"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_MODEL)"

# Read the key from the gateway, so that it never lands in a file or a deployment log
export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets --ids "$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_ID)/apiKeys/app-first-call" \
  --query primaryKey --output tsv)"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"
echo "🏷️ Model alias: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Install or upgrade the aigateway extension of the Azure CLI, which reads the key
irm https://aka.ms/aigateway-cli-install-ps | iex
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧩 aigateway extension $(az extension show --name aigateway --query version --output tsv) is installed" }

# Read the template's outputs: the gateway's runtime URL, the alias, and the gateway's resource ID
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL     = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL   = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_MODEL
$GATEWAY_ID             = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_ID

# Read the key from the gateway, so that it never lands in a file or a deployment log
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az aigateway api-key list-secrets --ids "$GATEWAY_ID/apiKeys/app-first-call" `
  --query primaryKey --output tsv
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"
Write-Host "🏷️ Model alias: $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

> **Checkpoint:** `azd up` ended with `SUCCESS`, and the last commands printed your gateway's runtime URL, for example
> `🌐 Runtime URL: https://aigw-abc123.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com`.

### Make your first call

Send a Chat Completions request to the gateway's OpenAI-compatible base URL, the way an app does: the alias in the
`model` field and the key in the `api-key` header.

```bash title="Bash"
# Call the model through the gateway, the way an app does: the alias in model, and the key in the api-key header
curl -sS "$AI_GATEWAY_URL/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"In one sentence, what does an AI gateway do?\"}]}" \
  | jq -r 'if .choices then "🤖 \(.choices[0].message.content)" else "⚠️ \(.error.message // .)" end'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Build the request: the alias in model, and one user message
$body = @{
  model    = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL
  messages = @(@{ role = "user"; content = "In one sentence, what does an AI gateway do?" })
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5

# Call the model through the gateway, the way an app does: with the key in the api-key header
$reply = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri "$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
  -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body
if ($?) { Write-Host "🤖 $($reply.choices[0].message.content)" }
```

> **Checkpoint:** the model answers in one sentence. Your gateway is live, and your app never needed a Foundry key:
> only the gateway's managed identity calls Foundry. If you get `403` or `404` in the first minute, the gateway's new
> role on the Foundry account is still taking effect. Wait a minute and run the call again.

To see what you created, open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway in the top
bar: **Models**, **Access** › **Keys**, and the **Catalog** playground.

### Clean up

To keep exploring, skip this step: [lab 03](../03-multi-provider-aliases/README.md) and the labs after it work on this
gateway. Otherwise, in the `ai-gateway/labs/quickstart` folder, delete everything that `azd up` created. `--purge` also purges
the Foundry account, which would otherwise stay soft-deleted for 48 hours and keep counting against your quota. It
takes about ten minutes.

```bash title="Bash"
# Delete everything that azd up created, and purge the Foundry account
azd down --purge --force &&
  echo "🧹 Everything that azd up created is deleted"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Delete everything that azd up created, and purge the Foundry account
azd down --purge --force
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 Everything that azd up created is deleted" }
```

> **Checkpoint:** `azd down` ended with `SUCCESS`. The resource group `rg-aigw-quickstart` is gone, and you can delete
> the `ai-gateway` folder.

# How Azure AI Gateway works

Every team that ships generative AI hits the same questions. Which models may we call, and with which keys?
Who spent the tokens? How do we stop one agent from starving everyone else, or from calling a tool it should
never touch? The **AI Gateway tier** of Azure API Management answers them in one place: apps and agents call one
gateway, and the gateway decides who gets in, which model or tool answers, what each call may cost, and what gets
recorded.

<!-- video: media/walkthrough.mp4 | Narrated walkthrough: how Azure AI Gateway works (3 min) -->

![Azure AI Gateway architecture: clients call one gateway that routes to model providers and tool sources](../assets/diagrams/architecture.svg "Apps, agents, and coding agents call one gateway. The gateway authenticates them, applies policies, routes model calls through aliases, federates tools, and emits OpenTelemetry.")

> [!NOTE]
> The AI Gateway tier runs in a growing list of regions: run the command in
> [Find the available regions](../SETUP.md#find-the-available-regions) to list them. For the
> gateway's pricing, see the [AI Gateway documentation](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs). Connected services, such
> as Microsoft Foundry inference and Application Insights, are billed normally.

## Before you begin

This lab is a guided reading. You don't need to deploy anything.

- If you already have a gateway, open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) in another tab and
  follow the portal tour at the end.
- If you don't have one yet, read on. You create your first gateway in
  [Provision your first AI gateway](../01-provision-gateway/README.md).

## How it works

The gateway sits on the path of every model call and every tool call. It has two faces:

- **Data plane**: the runtime endpoints your code calls, at `https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com`.
- **Control plane**: the product portal at [ai.gateway.azure.com](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and the Azure
  Resource Manager API for the `Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways` resource type, which you call with the
  `az aigateway` Azure CLI extension, Bicep, or any REST client.

| Building block | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Gateway** | An AI Gateway resource (`Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways`) in your subscription | `https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com` |
| **Backend model** | A model at a provider, such as a Foundry deployment or an Anthropic model | `gpt-6-luna` at Microsoft Foundry |
| **Alias** | The stable, gateway-wide name clients send in the `model` field | `chat` |
| **MCP server** | One governed MCP endpoint that federates tools from one or more sources | `/default/toolservers/<server-name>/mcp` |
| **Policy** | A rule on the gateway or on one asset: limits, budgets, safety, filters | Token rate limit, Cost limit |
| **Access** | How callers authenticate: API keys or Microsoft Entra ID roles | `api-key` header or Entra token |
| **Managed identity** | How the gateway authenticates to backends | Foundry User role on the Foundry account |
| **Monitoring** | OpenTelemetry metrics, logs, and traces for every call | Application Insights or any OTLP endpoint |

Model calls use protocols developers already know. The OpenAI-compatible base URL is
`https://<gateway-host>/default/models/openai/v1` (append `/responses` or `/chat/completions`), and
Anthropic Messages lives at `/default/models/anthropic/v1/messages`. The gateway passes requests through without
translating between OpenAI and Anthropic formats, so call each model on an interface it advertises.

## Follow one request

Press **Play** to send a request through the gateway. Then switch scenarios to see where each policy stops a
request and which status code the caller gets back.

<!-- widget: request-lifecycle -->

![Request lifecycle through the gateway](../assets/diagrams/request-lifecycle.svg "Every applicable policy is evaluated before the gateway forwards a request. If one blocks it, the backend is never called.")

Three rules explain almost every response you'll see in these labs:

1. **Policies run before the backend.** If any applicable policy blocks a request, the gateway answers right away
   and never calls the backend.
2. **Each block has a predictable status.** `401` for missing or invalid credentials, `403` for IP filters and
   cost limits (`LlmCostQuotaExceeded`), `429` with `Retry-After` for token and request rate limits, and `400` for
   content safety.
3. **Everything is recorded.** Allowed and blocked calls both show up in **Monitoring**, along with the policies
   that affected them.

## Models and aliases

A **backend model** is what a provider serves. An **alias** is what your clients call. Microsoft Foundry imports
create an alias for each model by default, and you can add more. Because clients only know the alias, you can move
it to a newer or cheaper model without a code change, and the alias keeps its own policies.

<!-- widget: alias-retarget -->

![Aliases decouple clients from backend models](../assets/diagrams/aliases.svg "Two aliases can share one backend model with different policies. Retargeting an alias needs no client change.")

You can put models from Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and
custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints behind aliases. You try it in
[Route models from several providers behind aliases](../03-multi-provider-aliases/README.md).

## MCP servers and tools

Agents need tools as much as models. An **MCP server** on the gateway gives agents one endpoint and one credential
for tools from remote MCP servers, OpenAPI specifications, built-in connectors, and Foundry Toolbox. Tool names are
namespaced per source, and **tool availability** decides which tools clients can see and call.

![MCP tool federation](../assets/diagrams/mcp-federation.svg "One MCP endpoint federates tools from several sources. Tool availability and policies apply to every call.")

## Policies and scopes

You add a policy at **gateway scope**, where it applies to every compatible asset including assets you add later,
or to **individual assets**: a backend model, an alias, or an MCP server. Pick an asset below to see every policy
that applies to it.

<!-- widget: policy-layers -->

| Policy | Applies to | When it blocks |
|---|---|---|
| **Token rate limit** | Models and aliases | `429` with `Retry-After` |
| **Request rate limit** | Models, aliases, and MCP servers | `429` with `Retry-After` |
| **Cost limit** | Models and aliases | `403` `LlmCostQuotaExceeded` |
| **Content safety** | Models, aliases, and MCP servers | `400` |
| **IP filter** | Models, aliases, and MCP servers | `403` |
| **Agent 365 tool threat protection** | MCP servers | Denies the tool call |

At gateway scope, the policy type decides which assets are relevant. A gateway-scope cost limit, for example,
tracks one budget across all models.

## Identities on both sides

The gateway separates **who is calling** from **how the gateway reaches the backend**. Callers use an API key or a
Microsoft Entra token with one of the AI Gateway data-plane roles. The gateway uses its own managed identity, or a
provider key it stores, to call backends. Callers never see backend credentials.

![Identity boundaries](../assets/diagrams/identity-boundaries.svg "Inbound and outbound identities are authorized separately.")

## Observability

The gateway emits OpenTelemetry metrics, logs, and traces for model calls, tool calls, and policy decisions. Send
them to Application Insights to light up the built-in **Monitoring** dashboard, or to any OTLP endpoint.

![Observability with OpenTelemetry](../assets/diagrams/observability.svg "Signals flow to Application Insights, which powers the Monitoring dashboard, or to any OTLP endpoint.")

## Verify

Check your understanding before you move on.

<details>
<summary>An app sends <code>"model": "chat"</code>. What must <code>chat</code> be?</summary>

A callable **alias** on the gateway. The `model` field must exactly match an alias, not a provider deployment name.
</details>

<details>
<summary>A caller exceeds a token rate limit. Is the backend called?</summary>

No. The gateway answers `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After` and never forwards the request.
</details>

<details>
<summary>You add an IP filter at gateway scope, then add a new model next week. Is the new model protected?</summary>

Yes. Gateway-scope policies apply to every compatible asset, including assets you add later.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Which credential does the gateway use to call a Microsoft Foundry model?</summary>

Its own managed identity, which needs the **Foundry User** role on the Foundry account. The caller's key or token
is never forwarded.
</details>

> **Checkpoint**
> You can explain the request lifecycle, the difference between a backend model and an alias, and where gateway
> and asset policies apply.

# Provision your AI Gateway

Your platform team is about to put every model and tool that the company's apps and agents use behind one
governed entry point. Before anyone can publish a model, issue a key, or set a budget, you need the gateway
itself. In this lab you create a shared AI Gateway, find its runtime URL and managed identity, and learn your
way around the portal so you're ready for the rest of the labs.

<!-- video: media/walkthrough.mp4 | Narrated walkthrough: create an AI Gateway in the portal and tour it (3 min) -->

![What provisioning creates: you choose a name, resource group, and region; Azure creates the AI Gateway, its managed identity, and its connector gateway; you get a runtime URL, a default workspace, and the portal](../assets/diagrams/provisioning.svg "One gateway per environment is the usual starting point. Every later lab publishes models, tools, keys, and policies on it.")

## Before you begin

<!-- setup: permissions tools sign-in extension providers regions clone -->

Every later lab reuses this one-time setup.

> [!TIP]
> On the **Bicep + azd** track, `azd up` creates the resource group and the gateway and names them for you, so you
> can skip the variables at the end of this section.

- For the portal track: a browser and your Azure account.
- A region where the Foundry models of the later labs are available too.
- Recommended reading: [How AI Gateway works](../00-how-ai-gateway-works/README.md).

### Set your variables

Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
# Make the subscription that you use for the labs the current one, so that every command runs in it
az account set --subscription "<subscription-id>" &&
  echo "🆔 Current subscription: $(az account show --query name -o tsv)"

# Name the resource group and the gateway, and choose the region
export RG="<resource-group>"               # for example rg-ai-gateway-labs
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"                 # globally unique, 24 characters or fewer, part of the runtime URL
export LOCATION="<location>"               # a Name from the list of available regions, for example eastus2
echo "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY in $RG ($LOCATION)"

# Read the subscription ID, which the REST call for the connector gateway uses
export SUBSCRIPTION_ID="$(az account show --query id -o tsv)"
echo "🆔 Subscription ID: $SUBSCRIPTION_ID"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Make the subscription that you use for the labs the current one, so that every command runs in it
az account set --subscription "<subscription-id>"
if ($?) { Write-Host "🆔 Current subscription: $(az account show --query name -o tsv)" }

# Name the resource group and the gateway, and choose the region
$RG              = "<resource-group>"      # for example rg-ai-gateway-labs
$GATEWAY         = "<gateway>"             # globally unique, 24 characters or fewer, part of the runtime URL
$LOCATION        = "<location>"            # a Name from the list of available regions, for example eastus2
Write-Host "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY in $RG ($LOCATION)"

# Read the subscription ID, which the REST call for the connector gateway uses
$SUBSCRIPTION_ID = az account show --query id -o tsv
Write-Host "🆔 Subscription ID: $SUBSCRIPTION_ID"
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Create the resource group in the same region as the gateway, so that defaults line up. The gateway
> name must be 1–24 characters: letters, digits, and hyphens, starting with a letter and not ending with a hyphen.

## How it works

An AI Gateway is an Azure Resource Manager resource of type `Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways`. You manage it
in the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com), which is separate from the Azure portal, or through
Azure Resource Manager with the CLI, REST, or Bicep. Each gateway has a companion connector gateway
(`Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways`) with the same name. There's no capacity to size, so the only real decisions
are the name, the region, and the resource group.

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Resource type | `Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways` (API version `2025-09-01-preview`), plus `Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways` with the same name |
| Regions | The list grows over time. List them as in [Find the available regions](../SETUP.md#find-the-available-regions) |
| Name | 1–24 characters: letters, digits, and hyphens. It becomes the first label of the runtime host name |
| Runtime URL | `https://` + `properties.frontend.defaultHostname`, for example `https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com` |
| Runtime routes | Models under `/default/models/…`, MCP servers under `/default/toolservers/<server>/mcp` |
| Outbound identity | A system-assigned managed identity, used to call Foundry and other Microsoft Entra–protected backends |
| SKU | `Consumption`, which `az aigateway create` and the Bicep templates set. A template that omits `sku` creates a `Premium` gateway |
| Provisioning time | A few minutes, often less |

Everything you publish later lives in the gateway's `default` workspace. That's why every runtime route
starts with `/default/`. Applications authenticate **inbound** with an API key or a Microsoft Entra token. The
gateway authenticates **outbound** to each backend, usually with its managed identity, so apps never hold
provider credentials.

![AI Gateway architecture: apps and agents call one gateway that governs models and tools](../assets/diagrams/architecture.svg "Apps and agents call one runtime URL. The gateway applies access, policies, and telemetry before it routes to models and MCP servers.")

## Create the gateway

Pick one track. Each track produces the same result: a gateway named `<gateway>` in `<resource-group>`, with a
system-assigned managed identity. The Bicep + azd track picks the names for you: `aigw-` plus six unique characters,
in `rg-aigw-lab01`.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Sign in to the AI Gateway portal

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and sign in with your Azure account. If this is your
first gateway, the portal takes you straight into gateway creation. If you already have a gateway, open the
gateway switcher in the top bar and start creating a new one from there.

### Enter the gateway details

In **Create AI gateway**, enter a globally unique **Name** of 24 characters or fewer, or select
**Generate a new name**. Then choose the subscription, a **Resource group** (**New** or **Existing**), and the
**Region**. Under **Advanced**, keep **Enable system-assigned managed identity** selected, **Public network access** set to **Enabled**, and
**Public routing**. **Private routing** connects the gateway to private backends through a virtual network and
can only be chosen at creation. [Lab 18](../18-private-networking/README.md) covers it.

![What to choose in Create AI gateway: a unique name, a subscription, a resource group, and a region, with the Advanced defaults kept](../assets/diagrams/create-gateway.svg "Fill in the basics, keep the Advanced defaults, then select Create gateway.")

> [!NOTE]
> The subscription picker lists every subscription you can see. Subscriptions where you lack write permission
> for API Management and connector gateways are disabled, and the portal explains why.

### Watch it provision

Select **Create gateway**. The portal shows provisioning progress in place, and a new gateway is typically ready
in a few minutes.

### Open the setup guide on Home

When provisioning finishes, **Home** opens with a setup guide for publishing models, adding MCP servers, and
creating runtime access. Leave it for now. You publish your first model in the next lab, and the guide stays
on **Home** until you finish it.

> **Checkpoint**
> The gateway switcher in the top bar shows `<gateway>`, and **Home** shows the setup guide.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

If you haven't yet, [register the resource providers](../SETUP.md#register-the-resource-providers) in this
subscription: the gateway lives in `Microsoft.ApiManagement` and its connector gateway in `Microsoft.Web`.

### Create a resource group

```bash
# Create the resource group that holds the gateway, in the gateway's region
az group create --name "$RG" --location "$LOCATION" --output none &&
  echo "📦 Resource group $RG is ready in $LOCATION"
```

### Create the connector gateway

Every AI gateway has a companion `Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways` resource with the same name, and either one
can be created first. The `aigateway` extension creates only the AI gateway, so
create the connector gateway through the Azure Resource Manager REST API with `az rest`.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create the companion connector gateway through the REST API, because the aigateway extension doesn't create it
az rest --method put --output none \
  --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUBSCRIPTION_ID/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways/$GATEWAY?api-version=2026-05-01-preview" \
  --body "$(jq -cn --arg location "$LOCATION" '{location: $location, properties: {}}')" &&
  echo "🔌 Connector gateway $GATEWAY is ready"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Write the request body to a file, so that PowerShell passes the JSON to az rest unchanged
@{ location = $LOCATION; properties = @{} } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress | Set-Content body.json

# Create the companion connector gateway through the REST API, because the aigateway extension doesn't create it
az rest --method put --output none `
  --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUBSCRIPTION_ID/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways/${GATEWAY}?api-version=2026-05-01-preview" `
  --body "@body.json"
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔌 Connector gateway $GATEWAY is ready" }
Remove-Item body.json
```

### Create the AI gateway

`az aigateway create` only needs the name, the region, and the managed identity. It creates the gateway in the
`Consumption` SKU, and there's no capacity or publisher to set. The command waits until provisioning finishes,
usually within a few minutes.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create the gateway with a system-assigned managed identity, and wait until it's provisioned
az aigateway create -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --location "$LOCATION" --system-assigned true -o none &&
  echo "🚀 Gateway $GATEWAY is ready in $LOCATION"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Create the gateway with a system-assigned managed identity, and wait until it's provisioned
az aigateway create -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --location $LOCATION --system-assigned true -o none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🚀 Gateway $GATEWAY is ready in $LOCATION" }
```

> [!TIP]
> Add `--no-wait` to return right away, then run `az aigateway wait -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --created` when you
> need the gateway.

### Read the runtime URL and identity

```bash title="Bash"
# Show the gateway's state, its runtime host name, and the principal ID of its managed identity
echo "📊 Gateway $GATEWAY, its runtime host, and its identity:"
az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" \
  --query "{name:name, location:location, state:properties.provisioningState, host:properties.frontend.defaultHostname, principalId:identity.principalId}" \
  -o table
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Show the gateway's state, its runtime host name, and the principal ID of its managed identity
Write-Host "📊 Gateway $GATEWAY, its runtime host, and its identity:"
az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY `
  --query "{name:name, location:location, state:properties.provisioningState, host:properties.frontend.defaultHostname, principalId:identity.principalId}" `
  -o table
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The table shows `Succeeded`, a `Host` like `<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com`, and a `PrincipalId`
> GUID.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

**What you need:** the [Setup guide](../SETUP.md) tasks from **Before you begin**. `azd up` creates the resource
group and the gateway, so you don't need the variables.

### Review the template

`infra/gateway.bicep` declares the gateway. It follows the AI Gateway [reference sample](https://github.com/Azure-Samples/simple-foundry-hosted-agent-python-aigateway/blob/main/infra/ai-gateway/main.bicep). It creates the AI gateway
(`Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways`) in the `Consumption` SKU with a system-assigned identity, then a
`Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways` resource with the same name. There's no capacity or publisher to set. Keep both
resources together in your own templates, and set `sku`: without it, the gateway is created in the `Premium` SKU.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| `gatewayName` | Required. The gateway name, 24 characters or fewer |
| `location` | `eastus2` (default), or another region where AI Gateway is available |
| `tags` | Optional. Tags applied to both resources |
| `backendSubnetId` | Optional. A subnet for outbound virtual network integration, which can only be set at creation. See [Lab 18](../18-private-networking/README.md) |

<!-- include: infra/gateway.bicep -->

`infra/main.bicep` is the template that azd deploys. It creates the resource group `rg-<environment name>`, then
calls `infra/gateway.bicep` with the name `aigw-` plus six characters that are unique to your subscription,
environment, and region. Its outputs become azd environment values:

<!-- include: infra/main.bicep -->

Later labs reuse `infra/gateway.bicep` as a module. You can also deploy it on its own to a resource group you
already have, with `az deployment group create`, as **Go further** shows.

> [!TIP]
> Bicep has no type definitions yet for `Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways` and `Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways`.
> As in the reference sample, each `#disable-next-line BCP081` line silences the warning about it. Without these
> lines, the build shows `BCP081` warnings, which don't block the deployment.

### Deploy with azd up

Move into the lab's folder, create an azd environment named `aigw-lab01` in your current subscription, then provision
the resource group and the gateway. It takes about three minutes.

```bash title="Bash"
# Move into the lab's folder, which holds the azd project
cd ~/ai-gateway/labs/01-provision-gateway &&
  echo "📂 Lab folder: $(pwd)"

# Create an azd environment in your current subscription, so that azd doesn't prompt you
azd env new aigw-lab01 --location eastus2 --subscription "$(az account show --query id --output tsv)" &&
  echo "📝 azd environment aigw-lab01 deploys to eastus2"

# Provision the resource group, the gateway, and its connector gateway
azd up &&
  echo "🚀 Gateway $(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_NAME) is deployed"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Move into the lab's folder, which holds the azd project
Set-Location ~/ai-gateway/labs/01-provision-gateway
if ($?) { Write-Host "📂 Lab folder: $(Get-Location)" }

# Create an azd environment in your current subscription, so that azd doesn't prompt you
azd env new aigw-lab01 --location eastus2 --subscription (az account show --query id --output tsv)
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 azd environment aigw-lab01 deploys to eastus2" }

# Provision the resource group, the gateway, and its connector gateway
azd up
if ($?) { Write-Host "🚀 Gateway $(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_NAME) is deployed" }
```

For another region, use its name from [Find the available regions](../SETUP.md#find-the-available-regions).

### Read the outputs

Set the variables that **Verify** and **Go further** use from azd's environment values, then print the runtime URL
and the gateway's principal ID.

# Read the resource group, the gateway name, and the region from azd's environment values
