## Verify

<!-- steps -->

### Call the runtime URL

Read the host name from the gateway rather than building it yourself, then send a request without a key. Any
HTTP status proves that DNS, TLS, and the gateway are up. A new gateway with no models answers `404`; after you
add a model and a key in the next lab, a call without a key gets `400` or `401`.

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the runtime host name from the gateway, and build the runtime URL from it
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Call the Chat Completions route without a key, and print only the HTTP status that the gateway answers with
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "🌐 The gateway answered: HTTP %{http_code}\n" "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the runtime host name from the gateway, and build the runtime URL from it
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Call the Chat Completions route without a key, and print only the HTTP status that the gateway answers with
$status = (Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "$($env:AI_GATEWAY_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
  -SkipHttpErrorCheck).StatusCode
if ($?) { Write-Host "🌐 The gateway answered: HTTP $status" }
```

A `Could not resolve host` error means the gateway isn't ready yet. Wait a minute and try again.

### Find the gateway on Home

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com). If you created the gateway with the CLI or with Bicep
and azd, select it in the gateway switcher in the top bar. **Home** shows the setup guide for your new gateway.

### Check the managed identity

Select **Managed identities**. On the **Configure identities** tab, the system-assigned identity is enabled.
Its principal ID matches `principalId` from the CLI output, or `AI_GATEWAY_PRINCIPAL_ID` from azd. In later labs
you grant this identity access to Foundry so that the gateway can call your models without keys.

![The Managed identities page with the system-assigned identity enabled](../assets/screens/managed-identities.png "Managed identities › Configure identities shows the system-assigned identity with its principal ID and tenant ID. You can add user-assigned identities here too.")

Use the left navigation to get familiar with each area. You visit most of them in later labs.

## Go further

- **One gateway per environment.** Run `azd env new <name>` and `azd up` once for each of dev, test, and
  production: every azd environment gets its own resource group and gateway. Keep the template in source control
  next to your app.
- **Tag for ownership and chargeback.** The template's `tags` parameter applies the same tags to the gateway
  and its connector gateway, so set them when you create each environment's gateway. To add them to the gateway
  you have, deploy `infra/gateway.bicep` on its own from the lab folder:

  ```bash
  # Deploy the gateway's template again with tags, which updates the gateway and its connector gateway in place
  az deployment group create -g "$RG" --template-file infra/gateway.bicep --output none \
    --parameters gatewayName="$GATEWAY" location="$LOCATION" \
                 tags='{"workload":"ai-gateway-labs","owner":"platform-team","costCenter":"1234"}' &&
    echo "📝 Tags are set on gateway $GATEWAY and its connector gateway"
  ```
- **Use a user-assigned identity.** When several gateways must share one backend identity, add a
  user-assigned identity on **Managed identities**. See
  [Call backends with managed identities](../12-backend-identity/README.md).

### Delete the resource group

When you're done with all the labs, delete the resource group. That removes the gateway, its connector gateway,
and everything else in the group. The command asks for confirmation.

```bash title="Bash"
# Delete the resource group, with the gateway, its connector gateway, and everything else in it, after you confirm
az group delete --name "$RG" &&
  echo "🧹 Resource group $RG is deleted"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Delete the resource group, with the gateway, its connector gateway, and everything else in it, after you confirm
az group delete --name $RG
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 Resource group $RG is deleted" }
```

### Delete only the gateway

To keep the resource group, delete the AI gateway first and then its connector gateway. Deleting the gateway
also deletes everything you published on it.

```bash title="Bash"
# Delete the AI gateway, with everything that you published on it
az aigateway delete -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --yes &&
  echo "🧹 Gateway $GATEWAY is deleted"

# Delete its companion connector gateway, which has the same name
az resource delete -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --resource-type Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways --api-version 2026-05-01-preview &&
  echo "🧹 Connector gateway $GATEWAY is deleted"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Delete the AI gateway, with everything that you published on it
az aigateway delete -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --yes
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 Gateway $GATEWAY is deleted" }

# Delete its companion connector gateway, which has the same name
az resource delete -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --resource-type Microsoft.Web/connectorGateways --api-version 2026-05-01-preview
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 Connector gateway $GATEWAY is deleted" }
```

# Publish a Foundry model and make your first call

The first product team wants to use `gpt-6-luna`, which already runs in your Microsoft Foundry account. You
don't want to hand every team the Foundry endpoint and a provider key. In this lab you publish the deployment
through your gateway, give the team a runtime API key of its own, and make the first call from the playground,
a shell, and code. The gateway authenticates to Foundry with its own managed identity, so the app never sees a
Foundry credential.

![A request travels from the app through the gateway to the model and back](../assets/diagrams/request-lifecycle.svg "The gateway checks the caller's key, applies policies, calls the backend with its own identity, and records telemetry on the way back.")

## Before you begin

<!-- setup: tools sign-in extension clone -->

> [!TIP]
> On the **Bicep + azd** track, `azd up` creates its own gateway, Foundry account, model, and key, so you can skip
> this section. You need only the one-time setup above, plus the language runtime for the code track if you follow it.

- Complete [Provision your AI Gateway](../01-provision-gateway/README.md). You need the gateway, its resource
  group, and its runtime URL.
- A model deployment in a Microsoft Foundry (Azure AI Services) or Azure OpenAI account, for example
  `gpt-6-luna`. If you don't have one, deploy the optional template described below.
- Permission to grant the gateway access to the account: **Owner**, **User Access Administrator**, or **Role
  Based Access Control Administrator** on the Foundry account. You also need to change the gateway, for example
  **Contributor** on its resource group.
- For the code track: Python 3.9 or later, Node.js 22.18 or later, or the .NET 8 SDK.
- Run the scripts and samples from the lab's folder, `~/ai-gateway/labs/02-first-model-call`.

Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
# Name your gateway and its resource group, the Foundry account and its deployment, and the provider to create
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"
export FOUNDRY_RG="<foundry-resource-group>"      # resource group of the Foundry account
export FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT="<foundry-account-name>"   # the account name, not a project or deployment name
export DEPLOYMENT="gpt-6-luna"                    # the model deployment to publish
export PROVIDER="foundry-models"                  # CLI track: the gateway provider to create
echo "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY in $RG, deployment $DEPLOYMENT in Foundry account $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT"

# Read the gateway's resource ID, and build its runtime URL from its host name
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query id -o tsv)"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
echo "🆔 Gateway ID: $GATEWAY_ID"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Name your gateway and its resource group, the Foundry account and its deployment, and the provider to create
$RG              = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY         = "<gateway>"
$FOUNDRY_RG      = "<foundry-resource-group>"     # resource group of the Foundry account
$FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT = "<foundry-account-name>"       # the account name, not a project or deployment name
$DEPLOYMENT      = "gpt-6-luna"                   # the model deployment to publish
$PROVIDER        = "foundry-models"               # CLI track: the gateway provider to create
Write-Host "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY in $RG, deployment $DEPLOYMENT in Foundry account $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT"

# Read the gateway's resource ID, and build its runtime URL from its host name
$GATEWAY_ID = az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --query id -o tsv
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
Write-Host "🆔 Gateway ID: $GATEWAY_ID"
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"
```

<details>
<summary>No Foundry deployment yet? Create one with Bicep.</summary>

[infra/foundry.bicep](infra/foundry.bicep) creates an Azure AI Services account with a `gpt-6-luna`
`GlobalStandard` deployment, mirroring the reference sample. Pick a region where the model is available. Model

```bash
# Create the resource group for the Foundry account
az group create --name "$FOUNDRY_RG" --location eastus2 --output none &&
  echo "📦 Resource group $FOUNDRY_RG is ready in eastus2"

# Deploy the template: the Foundry account and its gpt-6-luna deployment, then read the deployment's resource ID

  --template-file infra/foundry.bicep \
  --parameters accountName="$FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT" deploymentName="$DEPLOYMENT" \
  --query properties.outputs.deploymentId.value -o tsv)" &&
  echo "🧠 Model deployment $DEPLOYMENT is ready: $DEPLOYMENT_ID"
```

## How it works

Publishing a model has three parts. A **model provider** tells the gateway where the Foundry account is and
how to authenticate to it. A **backend model** registers one deployment under that provider. A callable
**alias** is the stable name that clients send in the request `model` field. Importing from Foundry creates all
three for you.

Clients call one runtime URL with a gateway API key. The gateway validates the key before anything else, runs
the policies that apply, swaps the caller's key for its own managed identity token, and forwards the request
unchanged to Foundry. The response comes back as is, and the gateway records token usage for monitoring.

| Step | What happens | Where you set it |
|---|---|---|
| Inbound authentication | An active runtime key in the `api-key` header, or as `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (what the OpenAI SDKs send), or the call fails with `401` | **Access** › **Keys** |
| Routing | `/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions` or `/responses`, and `model` must equal an alias | Model details and its **Aliases** tab |
| Policies | Token limits, cost limits, and content safety run before the backend call | **Policies** (labs 06–09) |
| Backend authentication | The gateway's managed identity, with the **Foundry User** role on the account | Model provider |
| Telemetry | Tokens, latency, and the API key that made the call | **Monitoring** (lab 13) |

<!-- widget: request-lifecycle -->

## Publish the model and create a key

Pick one track. Each track publishes the deployment, gives you a callable alias, and creates a runtime API key.
The Bicep + azd track also creates its own gateway and Foundry deployment, so it doesn't need lab 01's gateway.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Import the deployment from Foundry

1. Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway in the top bar.
2. Select **Models** › **Add** › **Models from Microsoft Foundry**. (On **Home**, **Add from Microsoft Foundry** in
   the **Set up your gateway** guide starts the same import.)
3. Select the subscription and resource group of your Foundry account. The wizard discovers the deployments
   automatically. Deployments that are already in this gateway can't be selected again.
4. Select the `gpt-6-luna` deployment and keep **Managed identity** as the **Authentication method**.
5. Under **Aliases**, keep **Create an alias for each model** selected, then select **Add models**.

> [!NOTE]
> The gateway calls Foundry with its system-assigned managed identity, which needs the **Foundry User** role on
> the account. If your first call returns `403` from the backend, assign the role yourself and wait a few
> minutes for it to take effect:
>
> ```bash
> # Read the principal ID of the gateway's managed identity, and the Foundry account's resource ID
> PRINCIPAL_ID="$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query identity.principalId -o tsv)"
> FOUNDRY_ID="$(az cognitiveservices account show -g "$FOUNDRY_RG" -n "$FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT" --query id -o tsv)"
> echo "🪪 Gateway identity: $PRINCIPAL_ID"
>
> # Give the gateway's identity the Foundry User role on the account, so that it can call the model
> az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
>   --role "53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d" --scope "$FOUNDRY_ID" --output none &&
>   echo "🛡️ The gateway's identity has the Foundry User role on $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT"
> ```

### Copy the callable alias

Open the imported model on **Models**. The model details show its base URL and supported interfaces, such as
**OpenAI Chat Completions** and **OpenAI Responses**. Open the **Aliases** tab and copy the alias exactly as
shown, then save it in your shell. Portal imports usually name it after the provider and the deployment, for
example `<foundry-account-name>/gpt-6-luna`.

```bash title="Bash"
# Save the alias that apps send in the model field
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="<model-name>"    # the alias from the Aliases tab
echo "🏷️ Model alias: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Save the alias that apps send in the model field
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = "<model-name>"    # the alias from the Aliases tab
Write-Host "🏷️ Model alias: $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

### Create a runtime API key

1. Select **Access** › **Keys** › **Create API key**. Some portal versions show **Keys** directly in the left
   navigation.
2. In **Key name**, enter a name for the app that will use it, for example `app-first-call`, and select
   **Create**.
3. Copy the value from **API key created successfully**, for example with **Copy & done**. Copy it now: treat
   the value as shown only once.
4. Paste it into your shell without echoing it or writing it to a file:

```bash title="Bash"
# Paste the key without showing it, and export it for the calls and samples that follow
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Paste the key without showing it, into the environment variable that the calls and samples read
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

> **Checkpoint**
> **Models** lists the Foundry deployment, its **Aliases** tab shows an alias, and **Access** › **Keys** shows
> `app-first-call`.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Look up the Foundry account

Use the account name and resource group to look up its resource ID and endpoint. No need to copy a long ID from
the portal.

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the Foundry account's resource ID and endpoint, which the provider and the model use
export FOUNDRY_ID="$(az cognitiveservices account show -g "$FOUNDRY_RG" -n "$FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT" --query id -o tsv)"
FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT="$(az cognitiveservices account show -g "$FOUNDRY_RG" -n "$FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT" --query properties.endpoint -o tsv)"
export FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT="${FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT%/}/"    # the provider expects a trailing slash
echo "🆔 Foundry account ID: $FOUNDRY_ID"
echo "🌐 Foundry endpoint: $FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the Foundry account's resource ID and endpoint, with the trailing slash that the provider expects
$FOUNDRY_ID       = az cognitiveservices account show -g $FOUNDRY_RG -n $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT --query id -o tsv
$FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT = (az cognitiveservices account show -g $FOUNDRY_RG -n $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT --query properties.endpoint -o tsv).TrimEnd('/') + '/'
Write-Host "🆔 Foundry account ID: $FOUNDRY_ID"
Write-Host "🌐 Foundry endpoint: $FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT"
```

### Grant the gateway access to the account

The portal import does three things for you: it grants the gateway's identity access to the account, creates the
provider, and registers the deployments. From the command line, you do each step yourself. First, give the gateway's
system-assigned identity the **Foundry User** role on the account.

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the principal ID of the gateway's system-assigned managed identity
PRINCIPAL_ID="$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query identity.principalId -o tsv)"
echo "🪪 Gateway identity: $PRINCIPAL_ID"

# Give the identity the Foundry User role on the account, so that the gateway can call its deployments
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d" --scope "$FOUNDRY_ID" --query id -o tsv &&
  echo "🛡️ The gateway's identity has the Foundry User role on $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the principal ID of the gateway's system-assigned managed identity
$PRINCIPAL_ID = az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --query identity.principalId -o tsv
Write-Host "🪪 Gateway identity: $PRINCIPAL_ID"

# Give the identity the Foundry User role on the account, so that the gateway can call its deployments
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id $PRINCIPAL_ID --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal `
  --role "53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d" --scope $FOUNDRY_ID --query id -o tsv
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ The gateway's identity has the Foundry User role on $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT" }
```

### Create the Foundry provider

The provider tells the gateway where the account is and to authenticate with its managed identity.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create a Foundry provider that points at the account and signs in with the gateway's managed identity
az aigateway model-provider create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$PROVIDER" \
  --kind Foundry --display-name "Foundry models" \
  --foundry "$(jq -cn --arg endpoint "$FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT" --arg id "$FOUNDRY_ID" '{
      endpoint: $endpoint, resourceIds: [$id],
      authentication: {kind: "ManagedIdentity",
                       managedIdentity: {resource: "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/"}}}')" \
  --query "{name:name, kind:properties.kind, endpoint:properties.foundry.endpoint}" &&
  echo "🔌 Model provider $PROVIDER points at $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Write the provider's Foundry settings to a file, so that PowerShell passes the JSON to az unchanged
@{
  endpoint       = $FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT
  resourceIds    = @($FOUNDRY_ID)
  authentication = @{ kind = "ManagedIdentity"; managedIdentity = @{ resource = "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/" } }
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content foundry.json

# Create a Foundry provider that points at the account and signs in with the gateway's managed identity
az aigateway model-provider create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $PROVIDER `
  --kind Foundry --display-name "Foundry models" --foundry "@foundry.json" `
  --query "{name:name, kind:properties.kind, endpoint:properties.foundry.endpoint}"
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔌 Model provider $PROVIDER points at $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT" }
Remove-Item foundry.json
```

### Register the deployment

A backend model registers one deployment under the provider. Name it after the deployment.

```bash title="Bash"
# Register the deployment as a backend model under the provider, with the endpoints that apps can call
az aigateway model create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" -n "$DEPLOYMENT" \
  --display-name "$DEPLOYMENT" --api-format OpenAIChatCompletions \
  --supported-endpoints /openai/v1/chat/completions /openai/v1/responses \
  --deployment-config "{resourceId:$FOUNDRY_ID/deployments/$DEPLOYMENT,modelName:$DEPLOYMENT}" \
  --query "{name:name, deployment:properties.deployment.modelName}" &&
  echo "🧠 Model $DEPLOYMENT is registered under $PROVIDER"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Register the deployment as a backend model under the provider, with the endpoints that apps can call
az aigateway model create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER -n $DEPLOYMENT `
  --display-name $DEPLOYMENT --api-format OpenAIChatCompletions `
  --supported-endpoints /openai/v1/chat/completions /openai/v1/responses `
  --deployment-config "{resourceId:$FOUNDRY_ID/deployments/$DEPLOYMENT,modelName:$DEPLOYMENT}" `
  --query "{name:name, deployment:properties.deployment.modelName}"
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧠 Model $DEPLOYMENT is registered under $PROVIDER" }
```

`--deployment-config` uses the Azure CLI shorthand syntax, so the same value works in Bash and PowerShell.

To publish more deployments, repeat this step and the next one for each name that
`az cognitiveservices account deployment list -g "$FOUNDRY_RG" -n "$FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT" --query "[].name" -o tsv`
returns.

> [!TIP]
> `az aigateway model create --foundry-resource-id "$FOUNDRY_ID" --deployment "$DEPLOYMENT"` does the last three
> steps in one command, like the portal import: it grants the gateway's identity **Foundry User** on the account,
> creates a provider named after the account, and registers the deployment. You can run it again safely. It doesn't
> publish an alias, so you still run the next step. This lab creates each piece itself so you see how they fit together.

### Publish an alias

Clients send an alias in the request `model` field, not the backend model name. Publish one named after the
deployment that points at the model you registered.

```bash title="Bash"
# Name the alias after the deployment, and build the resource ID of the model that it points at
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$DEPLOYMENT"
MODEL_ID="$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$DEPLOYMENT"

# Publish the alias, which prints its name and the model that it points at
az aigateway model-alias create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" \
  --backend-model resource-id="$MODEL_ID" \
  --query "{alias:properties.aliasName, target:properties.backendModels[0].resourceId}" &&
  echo "🏷️ Alias $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL is ready"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Name the alias after the deployment, and build the resource ID of the model that it points at
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = $DEPLOYMENT
$MODEL_ID = "$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$DEPLOYMENT"

# Publish the alias, which prints its name and the model that it points at
az aigateway model-alias create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL `
  --backend-model resource-id="$MODEL_ID" `
  --query "{alias:properties.aliasName, target:properties.backendModels[0].resourceId}"
if ($?) { Write-Host "🏷️ Alias $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL is ready" }
```

The command warns that the service doesn't enforce atomic alias creation. That's expected: it only matters when
two people create the same alias at the same time. If the alias already exists, `create` fails; change it with
`az aigateway model-alias update` and the same arguments instead.

### Create a runtime API key

`api-key create` returns metadata only. Read the generated value with `list-secrets` straight into a variable so
it never appears on screen. The service assigns the key's display name itself, so any `--display-name` works.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create a runtime API key for your app, which prints its name and state but not its value
az aigateway api-key create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n app-first-call --display-name app-first-call \
  --query "{name:name, state:properties.state}" &&
  echo "🔑 API key app-first-call is ready"

# Read the key's value straight into an environment variable, so that it never shows on screen
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n app-first-call \
  --query primaryKey -o tsv)" && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Create a runtime API key for your app, which prints its name and state but not its value
az aigateway api-key create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n app-first-call --display-name app-first-call `
  --query "{name:name, state:properties.state}"
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔑 API key app-first-call is ready" }

# Read the key's value straight into an environment variable, so that it never shows on screen
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n app-first-call `
  --query primaryKey -o tsv
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

> **Checkpoint**
> `az aigateway model list -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --query "[].{name:name, provider:properties.providerKind}" -o table`
> lists your deployment with the provider `Foundry`, the alias command returned your model's ID as `target` and
> printed `🏷️ Alias gpt-6-luna is ready`, and
> `az aigateway api-key list -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --query "[].{name:name, state:properties.state}" -o table`
> shows `app-first-call` as `active`, next to the built-in `master` key.

### Review the templates

`infra/main.bicep` creates the resource group `rg-<environment name>` and composes three templates. It calls lab
01's [gateway.bicep](../01-provision-gateway/infra/gateway.bicep) for the gateway, `infra/foundry.bicep` for the
Foundry account and its `gpt-6-luna` deployment, and then `infra/publish-model.bicep` to publish the deployment
through the gateway:

<!-- include: infra/main.bicep -->

`infra/foundry.bicep` creates an Azure AI Services account with local key authentication disabled, and a
`gpt-6-luna` `GlobalStandard` deployment. Skip it in your own templates if you already have a deployment:

<!-- include: infra/foundry.bicep -->

`infra/publish-model.bicep` adds to the gateway. It grants the gateway's identity the **Foundry User** role on the
account (in the account's own resource group, with
[foundry-user-role.bicep](infra/foundry-user-role.bicep)), and only then creates a Foundry model provider that
authenticates with the managed identity. It registers the deployment as a backend model with a per-caller token
limit, publishes an alias, and creates a runtime API key. It only references the gateway and the account, so you
can also deploy it on its own to a gateway you already have, with `az deployment group create`:

### Deploy with azd up

### Read the outputs and the key

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the names that the next sections and Verify use from azd's environment values
export RG="$(azd env get-value AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP)"
```

### Change the token limit

The template gives each caller 10,000 tokens per minute on the model. The value comes from the
`TOKENS_PER_MINUTE` azd environment value, with the default in `infra/main.parameters.json`. To change it, set the
value and provision again. Only the model changes.

```bash title="Bash"
# Set the tokens per minute that each caller can use on the model
azd env set TOKENS_PER_MINUTE 20000 &&
  echo "📝 TOKENS_PER_MINUTE is 20000"

# Provision again, which updates only the model
azd provision &&
  echo "🛡️ Token limit of 20,000 tokens per minute per caller is on $DEPLOYMENT"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Set the tokens per minute that each caller can use on the model
azd env set TOKENS_PER_MINUTE 20000
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 TOKENS_PER_MINUTE is 20000" }

# Provision again, which updates only the model
azd provision
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Token limit of 20,000 tokens per minute per caller is on $DEPLOYMENT" }
```

## Make your first call

Use the same alias and key everywhere. The gateway exposes the OpenAI-compatible base URL
`<gateway URL>/default/models/openai/v1`, so OpenAI SDKs only need a different base URL and the runtime key.

<!-- track: portal | Playground -->

### Try the model in Catalog

1. Select **Catalog** and pick your model.
2. Send a prompt in the built-in playground, for example `Write a one-sentence status update.`
3. Copy the endpoint and the code samples (cURL, PowerShell 7+, Python, TypeScript, and .NET) for your app.

> [!TIP]
> If the playground asks you to **Sign in again**, your portal session expired. Sign in and resend the prompt.

<!-- track: cli | curl and PowerShell -->

### Call Chat Completions

```bash title="Bash"
# Call Chat Completions through the gateway: the alias in model, and the runtime key in the api-key header
curl -sS "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Write a one-sentence status update.\"}]}" \
  | jq -r 'if .choices then "🤖 \(.choices[0].message.content)" else "⚠️ \(.error.message // .)" end'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Build the request: the alias in model, and one user message
$body = @{
  model    = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL
  messages = @(@{ role = "user"; content = "Write a one-sentence status update." })
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5

# Call Chat Completions through the gateway, with the runtime key in the api-key header
$reply = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post `
  -Uri "$($env:AI_GATEWAY_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
  -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body
if ($?) { Write-Host "🤖 $($reply.choices[0].message.content)" }
```

### Call the Responses API

```bash title="Bash"
# Call the Responses API through the gateway, with the same alias and key, and print the reply's text
curl -sS "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/responses" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"input\":\"Summarize what an AI gateway does in one sentence.\"}" \
  | jq -r 'if .output then "🤖 \([.output[] | select(.type == "message") | .content[] | select(.type == "output_text") | .text] | join(""))" else "⚠️ \(.error.message // .)" end'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Build the request: the alias in model, and the prompt in input
$body = @{ model = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL; input = "Summarize what an AI gateway does in one sentence." } |
  ConvertTo-Json

# Call the Responses API through the gateway, and print the text of the reply's message
$reply = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post `
  -Uri "$($env:AI_GATEWAY_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/default/models/openai/v1/responses" `
  -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body
if ($?) { Write-Host "🤖 $(($reply.output | Where-Object type -eq "message").content.text -join '')" }
```


### Call the model from code

The OpenAI SDKs send their API key as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`, which the model endpoint accepts, so the
runtime key goes straight into the SDK. Don't also add an `api-key` default header: the gateway rejects a request
that has both with `400`. The .NET sample uses `HttpClient`, like the .NET samples in the AI Gateway docs, so it
sends the `api-key` header explicitly.

```python title="Python"
import os

from openai import OpenAI

gateway_url = os.environ["AI_GATEWAY_URL"].rstrip("/")
model = os.environ["AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"]

client = OpenAI(
    base_url=f"{gateway_url}/default/models/openai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY"],
)

response = client.responses.create(model=model, input="Write a one-sentence status update.")
print(f"Responses API:    {response.output_text}")

completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=model,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Describe an AI gateway in one sentence."}],
)
print(f"Chat Completions: {completion.choices[0].message.content}")
```

```typescript title="TypeScript"
import OpenAI from "openai";

const gatewayUrl = process.env.AI_GATEWAY_URL!.replace(/\/+$/, "");
const model = process.env.AI_GATEWAY_MODEL!;

const client = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: `${gatewayUrl}/default/models/openai/v1`,
  apiKey: process.env.AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY!,
});

const response = await client.responses.create({ model, input: "Write a one-sentence status update." });
console.log(`Responses API:    ${response.output_text}`);

const completion = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model,
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Describe an AI gateway in one sentence." }],
});
console.log(`Chat Completions: ${completion.choices[0].message.content}`);
```

```csharp title="C#"
using System.Net.Http.Json;
using System.Text.Json;

var gatewayUrl = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("AI_GATEWAY_URL")!.TrimEnd('/');
var model = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("AI_GATEWAY_MODEL")!;

using var http = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri($"{gatewayUrl}/default/models/openai/v1/") };
http.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add("api-key", Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY"));

using var reply = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("chat/completions", new
{
    model,
    messages = new[] { new { role = "user", content = "Describe an AI gateway in one sentence." } },
});
reply.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
using var json = JsonDocument.Parse(await reply.Content.ReadAsStringAsync());
Console.WriteLine(json.RootElement.GetProperty("choices")[0].GetProperty("message").GetProperty("content").GetString());
```

The full samples in `infra` also call the Responses API from C# and print token usage: open
[first-call.py](infra/first-call.py), [first-call.ts](infra/first-call.ts), and
[dotnet/Program.cs](infra/dotnet/Program.cs).

## Verify

<!-- steps -->

### Confirm the model is published

```bash title="Bash"
# List the models that the gateway publishes, with the kind of provider of each
echo "🧠 Models on gateway $GATEWAY:"
az aigateway model list -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --query "[].{name:name, provider:properties.providerKind}" -o table
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# List the models that the gateway publishes, with the kind of provider of each
Write-Host "🧠 Models on gateway ${GATEWAY}:"
az aigateway model list -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --query "[].{name:name, provider:properties.providerKind}" -o table
```

The list includes your deployment. In the portal, **Catalog** lists the model too.

### Get a 200 with the key

```bash title="Bash"
# Call Chat Completions with the key, and print only the HTTP status
STATUS="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"ping\"}]}")" &&
  echo "🔑 With the key: HTTP $STATUS"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Build a short request: the alias in model, and one user message
$body = @{ model = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL; messages = @(@{ role = "user"; content = "ping" }) } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5

# Call Chat Completions with the key, and print only the HTTP status
$status = (Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri "$($env:AI_GATEWAY_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
  -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body -SkipHttpErrorCheck).StatusCode
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔑 With the key: HTTP $status" }
```

Expect `🔑 With the key: HTTP 200`.

### Get a 401 without the key

Send the same request without the `api-key` header. The gateway rejects it before any policy runs or the
backend is called.

```bash title="Bash"
# Send the same request without the api-key header, and print only the HTTP status
STATUS="$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"ping\"}]}")" &&
  echo "🚦 Without a key: HTTP $STATUS"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Send the same request without the api-key header, and print only the HTTP status
$status = (Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri "$($env:AI_GATEWAY_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
  -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body -SkipHttpErrorCheck).StatusCode
if ($?) { Write-Host "🚦 Without a key: HTTP $status" }
```

Expect `🚦 Without a key: HTTP 401`.

### Check that the alias is what clients call

Change one character in `model` and resend the request with the key. The call fails with `404` and
`model_not_found` because `model` must match an alias exactly. Backend model names and Foundry deployment names
aren't callable unless an alias with that name exists.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> You got `200` with the key, `401` without it, and an error for a name that isn't an alias.

### Delete what you published

When you're done with the labs, delete the key, the alias, and the provider, then remove the role assignment that
the gateway received on the Foundry account. Delete the alias first: deleting the provider also deletes its
models, but not the aliases that point at them. Deleting a model from the gateway doesn't delete the Foundry
deployment. The commands use the names from the CLI track. If you imported in the portal, use the provider
and alias names shown on **Models**.

```bash title="Bash"
# Delete the runtime API key, so that it stops working
az aigateway api-key delete -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n app-first-call --yes &&
  echo "🧹 API key app-first-call is deleted"

# Delete the alias first: deleting the provider doesn't delete the aliases that point at its models
az aigateway model-alias delete -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$DEPLOYMENT" --yes &&
  echo "🧹 Alias $DEPLOYMENT is deleted"

# Delete the provider, with its models. The Foundry deployment stays.
az aigateway model-provider delete -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$PROVIDER" --yes &&
  echo "🧹 Model provider $PROVIDER is deleted"

# Read the principal ID of the gateway's identity, and the Foundry account's resource ID
PRINCIPAL_ID="$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query identity.principalId -o tsv)"
FOUNDRY_ID="$(az cognitiveservices account show -g "$FOUNDRY_RG" -n "$FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT" --query id -o tsv)"
echo "🪪 Gateway identity: $PRINCIPAL_ID"

# Remove the Foundry User role that the gateway's identity has on the account
az role assignment delete --assignee "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --role "53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d" --scope "$FOUNDRY_ID" &&
  echo "🧹 The gateway's Foundry User role on $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT is removed"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Delete the runtime API key, so that it stops working
az aigateway api-key delete -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n app-first-call --yes
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 API key app-first-call is deleted" }

# Delete the alias first: deleting the provider doesn't delete the aliases that point at its models
az aigateway model-alias delete -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $DEPLOYMENT --yes
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 Alias $DEPLOYMENT is deleted" }

# Delete the provider, with its models. The Foundry deployment stays.
az aigateway model-provider delete -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $PROVIDER --yes
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 Model provider $PROVIDER is deleted" }

# Read the principal ID of the gateway's identity, and the Foundry account's resource ID
$PRINCIPAL_ID = az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --query identity.principalId -o tsv
$FOUNDRY_ID = az cognitiveservices account show -g $FOUNDRY_RG -n $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT --query id -o tsv
Write-Host "🪪 Gateway identity: $PRINCIPAL_ID"

# Remove the Foundry User role that the gateway's identity has on the account
az role assignment delete --assignee $PRINCIPAL_ID --role "53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d" --scope $FOUNDRY_ID
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 The gateway's Foundry User role on $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT is removed" }
```

If you created the Foundry account with `infra/foundry.bicep`, delete its resource group with
`az group delete --name "$FOUNDRY_RG"`.

# Publish models from any provider behind stable aliases

The support team wants to try Claude, and the batch team wants the same model for nightly summaries. You don't
want either team to hold an Anthropic key, and you don't want to edit their code every time you switch models.
In this lab you add Anthropic as a provider whose key only the gateway knows, publish two Claude models behind
aliases such as `support-chat`, and then point `support-chat` at a bigger model while the clients keep sending
the same name.

![Clients call an alias, and the alias points to a backend model of a provider](../assets/diagrams/aliases.svg "An alias is the stable name in the request's model field. You can point it at a different backend model at any time.")

<!-- widget: alias-retarget {"alias":"team-chat","targets":[{"provider":"Microsoft Foundry","model":"gpt-6-luna","note":"Lower cost","logo":"microsoft-foundry"},{"provider":"Microsoft Foundry","model":"gpt-6.1-sol","note":"Higher quality","logo":"microsoft-foundry"},{"provider":"OpenAI","model":"gpt-6-luna","note":"Custom provider","logo":"openai"}]} -->

## Before you begin

> section, except for the Anthropic key. You need only that key and the one-time setup above.

- Complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md). You need the
  gateway, a runtime API key, and the Foundry alias you created there.
- An API key from the [Claude Console](https://console.anthropic.com) that can call two models, for example
  `claude-haiku-5-5` and `claude-sonnet-5-5`. To use another provider instead, see the values in

- Permission to change the gateway, for example **Contributor** on its resource group.
- Run the scripts and samples from the lab's folder, `~/ai-gateway/labs/03-multi-provider-aliases`.

```bash title="Bash"
# Name your gateway, the provider that you create in this lab, and the two Anthropic models
```

## How it works

The gateway publishes models in three layers:

| Object | What it holds | Unique within | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Model provider** | A backend endpoint and the credential the gateway uses to call it | The gateway | `anthropic`, key sent in `x-api-key` |
| **Backend model** | A model that the provider serves, and the interfaces it supports | Its provider | `claude-haiku-5-5` |
| **Alias** | The callable name that clients put in the `model` field. It points to one or more backend models and can carry its own policies. | The gateway | `support-chat` |

Clients only ever see the gateway URL, their runtime key, and the alias. The provider key stays in the gateway.
In this lab each alias points to one backend model. To split traffic across several backend models by priority
and weight, see [Route an alias across models by priority and weight](../22-model-routing/README.md).

Each interface has its own route under `https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/models`:

| Interface | Route |
|---|---|
| OpenAI Chat Completions | `/openai/v1/chat/completions` |
| OpenAI Responses | `/openai/v1/responses` |
| Anthropic Messages | `/anthropic/v1/messages` |

Every model runs in passthrough mode. The gateway keeps the provider's request and response format and doesn't
translate between OpenAI and Anthropic, so call each model on an interface it advertises, and retarget an
alias only to a model that supports the same interface.

## Add Anthropic as a custom provider

The gateway connects to these providers. Microsoft Foundry and Azure OpenAI can use the gateway's managed
identity. Every other provider is a custom provider, and the gateway stores its API key.

| | Provider | How you add it | Gateway authenticates with |
|---|---|---|---|
| <img src="../assets/providers/microsoft-foundry.png" alt="" height="24"> | Microsoft Foundry | **Models from Microsoft Foundry** | Managed identity (recommended) or API key |
| <img src="../assets/providers/azure-openai.png" alt="" height="24"> | Azure OpenAI | **Models from Microsoft Foundry** | Managed identity (recommended) or API key |
| <img src="../assets/providers/openai.png" alt="" height="24"> | OpenAI | **Models from a custom provider** | API key |
| <img src="../assets/providers/anthropic.png" alt="" height="24"> | Anthropic | **Models from a custom provider** | API key |
| <img src="../assets/providers/aws-bedrock.png" alt="" height="24"> | AWS Bedrock | **Models from a custom provider** | API key |
| <img src="../assets/providers/google-vertex.png" alt="" height="24"> | Google Vertex AI | **Models from a custom provider** | API key |
| <img src="../assets/providers/custom-models.png" alt="" height="24"> | Any other OpenAI-compatible endpoint | **Models from a custom provider** | API key |

Pick one track. Every track creates the same result: a provider named `anthropic`, two backend models, and two
aliases. `support-chat` points to the fast model, and `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5` points to the bigger one. The
Bicep + azd track also declares the `batch-chat` alias and the token limits of the next section.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Start the custom provider wizard

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **Models** › **Add** › **Models from a custom provider**. **Add custom provider** in the
**Set up your gateway** guide on **Home** opens the same wizard.

On the **Provider** step, select **Create new provider** and fill in **Basic info**:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Display name** | `Anthropic` |
| **Provider name** | `anthropic` (used in the resource ID; you can't change it later) |
| **Description** | Optional |

Select **Next**.

### Connect the endpoint

On the **Endpoint** step, fill in **Endpoint and authentication**:

| Field | Value for Anthropic |
|---|---|
| **Base endpoint URL** | `https://api.anthropic.com` |
| **Header name** | `x-api-key` |
| **API key** | Your Anthropic API key |
| **Authentication scheme** | Leave **Include Bearer in the authorization header value** cleared. Anthropic expects the raw key. |

The wizard lists the provider's models by calling `<base endpoint URL>/v1/models`, so leave `/v1` off the base
URL. The key is stored in the gateway. Apps that call the gateway never receive it.

For other providers, change these values:

| Provider | Base endpoint URL | Header name | Authentication scheme |
|---|---|---|---|
| OpenAI | `https://api.openai.com` | `Authorization` | Selected, so the gateway sends `Bearer <key>` |
| Other OpenAI-compatible endpoints | The URL in front of `/v1/...` | The header the endpoint expects | As the endpoint expects |
| AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI | The provider's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, without the `/v1/...` path | The header that the provider's API key goes in | As the provider expects |

Select **Next**.

### Choose the models and their aliases

The **Models** step shows **Discovering available models…** while it calls the provider. Then select **Add** ›
**Individual model** and add each model:

| Field | First model | Second model |
|---|---|---|
| **Backend model** | `claude-haiku-5-5` | `claude-sonnet-5-5` |
| **Supported endpoints** | **Anthropic messages** | **Anthropic messages** |
| **Callable alias** | Change it to `support-chat` | Keep the default, `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5` |

If discovery fails or times out, you can still add the models by hand. Select **Add models**.

> **Checkpoint**
> **Models** lists the two Claude models of the `Anthropic` provider and the aliases `support-chat` and
> `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5`. Open a model: its **Overview** shows the Anthropic Messages endpoint,
> `https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/models/anthropic/v1/messages`.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Check the variables

The provider, its models, and the aliases are child resources of the gateway's `default` workspace. You set
`RG`, `GATEWAY`, `WS` (the workspace URL), and `API` in [Before you begin](#before-you-begin). Check that they
point at your gateway by listing its model providers. The command is the same in Bash and PowerShell.

```bash
# List the gateway's model providers, to check that the variables point at your gateway
echo "🔌 Model providers on your gateway:"
az aigateway model-provider list -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -o table
```

The table lists the provider from lab 02, of kind `Foundry`. If the command fails, set the variables again.

### Create the provider

The command reads the Anthropic key from a hidden prompt, so it never lands in your shell history. The command
output, like `az aigateway model-provider show`, never includes the key.

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the Anthropic key from a hidden prompt, so that it never lands in your shell history
read -rsp "Anthropic API key: " ANTHROPIC_API_KEY && echo
echo "🔑 Anthropic key: in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (${#ANTHROPIC_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"

# Add Anthropic as a custom provider: the gateway stores the key and sends it in the x-api-key header
az aigateway model-provider create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$PROVIDER" \
  --kind Custom --display-name "Anthropic" \
  --custom "$(jq -cn --arg key "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY" '{
      endpoint: "https://api.anthropic.com",
      authentication: {kind: "ApiKey", apiKey: {headerName: "x-api-key", value: $key}}}')" \
  --query "{name:name,kind:properties.kind,endpoint:properties.custom.endpoint}" &&
  echo "🔌 Model provider $PROVIDER is ready, and its key stays in the gateway"

# Clear the key from your shell, now that the gateway stores it
unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY &&
  echo "🧹 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is cleared from this shell"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the Anthropic key from a hidden prompt, so that it never lands in your shell history
$key = Read-Host "Anthropic API key" -MaskInput
Write-Host "🔑 Anthropic key: in the key variable ($($key.Length) characters, not shown)"

# Write the provider settings to a file: the endpoint, and the key that the gateway sends in the x-api-key header
@{
  endpoint       = 'https://api.anthropic.com'
  authentication = @{ kind = 'ApiKey'; apiKey = @{ headerName = 'x-api-key'; value = $key } }
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content -Path custom.json

# Add Anthropic as a custom provider: the gateway stores the key, and apps never receive it
az aigateway model-provider create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $PROVIDER `
  --kind Custom --display-name "Anthropic" --custom '@custom.json' `
  --query "{name:name,kind:properties.kind,endpoint:properties.custom.endpoint}"
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔌 Model provider $PROVIDER is ready, and its key stays in the gateway" }

# Delete the file and the variable right away, because they held the key
Remove-Item custom.json; Remove-Variable key
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 custom.json and the key variable are deleted" }
```

For OpenAI, use `https://api.openai.com`, the header `Authorization`, and the value `Bearer <key>`.

### Register the backend models

A backend model names one of the provider's models. Its name (`--name`) may only contain lowercase letters, digits,
and hyphens. If the provider's model ID contains other characters, replace them with `-` in `--name` and keep the
real ID in `modelName`.

```bash title="Bash"
# Register both Claude models as backend models of the provider, on the Anthropic Messages path, /v1/messages
for MODEL in "$FAST_MODEL" "$SMART_MODEL"; do
  az aigateway model create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" -n "$MODEL" \
    --display-name "$MODEL" --supported-endpoints /v1/messages --deployment-config "{modelName:$MODEL}" \
    --query "{name:name,endpoints:properties.supportedEndpoints}" -o json &&
    echo "🧠 Backend model $MODEL is published through $PROVIDER"
done
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Register both Claude models as backend models of the provider, on the Anthropic Messages path, /v1/messages
foreach ($model in $FAST_MODEL, $SMART_MODEL) {
  az aigateway model create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER -n $model `
    --display-name $model --supported-endpoints /v1/messages --deployment-config "{modelName:$model}" `
    --query "{name:name,endpoints:properties.supportedEndpoints}" -o json
  if ($?) { Write-Host "🧠 Backend model $model is published through $PROVIDER" }
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> The provider settings and model bodies mirror what the portal sends. For custom providers, `supportedEndpoints`
> holds the provider path: `/v1/messages` for Anthropic, `/v1/chat/completions` or `/v1/responses` for
> OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Leave out `--api-format` for custom providers. If the service rejects either
> command, create the provider and models with the **Portal** tab, then continue here with the aliases.

### Create the aliases

An alias lists its backend models by resource ID in `properties.backendModels`. Here each alias has one. The
callable name goes in `properties.aliasName`, which `--routing-name` sets, and `-n` sets the resource name.
Callable names may contain `/`, but resource names can't, so the script derives the resource name the same way
the portal does: `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5` is stored as `anthropic-claude-sonnet-5-5`.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create the support-chat alias on the fast model
./infra/alias.sh put support-chat "$PROVIDER" "$FAST_MODEL" &&
  echo "🏷️ Alias support-chat is ready"

# Create an alias for the bigger model, named after the provider and the model, as the portal does
./infra/alias.sh put "$PROVIDER/$SMART_MODEL" "$PROVIDER" "$SMART_MODEL" &&
  echo "🏷️ Alias $PROVIDER/$SMART_MODEL is ready"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Create the support-chat alias on the fast model
./infra/alias.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY put support-chat $PROVIDER $FAST_MODEL
if ($?) { Write-Host "🏷️ Alias support-chat is ready" }

# Create an alias for the bigger model, named after the provider and the model, as the portal does
./infra/alias.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY put "$PROVIDER/$SMART_MODEL" $PROVIDER $SMART_MODEL
if ($?) { Write-Host "🏷️ Alias $PROVIDER/$SMART_MODEL is ready" }
```

On GitHub, open [alias.sh](infra/alias.sh) or [alias.ps1](infra/alias.ps1). For a new alias, each `put` runs a
command like this. For an alias that already exists, it runs `az aigateway model-alias update` with the same
arguments.

```text
az aigateway model-alias create -g <resource-group> --gateway-name <gateway> -n support-chat \
  --routing-name support-chat \
  --backend-model resource-id=.../workspaces/default/modelProviders/anthropic/models/claude-haiku-5-5 \
  --policies '[]' --only-show-errors -o none
```

> **Checkpoint**
> `./infra/alias.sh list` shows `support-chat` → `anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5` and
> `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5` → `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5`, next to your Foundry alias from lab 02.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

**What you need:** only the one-time setup from **Before you begin**. This track doesn't use your gateway from earlier
labs: `azd up` creates a new one, so it works on its own.

### Choose what to declare

The provider, its models, and the aliases are child resources of the gateway's `default` workspace:
`modelProviders`, `modelProviders/models`, and `aliases`. The template declares the same bodies as the Azure CLI
track. The Anthropic key is a `@secure()` parameter: the gateway stores it, and it never shows in the deployment
history, the outputs, or the `az aigateway model-provider show` output.

| azd environment value | Parameter | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | `anthropicApiKey` | None. `azd up` asks for it if you don't set it. |
| `FAST_MODEL` | `fastModel` | `claude-haiku-5-5` |
| `SMART_MODEL` | `smartModel` | `claude-sonnet-5-5` |
| `SUPPORT_CHAT_MODEL` | `supportChatModel` | The fast model |
| `SUPPORT_CHAT_TOKENS_PER_MINUTE` | `supportChatTokensPerMinute` | `20000` |
| `BATCH_CHAT_TOKENS_PER_MINUTE` | `batchChatTokensPerMinute` | `2000` |

### Review the templates

`infra/main.bicep` creates the resource group `rg-<environment name>` and calls the quick start's
[resources.bicep](../quickstart/infra/resources.bicep) for the gateway, the Foundry model, its default alias, and the
runtime key. Then it calls `infra/anthropic-aliases.bicep` with the Anthropic key and the model names:

`infra/anthropic-aliases.bicep` declares the provider, the two backend models, and the three aliases, each with its
callable name in `aliasName` and its token limit in `policies`. It only references the gateway, so you can also

### Deploy with azd up

Move into the lab's folder, create an azd environment named `aigw-lab03` in your current subscription, and give it the
Anthropic key from a hidden prompt, so that it never lands in your shell history. Then provision everything. It takes
about three minutes.

```bash title="Bash"
# Move into the lab's folder, which holds the azd project
cd ~/ai-gateway/labs/03-multi-provider-aliases &&
  echo "📂 Lab folder: $(pwd)"

# Create an azd environment in your current subscription, so that azd doesn't prompt you
azd env new aigw-lab03 --location eastus2 --subscription "$(az account show --query id --output tsv)" &&
  echo "📝 azd environment aigw-lab03 deploys to eastus2"

# Read the Anthropic key from a hidden prompt, so that it never lands in your shell history
read -rsp "Anthropic API key: " ANTHROPIC_API_KEY && echo
echo "🔑 Anthropic key: in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (${#ANTHROPIC_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"

# Store the key in the azd environment, which passes it to the template's secure parameter
azd env set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY" &&
  echo "📝 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set in the azd environment"

# Clear the key from your shell, now that the azd environment holds it
unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY &&
  echo "🧹 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is cleared from this shell"

# Provision the gateway, the Foundry model, the key, the Anthropic provider, its models, and the aliases
azd up &&
  echo "🚀 Gateway deployed: $(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Move into the lab's folder, which holds the azd project
Set-Location ~/ai-gateway/labs/03-multi-provider-aliases
if ($?) { Write-Host "📂 Lab folder: $(Get-Location)" }

# Create an azd environment in your current subscription, so that azd doesn't prompt you
azd env new aigw-lab03 --location eastus2 --subscription (az account show --query id --output tsv)
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 azd environment aigw-lab03 deploys to eastus2" }

# Read the Anthropic key from a hidden prompt, so that it never lands in your shell history
$key = Read-Host "Anthropic API key" -MaskInput
Write-Host "🔑 Anthropic key: in the key variable ($($key.Length) characters, not shown)"

# Store the key in the azd environment, which passes it to the template's secure parameter
azd env set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY $key
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set in the azd environment" }

# Clear the key from your shell, now that the azd environment holds it
Remove-Variable key
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 The key variable is cleared from this shell" }

# Provision the gateway, the Foundry model, the key, the Anthropic provider, its models, and the aliases
azd up
if ($?) { Write-Host "🚀 Gateway deployed: $(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL)" }
```

For another region, pick one where AI Gateway and the `gpt-6-luna` model are available, as in [Find the available
regions](../SETUP.md#find-the-available-regions). azd keeps the key in `.azure/aigw-lab03/.env`,
which `.azure/.gitignore` keeps out of Git. If your Claude Console key can't call the default models, set `FAST_MODEL`
and `SMART_MODEL` with `azd env set` before `azd up`.

### Read the outputs and the key

Set the variables that the next sections and **Verify** use from azd's environment values, and read the gateway's



## Call Claude through the gateway

Send a native Anthropic Messages request to the gateway's Anthropic route. Three things differ from a direct
call to Anthropic: the URL is the gateway's, the `api-key` header carries your gateway runtime key, and `model`
is the alias. Keep the `anthropic-version` header that the Messages API expects.

```bash title="Bash"
# Call support-chat with the native Messages API: your runtime key in api-key, and the alias in model
curl -sS "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/anthropic/v1/messages" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" \
  -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "support-chat", "max_tokens": 1024,
       "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "In one sentence, what is an AI gateway?"}]}' \
  | jq -r 'if .content then
             "🧠 Backend model: \(.model)",
             "🤖 \([.content[] | select(.type == "text") | .text] | join(""))",
             "📊 Usage: \(.usage | tojson)"
           else "⚠️ \(.error.message // .)" end'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Build the request: your runtime key in api-key, the Messages API version, and the alias in model
$headers = @{ 'api-key' = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY; 'anthropic-version' = '2023-06-01' }
$body = @{
  model      = 'support-chat'
  max_tokens = 1024
  messages   = @(@{ role = 'user'; content = 'In one sentence, what is an AI gateway?' })
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5

# Call support-chat on the gateway's Anthropic route, and print the backend model, the reply, and the usage
$r = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri "$($env:AI_GATEWAY_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/default/models/anthropic/v1/messages" `
  -Headers $headers -ContentType 'application/json' -Body $body
if ($?) {
  Write-Host "🧠 Backend model: $($r.model)"
  Write-Host "🤖 $((@($r.content) | Where-Object type -eq 'text' | ForEach-Object text) -join '')"
  Write-Host "📊 Usage: $($r.usage | ConvertTo-Json -Compress)"
}
```

The response uses Anthropic's own format, with `content` blocks, `stop_reason`, and `usage.input_tokens`. It
doesn't use OpenAI's `choices`. The `model` field names the backend model that answered, for example
`claude-haiku-5-5`. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 think adaptively by default, so `content` can start
with a `thinking` block, and thinking counts toward `max_tokens`. Read the `text` blocks and leave headroom in
`max_tokens`.

> **Checkpoint**
> The call prints a `🤖` Claude reply and `🧠 Backend model: claude-haiku-5-5`. Your app never sent an Anthropic
> key.

## Give one backend model two aliases

The batch team's nightly job shouldn't be able to use up the capacity that the support app needs. Point a second
alias, `batch-chat`, at the same fast model and give each alias its own per-caller token limit: 2,000 tokens per
minute for `batch-chat` and 20,000 for `support-chat`. Alias policies apply only to callers that use that name.
Policies on the backend model apply to every alias that targets it.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Add the batch-chat alias

Select **Models** › **Aliases** › **Add alias**. The **Create alias** wizard has four steps:

| Step | What to do |
|---|---|
| **Basics** | Set **Alias name** to `batch-chat` and **Description** to `Nightly batch summaries`. |
| **Select models** | Under **Available backend models**, select `claude-haiku-5-5` from the `Anthropic` provider. |
| **Priority and weights** | Keep the defaults, priority `0` and weight `1`. With one backend model, it gets all requests. |
| **Review** | Check the summary. |

Select **Create**. You can also start from **Models** › **Add** › **Alias for an existing model**.

### Limit each alias

Select **Policies** › **Add policy**. On the **Type** step, select **Token rate limit**, then **Next**. On the
**Scope** step, select **Individual assets**, select the `batch-chat` alias, then **Next**. On the
**Configure** step, set **Time period** to **Per minute**, **Allowed tokens** to `2000`, and **Counter
dimensions** to **Caller identity**. Select **Create**.

Repeat for the `support-chat` alias with `20000` **Allowed tokens**.

> **Checkpoint**
> **Policies** lists two **Token rate limit** policies, one scoped to `batch-chat` and one scoped to
> `support-chat`.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Put both aliases with their limits

The optional fourth argument adds a per-caller token limit to the alias. It's the same `tokenLimit` policy
object that models use.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create batch-chat on the fast model, with a per-caller limit of 2,000 tokens per minute
./infra/alias.sh put batch-chat   "$PROVIDER" "$FAST_MODEL" 2000 &&
  echo "🛡️ Token limit of 2,000 tokens per minute is on batch-chat"

# Give support-chat, on the same model, its own per-caller limit of 20,000 tokens per minute
./infra/alias.sh put support-chat "$PROVIDER" "$FAST_MODEL" 20000 &&
  echo "🛡️ Token limit of 20,000 tokens per minute is on support-chat"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Create batch-chat on the fast model, with a per-caller limit of 2,000 tokens per minute
./infra/alias.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY put batch-chat   $PROVIDER $FAST_MODEL 2000
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Token limit of 2,000 tokens per minute is on batch-chat" }

# Give support-chat, on the same model, its own per-caller limit of 20,000 tokens per minute
./infra/alias.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY put support-chat $PROVIDER $FAST_MODEL 20000
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Token limit of 20,000 tokens per minute is on support-chat" }
```

The command now passes a policy in `--policies`:

```json
[ { "type": "tokenLimit", "count": 2000, "period": "minute", "counterKey": ["identity"] } ]
```

`put` replaces the alias's whole `policies` list, so a `put` without a limit removes it. To change only the
target, use `retarget` in the next section.

> **Checkpoint**
> Each command prints the alias with `tokenLimit 2000/minute` or `tokenLimit 20000/minute`.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Check the declared limits

`azd up` already created `batch-chat` and both limits: `anthropic-aliases.bicep` declares each alias with a
`tokenLimit` policy, the same object that the Azure CLI track passes in `--policies`. Show the `batch-chat` alias.

```bash title="Bash"
# Show the policies that the template declared on the batch-chat alias
echo "🛡️ Policies on batch-chat:"
./infra/alias.sh show batch-chat | jq '.properties.policies'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Show the policies that the template declared on the batch-chat alias
Write-Host "🛡️ Policies on batch-chat:"
(./infra/alias.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY show batch-chat | ConvertFrom-Json).properties.policies
```

To change a limit, set `BATCH_CHAT_TOKENS_PER_MINUTE` or `SUPPORT_CHAT_TOKENS_PER_MINUTE` with `azd env set`, then
run `azd provision`.

> **Checkpoint**
> The output lists one `tokenLimit` policy with `"count": 2000`, `"period": "minute"`, and
> `"counterKey": ["identity"]`.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Retarget an alias without touching clients

The support team wants better answers. Point `support-chat` at the bigger model. The clients keep sending
`"model": "support-chat"`, and the alias keeps its 20,000-token limit.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Edit the alias

In **Models** › **Aliases**, open the `support-chat` alias and select **Edit**. **Edit alias** has the same
steps as **Create alias**. On **Select models**, clear `claude-haiku-5-5` and select `claude-sonnet-5-5` from
the `Anthropic` provider. Keep the defaults on **Priority and weights**, select **Next** until you reach
**Review**, then select **Save**. New requests use the selected backend model immediately.

![The Priority and weights step of the alias wizard, with a backend model at priority 0 and two at priority 1 split 75/25](../assets/screens/models-alias-routing.png "Edit alias changes the backend models behind the name. The alias name that clients send stays the same. With several backend models, Priority and weights decides which one serves each request, as in lab 22.")

### Check that the policy stayed

On the `support-chat` alias page, select the **Policies** tab.

> **Checkpoint**
> The alias page shows `claude-sonnet-5-5` on the **Backend models** tab, and the **Policies** tab still lists the
> 20,000-token **Token rate limit**.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Update only the backend model

`retarget` runs `az aigateway model-alias update` with only `--backend-model`. The command changes only the
properties you pass, so the alias name, description, and policies stay as they are.

```bash title="Bash"
# Point support-chat at the bigger model, and keep its name, description, and token limit
./infra/alias.sh retarget support-chat "$PROVIDER" "$SMART_MODEL" &&
  echo "🏷️ Alias support-chat now points to $PROVIDER/$SMART_MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Point support-chat at the bigger model, and keep its name, description, and token limit
./infra/alias.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY retarget support-chat $PROVIDER $SMART_MODEL
if ($?) { Write-Host "🏷️ Alias support-chat now points to $PROVIDER/$SMART_MODEL" }
```

```text
az aigateway model-alias update -g <resource-group> --gateway-name <gateway> -n support-chat \
  --backend-model resource-id=.../modelProviders/anthropic/models/claude-sonnet-5-5 --only-show-errors -o none
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The output shows `support-chat` → `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5` and still `tokenLimit 20000/minute`.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Change the backend model in the environment

The template points `support-chat` at the model in `SUPPORT_CHAT_MODEL`, and the fast model when it's empty. Set it
to the bigger model and provision again. The deployment replaces the whole alias, but the template declares the
policy with it, so the limit stays.

```bash title="Bash"
# Point support-chat at the bigger model in the azd environment
azd env set SUPPORT_CHAT_MODEL "$SMART_MODEL" &&
  echo "📝 SUPPORT_CHAT_MODEL is $SMART_MODEL"

# Deploy the template again: it replaces the alias, with the new backend model and the same token limit

```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Point support-chat at the bigger model in the azd environment
```

```text
Reply:   An AI gateway sits between your apps and AI models to ...
```

> **Checkpoint**
> `support-chat` now answers with Sonnet and `batch-chat` with Haiku, and you didn't change the client request.

## Go further

- **Use the Anthropic SDK.** Point the SDK at the gateway's Anthropic base URL. The SDK appends `/v1/messages`
  itself and sends `anthropic-version` for you.

  ```python
  import os
  from anthropic import Anthropic  # pip install anthropic

  client = Anthropic(
      base_url=os.environ["AI_GATEWAY_URL"].rstrip("/") + "/default/models/anthropic",
      api_key="unused",  # required by the SDK; the gateway reads the api-key header
      default_headers={"api-key": os.environ["AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY"]},
  )
  message = client.messages.create(
      model="support-chat",
      max_tokens=1024,
      messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}],
  )
  print(message.model, "".join(block.text for block in message.content if block.type == "text"))
  ```

- **Move one alias between providers.** Add OpenAI as a second custom provider with the values from the
  provider table, and register `gpt-6-luna` with **OpenAI chat completions**. Create an alias such as
  `team-chat` on your Foundry `gpt-6-luna`, then retarget it to the OpenAI model. Both speak Chat Completions,
  so clients don't notice the switch.
- **Layer the limits.** Add a token limit to the `claude-haiku-5-5` backend model as in
  [Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md). It applies to every alias that
  targets the model, on top of each alias's own limit.

# Route an alias across models by priority and weight

Your team wants to try `gpt-6.1-sol`, but every app already sends `"model": "chat"`, and nobody wants a big-bang
switch. In this lab you put the current model and the new one behind the same alias, send a fifth of the traffic
to the new model, count where the requests land, and then use priority to choose which model is preferred. The
apps never change the model name they send.

![Clients call one alias. The gateway prefers the backend models with the lowest priority number and splits their traffic by weight](../assets/diagrams/alias-routing.svg "Priority picks the tier. Weight splits the traffic inside it.")

<!-- widget: alias-routing {"alias":"chat"} -->
