## How it works

An alias holds a list of backend models. Each one has a priority and a weight:

| Setting | Values | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Priority** | Whole number from 0 to 100 | `0` | Lower numbers are preferred. Requests go to the backend models with the lowest priority number. |
| **Weight** | Whole number from 1 to 100 | `1` | Splits traffic among the backend models that share a priority, in proportion to their weights. |

A backend model's **Share within priority** is its weight divided by the sum of the weights at its priority.
Weights `80` and `20` give 80% and 20%; weights `3` and `1` give 75% and 25%. With one backend model, the alias
behaves like the single-target aliases of labs 02 and 03.

Pick the values from the job you need to do:

| Scenario | Priority | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| **Canary a new model version** | Same for both | Small share for the new version, for example `95` and `5`, then raise it |
| **A/B test two models** | Same for both | Equal, for example `50` and `50` |
| **Balance deployments** across regions or providers | Same for all | In proportion to each deployment's capacity, for example `3` and `1` |
| **Prefer purchased capacity** | Provisioned deployment `0`, pay-as-you-go `1` | Any |

A few rules keep every request answerable:

- Each backend model can appear only once in an alias.
- All backend models must support at least one interface in common, for example **OpenAI Chat Completions**.
  Mixing an Anthropic Messages model with an OpenAI model in one alias fails.
- The response tells you which backend served the request: the `model` field holds the backend's model name and
  version, for example `gpt-6.1-sol-2026-09-29`, and Foundry models also return an `x-ms-served-model` header.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Priority sets a preference, not a guaranteed failover. In our tests, when the preferred backend returned an error
> such as `429` or `404`, the gateway passed that error to the client instead of retrying a lower-priority
> backend. Test how your gateway behaves under throttling before you rely on priority for
> availability, and keep retries in your clients.

## Split traffic 80/20 between two models

Register the candidate model in the gateway, then create the `chat` alias with both models at priority `0` and
weights `80` and `20`.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Import the candidate model

1. Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway in the top bar.
2. Select **Models** › **Add** › **Models from Microsoft Foundry**.
3. Select the subscription and resource group of your Foundry account, then select the `gpt-6.1-sol`
   deployment. Keep **Managed identity** as the **Authentication method**.
4. Select **Add models**. If the wizard also creates an alias named after the model, keep it; this lab doesn't
   use it.

### Create the chat alias

1. Select **Models** › **Aliases** › **Add alias**.
2. On **Basics**, set **Alias name** to `chat` and **Description** to `Canary: 80/20 between the current and the
   new model`. Select **Next**.
3. On **Select models**, select `gpt-6-luna` and `gpt-6.1-sol` in **Available backend models**. Select **Next**.
4. On **Priority and weights**, keep **Priority** at `0` for both models. Set **Weight** to `80` for
   `gpt-6-luna` and `20` for `gpt-6.1-sol`. **Share within priority** shows `80%` and `20%`. Select **Next**.
5. On **Review**, check the shares, then select **Create**.

![The Priority and weights step of Create alias, with Priority, Weight, and Share within priority columns for each backend model](../assets/screens/models-alias-routing.png "Priority and weights. This example from the product documentation uses three GPT-4o deployments: one at priority 0, and two at priority 1 that split 75/25.")

> **Checkpoint**
> **Models** › **Aliases** lists `chat`. Its **Backend models** tab shows `gpt-6-luna` and `gpt-6.1-sol`, both at
> priority `0`, with weights `80` and `20`.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Register the candidate model

A backend model registers one deployment under the provider. This is the same command as in lab 02, with the
model version.

```bash title="Bash"
# Register the candidate deployment as a backend model under the provider, with its model version
az aigateway model create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" -n "$CANDIDATE" \
  --display-name "$CANDIDATE" --api-format OpenAIChatCompletions \
  --supported-endpoints /openai/v1/chat/completions /openai/v1/responses \
  --deployment-config "{resourceId:$FOUNDRY_ID/deployments/$CANDIDATE,modelName:$CANDIDATE,modelVersion:$CANDIDATE_VERSION}" \
  --query "{name:name, version:properties.deployment.modelVersion}" &&
  echo "🧠 Model $CANDIDATE is published through $PROVIDER"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Register the candidate deployment as a backend model under the provider, with its model version
az aigateway model create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER -n $CANDIDATE `
  --display-name $CANDIDATE --api-format OpenAIChatCompletions `
  --supported-endpoints /openai/v1/chat/completions /openai/v1/responses `
  --deployment-config "{resourceId:$FOUNDRY_ID/deployments/$CANDIDATE,modelName:$CANDIDATE,modelVersion:$CANDIDATE_VERSION}" `
  --query "{name:name, version:properties.deployment.modelVersion}"
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧠 Model $CANDIDATE is published through $PROVIDER" }
```

### Create the chat alias

Each `--backend-model` adds an entry to the alias's `backendModels` list, with a `resource-id`, a `priority`, and
a `weight`. With more than one backend model, each entry needs both a priority and a weight.

```bash title="Bash"
# Build the resource ID prefix of the provider's backend models, which each --backend-model entry uses
export MODELS="$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models"

# Create the alias with both backend models at priority 0 and weights 80 and 20, then print each one's routing
echo "🏷️ Alias $ALIAS routes to:"
az aigateway model-alias create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$ALIAS" \
  --description "Canary: 80/20 between the current and the new model" \
  --backend-model resource-id="$MODELS/$PRIMARY" priority=0 weight=80 \
  --backend-model resource-id="$MODELS/$CANDIDATE" priority=0 weight=20 \
  --only-show-errors --query properties.backendModels -o json |
  jq -r '.[] | "\(.resourceId | split("/") | last)  priority \(.priority)  weight \(.weight)"'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Build the resource ID prefix of the provider's backend models, which each --backend-model entry uses
$MODELS = "$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models"

# Create the alias with both backend models at priority 0 and weights 80 and 20, then print each one's routing
Write-Host "🏷️ Alias $ALIAS routes to:"
az aigateway model-alias create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $ALIAS `
  --description "Canary: 80/20 between the current and the new model" `
  --backend-model resource-id="$MODELS/$PRIMARY" priority=0 weight=80 `
  --backend-model resource-id="$MODELS/$CANDIDATE" priority=0 weight=20 `
  --only-show-errors --query properties.backendModels -o json |
  ConvertFrom-Json | ForEach-Object { '{0}  priority {1}  weight {2}' -f ($_.resourceId -split '/')[-1], $_.priority, $_.weight }
```

If the alias already exists, `create` fails. Change it with `az aigateway model-alias update` and the same
arguments instead.

> **Checkpoint**
> The output shows `gpt-6-luna  priority 0  weight 80` and `gpt-6.1-sol  priority 0  weight 20`.

### Read the outputs and the key

Set the variables that the next sections and **Verify** use from azd's environment values, read the key from the
gateway so that it never shows on screen, then print the alias's routes.

```bash title="Bash"
# Read azd's outputs into the variables that the next sections use, and build the backend models' ID prefix
export RG="$(azd env get-value AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP)"
export GATEWAY="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_NAME)"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_ID)"
export PROVIDER="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_PROVIDER)"
export PRIMARY="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_BACKEND_MODEL)"
export CANDIDATE="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_CANDIDATE_MODEL)"
export ALIAS="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_MODEL)"
export MODELS="$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL)"
echo "📝 Alias $ALIAS routes between $PRIMARY and $CANDIDATE on gateway $GATEWAY in $RG"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Read the app-first-call key from the gateway, so that it never shows on screen or lands in a file
export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets --ids "$GATEWAY_ID/apiKeys/app-first-call" \
  --query primaryKey --output tsv)"
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"

# Print the alias's backend models, with the priority and the weight of each one
echo "🏷️ Alias $ALIAS routes to:"
az aigateway model-alias show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$ALIAS" --query properties.backendModels -o json |
  jq -r '.[] | "\(.resourceId | split("/") | last)  priority \(.priority)  weight \(.weight)"'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read azd's outputs into the variables that the next sections use, and build the backend models' ID prefix
$RG                     = azd env get-value AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP
$GATEWAY                = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_NAME
$GATEWAY_ID             = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_ID
$PROVIDER               = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_PROVIDER
$PRIMARY                = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_BACKEND_MODEL
$CANDIDATE              = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_CANDIDATE_MODEL
$ALIAS                  = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_MODEL
$MODELS                 = "$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL     = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL
Write-Host "📝 Alias $ALIAS routes between $PRIMARY and $CANDIDATE on gateway $GATEWAY in $RG"
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Read the app-first-call key from the gateway, so that it never shows on screen or lands in a file
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az aigateway api-key list-secrets --ids "$GATEWAY_ID/apiKeys/app-first-call" `
  --query primaryKey --output tsv
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"

# Print the alias's backend models, with the priority and the weight of each one
Write-Host "🏷️ Alias $ALIAS routes to:"
az aigateway model-alias show -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $ALIAS --query properties.backendModels -o json |
  ConvertFrom-Json | ForEach-Object { '{0}  priority {1}  weight {2}' -f ($_.resourceId -split '/')[-1], $_.priority, $_.weight }
```

> **Checkpoint**
> `azd up` ended with `SUCCESS`, and the last command printed `gpt-6-luna  priority 0  weight 80` and
> `gpt-6.1-sol  priority 0  weight 20`.

## Watch the split

Send 20 requests to `chat` and count which backend model answered each one. The script sends one request every
half second and reads the `model` field of each response.

```bash title="Bash"
# Send 20 requests to the alias, one every half second, and count which backend model answered each one
echo "📊 Counting the backend models that serve $ALIAS, one request every half second"
./infra/count-models.sh "$ALIAS" 20
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Send 20 requests to the alias, one every half second, and count which backend model answered each one
Write-Host "📊 Counting the backend models that serve $ALIAS, one request every half second"
./infra/count-models.ps1 -Alias $ALIAS -Count 20
```

```text
Requests per backend model:
  16 gpt-6-luna-2026-09-22
   4 gpt-6.1-sol-2026-09-29
```

In our tests the gateway interleaved the two models, four requests to `gpt-6-luna` and then one to
`gpt-6.1-sol`, so 20 requests split exactly 16 and 4. Plan around the shares, not the exact order.

To see the header for a single call:

```bash title="Bash"
# Send one request to the alias, and print only the x-ms-served-model header of the response
echo "🧠 Backend model that served one request to $ALIAS:"
curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null "$AI_GATEWAY_URL/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\": \"$ALIAS\", \"max_completion_tokens\": 16, \"messages\": [{\"role\": \"user\", \"content\": \"Hi\"}]}" |
  grep -i "^x-ms-served-model"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Build a short request to the alias, capped at 16 completion tokens
$body = @{ model = $ALIAS; max_completion_tokens = 16; messages = @(@{ role = "user"; content = "Hi" }) } | ConvertTo-Json -Compress

# Send it, and print only the x-ms-served-model header of the response
Write-Host "🧠 Backend model that served one request to ${ALIAS}:"
(Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri "$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
  -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body).Headers["x-ms-served-model"]
```

> **Checkpoint**
> About four of every five requests show `gpt-6-luna-…`, and the rest show `gpt-6.1-sol-…`. The client sent
> `"model": "chat"` every time.

## Prefer one model by priority

The canary looks good, but finance wants `gpt-6-luna` to handle the traffic until the new model is approved.
Give `gpt-6.1-sol` priority `1`. It stays in the alias, ready to promote, but requests go to `gpt-6-luna`.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Edit the alias

1. In **Models** › **Aliases**, open `chat` and select **Edit**.
2. Select **Next** until you reach **Priority and weights**.
3. Set **Priority** to `1` for `gpt-6.1-sol` and set both weights to `1`. `gpt-6-luna` now shows `100%` at
   priority `0`, and `gpt-6.1-sol` shows `100%` at priority `1`.
4. Select **Next**, then **Save**. New requests use the new settings immediately.

> **Checkpoint**
> The alias **Backend models** tab shows `gpt-6-luna` at priority `0` and `gpt-6.1-sol` at priority `1`.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Update the priorities

`model-alias update` replaces the whole `backendModels` list, so pass both backend models.

```bash title="Bash"
# Prefer gpt-6-luna: it keeps priority 0, and the candidate moves to priority 1, both with weight 1
echo "🏷️ Alias $ALIAS now routes to:"
az aigateway model-alias update -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$ALIAS" \
  --description "Prefer the current model" \
  --backend-model resource-id="$MODELS/$PRIMARY" priority=0 weight=1 \
  --backend-model resource-id="$MODELS/$CANDIDATE" priority=1 weight=1 \
  --only-show-errors --query properties.backendModels -o json |
  jq -r '.[] | "\(.resourceId | split("/") | last)  priority \(.priority)  weight \(.weight)"'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Prefer gpt-6-luna: it keeps priority 0, and the candidate moves to priority 1, both with weight 1
Write-Host "🏷️ Alias $ALIAS now routes to:"
az aigateway model-alias update -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $ALIAS `
  --description "Prefer the current model" `
  --backend-model resource-id="$MODELS/$PRIMARY" priority=0 weight=1 `
  --backend-model resource-id="$MODELS/$CANDIDATE" priority=1 weight=1 `
  --only-show-errors --query properties.backendModels -o json |
  ConvertFrom-Json | ForEach-Object { '{0}  priority {1}  weight {2}' -f ($_.resourceId -split '/')[-1], $_.priority, $_.weight }
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The output shows `gpt-6-luna  priority 0  weight 1` and `gpt-6.1-sol  priority 1  weight 1`.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Provision the priority strategy

Set `ROUTING_STRATEGY` to `priority` and provision again. Only the alias changes: `gpt-6-luna` keeps priority `0`,
and `gpt-6.1-sol` gets priority `1`.

```bash title="Bash"
# Switch the template's routing strategy from the weighted split to priority
azd env set ROUTING_STRATEGY priority &&
  echo "📝 ROUTING_STRATEGY is priority"

# Provision again: only the alias changes
azd provision &&
  echo "🚀 The $ALIAS alias now prefers $PRIMARY"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Switch the template's routing strategy from the weighted split to priority
azd env set ROUTING_STRATEGY priority
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 ROUTING_STRATEGY is priority" }

# Provision again: only the alias changes
azd provision
if ($?) { Write-Host "🚀 The $ALIAS alias now prefers $PRIMARY" }
```

To go back to the weighted split, run `azd env set ROUTING_STRATEGY weighted` and `azd provision`. Change
`ROUTING_CANDIDATE_WEIGHT` the same way to canary in steps.

> **Checkpoint**
> `azd provision` ended with `SUCCESS`. **Read the alias** in **Verify** shows `gpt-6-luna  priority 0  weight 1`
> and `gpt-6.1-sol  priority 1  weight 1`.

## Go further

- **Canary in steps.** Move the weights from `95`/`5` to `80`/`20` to `50`/`50` while you watch errors, latency,
  and cost per model in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md). Weights must be at least
  `1`, so to stop sending traffic to a model, give it a higher priority number or remove it from the alias.
- **Prefer provisioned throughput.** Put a provisioned deployment at priority `0` and a pay-as-you-go
  deployment of the same model at priority `1`, so purchased capacity is used first. Test what happens when the
  provisioned deployment is saturated before you depend on it.
- **Balance regions or providers.** Register the same model from two Foundry accounts, or from Foundry and a
  custom provider, and give them weights in proportion to their quota.
- **Limit each model and the alias.** A token limit on a backend model, as in
  [Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md), applies to that model. A limit
  on the alias applies to every request that calls `chat`.

# Stream responses and count every token

Chat apps and agents stream their replies: the model sends text a few tokens at a time, so people start reading
after a second or two instead of waiting for the whole answer. Streaming used to be a blind spot for governance,
because a streamed Chat Completions response only reports token usage when the client asks for it. In this lab you
stream through the gateway with curl, PowerShell, and the OpenAI SDKs, read every event the client receives, and
then prove that a token limit still counts every streamed token.

![A streamed request passes the gateway's limits before the stream starts, and the gateway captures usage while the stream flows back to the client](../assets/diagrams/streaming-usage.svg "Token and cost limits are checked before the stream starts. While the stream flows back, the gateway records its token usage for limits, budgets, and Monitoring.")

<!-- widget: stream-usage -->

## How it works

Add `"stream": true` to a Chat Completions request and the gateway answers with `Content-Type:
text/event-stream`. The body is a series of server-sent events (SSE): each one is a `data:` line with a JSON chunk,
followed by a blank line. The gateway passes each chunk on as the model produces it, and the response carries
`x-accel-buffering: no`, which tells proxies such as NGINX not to hold it back.

This is what a streamed reply from a Foundry model looks like through the gateway:

| Chunk | `choices` | What it carries |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt filter results | Empty `[]` | Content safety results for the prompt. `id` and `model` are empty strings. |
| Role | One choice | `delta.role` is `assistant` and `delta.content` is an empty string. |
| Content deltas | One choice | `delta.content` holds the next few characters of the reply. `usage` is `null`. |
| Finish | One choice | `finish_reason` is `stop`, or `length` when the reply hits `max_completion_tokens`. |
| Usage | Empty `[]` | `usage` with `prompt_tokens`, `completion_tokens`, and `total_tokens`. Sent when the client sets `stream_options.include_usage`. |
| `data: [DONE]` | Not JSON | The end of the stream. Stop reading. |

Two chunks have an empty `choices` array, so code that reads `choices[0]` on every chunk crashes on the first one.

**Where the gateway counts tokens.** A token limit or cost limit is checked **before** the gateway forwards the
request. When a counter is exhausted, the client gets an ordinary JSON error, such as `429` with `Retry-After`, and no
stream starts. Once a stream starts, it runs to the end, even if it takes the counter past the limit; the next request
is throttled. While the stream flows, the gateway records its token usage for token limits, cost limits, and
Monitoring.

**Usage without `include_usage`.** Since the [September 24, 2026 release](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/releases/2026-09-24),
the gateway makes sure it has a usage record for every streamed Chat Completions response, even when the client
doesn't set `stream_options.include_usage`, so the counters stay accurate. The release notes ask clients that parse
the events themselves to accept a usage-only chunk before `[DONE]`, even when they didn't ask for one. In our test
run in October 2026, a client that didn't set `include_usage` received no usage chunk, yet the token limit counted its
tokens exactly as it did for a client that asked. So write your client to work either way: skip chunks with an empty
`choices` array, and take usage from whichever chunk carries it.

The Responses API streams typed events instead: each `data:` line follows an `event:` line, and the last event,
`response.completed`, always carries the usage.

## Stream a response

Pick a track. Both stream the same request through the gateway and show the text as it arrives, the events, and
the usage.

<!-- track: cli | curl and PowerShell -->

### Watch the raw events

curl buffers its output by default; `-N` turns that off, so each event prints the moment it arrives. PowerShell's
`Invoke-RestMethod` and `Invoke-WebRequest` wait for the whole body, so the PowerShell script reads the stream
with `HttpClient`.

```bash title="Bash"
# Ask for a streamed reply: -N turns off curl's buffering, so that each event prints the moment it arrives
echo "🤖 Raw server-sent events from the $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL alias:"
curl -sSN "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"stream\":true,\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Say hello in five words.\"}]}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Ask for a streamed reply: with -Raw, the script prints every server-sent event line the moment it arrives
Write-Host "🤖 Raw server-sent events from the $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL alias:"
./infra/stream-chat.ps1 -Raw -Prompt "Say hello in five words."
```

Expected output (shortened; your text and IDs differ):

```text
🤖 Raw server-sent events from the gpt-6-luna alias:
data: {"choices":[],"created":0,"id":"","model":"","object":"","prompt_filter_results":[{"prompt_index":0,"content_filter_results":{…}}]}

data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"","refusal":null,"role":"assistant"},"finish_reason":null,"index":0,…}],"model":"gpt-6-luna-2026-09-22","object":"chat.completion.chunk",…,"usage":null}

data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"Hi"},"finish_reason":null,"index":0,…}],…,"usage":null}

data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":" there"},"finish_reason":null,"index":0,…}],…,"usage":null}

…

data: {"choices":[{"delta":{},"finish_reason":"stop","index":0,…}],…,"usage":null}

data: [DONE]
```

### Stream the Responses API

The Responses API names every event. List the event types in order, then read the usage from `response.completed`:

```bash title="Bash"
# Stream a Responses API reply into a file, so that you can count its events
curl -sSN "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/responses" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"stream\":true,\"input\":\"Say hello in five words.\"}" > events.txt &&
  echo "🤖 Stream received from the $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL alias"

# Count each run of the same event type, in order
echo "📊 Event types, in order:"
grep '^event:' events.txt | uniq -c

# Read the usage from the response.completed event, then delete the file
echo "📊 Usage from response.completed:"
sed -n 's/^data: {/{/p' events.txt | jq -c 'select(.type == "response.completed") | .response.usage'
rm events.txt
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Build a streamed Responses API request
$body = @{ model = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL; stream = $true; input = "Say hello in five words." } | ConvertTo-Json

# Send it: Invoke-WebRequest waits for the whole stream, which is fine here because you only count its events
$r = Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri "$($env:AI_GATEWAY_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/default/models/openai/v1/responses" `
  -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body
if ($?) { Write-Host "🤖 Stream received from the $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL alias" }

# Count each run of the same event type, in order, the way uniq -c does
Write-Host "📊 Event types, in order:"
$lines = $r.Content -split "`n"
$prev = $null; $n = 0
foreach ($e in $lines -match '^event:') { if ($e -eq $prev) { $n++ } else { if ($prev) { '{0,4} {1}' -f $n, $prev }; $prev = $e; $n = 1 } }
'{0,4} {1}' -f $n, $prev

# Read the usage from the response.completed event
Write-Host "📊 Usage from response.completed:"
($lines -match '^data: \{' | ForEach-Object { $_.Substring(6) | ConvertFrom-Json } |
  Where-Object type -eq 'response.completed').response.usage | ConvertTo-Json -Compress
```

Expected output (your counts differ):

```text
🤖 Stream received from the gpt-6-luna alias
📊 Event types, in order:
   1 event: response.created
   1 event: response.in_progress
   1 event: response.output_item.added
   1 event: response.output_item.done
   1 event: response.output_item.added
   1 event: response.content_part.added
   7 event: response.output_text.delta
   1 event: response.output_text.done
   1 event: response.content_part.done
   1 event: response.output_item.done
   1 event: response.completed
📊 Usage from response.completed:
{"input_tokens":12,"input_tokens_details":{"cache_write_tokens":0,"cached_tokens":0},"output_tokens":66,"output_tokens_details":{"reasoning_tokens":53},"total_tokens":78}
```

The first `output_item` pair is the model's reasoning item; the second is the message that carries the text. The
`reasoning_tokens` count shows why the first token can take a moment with a reasoning model.

### Stream from code

Pass `stream=True` and iterate over the chunks. Skip chunks without `choices`, and keep the usage from the chunk that
has it.

```python title="Python"
stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=model,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain in two sentences why streaming makes chat apps feel faster."}],
    stream=True,
    stream_options={"include_usage": True},
)
usage = None
for chunk in stream:
    if chunk.usage:
        usage = chunk.usage
    if not chunk.choices:  # the prompt filter chunk and the usage chunk
        continue
    print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", end="", flush=True)
print(f"\nTokens used: {usage.total_tokens if usage else 'no usage chunk'}")
```

```typescript title="TypeScript"
const stream = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model,
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Explain in two sentences why streaming makes chat apps feel faster." }],
  stream: true,
  stream_options: { include_usage: true },
});
let usage: OpenAI.CompletionUsage | undefined;
for await (const chunk of stream) {
  if (chunk.usage) usage = chunk.usage;
  // choices[0] is undefined on the prompt filter chunk and the usage chunk.
  process.stdout.write(chunk.choices[0]?.delta?.content ?? "");
}
console.log(`\nTokens used: ${usage?.total_tokens ?? "no usage chunk"}`);
```

The Responses API streams typed events. Print `response.output_text.delta` events and read the usage from
`response.completed`:

```python title="Python"
for event in client.responses.create(model=model, input="Write a one-sentence status update.", stream=True):
    if event.type == "response.output_text.delta":
        print(event.delta, end="", flush=True)
    elif event.type == "response.completed":
        print(f"\nTokens used: {event.response.usage.total_tokens}")
```

```typescript title="TypeScript"
const events = await client.responses.create({ model, input: "Write a one-sentence status update.", stream: true });
for await (const event of events) {
  if (event.type === "response.output_text.delta") process.stdout.write(event.delta);
  else if (event.type === "response.completed") console.log(`\nTokens used: ${event.response.usage?.total_tokens}`);
}
```

The full samples create the client, time the first token, and print both streams: open [stream.py](infra/stream.py)
and [stream.ts](infra/stream.ts).

## Put a token limit on a streaming alias

To find out whether the gateway counts streamed tokens, give a new alias, `<model-name>-stream`, a deliberately low
limit: **1,000 tokens per minute for each caller identity**. It targets the same backend model as your alias from
lab 02, so clients that call that alias aren't affected.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Create the alias

1. Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway in the top bar.
2. Select **Models** › **Aliases** › **Add alias**.
3. On **Basics**, set **Alias name** to `<model-name>-stream`, for example `gpt-6-luna-stream`. Select **Next**.
4. On **Select models**, select your model in **Available backend models**. Select **Next**.
5. Keep the defaults on **Priority and weights**, select **Next**, then select **Create** on **Review**.

### Add the token limit

1. Select **Policies** › **Add policy**. On the **Type** step, under **Cost & Rate Limits**, select
   **Token rate limit**, then **Next**.
2. On the **Scope** step, select **Individual assets**, select the `<model-name>-stream` alias, then **Next**.
3. On the **Details** step, set **Time period** to **Per minute**, **Allowed tokens** to `1000`, and
   **Counter dimensions** to **Caller identity**. Select **Create**.

![The Add policy wizard on the Type step](../assets/screens/policy-add-wizard.png "Policies › Add policy opens a three-step wizard: Type, Scope, Configure.")

> **Checkpoint**
> **Models** › **Aliases** lists `<model-name>-stream`, and **Policies** lists a **Token rate limit** of 1,000
> tokens per minute scoped to it.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Create the alias with its token limit

An alias carries its own `policies` array, so one command creates the alias and its limit together.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create the streaming alias for the same backend model, with its own token limit of 1,000 tokens per minute
# for each caller identity, and show the alias and its policies
echo "🏷️ Alias $STREAM_ALIAS and its policies:"
az aigateway model-alias create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$STREAM_ALIAS" \
  --description "Streaming lab: 1,000 tokens per minute for each caller" \
  --backend-model resource-id="$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL" \
  --policies '[{"type": "tokenLimit", "count": 1000, "period": "minute", "counterKey": ["identity"]}]' \
  --only-show-errors --query "{alias:name, policies:properties.policies}" -o json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Write the token limit of 1,000 tokens per minute for each caller identity to a file, so that PowerShell
# passes the JSON to az unchanged
ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress -InputObject @(
  @{ type = "tokenLimit"; count = 1000; period = "minute"; counterKey = @("identity") }
) | Set-Content policies.json

# Create the streaming alias for the same backend model, with that limit, and show the alias and its policies
Write-Host "🏷️ Alias $STREAM_ALIAS and its policies:"
az aigateway model-alias create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $STREAM_ALIAS `
  --description "Streaming lab: 1,000 tokens per minute for each caller" `
  --backend-model resource-id="$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL" `
  --policies "@policies.json" `
  --only-show-errors --query "{alias:name, policies:properties.policies}" -o json
Remove-Item policies.json
```

If the alias already exists, `create` fails. Change it with `az aigateway model-alias update` and the same
arguments instead.

> **Checkpoint**
> The output shows your alias and one policy with `"type": "tokenLimit"`, `"count": 1000`, `"period": "minute"`,
> `"counterKey": ["identity"]`, and `"scope": "resource"`.

## Verify

Send bursts of streamed requests that each use about 220 tokens: first without asking for usage, then with it. If the
gateway only counted the tokens that clients report, the first burst would never be throttled.

<!-- steps -->

### Stream a burst without asking for usage

For each request, the script prints the status, `Retry-After`, the number of events, and the usage chunk, if any.

```bash title="Bash"
# Send 8 streamed requests to the streaming alias, without asking for usage
echo "🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests after about 1,000 tokens, with no usage chunks:"
./infra/stream-burst.sh "$STREAM_ALIAS" 8
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Send 8 streamed requests to the streaming alias, without asking for usage
Write-Host "🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests after about 1,000 tokens, with no usage chunks:"
./infra/stream-burst.ps1 -Model $STREAM_ALIAS -Requests 8
```

On GitHub, open [stream-burst.sh](infra/stream-burst.sh) or [stream-burst.ps1](infra/stream-burst.ps1).

Expected output (your counts differ):

```text
🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests after about 1,000 tokens, with no usage chunks:
Request  Status  Retry-After  Events  Usage chunk
1        200     -            209     none
2        200     -            187     none
3        200     -            207     none
4        200     -            200     none
5        200     -            196     none
6        200     -            191     none
7        429     2            -       Token limit is exceeded. Try again in 2 seconds.
8        429     1            -       Token limit is exceeded. Try again in 1 seconds.
```

No stream carried a usage chunk, yet the gateway throttled request 7, after about 1,300 tokens. If it had
counted only the prompts, about 25 tokens each, the alias would have allowed roughly 40 requests.

> [!NOTE]
> A new alias or policy can take up to a minute to apply, and the counters catch up within a few seconds, so a fast
> burst can go a few hundred tokens past the limit. If every request returns `200`, wait a minute and run it again.

### Stream a burst with usage

Wait a minute for the window to reset, then run the same burst with `include_usage`:

```bash title="Bash"
# Wait a minute, so that the token limit's window resets
echo "⏳ Waiting 60 seconds for the token limit's window to reset"
sleep 60

# Send the same burst with stream_options.include_usage, so that each stream ends with a usage chunk
echo "🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests at the same point, now with usage chunks:"
./infra/stream-burst.sh --usage "$STREAM_ALIAS" 8
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Wait a minute, so that the token limit's window resets
Write-Host "⏳ Waiting 60 seconds for the token limit's window to reset"
Start-Sleep 60

# Send the same burst with stream_options.include_usage, so that each stream ends with a usage chunk
Write-Host "🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests at the same point, now with usage chunks:"
./infra/stream-burst.ps1 -Model $STREAM_ALIAS -Requests 8 -Usage
```

Expected output:

```text
⏳ Waiting 60 seconds for the token limit's window to reset
🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests at the same point, now with usage chunks:
Request  Status  Retry-After  Events  Usage chunk
1        200     -            196     218 tokens
2        200     -            186     208 tokens
3        200     -            196     218 tokens
4        200     -            191     213 tokens
5        200     -            211     233 tokens
6        200     -            191     213 tokens
7        429     1            -       Token limit is exceeded. Try again in 1 seconds.
8        200     -            193     215 tokens
```

The throttle point is the same: the gateway counted the streams the same way whether or not the client asked for
usage. Request 8 succeeds again because it was sent after the `Retry-After` wait.

### Inspect a throttled streaming request

Run the burst once more and, while the alias is throttled, look at a full response:

```bash
# Send one streamed request while the alias is throttled: -i prints the status line and the headers too
echo "🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests while the limit is active, as plain JSON:"
curl -sS -i "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$STREAM_ALIAS\",\"stream\":true,\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"ping\"}]}"
```

Expected output, when the limit is active:

```text
🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests while the limit is active, as plain JSON:
HTTP/2 429
content-type: application/json
retry-after: 3
content-length: 84

{ "statusCode": 429, "message": "Token limit is exceeded. Try again in 3 seconds." }
```

The throttled answer is plain JSON, not an event stream, because the gateway refused the request before it reached
the model. Check the status code before you start reading events, and honor `Retry-After`.

### Find the streamed calls in Monitoring

If you configured Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), open
**Monitoring**. The streamed requests show their token counts next to the non-streamed ones, and the throttled
requests appear as `429` outcomes.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> Both bursts were throttled at the same request, the burst without `include_usage` included, and the throttled
> request returned a JSON `429` with `Retry-After` instead of a stream.

## Go further

- **Cap spend for streams.** A cost limit is estimated from the same usage record, so streamed calls count against
  budgets too. Try it in [Enforce cost budgets](../07-cost-budgets/README.md).
- **Shorten the time to the first token.** Reasoning models think before they write. For chat that needs a quick
  first word, set `reasoning_effort` to `low` or `none` where the model supports it, as the scripts in this lab do.
- **Stream from an agent.** Agent frameworks stream through the same endpoint. See
  [Connect agent frameworks to models and tools](../15-agent-frameworks/README.md).
- **Check your proxies.** Anything between the client and the gateway, such as a reverse proxy or an API layer of your
  own, must pass `text/event-stream` responses through without buffering.

## Clean up

Delete the streaming alias. Its token limit goes with it, and the backend model and your alias from lab 02 stay.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

# Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint

Your agent teams want tools: documentation search, ticketing, internal APIs. If every agent connects to every
tool server directly, you end up with credentials in many places and no single point of control. In this lab
the platform team publishes **one governed MCP endpoint** on the gateway, starting with the public Microsoft
Learn MCP server, so agents get tools through the same front door they already use for models.

![One MCP endpoint on the gateway federates tools from several backends](../assets/diagrams/mcp-federation.svg "Clients connect to one MCP endpoint. The gateway authenticates them, applies policies, and federates the namespaced tools of every backend.")

## Before you begin

  one yet, create it in the portal under **Access** › **Keys**, or, after

  `az aigateway api-key create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n app-first-call --display-name app-first-call`

## How it works

An **MCP server** in AI Gateway is a federation point. You give it one or more **backends**, and the gateway
publishes all their tools at one Streamable HTTP endpoint:
`https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/toolservers/<server-name>/mcp`.

| Backend type | What you provide | What clients see |
|---|---|---|
| **MCP server** (remote) | A URL that speaks SSE or Streamable HTTP | The server's tools |
| **OpenAPI spec** | A JSON or YAML OpenAPI document (upload, URL, or inline) | Selected operations as tools. The operation summary or description becomes the tool description. |
| **Built-in connector** | A managed connection to a SaaS app, such as Microsoft 365, SharePoint, GitHub, or Salesforce | The connector's operations as tools |
| **Foundry Toolbox** | A Microsoft Foundry Toolbox source | The toolbox's tools |

Each backend can have a **namespace**. The gateway prefixes that backend's tools with it, as in
`learn_microsoft_docs_search`, so two backends can expose tools with the same name without conflict.

The gateway authenticates **clients**. In this lab they send a runtime key in the `api-key` header.
It authenticates to each **backend** separately, with **None**, **API key** (a header name and value),
**OAuth 2.0**, or **Managed identity**. Backend credentials are stored securely, are never exposed to clients,
and appear under **Connections**.

> [!NOTE]
> Registering a backend doesn't mean that AI Gateway translates every backend protocol into MCP. Pick the
> backend type that matches what the backend actually serves.

## Register the Learn MCP server

Pick one track. Each track creates the same MCP server: **`learn`**, with one backend, the public Microsoft
Learn MCP server at `https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp`, under the namespace `learn`. That server needs no
credentials, so the backend authentication is **None**.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Start the workflow

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **MCP servers** › **Add MCP server**. The full-page **Create MCP server** workflow has three steps:
**Basic info**, **Backends**, and **Tools**.

### Describe the server

On **Basic info**, set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Name** | `learn` (part of the endpoint URL; it can't be changed after creation) |
| **Display name** | `Microsoft Learn` |
| **Description** | `Search and fetch official Microsoft documentation and code samples.` |

Agents and people read the description to decide when to use the server, so keep it specific. Select **Next**.

### Add the Learn backend

On **Backends**, select **Add backend**. In **Choose a backend type**, select **MCP server**, then set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **URL** | `https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp` |
| **Namespace** | `learn` |
| **Authentication** | **None** |

The backend appears in the table with its **URL**, **Type**, **Authentication**, **Namespace**, and
**Required** columns. Leave **Required** on. Select **Next**.

### Publish all tools

On **Tools**, under **Tool availability**, keep **Allow all tools** ("Expose every tool from these backends,
including tools added in the future."). You narrow this down in
[Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md). Select **Create**.

### Copy the endpoint

The server's details page opens. When **Provisioning** shows that the server is ready, copy the
**Endpoint URL**. It ends in `/default/toolservers/learn/mcp`.

> **Checkpoint**
> **MCP servers** lists `learn`, and its details page shows an **Endpoint URL** and one backend with the
> namespace `learn`.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Create the registration

`az aigateway mcp create` registers the MCP server. `--endpoints` takes the backends as a JSON array.

```bash title="Bash"
# Register the learn MCP server, with the public Learn MCP server as its one backend, under the namespace learn
az aigateway mcp create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n learn \
  --display-name "Microsoft Learn" \
  --description "Search and fetch official Microsoft documentation and code samples." \
  --endpoints '[{"kind": "mcp", "namespace": "learn", "required": true,
                 "mcp": {"transport": "streamableHttp", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp"}}]' \
  --query "{name:name,mcpEndpoint:properties.gatewayEndpoints[0].url}" &&
  echo "🔌 MCP server learn is ready"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Write the backends to a file, so that PowerShell passes the JSON to az unchanged
ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress -InputObject @(
  @{ kind = 'mcp'; namespace = 'learn'; required = $true
     mcp  = @{ transport = 'streamableHttp'; url = 'https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp' } }
) | Set-Content -Path endpoints.json

# Register the learn MCP server, with the public Learn MCP server as its one backend, under the namespace learn
az aigateway mcp create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n learn `
  --display-name "Microsoft Learn" `
  --description "Search and fetch official Microsoft documentation and code samples." `
  --endpoints "@endpoints.json" `
  --query "{name:name,mcpEndpoint:properties.gatewayEndpoints[0].url}"
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔌 MCP server learn is ready" }
Remove-Item endpoints.json
```

`-n learn` is the MCP server name. `mcp create` fails with `This MCP registration already exists; use mcp update.`
if the name is taken, so change an existing registration with `az aigateway mcp update` or the `mcp source`
commands, as in the next section.

### Confirm the registration

The commands are the same in Bash and PowerShell.

```bash
# List the MCP servers on your gateway
echo "🔌 MCP servers on your gateway:"
az aigateway mcp list -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -o table

# Show the backends and the endpoint URL of learn
echo "🔌 Backends and endpoint of learn:"
az aigateway mcp show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n learn --query "properties.{endpoints:endpoints,url:gatewayEndpoints[0].url}"
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The table shows `learn` with `Microsoft Learn` in the **DisplayName** column and `1` in the **Sources** column.
> The second command returns one endpoint with `"namespace": "learn"` and `"kind": "mcp"`, and a `url` that ends
> in `/default/toolservers/learn/mcp`.

`azd up` creates a new one, so it works on its own.

## Federate a second backend

Federation pays off when one endpoint combines several backends. To see it without extra credentials, add the
same public Learn server again under a second namespace, `docs`. Both backends expose a tool called
`microsoft_docs_search`, and the namespaces keep them apart. Mark the new backend as **not required**: if an
optional backend is unavailable, the gateway skips it instead of failing the whole MCP server.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Add the backend

On the `learn` details page, select **Edit**, then go to **Backends**. Select **Add backend** › **MCP server**
and set **URL** to `https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp`, **Namespace** to `docs`, and **Authentication** to
**None**. In the backends table, turn **Required** off for the new row. Select **Save**.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Add the source

`az aigateway mcp source add` appends one backend and changes only the list of backends. Other settings, such as
the description and policies, stay as they are.

```bash title="Bash"
# Add the Learn MCP server again as an optional backend, under the namespace docs, and list the backends
az aigateway mcp source add -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n learn \
  --namespace docs --kind mcp --required false \
  --mcp '{"transport": "streamableHttp", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp"}' \
  --query "[].{namespace:namespace,required:required,url:mcp.url}" -o table &&
  echo "🔌 Backend docs is added to learn, as optional"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Write the backend's settings to a file, so that PowerShell passes the JSON to az unchanged
@{ transport = 'streamableHttp'; url = 'https://learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp' } |
  ConvertTo-Json -Compress | Set-Content -Path mcp.json

# Add the Learn MCP server again as an optional backend, under the namespace docs, and list the backends
az aigateway mcp source add -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n learn `
  --namespace docs --kind mcp --required false --mcp "@mcp.json" `
  --query "[].{namespace:namespace,required:required,url:mcp.url}" -o table
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔌 Backend docs is added to learn, as optional" }
Remove-Item mcp.json
```

The table lists every backend of the server. The command fails with "A source with namespace 'docs' already
exists on this MCP server registration." if you run it twice. For a backend that needs a key, pass the key with
`--credentials`.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Add the second namespace

When `secondNamespace` isn't empty, the template adds a second endpoint with `required: false`. Set it in the azd
environment and provision again. Only the MCP server changes.

```bash title="Bash"
# Add the second namespace in the azd environment
azd env set MCP_SECOND_NAMESPACE docs &&
  echo "📝 MCP_SECOND_NAMESPACE is docs"

# Deploy the template again: it adds the optional docs backend to the learn MCP server
azd provision &&
  echo "🔌 MCP server learn now has the optional docs backend"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Add the second namespace in the azd environment
azd env set MCP_SECOND_NAMESPACE docs
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 MCP_SECOND_NAMESPACE is docs" }

# Deploy the template again: it adds the optional docs backend to the learn MCP server
azd provision
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔌 MCP server learn now has the optional docs backend" }
```

<!-- /tracks -->

> [!TIP]
> In production, the second backend is a different service. For an internal REST API, choose **OpenAPI spec**
> and point **Spec source** › **Fetch from URL** at its OpenAPI document. For an API that needs a key, set
> **Authentication** to **API key** with the **Header name** and **Key value** the backend expects. Clients
> never see that key.

> **Checkpoint**
> The `learn` server has two backends: `learn` (required) and `docs` (optional).

## Choose supported MCP versions

MCP is versioned by date. A client opens a connection by naming the protocol version it speaks, and the server
answers with the version both sides will use. AI Gateway negotiates one version for the whole MCP server, so
that version must work with **every backend** behind it.

| Supported MCP versions | What clients get |
|---|---|
| Not configured | The legacy defaults: `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`, and `2024-11-05`. The portal labels them **Legacy defaults**. |
| A list that you choose | Version restrictions. Clients negotiate only a version in the list, and a request whose `MCP-Protocol-Version` header names any other version is rejected with `400`. |

You can choose `2026-07-28`, `2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`, and `2024-11-05`. Version
`2026-07-28` is the stateless revision of the specification: it replaces the `initialize` handshake and
sessions with a `server/discover` request, and every request carries `MCP-Protocol-Version`, `Mcp-Method`, and
`Mcp-Name` headers plus metadata in `params._meta`. Select it only when every backend supports it, and use an
MCP SDK that implements it rather than hand-written requests.

In this lab, pin the server to `2025-06-18`. At the time of writing, that's the version the Microsoft Learn MCP
server negotiates, so both backends, `learn` and `docs`, support it.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Pin the version

1. On the `learn` details page, find **Supported MCP versions**. Unless you changed it, it lists the legacy
   defaults.
2. Select **Edit**. On **Basic info**, open **Supported MCP versions** and keep only `2025-06-18` selected.
3. Go to **Backends**. Because the list changed, the portal asks you to recheck the backends: "Supported MCP
   versions changed. Edit and save each external MCP backend before saving this server." For each backend row,
   select **Edit**, then **Save** in **Edit MCP backend**. The portal checks which versions the backend
   supports before it saves the row.
4. Select **Save**.

If a backend doesn't support a selected version, **Edit MCP backend** shows "Backend isn't compatible with all
configured MCP versions." and lists the versions the backend reports. Return to **Basic info** and change the
list, or update the backend.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Set the versions

The `aigateway` extension doesn't set MCP protocol versions yet, so call the Azure Resource Manager REST API with
`az rest`. A `PATCH` that sends only `properties.versions` keeps the backends, tool rules, and policies as they are.

```bash title="Bash"
# Pin learn to MCP version 2025-06-18 with a PATCH that changes only properties.versions
az rest --method patch --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" \
  --body '{"properties": {"versions": ["2025-06-18"]}}' --query properties.versions &&
  echo "📝 MCP server learn supports only MCP version 2025-06-18"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Write the request body to a file, so that PowerShell passes the JSON to az unchanged
@{ properties = @{ versions = @('2025-06-18') } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5 -Compress | Set-Content -Path body.json

# Pin learn to MCP version 2025-06-18 with a PATCH that changes only properties.versions
az rest --method patch --url "$WS/toolServers/learn?$API" --body '@body.json' --query properties.versions
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 MCP server learn supports only MCP version 2025-06-18" }
Remove-Item body.json
```

Unlike the portal, the API doesn't ask the backends which versions they support. If you list a version that a
backend can't speak, the `PATCH` succeeds and clients that negotiate that version fail. See
[Troubleshooting](../TROUBLESHOOTING.md#lab-04-federate-mcp-tools).

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Pin the versions

The `supportedVersions` parameter takes a comma-separated list, such as `2025-06-18` or `2026-07-28,2025-06-18`,
and azd fills it from `MCP_SUPPORTED_VERSIONS`. Set it and provision again. The azd environment keeps
`MCP_SECOND_NAMESPACE`, so both backends stay.

```bash title="Bash"
# Pin learn to MCP version 2025-06-18 in the azd environment
azd env set MCP_SUPPORTED_VERSIONS 2025-06-18 &&
  echo "📝 MCP_SUPPORTED_VERSIONS is 2025-06-18"

# Deploy the template again: it sets the supported versions of the learn MCP server
azd provision &&
  echo "🚀 MCP server learn is deployed with MCP version 2025-06-18"

# Show the versions that learn supports now
echo "📝 Supported MCP versions of learn:"
az aigateway mcp show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n learn --query properties.versions
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Pin learn to MCP version 2025-06-18 in the azd environment
azd env set MCP_SUPPORTED_VERSIONS 2025-06-18
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 MCP_SUPPORTED_VERSIONS is 2025-06-18" }

# Deploy the template again: it sets the supported versions of the learn MCP server
azd provision
if ($?) { Write-Host "🚀 MCP server learn is deployed with MCP version 2025-06-18" }

# Show the versions that learn supports now
Write-Host "📝 Supported MCP versions of learn:"
az aigateway mcp show -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n learn --query properties.versions
```

The last command prints a list that holds only `2025-06-18`. An empty value doesn't clear a list that the server already has, so
to change the versions later, set another list.

<!-- /tracks -->

### Check the negotiated version

Ask for an older version. The gateway answers with the version it will use:

```bash title="Bash"
# Send an initialize request that asks for 2025-03-26, with your runtime key in api-key
echo "🔌 initialize response from learn:"
curl -sS "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/toolservers/learn/mcp" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-03-26",
       "capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1.0"}}}'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Build an initialize request that asks for 2025-03-26, with your runtime key in api-key
$mcp     = "$($env:AI_GATEWAY_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/default/toolservers/learn/mcp"
$headers = @{ 'api-key' = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY; Accept = 'application/json, text/event-stream' }
$body    = '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-03-26",
             "capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"pwsh","version":"1.0"}}}'

# Send it, and print the response, with the version that the gateway chose
Write-Host "🔌 initialize response from learn:"
(Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri $mcp -Headers $headers -ContentType 'application/json' -Body $body).Content
```

The result includes `"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18"`. Now send a request that names a version outside the list:

```bash title="Bash"
# Send tools/list with MCP version 2026-07-28, which isn't in the list
echo "🚦 Expect 400 Bad Request for MCP version 2026-07-28:"
curl -sS -w "\n🚦 HTTP %{http_code}\n" "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/toolservers/learn/mcp" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" -H "MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Send tools/list with MCP version 2026-07-28, which isn't in the list
Write-Host "🚦 Expect 400 Bad Request for MCP version 2026-07-28:"
$r = Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri $mcp -SkipHttpErrorCheck -ContentType 'application/json' `
  -Headers ($headers + @{ 'MCP-Protocol-Version' = '2026-07-28' }) -Body '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
if ($?) { Write-Host "🚦 HTTP $($r.StatusCode) $($r.Content)" }
```

The gateway rejects it with `🚦 HTTP 400` and `Unsupported MCP-Protocol-Version` before any backend is called.

> **Checkpoint**
> **Supported MCP versions** shows `2025-06-18` on the details page and in **Catalog**, an `initialize` request
> for `2025-03-26` returns `2025-06-18`, and a `2026-07-28` request is rejected with `400`.

## Connect a client

Any MCP-compatible client or agent framework can use the endpoint. Store the runtime key in the client's
secret store, never in a file that you commit.

deep link) and **mcp.json** (raw configuration for any MCP-aware client). Replace any key placeholder with your
runtime key in the client's secret prompt, not in a committed file.

## Verify

<!-- steps -->

### List the published tools

MCP clients start with a handshake: `initialize`, then `notifications/initialized`, then `tools/list`. The
script runs that handshake through your gateway, reads JSON or server-sent event (SSE) responses, and prints
every published tool. Run it from the lab folder.

```bash title="Bash"
# Run the MCP handshake through your gateway, and list every tool that learn publishes
echo "🛠️ Tools on learn:"
./infra/list-tools.sh learn
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Run the MCP handshake through your gateway, and list every tool that learn publishes
Write-Host "🛠️ Tools on learn:"
./infra/list-tools.ps1 -Server learn
```

On GitHub, open [list-tools.sh](infra/list-tools.sh) or [list-tools.ps1](infra/list-tools.ps1).

Expected output (descriptions are shortened, and the tool list can change as the Learn server evolves):

```text
🛠️ Tools on learn:
MCP endpoint: https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/toolservers/learn/mcp
Server: <server-name-reported-by-the-gateway>  protocol: <negotiated-version>

Tool                                          Description
learn_microsoft_docs_search                   Search official Microsoft/Azure documentation to find the most relevan
learn_microsoft_code_sample_search            Search for code snippets and examples in official Microsoft Learn docu
learn_microsoft_docs_fetch                    Fetch and convert a Microsoft Learn documentation webpage to markdown
docs_microsoft_docs_search                    Search official Microsoft/Azure documentation to find the most relevan
docs_microsoft_code_sample_search             Search for code snippets and examples in official Microsoft Learn docu
docs_microsoft_docs_fetch                     Fetch and convert a Microsoft Learn documentation webpage to markdown

6 tools published
```

Each tool carries its backend's namespace. Use the exact names that your output shows in the next steps.

### Call a tool through the gateway

```bash title="Bash"
# List the tools again, then call learn_microsoft_docs_search with a question
echo "🛠️ Tools on learn, and a call to learn_microsoft_docs_search:"
./infra/list-tools.sh learn learn_microsoft_docs_search "How do I add a token limit in AI Gateway?"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# List the tools again, then call learn_microsoft_docs_search with a question
Write-Host "🛠️ Tools on learn, and a call to learn_microsoft_docs_search:"
./infra/list-tools.ps1 -Server learn -Tool learn_microsoft_docs_search -Query "How do I add a token limit in AI Gateway?"
```

After the tool list, the script prints the start of the search results that Microsoft Learn returned through
your gateway.

### Send a raw JSON-RPC request

The docs show the smallest possible request: a single JSON-RPC `tools/list` call. Streamable HTTP clients
should also accept both JSON and SSE responses.

```bash
# Send a single tools/list request, with your runtime key in api-key
echo "🛠️ tools/list response from learn:"
curl -sS "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/toolservers/learn/mcp" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
```

The answer is JSON or an SSE `data:` line with a `result.tools` array. If the server answers with a JSON-RPC
`error` instead, it requires the full handshake. Use the script, which runs it for you.

### Prove that the gateway checks the caller

Send the same request without the key:

```bash
# Send the same request without the api-key header
echo "🚦 Expect 401 Unauthorized without a key:"
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "🚦 HTTP %{http_code}\n" "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/toolservers/learn/mcp" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
```

The gateway rejects the request, typically with `🚦 HTTP 401`, and no backend is called. Microsoft Learn is public,
but your MCP endpoint isn't.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The script lists namespaced tools from both backends, a tool call returns Microsoft Learn content, and a
> request without a key is rejected.

## Go further

- **Control the catalog.** Publish only approved tools, block risky ones, and rate-limit the server in
  [Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md).
- **Screen tool traffic.** Content safety also screens tool inputs and responses on MCP servers. See
  [Screen prompts and responses with content safety](../08-content-safety/README.md).
- **Go keyless.** Grant callers the **AI Gateway User** role and send a Microsoft Entra token instead of a
  runtime key. See [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md).
- **Watch tool traffic.** When Application Insights is configured, tool executions appear in **Monitoring** ›
  **Tools**. See [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md).
- **Onboard GitHub.** Add the GitHub MCP server, `https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/`, as an **MCP server**
  backend with **API key** authentication: **Header name** `Authorization` and **Key value**
  `Bearer <your-github-token>`. The gateway stores the token, and clients never see it.
- **Give tools to an agent.** Point an agent framework at the endpoint in [Connect agent frameworks to models and tools](../15-agent-frameworks/README.md).

## Clean up

MCP servers don't add charges beyond the gateway itself. Keep `learn` if you continue with
[Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md), which builds on it.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Remove the second backend or the server

To remove only the `docs` backend, select **Edit** on the `learn` details page, delete its row on **Backends**,
and select **Save**. To remove the whole server, select **Delete** on the details page.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Remove the second source or the server

```bash title="Bash"
# Remove only the optional backend
az aigateway mcp source remove -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n learn --namespace docs --query "[].namespace" &&
  echo "🧹 Backend docs is removed from learn"

# Or remove the whole MCP server
az aigateway mcp delete -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n learn --yes &&
  echo "🧹 MCP server learn is deleted"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Remove only the optional backend
az aigateway mcp source remove -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n learn --namespace docs --query "[].namespace"
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 Backend docs is removed from learn" }

# Or remove the whole MCP server
az aigateway mcp delete -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n learn --yes
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 MCP server learn is deleted" }
```

`mcp source remove` prints the backends that remain. An MCP server needs at least one backend, so the command
refuses to remove the last one with "Cannot remove the last source." Delete the server instead.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Delete everything azd created

In the `ai-gateway/labs/04-federate-mcp-tools` folder, delete the resource group with the gateway, the `learn` MCP
server, and the key. [`--purge`](../SETUP.md#delete-what-azd-created) also purges soft-deleted resources. It takes
about ten minutes.

```bash
# Delete the resource group with everything that azd up created, and purge soft-deleted resources
azd down --purge --force &&
  echo "🧹 Everything that azd up created is deleted"
```

To keep this gateway instead, skip `azd down`. To go back to one backend, run
`azd env set MCP_SECOND_NAMESPACE ""`, then `azd provision`.

<!-- track: code | Code -->

### Remove the client configuration

Delete the `ai-gateway-learn` entry from `.vscode/mcp.json` and the `.venv` folder you created.

<!-- /tracks -->

Keep your gateway from lab 01: the next labs reuse it. `azd down` doesn't touch it, because the Bicep + azd track
created its own gateway.

# Control which tools agents can call

The `learn` MCP server that you federated now publishes every tool from two backends. Your security team has
two requests: agents should **search** documentation but not fetch arbitrary pages, and the code sample tool
stays off until its review is done. Operations adds a third: a looping agent must not flood the backends. In
this lab you publish only the approved tools, block one explicitly, and give each caller a request budget.

![Tool controls on the MCP server decide which federated tools agents can list and call](../assets/diagrams/mcp-federation.svg "The gateway applies tool availability, blocked tools, and policies on the MCP server before it calls any backend.")

<!-- widget: tool-patterns {"tools":["learn_microsoft_docs_search","learn_microsoft_code_sample_search","learn_microsoft_docs_fetch","docs_microsoft_docs_search","docs_microsoft_code_sample_search","docs_microsoft_docs_fetch"],"allow":["*_search"],"block":["*code_sample*"]} -->

## Before you begin

<!-- setup: tools sign-in extension clone -->

> [!TIP]
> On the **Bicep + azd** track, `azd up` creates its own gateway, the `learn` MCP server with its tool controls and
> request rate limit, and a key, so you can skip this section. You need only the one-time setup above.

- Complete [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md). You need the `learn`
  MCP server with its `learn` and `docs` backends, and a runtime API key from **Access** › **Keys**.
- Permission to change the gateway, for example **Contributor** on the resource group.
- Run the scripts and samples from the lab's folder, `~/ai-gateway/labs/05-mcp-tool-controls`.

Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
# Name the resource group and the gateway that hold the learn MCP server from lab 04
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"
echo "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY in $RG"

# Read the gateway's runtime URL, which every MCP endpoint starts with

echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"

# Paste the runtime key that you created in Access › Keys, without showing it

Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

## How it works

An MCP server has three layers of tool control. The gateway applies all of them before it calls a backend.

| Control | Where | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Tool availability** | The server's **Tools** step | **Allow all tools** publishes every tool, including tools that backends add later. **Select exact tools** (a static list) or name patterns publish only matching tools. Tools that don't match aren't listed and can't be called. |
| **Blocked tools** | The server's **Tools** step | Names or patterns that the gateway refuses to run. Blocked patterns take precedence over the allow list. Blocked tools remain visible to clients, but the gateway blocks their execution. |
| **MCP server access** | The server's **Basic info** step, in edit mode | **Active** or **Blocked**. Blocked MCP servers can't be reached by clients, whatever their tool rules say. |
| **Request rate limit** policy | **Policies** | A number of **Calls** per **Renewal period** for each counter. Over the limit, the gateway answers `429` with `Retry-After`. |

Patterns use `*` for any number of characters and `?` for exactly one. This lab uses `*_search` to allow
both search tools and `*code_sample*` to block the code sample tool. Both patterns match whether or not you
include the namespace prefix, such as `learn_`, so they cover every backend of the server.

> [!NOTE]
> The `aigateway` extension doesn't set tool availability, blocked tools, or server access yet, so the Azure CLI
> track covers only the request rate limit. Configure the rest in the portal, or declare them with the
> **Bicep + azd** track: they're the MCP server's `allowList`, `blocked`, and `accessState` properties.

## Publish only approved tools

Pick one track. Both publish the same catalog on the `learn` server: the tools that match `*_search`, with
`*code_sample*` blocked. Make sure the patterns cover every tool that your agents legitimately need before you
save. Tools that don't match are no longer listed or callable.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Open the Tools step

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway. Select **MCP servers**,
open `learn`, select **Edit**, and go to the **Tools** step.

### Allow the search tools by pattern

Under **Tool availability**, select **Match tools by name pattern**. Depending on your portal version, the
option is labeled **Use name patterns**, and **Select exact tools** is also offered. In
**Allowed tool name patterns**, enter `*_search`. If your portal shows **Add pattern**, use it to add each
pattern on its own row.

### Block the code sample tool

Under **Blocked tools**, select **Add blocked tool** (or **Add**). In **Tool name or pattern**, enter
`*code_sample*` and select **Add**. The pattern appears under **Blocked tools**, with a note on whether it
matches tools in the discovered catalog.

![The Tools step with an allowed tool name pattern and a blocked pattern](../assets/screens/mcp-tool-controls.png "Edit MCP server › Tools: allowed name patterns publish matching tools, and blocked patterns stop matching tools from running. This example uses a pet store backend.")

### Save the server

Select **Save**.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

**What you need:** only the one-time setup from **Before you begin**. This track doesn't use your gateway or `learn`
server from lab 04: `azd up` creates a new gateway with its own `learn` server, so it works on its own.

### Review the templates

`infra/main.bicep` creates the resource group `rg-<environment name>` and calls lab 01's
[gateway.bicep](../01-provision-gateway/infra/gateway.bicep) for a gateway with no model. Then it calls
`infra/controlled-tool-server.bicep` with the tool controls, which azd fills from environment values:

| Parameter | azd environment value | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `allowedTools` | `MCP_ALLOWED_TOOLS` | `["*_search"]` |
| `blockedTools` | `MCP_BLOCKED_TOOLS` | `["*code_sample*"]` |
| `serverAccess` | `MCP_SERVER_ACCESS` | `active` |
| `callsPerPeriod` | `REQUEST_RATE_LIMIT` | `5` |
| `periodSeconds` | `REQUEST_RATE_LIMIT_PERIOD` | `30` |
| `counterKey` | `REQUEST_RATE_LIMIT_COUNTER_KEY` | `["identity"]` |

<!-- include: infra/main.bicep -->

`infra/controlled-tool-server.bicep` declares the `learn` server of lab 04, with its `learn` and `docs` backends,
plus the tool controls: `allowList` is **Tool availability** (`["*"]` is **Allow all tools**), `blocked` is
**Blocked tools**, and `accessState` is **MCP server access**. Its `policies` array holds the request rate limit
of [Rate-limit the MCP server](#rate-limit-the-mcp-server). It also creates the `app-first-call` key.

<!-- include: infra/controlled-tool-server.bicep -->

> [!WARNING]
> A Bicep deployment sends a `PUT`, which replaces the whole MCP server, including backends, tool rules, and
> policies that you added in the portal. Keep the template as the only source of truth for this server, and change
> it with `azd provision`.

### Read the outputs and the key

Set the variables that the next sections and **Verify** use from azd's environment values, and read the key from
the gateway, so that it never shows on screen.

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the template's outputs: the resource group, the gateway, and its runtime URL
export RG="$(azd env get-value AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP)"
export GATEWAY="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_NAME)"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL)"
echo "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY in $RG"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Read the key from the gateway, so that it never lands in a file or a deployment log
export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets --ids "$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_ID)/apiKeys/app-first-call" \
  --query primaryKey --output tsv)"
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"

# Show the tools that the learn MCP server publishes and the tools it blocks
echo "🛠️ Tool controls on the learn MCP server:"
az aigateway mcp show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n learn --query "properties.{allowList:allowList,blocked:blocked}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the template's outputs: the resource group, the gateway, its runtime URL, and its resource ID
$RG                     = azd env get-value AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP
$GATEWAY                = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_NAME
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL     = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL
$GATEWAY_ID             = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_ID
Write-Host "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY in $RG"
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Read the key from the gateway, so that it never lands in a file or a deployment log
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az aigateway api-key list-secrets --ids "$GATEWAY_ID/apiKeys/app-first-call" `
  --query primaryKey --output tsv
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"

# Show the tools that the learn MCP server publishes and the tools it blocks
Write-Host "🛠️ Tool controls on the learn MCP server:"
az aigateway mcp show -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n learn --query "properties.{allowList:allowList,blocked:blocked}"
```

> **Checkpoint**
> `azd up` ended with `SUCCESS`, and the last command printed `"allowList": ["*_search"]` and
> `"blocked": ["*code_sample*"]`.

The server already has the request rate limit, 5 calls per 30 seconds for each key, so wait 30 seconds between
script runs.

## Take the whole server offline

Sometimes you need to stop all tool traffic at once, for example while you investigate a misbehaving backend.
Blocking the server keeps its backends, tool rules, and policies, so you can turn it back on in one step.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Block the server

On the `learn` details page, select **Edit**. On **Basic info**, set **MCP server access** to **Blocked**, then
select **Save**.

### Confirm that clients can't connect

```bash title="Bash"
# Try to connect to the blocked server: the MCP handshake fails before any backend is called
echo "🚦 Expect initialize to fail with AccessBlockedByGateway:"
./infra/list-tools.sh learn
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Try to connect to the blocked server: the MCP handshake fails before any backend is called
Write-Host "🚦 Expect initialize to fail with AccessBlockedByGateway:"
./infra/list-tools.ps1 -Server learn
```

The script stops at `initialize`. The gateway answers with HTTP `200` and a JSON-RPC error,
`Access to MCP server 'learn' is blocked.`, with the code `AccessBlockedByGateway`. No backend is called.

### Turn the server back on

Select **Edit** again, set **MCP server access** to **Active**, and select **Save**. Run the script again to
confirm that the four tools are back.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Block the server

Set `MCP_SERVER_ACCESS` to `blocked` and provision again. Only the MCP server changes.

```bash title="Bash"
# Set the server's access to blocked in the azd environment
azd env set MCP_SERVER_ACCESS blocked &&
  echo "📝 MCP_SERVER_ACCESS is blocked"

# Provision again, which updates only the MCP server
azd provision &&
  echo "🔌 The learn MCP server is blocked"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Set the server's access to blocked in the azd environment
azd env set MCP_SERVER_ACCESS blocked
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 MCP_SERVER_ACCESS is blocked" }

# Provision again, which updates only the MCP server
azd provision
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔌 The learn MCP server is blocked" }
```

### Confirm that clients can't connect

```bash title="Bash"
# Try to connect to the blocked server: the MCP handshake fails before any backend is called
echo "🚦 Expect initialize to fail with AccessBlockedByGateway:"
./infra/list-tools.sh learn
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Try to connect to the blocked server: the MCP handshake fails before any backend is called
Write-Host "🚦 Expect initialize to fail with AccessBlockedByGateway:"
./infra/list-tools.ps1 -Server learn
```

The script stops at `initialize`. The gateway answers with HTTP `200` and a JSON-RPC error,
`Access to MCP server 'learn' is blocked.`, with the code `AccessBlockedByGateway`. No backend is called.

### Turn the server back on

```bash title="Bash"

azd env set MCP_SERVER_ACCESS active &&
  echo "📝 MCP_SERVER_ACCESS is active"

```
