## Rate-limit the MCP server

A request rate limit counts calls instead of tokens. That suits tools, where one agent in a loop can send
hundreds of calls a minute. Pick one track. Each produces the same policy on the `learn` server: **5 calls per
30 seconds for each caller identity**. The limit is deliberately low so you can trigger it quickly.

<!-- widget: request-rate {"calls":5,"window":30} -->

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Start the policy wizard

Select **Policies** › **Add policy**. On the **Type** step, under **Cost & Rate Limits**, select
**Request rate limit**, then **Next**.

### Choose the MCP server

On the **Scope** step, select **Individual assets** ("Apply only to selected models, aliases, or MCP servers").
Select the `learn` MCP server, then **Next**.

### Configure the limit

On the **Details** step (**Configure** in some portal versions), under **Parameters**, set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Calls** | `5` |
| **Renewal period** | **30 seconds** |
| **Counter dimensions** | **Caller identity** |

The other renewal periods are **60 seconds**, **2 minutes**, and **5 minutes**. **Caller identity** gives each API
key, and each Entra caller, its own counter. If you select no counter dimension, all callers share one
counter. Select **Create**.

> **Checkpoint**
> **Policies** lists a **Request rate limit** with the `learn` MCP server as its scope.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Read the current policies

Policies live inline in the MCP server's `properties.policies` array. `az aigateway mcp update --policies`
**replaces the whole array**, so always read it first and keep the policies you didn't mean to change.

The command is the same in Bash and PowerShell.

```bash
# Read the policies on the learn MCP server, so that you can keep the ones you don't change
echo "🛡️ Policies on the learn MCP server:"
az aigateway mcp show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n learn --query properties.policies
```

The `mcp show` command prints nothing if the server has never had a policy, and `[]` if you removed its last one.

### Replace the request rate limit and keep everything else

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the whole MCP server, keep every policy except the request rate limit, and add the new one:
# 5 calls per 30 seconds for each caller identity, in a file that --policies reads with the @ prefix
az aigateway mcp show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n learn -o json | jq -c '
    [(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "requestRateLimit")]
    + [{type: "requestRateLimit", callsPerPeriod: 5, periodSeconds: 30, counterKey: ["identity"]}]' > policies.json &&
  echo "📄 policies.json has the merged policies"

# Replace the server's whole policies array with the file, show the result, and delete the file
az aigateway mcp update -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n learn --policies @policies.json \
  --query properties.policies &&
  echo "🛡️ Request rate limit of 5 calls per 30 seconds is on learn"
rm policies.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the whole MCP server, keep every policy except the request rate limit, and add the new one:
# 5 calls per 30 seconds for each caller identity
$current  = az aigateway mcp show -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n learn -o json | ConvertFrom-Json
$policies = @($current.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'requestRateLimit' })
$policies += [pscustomobject]@{ type = 'requestRateLimit'; callsPerPeriod = 5; periodSeconds = 30; counterKey = @('identity') }
Write-Host "📝 Policies to write: $($policies.Count), including the request rate limit"

# Write the merged array to a file, which --policies reads with the @ prefix
ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress -InputObject $policies | Set-Content -Path policies.json
if ($?) { Write-Host "📄 policies.json has the merged policies" }

# Replace the server's whole policies array with the file, show the result, and delete the file
az aigateway mcp update -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n learn --policies "@policies.json" `
  --query properties.policies
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Request rate limit of 5 calls per 30 seconds is on learn" }
Remove-Item policies.json
```

The commands read the whole MCP server, not just `properties.policies`, because the array is missing until the
server has had a policy. `mcp update` changes only the properties you pass, so the backends and versions stay as
they are. `periodSeconds` is the renewal period in seconds. The portal offers `30`, `60`, `120`, and
`300`. `counterKey` is an array with `identity`, `ipAddress`, or both. An empty array gives all callers one
shared counter.

> [!TIP]
> The same read, merge, and replace pattern sets policies on models, aliases, and the `default` workspace.

> **Checkpoint**
> `mcp update` returns your other policies unchanged plus one entry like this:
>
> ```json
> {
>   "callsPerPeriod": 5,
>   "counterKey": ["identity"],
>   "periodSeconds": 30,
>   "scope": "resource",
>   "type": "requestRateLimit"
> }
> ```

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Check the policy

`azd up` already added the request rate limit: the template's `policies` array holds one `requestRateLimit` entry
with `callsPerPeriod`, `periodSeconds`, and `counterKey`. The command is the same in Bash and PowerShell.

```bash
# Read the policies on the learn MCP server that azd up created
echo "🛡️ Policies on the learn MCP server:"
az aigateway mcp show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n learn --query properties.policies
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The command prints one policy with `"type": "requestRateLimit"`, `"callsPerPeriod": 5`, `"periodSeconds": 30`,
> `"counterKey": ["identity"]`, and `"scope": "resource"`.

### Change the limit

To count calls per client IP address instead of per key, set `REQUEST_RATE_LIMIT_COUNTER_KEY` to a JSON array and
provision again. `REQUEST_RATE_LIMIT` and `REQUEST_RATE_LIMIT_PERIOD` work the same way, and
`REQUEST_RATE_LIMIT` `0` removes the policy.

```bash title="Bash"
# Count calls per client IP address instead of per key, in the azd environment
azd env set REQUEST_RATE_LIMIT_COUNTER_KEY '["ipAddress"]' &&
  echo "📝 REQUEST_RATE_LIMIT_COUNTER_KEY is set to ipAddress"

# Provision again, which updates the learn MCP server's request rate limit
azd provision &&
  echo "🛡️ The request rate limit on learn counts calls per client IP address"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Count calls per client IP address instead of per key, in the azd environment
azd env set REQUEST_RATE_LIMIT_COUNTER_KEY '["ipAddress"]'
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 REQUEST_RATE_LIMIT_COUNTER_KEY is set to ipAddress" }

# Provision again, which updates the learn MCP server's request rate limit
azd provision
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ The request rate limit on learn counts calls per client IP address" }
```

Use `'["identity","ipAddress"]'` for both. Set it back to `'["identity"]'` before **Verify**.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Verify

The rate limit counts the calls you make while you verify, too. Every MCP request counts, including the two
handshake messages that each script run starts with. Wait 30 seconds between steps so each one starts with a
fresh window.

<!-- steps -->

### Call a blocked tool

The code sample tool is still listed, but the gateway refuses to run it:

```bash title="Bash"
# List the tools, then try to call the code sample tool, which is listed but blocked
echo "🚦 Expect the call to learn_microsoft_code_sample_search to fail:"
./infra/list-tools.sh learn learn_microsoft_code_sample_search "Python MCP client"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# List the tools, then try to call the code sample tool, which is listed but blocked
Write-Host "🚦 Expect the call to learn_microsoft_code_sample_search to fail:"
./infra/list-tools.ps1 -Server learn -Tool learn_microsoft_code_sample_search -Query "Python MCP client"
```

The tool list prints as before, and then the script reports that the `tools/call` request failed and prints
the gateway's error. The Learn backend never receives the call.

### Run the burst

Wait 30 seconds, then send a handshake followed by eight `tools/list` requests:

```bash title="Bash"
# Send the MCP handshake and eight tools/list requests, and print the status and Retry-After of each one
echo "🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests after the limit of 5 calls per 30 seconds:"
./infra/trigger-request-rate.sh learn 8
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Send the MCP handshake and eight tools/list requests, and print the status and Retry-After of each one
Write-Host "🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests after the limit of 5 calls per 30 seconds:"
./infra/trigger-request-rate.ps1 -Server learn -Requests 8
```

On GitHub, open [trigger-request-rate.sh](infra/trigger-request-rate.sh) or
[trigger-request-rate.ps1](infra/trigger-request-rate.ps1).

Expected output (your `Retry-After` values will differ):

```text
🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests after the limit of 5 calls per 30 seconds:
Request  Method                      Status  Retry-After
1        initialize                  200     -
2        notifications/initialized   202     -
3        tools/list                  200     -
4        tools/list                  200     -
5        tools/list                  200     -
6        tools/list                  200     -
7        tools/list                  200     -
8        tools/list                  429     4
9        tools/list                  429     3
10       tools/list                  429     2

Last response body:
{ "statusCode": 429, "message": "Rate limit is exceeded. Try again in 2 seconds." }
```

The counter is approximate, so the gateway can let a call or two beyond the limit through before the first
`429`. `Retry-After` counts down to the end of the current 30-second window, so it can be anything from 1 to 30
seconds.

### Inspect one throttled response

Right after the burst, while you're still throttled, send one raw request and look at the status line and
headers. If it returns `200`, the window has already renewed. Run the burst again, then this command.

```bash
# Send one raw tools/list request, and show its status line, headers, and body
echo "🚦 Expect HTTP 429 with a retry-after header:"
curl -i "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/toolservers/learn/mcp" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'
```

The status line is `HTTP/2 429`, the headers include `retry-after`, and the body is the same JSON error. The
`Retry-After` value tells the client how many seconds to wait. Agent frameworks should back
off for that long instead of retrying in a tight loop.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The `*_fetch` tools are no longer listed, a call to the blocked code sample tool fails, an allowed search
> tool works, and calls over the limit in a 30-second window get `429` with `Retry-After`.

## Go further

- **Prefer exact names for sensitive servers.** Patterns also publish tools that a backend adds later. Where
  your portal offers **Select exact tools**, use it for servers whose new tools need a review first.
- **Block destructive operations everywhere.** For a server built from an OpenAPI spec, keep
  **Allow all tools** and add blocked patterns such as `*_delete_*` so new read operations appear
  automatically but deletions never run.
- **Set a default for every MCP server.** Add a **Request rate limit** with **Gateway** scope in
  [Set gateway-wide policy baselines](../09-gateway-baselines/README.md).
- **Inspect tool calls for attacks.** Add Agent 365 tool threat protection in
  [Protect tool calls with Agent 365 threat protection](../19-tool-threat-protection/README.md).

## Clean up

A 5-call limit will throttle real agents. Remove it, and open the tool catalog again, before you continue.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Remove the policy and restore the catalog

1. Select **Policies**, open the **Request rate limit** that's scoped to `learn`, and delete it.
2. Open **MCP servers** › `learn` › **Edit** › **Tools**. Select **Allow all tools**, remove the
   `*code_sample*` blocked pattern, and select **Save**.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Remove the policy

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the whole MCP server, and keep every policy except the request rate limit, in a file for --policies
az aigateway mcp show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n learn -o json \
  | jq -c '[(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "requestRateLimit")]' > policies.json &&
  echo "📄 policies.json has every policy except the request rate limit"

# Replace the server's whole policies array with the file, show the result, and delete the file
az aigateway mcp update -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n learn --policies @policies.json \
  --query properties.policies &&
  echo "🧹 Request rate limit is removed from learn"
rm policies.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the whole MCP server, and keep every policy except the request rate limit
$current  = az aigateway mcp show -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n learn -o json | ConvertFrom-Json
$policies = @($current.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'requestRateLimit' })
Write-Host "📝 Policies to keep: $($policies.Count)"

# Write the remaining policies to a file, which --policies reads with the @ prefix
ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress -InputObject $policies | Set-Content -Path policies.json
if ($?) { Write-Host "📄 policies.json has every policy except the request rate limit" }

# Replace the server's whole policies array with the file, show the result, and delete the file
az aigateway mcp update -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n learn --policies "@policies.json" `
  --query properties.policies
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 Request rate limit is removed from learn" }
Remove-Item policies.json
```

Then restore the catalog in the portal: open **MCP servers** › `learn` › **Edit** › **Tools**, select
**Allow all tools**, remove the `*code_sample*` blocked pattern, and select **Save**.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Delete everything azd created

In the `ai-gateway/labs/05-mcp-tool-controls` folder, delete the resource group with the gateway, the `learn` MCP
server, and the key. [`--purge`](../SETUP.md#delete-what-azd-created) also purges soft-deleted resources. It takes
about ten minutes.

```bash
# Delete everything that azd up created, and purge the soft-deleted resources
azd down --purge --force &&
  echo "🧹 Everything that azd up created is deleted"
```

To keep this gateway for other labs instead, skip `azd down`. Open the catalog and remove the limit:

```bash
# Allow all tools, block none, and set the request rate limit to 0, which removes it
azd env set MCP_ALLOWED_TOOLS '["*"]'
azd env set MCP_BLOCKED_TOOLS '[]'
azd env set REQUEST_RATE_LIMIT 0 &&
  echo "📝 The azd environment allows all tools, blocks none, and has no request rate limit"

# Provision again, which updates only the learn MCP server
azd provision &&
  echo "🔌 The learn MCP server publishes every tool, with no request rate limit"
```

Keep the gateway, the `learn` MCP server, and your key from lab 04. The next labs reuse them. `azd down` doesn't
touch them, because the Bicep + azd track created its own gateway.

# Throttle tokens per caller with token limits

Your gateway now serves several apps from one model deployment. One batch job sends long prompts in a tight
loop and eats the deployment's tokens-per-minute (TPM) capacity, so every other app starts to fail. In this lab
you give each caller its own token allowance at the gateway, so a noisy neighbor gets a `429` with
`Retry-After` and everyone else keeps working.

![A token limit gives each caller its own allowance in front of a shared model deployment](../assets/diagrams/token-limits.svg "Each caller identity gets its own token counter. When a counter is exhausted, the gateway answers 429 without calling the backend.")

<!-- widget: token-limit {"limit":1000,"period":"minute"} -->

## Before you begin

<!-- setup: tools sign-in extension clone -->

> [!TIP]
> On the **Bicep + azd** track, `azd up` creates its own gateway, model, and key, so you can skip this section. You
> need only the one-time setup above.

- Complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md). You need a gateway, an imported
  model, a callable alias, and a runtime API key from **Access** › **Keys**.
- Permission to change the gateway, for example **Contributor** on the resource group.
- Run the scripts and samples from the lab's folder, `~/ai-gateway/labs/06-token-limits`.

Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
# Name the resource group, the gateway, the model provider, and the model that you published in lab 02
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
export PROVIDER="<provider-name>"          # for example foundry-models
export MODEL="<model-name>"                # the backend model name under that provider
echo "📝 Model $MODEL from $PROVIDER, on gateway $GATEWAY in $RG"

# Read the gateway's runtime URL
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Guess the alias from the model's deployment name
# Confirm it on the model's Aliases tab (lab 02), and replace it if it differs
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(az aigateway model show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" \
  -n "$MODEL" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv)"
echo "🏷️ Model alias: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Paste the runtime key that you created in Access › Keys, without showing it
# Don't commit the key or write it to a file
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Name the resource group, the gateway, the model provider, and the model that you published in lab 02
$RG         = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY    = "<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
$PROVIDER   = "<provider-name>"           # for example foundry-models
$MODEL      = "<model-name>"              # the backend model name under that provider
Write-Host "📝 Model $MODEL from $PROVIDER, on gateway $GATEWAY in $RG"

# Read the gateway's runtime URL
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Guess the alias from the model's deployment name
# Confirm it on the model's Aliases tab (lab 02), and replace it if it differs
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = az aigateway model show -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER `
  -n $MODEL --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv
Write-Host "🏷️ Model alias: $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Paste the runtime key that you created in Access › Keys, without showing it
# Don't commit the key or write it to a file
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

> [!TIP]
> Not sure which alias your clients call? Open the model in **Models** and check its **Aliases** tab. The value
> in the request `model` field must match an alias exactly.

## How it works

A token limit is a policy that the gateway evaluates **before** it forwards a request. It keeps a counter of
the tokens that each caller consumed in the current window. While the counter is under the limit, the request
goes through and the tokens in the response are added to the counter. When the counter reaches the limit, the
gateway answers `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header and never calls the backend.

| Setting | Portal label | JSON field | Values |
|---|---|---|---|
| Allowance | **Allowed tokens** | `count` | Positive integer |
| Window | **Time period** | `period` | `minute` (TPM), `hour`, `day` (quota) |
| Who gets a counter | **Counter dimensions** | `counterKey` | An array: `["identity"]` (each API key, or each Entra tenant + object ID), `["ipAddress"]`, or both |

You can attach a token limit to a **model** (applies to every alias that targets it), to an **alias** (only
callers that use that name), or to the **gateway** (a default for every compatible model, including models you
add later). Every applicable policy is checked, and any one of them can block the request.

> [!NOTE]
> The backend deployment has its own capacity, shown as **Token rate limit (TPM)** on the model's details page.
> The gateway limit is how you *share* that capacity fairly. Set per-caller limits so that the sum of your busiest
> callers stays below the deployment's TPM.

<!-- widget: policy-layers -->

## Add a token limit to the model

Pick one track. Each track produces the same policy on your model: **1,000 tokens per minute for each caller
identity**. The limit is deliberately low so you can trigger it in a few requests. The IaC track takes a
different route, explained in its first step.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Start the policy wizard

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **Policies** › **Add policy**. On the **Type** step, under **Cost & Rate Limits**, select
**Token rate limit**, then **Next**.

![The Add policy wizard on the Type step](../assets/screens/policy-add-wizard.png "Policies › Add policy opens a three-step wizard: Type, Scope, Configure.")

### Choose where the limit applies

On the **Scope** step, select **Individual assets** ("Apply only to selected models, aliases, or MCP servers").
Select your model, then **Next**.

> [!TIP]
> **Gateway** scope applies the limit to every compatible asset, including models you add later. It's a good
> default for production. You'll try it in [Go further](#go-further).

### Configure the allowance

On the **Details** step (**Configure** in some portal versions), under **Parameters**, set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Time period** | **Per minute** |
| **Allowed tokens** | `1000` |
| **Counter dimensions** | **Caller identity** |

Select **Create**. The policy appears in the **Policies** list with your model as its scope.

> **Checkpoint**
> **Policies** lists a **Token rate limit** for your model with 1,000 tokens per minute and the
> **Caller identity** counter.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Set the token limit

Policies live in the model's `properties.policies` array. `az aigateway model policy set-token-limit` adds the
token limit, or replaces the one that's there, and keeps every other policy on the model.

```bash title="Bash"
# Add a token limit to the model: 1,000 tokens per minute, with its own counter for each caller identity
az aigateway model policy set-token-limit -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" -n "$MODEL" \
  --token-limit 1000 --token-period minute --token-counter-key Identity &&
  echo "🛡️ Token limit of 1,000 tokens per minute is on $MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Add a token limit to the model: 1,000 tokens per minute, with its own counter for each caller identity
az aigateway model policy set-token-limit -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER -n $MODEL `
  --token-limit 1000 --token-period minute --token-counter-key Identity
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Token limit of 1,000 tokens per minute is on $MODEL" }
```

The command prints the model's policies. `--token-period` accepts `minute` (the default), `hour`, or `day`.
`--token-counter-key` accepts `Identity` (the default) or `IPAddress`. To count by both, as the portal's
**Counter dimensions** allows, use the **REST API** track.

### Confirm the policy

```bash title="Bash"
# List the model's policies, to check the token limit
echo "🛡️ Policies on ${MODEL}:"
az aigateway model policy list -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" -n "$MODEL" -o json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# List the model's policies, to check the token limit
Write-Host "🛡️ Policies on ${MODEL}:"
az aigateway model policy list -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER -n $MODEL -o json
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The output contains `"type": "tokenLimit"` with `"count": 1000`, `"period": "minute"`,
> `"counterKey": ["identity"]`, and `"scope": "resource"`, which the service adds to every model policy.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Read the current policies

Policies live inline in the model's `properties.policies` array. A `PATCH` **replaces the whole array**, so
always read it first and keep the policies you didn't mean to change.

```bash
# Read your subscription ID, and build the model's management URL, with the API version
SUB="$(az account show --query id -o tsv)"
URL="https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
echo "🆔 Subscription: $SUB"

# Read the model's policies, so that you can keep the ones you don't change
echo "🛡️ Policies on ${MODEL}:"
az rest --method get --url "$URL" --query properties.policies
```

### Replace the token limit and keep everything else

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the model, keep every policy except the token limit, and add the new one:
# 1,000 tokens per minute, with its own counter for each caller identity
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c '
  [(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "tokenLimit")]
  + [{"type":"tokenLimit","count":1000,"period":"minute","counterKey":["identity"]}]')"
echo "📝 Policies to write: $(jq length <<< "$POLICIES"), including the token limit"

# Replace the model's whole policies array with the merged one
az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}" &&
  echo "🛡️ Token limit of 1,000 tokens per minute is on $MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read your subscription ID, and build the model's management URL, with the API version
$SUB = az account show --query id -o tsv
$URL = "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL`?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
Write-Host "🆔 Subscription: $SUB"

# Read the model, keep every policy except the token limit, and add the new one:
# 1,000 tokens per minute, with its own counter for each caller identity
$current  = az rest --method get --url $URL | ConvertFrom-Json
$policies = @($current.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'tokenLimit' })
$policies += [pscustomobject]@{ type = 'tokenLimit'; count = 1000; period = 'minute'; counterKey = @('identity') }
Write-Host "📝 Policies to write: $($policies.Count), including the token limit"

# Write the request body to a file, which --body reads with the @ prefix, so that its quotes reach az intact
# Then replace the model's whole policies array, and delete the file
$body = @{ properties = @{ policies = $policies } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress
$body | Set-Content -Path patch.json
az rest --method patch --url $URL --body '@patch.json'
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Token limit of 1,000 tokens per minute is on $MODEL" }
Remove-Item patch.json
```

> **Checkpoint**
> Running the `GET` again returns your other policies unchanged plus one `tokenLimit` entry with
> `"counterKey": ["identity"]` and `"scope": "resource"`.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

**What you need:** only the one-time setup from **Before you begin**. This track doesn't use your gateway from lab 02:
`azd up` creates a new one, so it works on its own.

### Choose what to declare

A Bicep deployment sends a `PUT`, which replaces the whole resource. Redeclaring a model you imported in the
portal risks dropping settings you didn't copy. Instead, this template **adds a new alias**,
`<model-name>-limited`, that targets the same backend model and carries its own token limit. Existing clients
keep calling the original alias. Callers that you move to the new alias get the allowance.

This is also a common production pattern: one backend model, several aliases, and a different limit for each
audience (for example `gpt-chat` for interactive apps and `gpt-batch` for offline jobs).

### Review the templates

`infra/main.bicep` creates the resource group `rg-<environment name>` and calls the quick start's
[resources.bicep](../quickstart/infra/resources.bicep) for the gateway, the Foundry model, its default alias, and the
`app-first-call` key. Then it calls `infra/limited-alias.bicep` with the token limit:

<!-- include: infra/main.bicep -->

`infra/limited-alias.bicep` adds the alias. It only references the gateway, the provider, and the model, so you can
also deploy it on its own to a gateway you already have, with `az deployment group create`:

<!-- include: infra/limited-alias.bicep -->

### Deploy with azd up

Move into the lab's folder, create an azd environment named `aigw-lab06` in your current subscription, then provision
everything. It takes about three minutes.

```bash title="Bash"

cd ~/ai-gateway/labs/06-token-limits &&
  echo "📂 Lab folder: $(pwd)"

  echo "📝 azd environment aigw-lab06 deploys to eastus2"

azd up &&
  echo "🚀 Gateway deployed: $(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL)"
```

# Create an azd environment in your current subscription, so that azd doesn't prompt you

if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 azd environment aigw-lab06 deploys to eastus2" }

### Read the outputs and the key

Set the variables that **Verify** uses from azd's environment values, and read the key from the gateway, so that it
never shows on screen.

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the template's outputs: the resource group, the gateway, the provider, the backend model, the runtime URL,
# and the limited alias that apps send in the model field
export RG="$(azd env get-value AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP)"
export GATEWAY="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_NAME)"
export PROVIDER="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_PROVIDER)"
export MODEL="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_BACKEND_MODEL)"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL)"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_MODEL)"
echo "📝 Model $MODEL from $PROVIDER, on gateway $GATEWAY in $RG"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Read the key from the gateway, so that it never lands in a file or a deployment log
export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets --ids "$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_ID)/apiKeys/app-first-call" \
  --query primaryKey --output tsv)"
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
echo "🏷️ Model alias: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the template's outputs: the resource group, the gateway, the provider, the backend model, the runtime URL,
# the limited alias that apps send in the model field, and the gateway's resource ID
$RG                     = azd env get-value AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP
$GATEWAY                = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_NAME
$PROVIDER               = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_PROVIDER
$MODEL                  = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_BACKEND_MODEL
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL     = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL   = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_MODEL
$GATEWAY_ID             = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_ID
Write-Host "📝 Model $MODEL from $PROVIDER, on gateway $GATEWAY in $RG"
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Read the key from the gateway, so that it never lands in a file or a deployment log
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az aigateway api-key list-secrets --ids "$GATEWAY_ID/apiKeys/app-first-call" `
  --query primaryKey --output tsv
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"

```

> **Checkpoint**
> `azd up` ended with `SUCCESS`, and the last command printed the limited alias,
> `🏷️ Model alias: gpt-6-luna-limited`. In the portal, **Models** shows it next to `gpt-6-luna`, and **Policies**
> lists a **Token rate limit** scoped to it.

### Change the limit

The parameters come from azd environment values, with the defaults in `infra/main.parameters.json`. To count tokens
per client IP address instead of per key, set `TOKEN_LIMIT_COUNTER_KEY` to a JSON array and provision again. Only
the alias changes. `TOKEN_LIMIT` and `TOKEN_LIMIT_PERIOD` work the same way.

```bash title="Bash"
# Count tokens per client IP address instead of per key, in the azd environment
azd env set TOKEN_LIMIT_COUNTER_KEY '["ipAddress"]' &&
  echo "📝 TOKEN_LIMIT_COUNTER_KEY is set to ipAddress"

# Provision again, which updates only the limited alias
azd provision &&
  echo "🛡️ The token limit on the limited alias counts tokens per client IP address"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Count tokens per client IP address instead of per key, in the azd environment
azd env set TOKEN_LIMIT_COUNTER_KEY '["ipAddress"]'
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 TOKEN_LIMIT_COUNTER_KEY is set to ipAddress" }

# Provision again, which updates only the limited alias
azd provision
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ The token limit on the limited alias counts tokens per client IP address" }
```

Use `'["identity","ipAddress"]'` for both. Set it back to `'["identity"]'` before **Verify**, which proves the
counter is per key.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Verify

Send a burst of requests that each use about 225 tokens. With a 1,000-token budget, the first few succeed, and
then the gateway starts answering `429`.

<!-- steps -->

### Run the burst

From the lab folder, run the script for your shell. For each request it prints the status, `Retry-After`, the
tokens used, and the backend deployment's own `x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens` header.

```bash title="Bash"
# Send eight chat completions to the alias, and print the status, Retry-After, and tokens of each one
echo "🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests once the 1,000-token allowance runs out:"
./infra/trigger-token-limit.sh "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" 8
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Send eight chat completions to the alias, and print the status, Retry-After, and tokens of each one
Write-Host "🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests once the 1,000-token allowance runs out:"
./infra/trigger-token-limit.ps1 -Model $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL -Requests 8
```

On GitHub, open [trigger-token-limit.sh](infra/trigger-token-limit.sh) or
[trigger-token-limit.ps1](infra/trigger-token-limit.ps1).

Expected output (your token counts will differ):

```text
🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests once the 1,000-token allowance runs out:
Request  Status  Retry-After  Tokens used  Backend tokens left
1        200     -            231          9977
2        200     -            214          9977
3        200     -            220          9977
4        200     -            221          9977
5        200     -            223          9977
6        200     -            229          9977
7        429     1            -            -
8        200     -            222          9977
```

The gateway stops this caller once it passes 1,000 tokens, while the backend deployment still has most of its
capacity left: that's the point of a per-caller limit. `Retry-After` says how many seconds to wait, and a request sent
after that wait can succeed again, as request 8 shows. The gateway doesn't add its own remaining-tokens header, so
watch the status and `Retry-After`.

> [!NOTE]
> The gateway counts a request's tokens after the response, and its counters catch up within a few seconds, so a
> fast burst can go a few hundred tokens past the budget before the first `429`. A new or changed policy can also
> take up to a minute to apply. If every request returns `200`, wait a minute and run the burst again.

### Inspect one throttled response

Look at the full headers and body of a single throttled call:

```bash
# Send one raw chat completion while you're throttled, and show its status line, headers, and body
echo "🚦 Expect HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header:"
curl -i "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"ping\"}]}"
```

The status line is `HTTP/1.1 429`, and `Retry-After` tells the client how many seconds to wait. Well-behaved
SDKs, including the OpenAI SDKs, honor `Retry-After` automatically when they retry.

### Prove the counter is per caller

Create a second runtime key in **Access** › **Keys**, set it as `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` in a new terminal, and
run the burst again while the first key is still throttled. The second key starts with a full allowance,
because **Caller identity** gives every key its own counter.

### Find the throttled calls in Monitoring

If you configured Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), open
**Monitoring**. The dashboard shows `429` outcomes and policy impact next to token consumption, and the
**Traces** tab shows the policy span that blocked each request.

![The Monitoring overview showing requests, outcomes, and token consumption](../assets/screens/monitoring-overview.png "Monitoring shows throttled requests and token use per model and API key.")

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> You saw `200` responses until the allowance ran out, then `429` with `Retry-After`. A second key wasn't
> affected, and the backend received no calls while the limit was active.

## Go further

- **Set a gateway-wide default.** Add a second **Token rate limit** with **Gateway** scope and a generous
  allowance, such as `100000` per minute. New models get a guardrail the moment you import them, and you keep
  the stricter model or alias limits on top.
- **Add a daily quota.** Combine a per-minute limit (smooths bursts) with a **Per day** limit (caps total use).
  Both are checked on every request.
- **Limit by IP address.** For a public demo with one shared key, use **Caller IP address** so each visitor
  gets their own counter.
- **Budget in dollars instead of tokens.** Token counts don't reflect model prices. To cap spend, continue
  with [Enforce cost budgets](../07-cost-budgets/README.md).

## Clean up

The policy doesn't cost anything, but a 1,000-token limit will throttle real traffic. Remove it, or raise it
to a production value, before you continue.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Remove the policy

Select **Policies**, open the **Token rate limit** you created, and delete it. If you created a second runtime
key for testing, revoke it in **Access** › **Keys**.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Remove the policy

```bash title="Bash"
# Remove only the token limit from the model, and keep every other policy
az aigateway model policy remove -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" -n "$MODEL" \
  --remove-token-limit true &&
  echo "🧹 Token limit is removed from $MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Remove only the token limit from the model, and keep every other policy
az aigateway model policy remove -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER -n $MODEL `
  --remove-token-limit true
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 Token limit is removed from $MODEL" }
```

This removes only the token limit and keeps every other policy on the model. To keep a limit for real traffic
instead, run the **Set the token limit** step again with a production `count`, such as `100000`.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Remove the policy

```bash
# Read the model, and keep every policy except the token limit
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c '[(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "tokenLimit")]')"
echo "📝 Policies to keep: $(jq length <<< "$POLICIES")"

# Replace the model's whole policies array with the remaining policies
az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}" &&
  echo "🧹 Token limit is removed from $MODEL"
```

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Delete everything azd created

In the `ai-gateway/labs/06-token-limits` folder, delete the resource group with the gateway, the Foundry account, and
the limited alias. [`--purge`](../SETUP.md#delete-what-azd-created) also purges the soft-deleted Foundry account. It
takes about ten minutes.

```bash
# Delete everything that azd up created, and purge the soft-deleted Foundry account
azd down --purge --force &&
  echo "🧹 Everything that azd up created is deleted"
```

To keep this gateway for other labs instead, skip `azd down` and raise the limit to a production value:
`azd env set TOKEN_LIMIT 100000`, then `azd provision`.

<!-- /tracks -->

Keep the gateway, model, and key from lab 02: the next labs reuse them. `azd down` doesn't touch them, because
the Bicep + azd track created its own gateway.

# Enforce cost budgets with per-caller overrides

Your FinOps team has a problem that token limits can't solve: a thousand tokens on a premium reasoning model
costs many times more than a thousand tokens on a mini model, so "tokens per day" says nothing about the bill.
They want every app to have a **daily budget in dollars**, a bigger envelope for the production support bot,
and a separate allowance for a data science lead who signs in with Microsoft Entra ID. In this lab you set
that up as a cost limit at the gateway, so a caller who runs out of budget is stopped before the model is
called.

![A cost limit can apply to one model or to the whole gateway, with overrides for specific callers](../assets/diagrams/policy-scopes.svg "A cost limit attached to a model budgets spend on that model. Attached at gateway scope, it tracks one budget per caller across all models.")

<!-- widget: budget {"amount":5,"period":"day"} -->

## Before you begin

<!-- setup: tools sign-in extension clone -->

> [!TIP]
> On the **Bicep + azd** track, `azd up` creates its own gateway, model, and keys, so you can skip this section. You
> need only the one-time setup above.

- Complete [Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md). This lab reuses the
  **Policies** › **Add policy** wizard and the idea of per-caller counters.
- Complete [Issue and rotate runtime API keys](../10-api-keys/README.md). You need **two** runtime keys from
  **Access** › **Keys**, for example `app-dev` (gets the default budget) and `support-bot` (gets an override).
- Recommended: configure Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md)
  and send a few requests first, so **Monitoring** can show estimated spend before you choose a budget.
- Optional, for the Entra override: a user or service principal that can call the gateway with Microsoft
  Entra ID. [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md) shows how.
- Permission to change the gateway, for example **Contributor** on the resource group.
- Run the scripts and samples from the lab's folder, `~/ai-gateway/labs/07-cost-budgets`.

Set these variables once. Both tracks and the **Verify** section reuse them. Use the `app-dev` key here.

```bash title="Bash"
# Name your gateway, its model provider, and the backend model that gets the budget
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
export PROVIDER="<provider-name>"          # for example foundry-models
export MODEL="<model-name>"                # the backend model name under that provider

# Read the gateway's resource ID, and build the management URL of its default workspace for the az rest calls
export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query id -o tsv)"
export WS="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default"
echo "🆔 Gateway: $GATEWAY_ID"

# Read the gateway's runtime URL, which apps call
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Read the alias that apps send in the model field: for Foundry imports, it matches the deployment's model name
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(az aigateway model show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" \
  -n "$MODEL" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv)"
echo "🏷️ Model alias: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Paste the app-dev runtime key from Access › Keys, without showing it: don't commit it or write it to a file
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Name your gateway, its model provider, and the backend model that gets the budget
$RG         = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY    = "<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
$PROVIDER   = "<provider-name>"           # for example foundry-models
$MODEL      = "<model-name>"              # the backend model name under that provider

# Read the gateway's resource ID, and build the management URL of its default workspace for the az rest calls
$API        = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID = az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --query id -o tsv
$WS         = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default"
Write-Host "🆔 Gateway: $GATEWAY_ID"

# Read the gateway's runtime URL, which apps call
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Read the alias that apps send in the model field: for Foundry imports, it matches the deployment's model name
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = az aigateway model show -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER `
  -n $MODEL --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv
Write-Host "🏷️ Model alias: $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Paste the app-dev runtime key from Access › Keys, without showing it: don't commit it or write it to a file
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

## How it works

After each model response, the gateway **estimates its cost** from the tokens the provider reported and the
model's public pricing, broken down by token category. A cost limit adds that estimate to the caller's
counter for the current renewal period. Before it forwards the next request, the gateway checks the counter.
Once spend reaches the budget, the gateway answers `403` (`LlmCostQuotaExceeded` in the product docs) with the
message `LLM cost quota is exceeded` and never calls the backend. Responses also carry headers with the cost of the
call and the remaining budget.

| Setting | Portal label | JSON field | Values |
|---|---|---|---|
| Budget | **Budget amount** | `amount` | US dollars, for example `5` |
| Window | **Renewal period** | `period` | `hour`, `day`, `week`, `month`, `year` (**Hourly** … **Yearly**) |
| Who gets a counter | **Counter dimensions** (shown as **Budget counted by**) | `counterKey` | An array: `["identity"]` (the API key, or the Entra tenant ID + object ID) or `["ipAddress"]` |
| Exceptions | **Overrides** | `overrides` | A different `amount` for an API key (`apiKeyResourceId`) or Entra identity (`claims`) |
| Policy identity | Not shown | `id` | Stable ID. Editing the amount keeps accumulated spend. |

Renewal periods are **fixed calendar windows**, not rolling windows: a **Daily** budget starts fresh at the
beginning of each day, not 24 hours after the first call. Attach the policy to a **model** to budget spend on
that model, or at **Gateway** scope to track **one budget per caller across all models**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> A cost limit is a guardrail, not an invoice. Spend is estimated from public pricing, and because gateway
> instances update counters concurrently, concurrent requests can briefly **overshoot** the budget before every
> instance sees the latest spend.

<!-- widget: policy-layers -->

## Add a cost limit to the model

Pick one track. Each one produces the same default budget: **$5 per day for each caller identity**. The portal and
REST tracks put it on your model. The Bicep + azd track creates a new gateway and puts it on a new alias of the model.
The portal and Bicep + azd tracks also add the overrides for specific callers. The REST track points to the portal
for them.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Start the policy wizard

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **Policies** › **Add policy**. On the **Type** step, under **Cost & Rate Limits**, select
**Cost limit**, then **Next**.

### Choose where the budget applies

On the **Scope** step, select **Individual assets** ("Apply only to selected models, aliases, or MCP servers").
Select your model, then **Next**.

> [!TIP]
> Choose **Gateway** ("Apply to all compatible assets") when the budget should cover **every** model a caller
> uses, including models you import later. A gateway-scoped cost limit tracks one budget across all models
> instead of one per model.

### Set the default budget

On the **Details** step, under **Parameters**, set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Budget amount** | `5` (US dollars) |
| **Renewal period** | **Daily** |
| **Counter dimensions** | **Caller identity** |

Select **Next**.

> [!NOTE]
> **Caller identity** gives each API key, and each Entra caller, its own counter. If you select no dimension, every
> caller shares one counter for the policy. **Caller IP address** can't be combined with overrides: the portal asks
> you to remove all overrides or switch to caller identity before saving.

### Give an API key a bigger budget

On the **Overrides** step, under **API keys**, select **Add**. In the new row, pick your `support-bot` key in
**API key** and set **Budget amount** to `50`. Each key can have only one override.

### Give a Microsoft Entra identity its own budget

Under **Microsoft Entra identities**, select **Add**. In **Add Microsoft Entra identities override**, choose how
**Match requests by** works:

- **Specific Microsoft Entra identity**: search for a user by name or email. For a service principal, enter its
  **object ID**, not its application (client) ID.
- **Custom token claim combination**: add one or more **Claim name** and **Value** pairs, for example `appid`
  and the client ID of an internal app. Every claim condition must match the validated token.

Set **Budget amount** to `20`, then select **Add**.

![The Overrides step with one Microsoft Entra identity override and one custom token claims override](../assets/screens/policy-cost-limit-entra-overrides.png "Overrides (optional): API key overrides match a specific key; Microsoft Entra overrides match one identity or a combination of validated token claims. The first matching override wins.")

Overrides are evaluated in the order you add them, and the **first match wins**. A claim combination never
pools callers into a shared budget: with identity counting, each matching identity gets the override amount
on its own counter.

### Create the policy

Select **Create**. Back in **Policies**, open the new **Cost limit** to review it.

![The Cost limit details page showing behavior, configuration, and the assets it applies to](../assets/screens/policy-cost-limit-details.png "The details page explains the trigger and the 403 LlmCostQuotaExceeded response, and lists Budget amount, Renewal period, Budget counted by, and Applies to.")

> **Checkpoint**
> The **Cost limit** details page shows **Budget amount** $5.00, **Renewal period** **Daily**, **Budget
> counted by** **Caller identity**, and your model under **Applies to**. Select **Edit** to see your overrides.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Read the current policies

This track calls the Azure Resource Manager REST API with `az rest`, because the `aigateway` extension doesn't
set cost limits. Policies live inline in the model's `properties.policies` array. A `PATCH` **replaces the
whole array**, so always read it first and keep the policies you didn't mean to change.

```bash
# Read your subscription ID, and build the management URL of your model, which holds its policies
SUB="$(az account show --query id -o tsv)"
URL="https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
echo "🆔 Subscription: $SUB"

# Read the model's current policies, so that you know what the merge must keep
echo "🛡️ Policies on $MODEL:"
az rest --method get --url "$URL" --query properties.policies
```

### Add or update the cost limit and keep everything else

A cost limit carries a stable `id`. Editing the amount of an existing policy **keeps its accumulated spend**,
so the merge below updates an existing `costLimit` in place (keeping its `id` and any overrides) and only
creates a new one, with a fresh GUID, when none exists.

```bash title="Bash"
# Choose the default budget: 5 US dollars for each caller, renewed every day
BUDGET=5
PERIOD=day

# Read the policies, then update the cost limit in place, keeping its id and overrides,
# or add a new one with a fresh GUID when there's none
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c \
  --argjson amount "$BUDGET" --arg period "$PERIOD" --arg id "$(uuidgen | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z')" '
  .properties.policies // [] | . as $p
  | if any($p[]; .type == "costLimit")
    then [$p[] | if .type == "costLimit"
                 then (.amount = $amount | .period = $period | .counterKey = ["identity"])
                 else . end]
    else $p + [{"type":"costLimit","id":$id,"amount":$amount,"period":$period,"counterKey":["identity"]}]
    end')"

# Send the merged array back: a PATCH replaces the whole policies array
az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}" --output none &&
  echo "🛡️ Cost limit of \$$BUDGET per $PERIOD for each caller is on $MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Choose the default budget: 5 US dollars for each caller, renewed every day
$BUDGET = 5
$PERIOD = 'day'

# Read your subscription ID, and build the management URL of your model, which holds its policies
$SUB = az account show --query id -o tsv
$URL = "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL`?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
Write-Host "🆔 Subscription: $SUB"

# Read the policies, then update the cost limit in place, keeping its id and overrides,
# or add a new one with a fresh GUID when there's none
$current  = az rest --method get --url $URL | ConvertFrom-Json
$policies = @($current.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ })
$cost     = $policies | Where-Object { $_.type -eq 'costLimit' } | Select-Object -First 1
if ($cost) {
  $cost | Add-Member -NotePropertyName amount -NotePropertyValue $BUDGET -Force
  $cost | Add-Member -NotePropertyName period -NotePropertyValue $PERIOD -Force
  $cost | Add-Member -NotePropertyName counterKey -NotePropertyValue @('identity') -Force
} else {
  $policies += [pscustomobject]@{
    type = 'costLimit'; id = [guid]::NewGuid().ToString(); amount = $BUDGET; period = $PERIOD; counterKey = @('identity')
  }
}

# Send the merged array back from a file, which keeps the JSON quotes intact: a PATCH replaces the whole array
$body = @{ properties = @{ policies = $policies } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress
$body | Set-Content -Path patch.json
az rest --method patch --url $URL --body '@patch.json' --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Cost limit of `$$BUDGET per $PERIOD for each caller is on $MODEL" }
Remove-Item patch.json
```

`period` accepts `hour`, `day`, `week`, `month`, or `year`. `counterKey` is an array: `["identity"]`, or
`["ipAddress"]` to count per client IP address.

### Add overrides in the portal

Configure overrides for API keys and Microsoft Entra identities in the portal: select **Policies**, open the
**Cost limit**, select **Edit**, and use the **Overrides** step as described in the portal track. The merge
above keeps those overrides when you change the amount later.

> **Checkpoint**
> Running the `GET` again returns your other policies unchanged plus one `costLimit` entry with its `id`,
> `"amount": 5.0`, `"period": "day"`, `"counterKey": ["identity"]`, and `"scope": "resource"`.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

**What you need:** only the one-time setup from **Before you begin**. This track doesn't use your gateway from lab 02:
`azd up` creates a new one, so it works on its own.

### Choose what to declare

A Bicep deployment sends a `PUT`, which replaces the whole resource. Redeclaring a model you imported in the
portal risks dropping settings you didn't copy. Instead, this template **adds a new alias**,
`<model-name>-budget`, that targets the same backend model and carries the cost limit. Existing clients keep
calling the original alias. Callers that you move to the new alias get the budget.

The template also declares what the portal track picks by hand: the `app-dev` and `support-bot` runtime keys,
and two entries in the policy's `overrides` array. Overrides are evaluated in order, and the first match wins.

| Override | Matches | Budget |
|---|---|---|
| API key | `apiKeyResourceId`: the resource ID of the `support-bot` key | $50 per day |
| Microsoft Entra identity | `claims`: your tenant ID (`tid`) and object ID (`oid`) | $20 per day |

azd fills in the object ID of the account you signed in with. The policy `id` is a GUID that the template derives
from the gateway and the alias name, so it stays the same on every deployment, and a new amount keeps the spend
accumulated so far.

### Review the templates

`infra/main.bicep` creates the resource group `rg-<environment name>` and calls the quick start's
[resources.bicep](../quickstart/infra/resources.bicep) for the gateway, the Foundry model, its default alias, and the
`app-first-call` key. Then it calls `infra/budget-alias.bicep` with the budget and the overrides:

<!-- include: infra/main.bicep -->

`infra/budget-alias.bicep` adds the two keys and the alias. It only references the gateway, the provider, and the
model, so you can also deploy it on its own to a gateway you already have, with `az deployment group create`:

<!-- include: infra/budget-alias.bicep -->

### Deploy with azd up

Move into the lab's folder, create an azd environment named `aigw-lab07` in your current subscription, then provision
everything. It takes about three minutes.

```bash title="Bash"
# Move into the lab's folder, which holds the azd project
cd ~/ai-gateway/labs/07-cost-budgets &&
  echo "📂 Lab folder: $(pwd)"

# Create an azd environment in your current subscription, so that azd doesn't prompt you
azd env new aigw-lab07 --location eastus2 --subscription "$(az account show --query id --output tsv)" &&
  echo "📝 azd environment aigw-lab07 deploys to eastus2"

# Provision the gateway, the Foundry model, the app-dev and support-bot keys, and the budgeted alias
azd up &&
  echo "🚀 Gateway deployed: $(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Move into the lab's folder, which holds the azd project
Set-Location ~/ai-gateway/labs/07-cost-budgets
if ($?) { Write-Host "📂 Lab folder: $(Get-Location)" }

# Create an azd environment in your current subscription, so that azd doesn't prompt you
azd env new aigw-lab07 --location eastus2 --subscription (az account show --query id --output tsv)
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 azd environment aigw-lab07 deploys to eastus2" }

# Provision the gateway, the Foundry model, the app-dev and support-bot keys, and the budgeted alias
azd up
if ($?) { Write-Host "🚀 Gateway deployed: $(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL)" }
```

For another region, pick one where AI Gateway and the `gpt-6-luna` model are available, as in [Find the available
regions](../SETUP.md#find-the-available-regions).

### Read the outputs and the key

Set the variables that **Verify** and **Go further** use from azd's environment values, and read the `app-dev` key
from the gateway, so that it never shows on screen.

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the template's outputs: the resource group, the gateway, its model provider, and the backend model
export RG="$(azd env get-value AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP)"
export GATEWAY="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_NAME)"
export PROVIDER="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_PROVIDER)"
export MODEL="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_BACKEND_MODEL)"

# Read the gateway's resource ID, and build the management URL of its default workspace for the az rest calls
export API="api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
export GATEWAY_ID="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_ID)"
export WS="https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default"

# Read the gateway's runtime URL and the budgeted alias
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL)"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_MODEL)"

# Read the app-dev key from the gateway, so that it never lands in a file or a deployment log
export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets --ids "$GATEWAY_ID/apiKeys/app-dev" \
  --query primaryKey --output tsv)"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
echo "🏷️ Model alias: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the template's outputs: the resource group, the gateway, its model provider, and the backend model
$RG                     = azd env get-value AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP
$GATEWAY                = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_NAME
$PROVIDER               = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_PROVIDER
$MODEL                  = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_BACKEND_MODEL

# Read the gateway's resource ID, and build the management URL of its default workspace for the az rest calls
$API                    = "api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
$GATEWAY_ID             = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_ID
$WS                     = "https://management.azure.com$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default"

# Read the gateway's runtime URL and the budgeted alias
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL     = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL   = azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_MODEL

# Read the app-dev key from the gateway, so that it never lands in a file or a deployment log
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az aigateway api-key list-secrets --ids "$GATEWAY_ID/apiKeys/app-dev" `
  --query primaryKey --output tsv
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
Write-Host "🏷️ Model alias: $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

> **Checkpoint**
> `azd up` ended with `SUCCESS`, and the last command printed `🏷️ Model alias: gpt-6-luna-budget`.
> `az rest --url "$WS/aliases/$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL?$API" --query properties.policies` returns one `costLimit` entry
> with `"amount": 5.0`, `"period": "day"`, `"counterKey": ["identity"]`, and two `overrides`: `"amount": 50.0`
> with the `apiKeyResourceId` of `support-bot`, and `"amount": 20.0` with your `oid` and `tid` claims.

### Change the budget

The parameters come from azd environment values, with the defaults in `infra/main.parameters.json`:
`COST_LIMIT_AMOUNT` for the default budget, `COST_LIMIT_PERIOD` (`hour`, `day`, `week`, `month`, or `year`),
`COST_LIMIT_OVERRIDE_AMOUNT` for `support-bot`, and `COST_LIMIT_ENTRA_AMOUNT` for your identity. Change one with
`azd env set` and run `azd provision`: only the alias changes, and it keeps the policy `id`. **Verify** lowers
`COST_LIMIT_AMOUNT` this way.

<!-- /tracks -->

## Verify

A $5 budget takes a while to spend, so temporarily lower it, run a short series of requests with the `app-dev`
key (which has no override), and watch the gateway switch from `200` to `403`.

<!-- steps -->

### Lower the budget for the test

In the portal, open the **Cost limit**, select **Edit**, set **Budget amount** to `0.01`, and **Save**. On the
REST track, run the merge again with `BUDGET=0.01` (PowerShell: `$BUDGET = 0.01`).

If your model is an inexpensive mini or nano model, use `0.001` so a handful of calls is enough. Because
editing keeps accumulated spend, the very first request might already be blocked if `app-dev` spent more than
the new budget earlier today.

On the Bicep + azd track, a call to `gpt-6-luna` costs about $0.0001, so set the budget to `0.001`:

```bash title="Bash"
# Lower the default budget to $0.001 for each caller, in the azd environment
azd env set COST_LIMIT_AMOUNT 0.001 &&
  echo "📝 COST_LIMIT_AMOUNT is 0.001"

# Deploy the change: only the budgeted alias changes, and it keeps its policy id and the spend so far
azd provision &&
  echo "🛡️ Default budget on $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL is now \$0.001 for each caller"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Lower the default budget to $0.001 for each caller, in the azd environment
azd env set COST_LIMIT_AMOUNT 0.001
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 COST_LIMIT_AMOUNT is 0.001" }

# Deploy the change: only the budgeted alias changes, and it keeps its policy id and the spend so far
azd provision
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Default budget on $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL is now `$0.001 for each caller" }
```

### Run the requests

From the lab folder, run the script for your shell. It prints the status, the error code, the tokens used, and
any response header whose name mentions budget, cost, or remaining.

```bash title="Bash"
# Send 10 requests with the app-dev key, and print the status, the tokens used, and the budget headers of each
echo "🚦 Expect 403 once app-dev's estimated spend reaches the budget:"
./infra/trigger-cost-limit.sh "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" 10
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Send 10 requests with the app-dev key, and print the status, the tokens used, and the budget headers of each
Write-Host "🚦 Expect 403 once app-dev's estimated spend reaches the budget:"
./infra/trigger-cost-limit.ps1 -Model $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL -Requests 10
```

On GitHub, open [trigger-cost-limit.sh](infra/trigger-cost-limit.sh) or
[trigger-cost-limit.ps1](infra/trigger-cost-limit.ps1).

Example output with a $0.001 budget on the alias from the Bicep + azd track (your token counts, the number of
successful calls, and the header values will differ):

```text
🚦 Expect 403 once app-dev's estimated spend reaches the budget:
Request  Status  Error code               Tokens used  Budget headers
1        200     -                        223          …; x-alias-cost-per-day-remaining=…; x-alias-cost-per-day-consumed=0.000101900
2        200     -                        221          …; x-alias-cost-per-day-remaining=…; x-alias-cost-per-day-consumed=0.000100900
…
9        200     -                        …            …; x-alias-cost-per-day-remaining=0.000000000; …
10       403     -                        -            x-alias-cost-per-day-retry-after=1837
```

`x-alias-cost-per-day-consumed` is the estimated cost of the call, and `x-alias-cost-per-day-remaining` is what's
left of the budget. On a cost limit attached to the model, the headers start with `x-cost-` instead. A blocked
call has no error code in its body, so the script prints `-`, and `…-retry-after` gives the seconds until the caller
can try again. How many calls succeed depends on the model's price. A call or two more than you expect is the
small overshoot described in [How it works](#how-it-works).

### Inspect one blocked response

Look at the full headers and body of a single blocked call:

```bash
# Send one more request with the app-dev key, and show the whole response: the status line, the headers, and the body
echo "🚦 Expect 403 with the message LLM cost quota is exceeded:"
curl -i "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"ping\"}]}"
```

The status line is `HTTP/2 403`, and the body is
`{ "statusCode": 403, "message": "LLM cost quota is exceeded. Try again in 30 minutes and 36 seconds." }`, with your
own wait time. Scan the headers for the ones that report the cost and the remaining budget, and compare them with a
successful response from a key that still has budget.
Unlike a token limit, which frees up as the window rolls, the caller stays blocked until the next calendar
renewal period starts or you raise the budget.

### Prove the override and the per-caller counters

Set `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` to the `support-bot` key in a new terminal (repeat the variable block) and run the
script again. Every request succeeds, because that key has its own counter and a $50 override. On the Bicep + azd
track, read that key from the gateway instead:

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the support-bot key from the gateway, so that it never shows on screen
export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets --ids "$GATEWAY_ID/apiKeys/support-bot" \
  --query primaryKey --output tsv)"
echo "🔑 support-bot key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"

# Send the same 10 requests with support-bot, which has its own counter and a $50 override
echo "📊 Expect 200 for every request, because support-bot has its own \$50 budget:"
./infra/trigger-cost-limit.sh "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" 10
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the support-bot key from the gateway, so that it never shows on screen
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az aigateway api-key list-secrets --ids "$GATEWAY_ID/apiKeys/support-bot" `
  --query primaryKey --output tsv
Write-Host "🔑 support-bot key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"

# Send the same 10 requests with support-bot, which has its own counter and a $50 override
Write-Host "📊 Expect 200 for every request, because support-bot has its own `$50 budget:"
./infra/trigger-cost-limit.ps1 -Model $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL -Requests 10
```

If you added an Entra override (the Bicep + azd track adds one for you), call the gateway with that identity's
token as shown in
[Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md): it gets its own counter too, keyed
by tenant ID and object ID.

### Review estimated spend in Monitoring

If you configured Application Insights, open **Monitoring**. **Estimated model cost** and **Top models** show
the spend the gateway estimated, and the dashboard attributes it to individual API keys and models.

![The Monitoring overview with estimated model cost, model calls, and top models by estimated cost](../assets/screens/monitoring-overview.png "Monitoring estimates model cost from observed tokens and public pricing, and breaks it down by model and API key.")

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> `app-dev` got `200` responses until its estimated spend reached the budget, then `403` with
> `LLM cost quota is exceeded`. `support-bot` wasn't affected, and the backend received no calls from `app-dev` while
> it was blocked.

## Go further

- **Cap spend across all models.** Add a second **Cost limit** with **Gateway** scope, for example $200
  **Monthly**. Each caller then has one budget across every model, including models you import later. With
  REST, run the same merge against the gateway workspace:
  `https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default?api-version=2025-09-01-preview`
  (`"${WS}?$API"` from the variable block).
- **Combine with token limits.** Keep a per-minute **Token rate limit** to smooth bursts and a **Cost limit**
  to cap spend. Both are checked on every request, and either one can block.
- **Budget by role or app.** Use **Custom token claim combination** overrides, for example a `roles` claim with
  an app role value, so everyone with that role gets a different per-identity amount.
- **Chargeback by team.** Export `tid`, `oid`, or a custom claim to cost metrics in
  [Attribute tokens and cost with OpenTelemetry](../14-otel-chargeback/README.md).

## Clean up

A $0.01 budget blocks real traffic. Delete the policy, or raise it to a production value, before you continue.
Raising the amount takes effect immediately, because the accumulated spend is kept and compared with the new
budget.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Remove or raise the budget

Select **Policies**, open the **Cost limit** you created, and select **Delete**, or select **Edit** and set a
production **Budget amount**. If you created runtime keys only for this lab, revoke them in **Access** › **Keys**.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Remove the cost limit

```bash
# Read the policies, and keep every one except the cost limit
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c '[(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "costLimit")]')"

# Send the array back without the cost limit: a PATCH replaces the whole policies array
az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}" --output none &&
  echo "🧹 Cost limit is removed from $MODEL"
```

To keep the policy instead, run the merge again with a production budget, for example `BUDGET=100`.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Delete everything azd created

In the `ai-gateway/labs/07-cost-budgets` folder, delete the resource group with the gateway, the Foundry account, the
keys, and the budgeted alias. [`--purge`](../SETUP.md#delete-what-azd-created) also purges the soft-deleted Foundry
account. It takes about ten minutes.

```bash
# Delete everything that azd up created, and purge the Foundry account
azd down --purge --force &&
  echo "🧹 Everything that azd up created is deleted"
```

To keep this gateway for other labs instead, skip `azd down` and raise the budget to a production value:
`azd env set COST_LIMIT_AMOUNT 100`, then `azd provision`.

<!-- /tracks -->

Keep the gateway, model, and keys from earlier labs: the next labs reuse them. `azd down` doesn't touch them,
because the Bicep + azd track created its own gateway.

# Screen prompts and responses with content safety

Your gateway now serves a customer-facing assistant and several internal agents, on models from more than one
provider. Your responsible AI review asks for one consistent rule: every prompt and every response is screened
for harmful content, whichever model or tool handles it. In this lab you add a **content safety** policy at the
gateway, tune it per category, and see what a blocked call looks like to a client.

![The request lifecycle through authentication, policies, the backend, and telemetry](../assets/diagrams/request-lifecycle.svg "Content safety is one of the policies that the gateway evaluates on every request. When it blocks a call, the client gets 400.")

<!-- widget: request-lifecycle {"focus":"contentSafety"} -->

## Before you begin
