## How it works

A content safety policy screens prompts, tool inputs, and responses with Azure AI Content Safety. It rates
content in four categories: **Hate**, **Self-harm**, **Sexual**, and **Violence**. You set a severity threshold
for each category independently. When content reaches the threshold, the gateway blocks the call and returns
`400`. A blocked prompt never reaches the backend.

The threshold is the lowest severity that gets blocked, so a **lower** threshold blocks **more**:

| Portal label | CLI and REST value | What it blocks |
|---|---|---|
| **Strict** | `Low` | The most content: low, medium, and high severity |
| **Balanced** (default) | `Medium` | Medium and high severity |
| **Lenient** | `High` | Only the most concerning, high-severity content |
| **Off** | `None` | Nothing in this category |

You can attach content safety to **models** and **MCP servers**. On an MCP server, it screens the tool inputs
that agents send and the results that tools return. Every applicable policy is evaluated, and any one of them
can block the call.

> [!NOTE]
> Foundry deployments have their own **Content filter**, shown on the model's details page in **Models**. That
> filter runs inside Foundry, for that one deployment. The gateway policy runs before the backend, applies the
> same rules to models from any provider and to MCP tool traffic, and is managed by the platform team in one
> place. Keep both: a request has to pass each of them.

## Add content safety to the model

Pick one track. Each track produces the same policy: **Balanced** (`Medium`) for Hate, Self-harm, and Sexual,
and **Strict** (`Low`) for Violence. The portal, CLI, and REST tracks put it on your model. The Bicep + azd track
creates a new gateway and puts it on a new alias of the model. The stricter Violence threshold makes the test in
**Verify** more likely to show a block, using only a mild, non-graphic prompt.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Start the policy wizard

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **Policies** › **Add policy**. On the **Type** step, under **Security**, select **Content safety**, then
**Next**.

![The Add policy wizard on the Type step](../assets/screens/policy-add-wizard.png "Policies › Add policy opens a three-step wizard: Type, Scope, Details.")

### Choose the model

On the **Scope** step, select **Individual assets** ("Apply only to selected models, aliases, or MCP servers").
Select your model, then **Next**.

### Set the thresholds

On the **Details** step (**Configure** in some portal versions), under **Parameters**, choose how strictly
each category is filtered:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Hate** | **Balanced** |
| **Violence** | **Strict** |
| **Self-harm** | **Balanced** |
| **Sexual** | **Balanced** |

Select **Create**. The policy appears in the **Policies** list with your model as its scope.

> **Checkpoint**
> **Policies** lists a **Content safety** policy for your model.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Set the policy

Policies live in the model's `properties.policies` array. `az aigateway model policy set-content-safety` adds the
content safety policy, or replaces the one that's there, and keeps every other policy on the model.
`--content-safety` sets the threshold for all four categories, and `--violence-severity` overrides **Violence**.

```bash title="Bash"
# Screen the model at Medium (Balanced) in all four categories, with Low (Strict) for Violence
az aigateway model policy set-content-safety -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" -n "$MODEL" \
  --content-safety Medium --violence-severity Low --output none &&
  echo "🛡️ Content safety on $MODEL is Balanced (Medium), with Strict (Low) for Violence"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Screen the model at Medium (Balanced) in all four categories, with Low (Strict) for Violence
az aigateway model policy set-content-safety -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER -n $MODEL `
  --content-safety Medium --violence-severity Low --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Content safety on $MODEL is Balanced (Medium), with Strict (Low) for Violence" }
```

The command prints `🛡️ Content safety on <model-name> is Balanced (Medium), with Strict (Low) for Violence`. Each
threshold accepts `None`, `Low`, `Medium`, or `High`. To override another category, add `--hate-severity`,
`--self-harm-severity`, or `--sexual-severity`.

### Confirm the policy

```bash title="Bash"
# List the model's policies, to check the content safety thresholds
echo "🛡️ Policies on $MODEL:"
az aigateway model policy list -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" -n "$MODEL" -o json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# List the model's policies, to check the content safety thresholds
Write-Host "🛡️ Policies on ${MODEL}:"
az aigateway model policy list -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER -n $MODEL -o json
```

> **Checkpoint**
> The output contains `"type": "contentSafety"` with `"violenceSeverity": "Low"`, `"Medium"` for the other
> three categories, and `"scope": "resource"`, which the service adds to every model policy.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Read the current policies

Policies live inline in the model's `properties.policies` array. A `PATCH` **replaces the whole array**, so
always read it first and keep the policies you didn't mean to change.

```bash
# Read your subscription ID, and build the management URL of your model, which holds its policies
SUB="$(az account show --query id -o tsv)"
URL="https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
echo "🆔 Subscription: $SUB"

# Read the model's current policies, so that you know what the merge must keep
echo "🛡️ Policies on $MODEL:"
az rest --method get --url "$URL" --query properties.policies
```

### Replace the content safety policy and keep everything else

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the policies, drop any content safety policy, and add the new one: Medium, with Low for Violence
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c '
  [(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "contentSafety")]
  + [{"type":"contentSafety","hateSeverity":"Medium","violenceSeverity":"Low","sexualSeverity":"Medium","selfHarmSeverity":"Medium"}]')"

# Send the merged array back: a PATCH replaces the whole policies array
az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}" --output none &&
  echo "🛡️ Content safety on $MODEL is Balanced (Medium), with Strict (Low) for Violence"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read your subscription ID, and build the management URL of your model, which holds its policies
$SUB = az account show --query id -o tsv
$URL = "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$MODEL`?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
Write-Host "🆔 Subscription: $SUB"

# Read the policies, drop any content safety policy, and add the new one: Medium, with Low for Violence
$current  = az rest --method get --url $URL | ConvertFrom-Json
$policies = @($current.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'contentSafety' })
$policies += [pscustomobject]@{
  type = 'contentSafety'; hateSeverity = 'Medium'; violenceSeverity = 'Low'; sexualSeverity = 'Medium'; selfHarmSeverity = 'Medium'
}

# Send the merged array back from a file, which keeps the JSON quotes intact: a PATCH replaces the whole array
$body = @{ properties = @{ policies = $policies } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress
$body | Set-Content -Path patch.json
az rest --method patch --url $URL --body '@patch.json' --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Content safety on $MODEL is Balanced (Medium), with Strict (Low) for Violence" }
Remove-Item patch.json
```

> **Checkpoint**
> Running the `GET` again returns your other policies unchanged plus one `contentSafety` entry with
> `"violenceSeverity": "Low"` and `"scope": "resource"`.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

**What you need:** only the one-time setup from **Before you begin**. This track doesn't use your gateway from lab 02:
`azd up` creates a new one, so it works on its own.

### Choose what to declare

A Bicep deployment sends a `PUT`, which replaces the whole resource. Redeclaring a model you imported in the
portal risks dropping settings you didn't copy. Instead, this template **adds a new alias**,
`<model-name>-safe`, that targets the same backend model and carries the content safety policy. Existing clients
keep calling the original alias. Callers that you move to the new alias get screened.

The policy is one `contentSafety` object with a threshold for each category: `hateSeverity`, `selfHarmSeverity`,
`sexualSeverity`, and `violenceSeverity`. Each accepts the API values from [How it works](#how-it-works): `Low`,
`Medium`, `High`, or `None`.

### Review the templates

`infra/main.bicep` creates the resource group `rg-<environment name>` and calls the quick start's
[resources.bicep](../quickstart/infra/resources.bicep) for the gateway, the Foundry model, its default alias, and the
`app-first-call` key. Then it calls `infra/safe-alias.bicep` with the four thresholds:

<!-- include: infra/main.bicep -->

`infra/safe-alias.bicep` adds the alias. It only references the gateway, the provider, and the model, so you can
also deploy it on its own to a gateway you already have, with `az deployment group create`:

<!-- include: infra/safe-alias.bicep -->

### Change the thresholds

The parameters come from azd environment values, with the defaults in `infra/main.parameters.json`:
`CONTENT_SAFETY_HATE`, `CONTENT_SAFETY_SELF_HARM`, `CONTENT_SAFETY_SEXUAL`, and `CONTENT_SAFETY_VIOLENCE`. Change one
with `azd env set` and run `azd provision`: only the alias changes. **Verify** relaxes Violence this way.

## Verify

Test the policy with **benign prompts only**. You don't need harmful content to see how the gateway behaves,
and you should never write it to test a filter.

<!-- steps -->

### Run the test prompts

From the lab folder, run the script for your shell. It sends two prompts: a neutral question, and a request
for a short, non-graphic scene from a historical novel. It prints the status and the start of the response or
the error for each one.

```bash title="Bash"
# Send a neutral prompt and a mild fiction prompt through the screened alias
echo "🚦 Expect 200 for the neutral prompt, and 200 or 400 for the fiction prompt:"
./infra/test-content-safety.sh "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Send a neutral prompt and a mild fiction prompt through the screened alias
Write-Host "🚦 Expect 200 for the neutral prompt, and 200 or 400 for the fiction prompt:"
./infra/test-content-safety.ps1 -Model $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL
```

On GitHub, open [test-content-safety.sh](infra/test-content-safety.sh) or
[test-content-safety.ps1](infra/test-content-safety.ps1).

Example output:

```text
🚦 Expect 200 for the neutral prompt, and 200 or 400 for the fiction prompt:
Prompt    Status  Finish reason   Response or error
neutral   200     stop            Teams put an API gateway in front of AI models to centralize access con
fiction   400     -               <the gateway's content safety error message>
```

The neutral prompt returns `200`. The fiction prompt can go either way, and your results will vary: Content
Safety rates both the prompt and the model's response, and a mild battle scene sits close to the **Strict**
Violence threshold. If it returns `400`, the gateway blocked it and the error message says why. If it returns
`200`, the content was rated below the threshold.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> If the fiction prompt passes, don't make it more graphic to force a block. The point of this test is to
> understand thresholds with safe input, not to probe the filter. Use **Monitoring** and real, representative
> traffic in a test environment to tune thresholds.

### Relax one category

Set **Violence** back to **Balanced** (`Medium`) with the track you used, then run the script again. For
example, from the command line, set all four categories to `Medium`. The other three already are, so only
**Violence** changes, and the command keeps every other policy on the model:

```bash title="Bash"
# Set all four categories to Medium (Balanced): only Violence changes, and the other policies stay
az aigateway model policy set-content-safety -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" -n "$MODEL" \
  --content-safety Medium --output none &&
  echo "🛡️ Content safety on $MODEL is Balanced (Medium) for all four categories"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Set all four categories to Medium (Balanced): only Violence changes, and the other policies stay
az aigateway model policy set-content-safety -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER -n $MODEL `
  --content-safety Medium --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Content safety on $MODEL is Balanced (Medium) for all four categories" }
```

On the Bicep + azd track, set the environment value and provision again instead:

```bash title="Bash"
# Relax Violence to Medium (Balanced) in the azd environment
azd env set CONTENT_SAFETY_VIOLENCE Medium &&
  echo "📝 CONTENT_SAFETY_VIOLENCE is Medium"

# Provision again: only the screened alias changes
azd provision &&
  echo "🛡️ Content safety on $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL is Balanced (Medium) for all four categories"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Relax Violence to Medium (Balanced) in the azd environment
azd env set CONTENT_SAFETY_VIOLENCE Medium
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 CONTENT_SAFETY_VIOLENCE is Medium" }

# Provision again: only the screened alias changes
azd provision
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Content safety on $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL is Balanced (Medium) for all four categories" }
```

A prompt that **Strict** blocked is more likely to pass at **Balanced**. Prompts that passed before still pass.

### Check the Foundry content filter

Open **Models**, select your model, and find **Content filter** on its details page. That is the Foundry
deployment's own filter, separate from the gateway policy. When Foundry's filter acts instead of the gateway,
the error or the `finish_reason` comes from the backend, and it can mention `content_filter`.

### Find blocked calls in Monitoring

If you configured Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), open
**Monitoring** and look for `400` outcomes on your model. Review them before and after every threshold change.

A **Strict** threshold can block legitimate traffic. Remove the model policy before you continue. The next
lab sets a gateway-wide baseline instead.

### Remove the policy

Select **Policies**, open the **Content safety** policy that's scoped to your model, and delete it.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Remove the policy

```bash title="Bash"
# Remove only the content safety policy from the model, and keep its other policies
az aigateway model policy remove -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" -n "$MODEL" \
  --remove-content-safety true --output none &&
  echo "🧹 Content safety is removed from $MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Remove only the content safety policy from the model, and keep its other policies
az aigateway model policy remove -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER -n $MODEL `
  --remove-content-safety true --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 Content safety is removed from $MODEL" }
```

This removes only the content safety policy and keeps every other policy on the model.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Remove the policy

```bash
# Read the policies and drop the content safety policy, so that the others stay
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c '[(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "contentSafety")]')"

# Send the remaining policies back: a PATCH replaces the whole policies array
az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}" --output none &&
  echo "🧹 Content safety is removed from $MODEL"
```

# Set gateway-wide policy baselines

Your gateway now serves several models and MCP servers, and teams add new ones every week. Some assets have
carefully tuned policies, and some have none at all. The platform and security teams agree on a baseline that
every asset gets by default: a generous token limit, a request rate limit, **Balanced** content safety, and
runtime access only from approved networks. In this lab you apply that baseline once, at **Gateway** scope,
and keep tighter asset policies on top of it.

![Policies at gateway scope and on models, aliases, MCP servers, and future assets](../assets/diagrams/policy-scopes.svg "A Gateway scope policy covers every compatible asset, including assets added later. Asset policies add narrower rules on top.")

<!-- widget: policy-layers -->

## Before you begin

<!-- setup: tools sign-in extension clone -->

- Complete [Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md) and
  [Screen prompts and responses with content safety](../08-content-safety/README.md), including their
  **Clean up** sections. You need a gateway, an imported model, a callable alias, and a runtime API key from
  **Access** › **Keys**.
- Permission to change the gateway, for example **Contributor** on the resource group.
- The public IP addresses or CIDR ranges your callers use. Once the IP filter is on, calls from anywhere else get
  `403`.
- Run the scripts and samples from the lab's folder, `~/ai-gateway/labs/09-gateway-baselines`.

Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"
# Name your gateway, its model provider, and the backend model that the Verify section calls
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
export PROVIDER="<provider-name>"          # for example foundry-models
export MODEL="<model-name>"                # the backend model name under that provider

# Read the gateway's runtime URL, which apps call
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Read the alias that apps send in the model field: for Foundry imports, it matches the deployment's model name
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(az aigateway model show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" \
  -n "$MODEL" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv)"
echo "🏷️ Model alias: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys, without showing it: don't commit it or write it to a file
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"

# Read the public IP address that this machine uses on the internet
export MY_IP="$(curl -s https://api.ipify.org)"
echo "🌐 Public IP address: $MY_IP"

# Set the ranges that the IP filter allows
export ALLOWED_CIDRS="$MY_IP/32"           # comma-separated, for example "$MY_IP/32,198.51.100.0/24"
echo "📝 Ranges the IP filter allows: $ALLOWED_CIDRS"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Name your gateway, its model provider, and the backend model that the Verify section calls
$RG         = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY    = "<gateway>"                 # 24 characters or fewer
$PROVIDER   = "<provider-name>"           # for example foundry-models
$MODEL      = "<model-name>"              # the backend model name under that provider

# Read the gateway's runtime URL, which apps call
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Read the alias that apps send in the model field: for Foundry imports, it matches the deployment's model name
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = az aigateway model show -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER `
  -n $MODEL --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv
Write-Host "🏷️ Model alias: $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Paste the runtime key you created in Access › Keys, without showing it: don't commit it or write it to a file
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"

# Read the public IP address that this machine uses on the internet
$env:MY_IP = Invoke-RestMethod https://api.ipify.org
Write-Host "🌐 Public IP address: $env:MY_IP"

# Set the ranges that the IP filter allows
$env:ALLOWED_CIDRS = "$($env:MY_IP)/32"    # comma-separated, for example "$($env:MY_IP)/32,198.51.100.0/24"
Write-Host "📝 Ranges the IP filter allows: $env:ALLOWED_CIDRS"
```

## How it works

A policy with **Gateway** scope is stored on the gateway's `default` workspace instead of on one asset. It
applies to every compatible model, alias, and MCP server, including assets you add later, without another
policy update. Asset policies keep working alongside it. The gateway evaluates every applicable policy before
it forwards a request, and if any one of them blocks, the client gets an error and the backend is never
called. So an asset policy can make the rules **tighter** for one asset, but it can't loosen the baseline.

This lab's baseline:

| Policy | Applies to | Baseline value | Blocked calls get |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Token rate limit** | Models | 100,000 tokens per minute, per caller identity | `429` with `Retry-After` |
| **Request rate limit** | Models and MCP servers | 600 calls per 60 seconds, per caller identity | `429` with `Retry-After` |
| **Content safety** | Models and MCP servers | **Balanced** (`Medium`) for all four categories | `400` |
| **IP filter** | Models and MCP servers | **Allow listed IPs only**: your CIDR ranges | `403` |

A Gateway scope **Cost limit** is one budget across all models; you can add it in
[Enforce cost budgets with per-caller overrides](../07-cost-budgets/README.md). Agent 365 tool threat
protection can't be set at Gateway scope; it applies to individual MCP servers.

> [!WARNING]
> The IP filter applies to **runtime** calls. You keep managing the gateway in the portal and with the Azure
> CLI, so you can always fix the list. But every caller outside it gets `403`: teammates, CI pipelines, hosted
> agents, and your own machine when you switch networks or VPN. Remove it in [Clean up](#clean-up).

## Apply the baseline

Pick one track. Each track creates the same four policies at **Gateway** scope. The `aigateway` extension
doesn't set Gateway scope policies yet, so both scripted tracks call the Azure Resource Manager REST API with
`az rest` against the gateway's `default` workspace.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Add the token rate limit

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **Policies** › **Add policy**. On the **Type** step, select **Token rate limit**, then **Next**.

On the **Scope** step, select **Gateway** ("Apply to the entire gateway workspace, including applicable assets
added later."), then **Next**.

![The Add policy wizard on the Scope step with Gateway selected](../assets/screens/policy-gateway-scope.png "On the Scope step, Gateway applies the policy to every compatible asset, including assets added later.")

On the **Details** step (**Configure** in some portal versions), under **Parameters**, set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Time period** | **Per minute** |
| **Allowed tokens** | `100000` |
| **Counter dimensions** | **Caller identity** |

Select **Create**.

### Add the request rate limit

Select **Add policy** again. Select **Request rate limit**, then **Gateway** scope, and set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Calls** | `600` |
| **Renewal period** | **60 seconds** |
| **Counter dimensions** | **Caller identity** |

Select **Create**.

### Add content safety

Select **Add policy**. Under **Security**, select **Content safety**, then **Gateway** scope. Set **Hate**,
**Violence**, **Self-harm**, and **Sexual** to **Balanced**, then select **Create**.

### Add the IP filter

Select **Add policy**. Under **Security**, select **IP filter**, then **Gateway** scope, and set:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Action** | **Allow listed IPs only** |
| **IP addresses / CIDR ranges** | Your `ALLOWED_CIDRS` value, for example `198.51.100.7/32` |

Use CIDR notation for every entry: `/32` for a single IPv4 address. Check the value against `echo "$MY_IP"`
before you select **Create**.

> **Checkpoint**
> **Policies** lists four policies whose scope is **Gateway**: **Token rate limit**, **Request rate limit**,
> **Content safety**, and **IP filter**.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Read the Gateway scope policies

Gateway scope policies live inline in the `properties.policies` array of the gateway's `default` workspace.
A `PATCH` **replaces the whole array**, so always read it first and keep the policies you didn't mean to
change.

```bash title="Bash"
# Read your subscription ID, and build the management URL of the gateway's default workspace
SUB="$(az account show --query id -o tsv)"
URL="https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
echo "🆔 Subscription: $SUB"

# Read the Gateway scope policies, so that you know what the merge must keep
echo "🛡️ Gateway scope policies on $GATEWAY:"
az rest --method get --url "$URL" --query properties.policies
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read your subscription ID, and build the management URL of the gateway's default workspace
$SUB = az account show --query id -o tsv
$URL = "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/$GATEWAY/workspaces/default`?api-version=2025-09-01-preview"
Write-Host "🆔 Subscription: $SUB"

# Read the Gateway scope policies, so that you know what the merge must keep
Write-Host "🛡️ Gateway scope policies on ${GATEWAY}:"
az rest --method get --url $URL --query properties.policies
```

### Merge the baseline and keep everything else

The baseline replaces any existing policy of the same four types and keeps every other entry, such as a
Gateway scope cost limit.

```bash title="Bash"
# Build the four baseline policies, with your ranges in the IP filter
BASELINE="$(jq -cn --arg cidrs "$ALLOWED_CIDRS" '[
  {"type":"tokenLimit","count":100000,"period":"minute","counterKey":["identity"],"scope":"workspace"},
  {"type":"requestRateLimit","callsPerPeriod":600,"periodSeconds":60,"counterKey":["identity"],"scope":"workspace"},
  {"type":"contentSafety","hateSeverity":"Medium","violenceSeverity":"Medium","sexualSeverity":"Medium","selfHarmSeverity":"Medium"},
  {"type":"ipFilter","action":"Allow","cidrRanges":($cidrs | split(",") | map(gsub("\\s"; "")) | map(select(length > 0)))}
]')"

# Check the allowed ranges before you apply
echo "🛡️ IP filter in the baseline:"
jq '.[] | select(.type == "ipFilter")' <<<"$BASELINE"

# Read the policies, drop any policy of the four baseline types, and add the baseline
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c --argjson baseline "$BASELINE" '
  [(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type | IN($baseline[].type) | not)] + $baseline')"

# Send the merged array back: a PATCH replaces the whole policies array
az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}" --output none &&
  echo "🛡️ Baseline of four policies is on $GATEWAY at Gateway scope"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Build the four baseline policies, with your ranges in the IP filter
$baseline = @(
  [pscustomobject]@{ type = 'tokenLimit'; count = 100000; period = 'minute'; counterKey = @('identity'); scope = 'workspace' }
  [pscustomobject]@{ type = 'requestRateLimit'; callsPerPeriod = 600; periodSeconds = 60; counterKey = @('identity'); scope = 'workspace' }
  [pscustomobject]@{ type = 'contentSafety'; hateSeverity = 'Medium'; violenceSeverity = 'Medium'; sexualSeverity = 'Medium'; selfHarmSeverity = 'Medium' }
  [pscustomobject]@{ type = 'ipFilter'; action = 'Allow'; cidrRanges = @($env:ALLOWED_CIDRS -split ',' | ForEach-Object { $_.Trim() } | Where-Object { $_ }) }
)

# Check the allowed ranges before you apply
Write-Host "🛡️ IP filter in the baseline:"
$baseline | Where-Object type -eq 'ipFilter' | ConvertTo-Json

# Read the policies, drop any policy of the four baseline types, and add the baseline
$current  = az rest --method get --url $URL | ConvertFrom-Json
$policies = @($current.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -notin $baseline.type })
$policies += $baseline

# Send the merged array back from a file, which keeps the JSON quotes intact: a PATCH replaces the whole array
$body = @{ properties = @{ policies = $policies } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress
$body | Set-Content -Path patch.json
az rest --method patch --url $URL --body '@patch.json' --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Baseline of four policies is on $GATEWAY at Gateway scope" }
Remove-Item patch.json
```

> [!NOTE]
> When you create a token or request rate limit at **Gateway** scope, the portal writes `"scope": "workspace"`
> into the policy object. The REST and Policy as code tracks include the same field so that every track creates
> the same policy. `counterKey` is an array: `["identity"]` gives each API key or Entra caller its own counter.
> If the API rejects a field, create the policy once in the portal, then copy its shape from the `GET` response.

> **Checkpoint**
> Running the `GET` again returns your other policies unchanged plus `tokenLimit` and `requestRateLimit` entries
> with `"counterKey": ["identity"]` and `"scope": "workspace"`, and `contentSafety` and `ipFilter` entries
> with your ranges in `cidrRanges`. The service adds `"scope": "resource"` to the last two.

<!-- track: iac | Policy as code -->

### Choose what to declare

Gateway scope policies live on the gateway's `default` workspace. The sample Bicep templates only reference
that workspace as `existing`. Declaring it in your own template would send a `PUT` that replaces the whole
workspace resource, including settings that the template doesn't list. Instead, keep the baseline in a policy
file that goes through code review, and apply it with a script that does the same `GET`, merge, and `PATCH` as
the REST track.

### Review the policy file

<!-- include: infra/baseline-policies.json -->

On GitHub, open [infra/baseline-policies.json](infra/baseline-policies.json).

The `ipFilter` entry holds a placeholder from the `203.0.113.0/24` documentation range. The script never applies
it: it replaces `cidrRanges` with your `ALLOWED_CIDRS` value and stops if that value is missing or isn't in CIDR
notation.

### Preview the change

From the lab folder, print the merged policy array without changing anything:

```bash title="Bash"
# Print the merged policy array, without changing anything on the gateway
./infra/apply-baseline.sh --dry-run &&
  echo "💡 Nothing is applied yet: review the policies above, then apply them"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Print the merged policy array, without changing anything on the gateway
./infra/apply-baseline.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY -DryRun
if ($?) { Write-Host "💡 Nothing is applied yet: review the policies above, then apply them" }
```

The PowerShell script reads `$env:ALLOWED_CIDRS` unless you pass `-AllowedCidrs`.

### Apply it

```bash title="Bash"
# Merge the baseline into the Gateway scope policies, and keep every other policy
./infra/apply-baseline.sh &&
  echo "🛡️ Baseline of four policies is on $GATEWAY at Gateway scope"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Merge the baseline into the Gateway scope policies, and keep every other policy
./infra/apply-baseline.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Baseline of four policies is on $GATEWAY at Gateway scope" }
```

On GitHub, open [infra/apply-baseline.sh](infra/apply-baseline.sh) or
[infra/apply-baseline.ps1](infra/apply-baseline.ps1).

> reviewers see the exact policy array before it's applied.

> **Checkpoint**
> The script prints four Gateway scope policies (`tokenLimit`, `requestRateLimit`, `contentSafety`, and
> `ipFilter`) plus any other policies you already had.

### Call the model from your IP address

Expected output:

```text
🤖 Expect Status: 200 and a reply, because your IP address is on the allow list:
Status: 200
Reply:  A gateway-wide policy baseline is a default set of rules that applies to every asset ...
```

Your call passed all four baseline policies: your IP address is on the allow list, you're far below both rate
limits, and the prompt is benign. If you completed
[Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md), run
`../04-federate-mcp-tools/infra/list-tools.sh learn` (PowerShell:
`../04-federate-mcp-tools/infra/list-tools.ps1 -Server learn`). The MCP server is covered by the same IP
filter, request rate limit, and content safety policies, and it still lists its tools.

### Layer a stricter model policy

Add a deliberately low token limit to your model only, the same one you used in lab 06.
`az aigateway model policy set-token-limit` keeps every other policy on the model:

```bash title="Bash"
# Add a low token limit to the model only: 1,000 tokens per minute for each caller
az aigateway model policy set-token-limit -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" -n "$MODEL" \
  --token-limit 1000 --output none &&
  echo "🛡️ Token limit of 1,000 tokens per minute for each caller is on $MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Add a low token limit to the model only: 1,000 tokens per minute for each caller
az aigateway model policy set-token-limit -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER -n $MODEL `
  --token-limit 1000 --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Token limit of 1,000 tokens per minute for each caller is on $MODEL" }
```

Then send a burst with the script from lab 06:

```bash title="Bash"
# Send a burst of eight requests with the script from lab 06
echo "🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests after three or four requests:"
../06-token-limits/infra/trigger-token-limit.sh "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" 8
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Send a burst of eight requests with the script from lab 06
Write-Host "🚦 Expect 429 Too Many Requests after three or four requests:"
../06-token-limits/infra/trigger-token-limit.ps1 -Model $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL -Requests 8
```

After three or four requests, the gateway returns `429`. The baseline allows 100,000 tokens per minute, but the
model's tighter limit is evaluated too, and it blocks. Remove the model limit and run the burst again:

```bash title="Bash"
# Remove only the token limit from the model, and keep its other policies
az aigateway model policy remove -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" -n "$MODEL" \
  --remove-token-limit true --output none &&
  echo "🧹 Token limit is removed from $MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Remove only the token limit from the model, and keep its other policies
az aigateway model policy remove -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER -n $MODEL `
  --remove-token-limit true --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 Token limit is removed from $MODEL" }
```

All eight requests now return `200`, because only the generous baseline applies.

### See the IP filter block a call (optional)

Point the allow list at a documentation address that can't be yours, call the model, then restore your range.

- **Portal:** in **Policies**, select **Edit** on the **IP filter** policy, set the ranges to
  `203.0.113.10/32`, and save.
- **Script (Bash):** `ALLOWED_CIDRS="203.0.113.10/32" ./infra/apply-baseline.sh`
- **Script (PowerShell):** `./infra/apply-baseline.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY -AllowedCidrs "203.0.113.10/32"`

Run `check-call` again. It now returns `Status: 403`, and the request never reaches the model. Restore your
range in the portal, or run the script again without the override (`./infra/apply-baseline.sh`, or the
PowerShell script without `-AllowedCidrs`), and check that `check-call` returns `200`. If you still see the old
result, wait a minute and retry.

### Watch outcomes in Monitoring

If you configured Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), open
**Monitoring** and compare `400`, `403`, and `429` outcomes before and after the baseline. A sudden rise in
`403` usually means a caller's network isn't on the allow list.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> **Policies** shows four **Gateway** scope policies. Your own call returned `200`, a stricter model limit
> still returned `429` on top of the baseline, and you know how a blocked IP address looks (`403`).

## Go further

- **Cap spend gateway-wide.** Add a **Cost limit** with **Gateway** scope for one budget across all models, as
  described in [Enforce cost budgets with per-caller overrides](../07-cost-budgets/README.md).
- **Tighten tool traffic.** Keep the baseline and add stricter controls to individual MCP servers in
  [Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md) and
  [Protect tool calls with Agent 365 threat protection](../19-tool-threat-protection/README.md).
- **Keep the allow list for inbound traffic.** Inbound private endpoints and turning off public network access
  aren't available for AI Gateway yet, so the IP filter is how you restrict who can call the gateway. To keep
  the gateway's traffic to your backends private, see
  [Lock down backend traffic with private networking](../18-private-networking/README.md).
- **Count Entra callers.** With `identity` counters, each Entra caller gets its own allowance. Move clients to
  keyless calls in [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md).

## Clean up

Remove the baseline before you continue, especially the IP filter: later labs call the gateway from hosted
agents and other networks, which would get `403`. In your own environment, you can keep the other three
policies and replace the IP filter with your organization's egress ranges.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Remove the baseline

Select **Policies**. For each of the four policies with **Gateway** scope, select **Delete**. Remove the
**IP filter** first.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Remove the baseline

```bash
# Read the Gateway scope policies and drop the four baseline types, so that the others stay
POLICIES="$(az rest --method get --url "$URL" | jq -c '[(.properties.policies // [])[]
  | select(.type | IN("tokenLimit","requestRateLimit","contentSafety","ipFilter") | not)]')"

# Send the remaining policies back: a PATCH replaces the whole policies array
az rest --method patch --url "$URL" --body "{\"properties\":{\"policies\":$POLICIES}}" --output none &&
  echo "🧹 Baseline is removed from $GATEWAY"
```

Every other Gateway scope policy stays.

<!-- track: iac | Policy as code -->

### Remove the baseline

```bash title="Bash"
# Remove the policy types listed in baseline-policies.json from Gateway scope, and keep every other policy
./infra/apply-baseline.sh --remove &&
  echo "🧹 Baseline is removed from $GATEWAY"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Remove the policy types listed in baseline-policies.json from Gateway scope, and keep every other policy
./infra/apply-baseline.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY -Remove
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 Baseline is removed from $GATEWAY" }
```

The script removes the policy types listed in `baseline-policies.json` and keeps every other Gateway scope
policy.

<!-- /tracks -->

Keep the gateway, model, and key. The next labs reuse them.

# Issue and rotate runtime API keys

Three callers now use your gateway: the `app-dev` web app, the `support-bot` agent, and a data scientist's
notebook that was shared with the whole company, key included. In this lab you give each caller its own runtime
API key, keep the values in a secret store, rotate the bot's key without taking it offline, and revoke the
leaked notebook key. Because every key is a separate caller identity, you can also see who used what.

![Callers reach the gateway with an API key or a Microsoft Entra token, and the gateway reaches providers with its own credentials](../assets/diagrams/identity-boundaries.svg "Inbound, apps send an api-key header or a Microsoft Entra token. Outbound, the gateway uses its managed identity or a provider key that it stores. Callers never receive backend credentials.")

<!-- widget: request-lifecycle {"focus":"auth"} -->

## Before you begin

<!-- setup: tools sign-in extension clone -->

> [!TIP]
> On the **Bicep + azd** track, `azd up` creates its own gateway, model, and keys, so you can skip this section. You
> need only the one-time setup above.

- Complete [Provision your AI Gateway](../01-provision-gateway/README.md). You need the gateway, its resource
  group, and its runtime URL.
- Recommended: complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md),
  so you have a model alias to call. The checks in this lab call that alias. The gateway answers `404` for an
  alias it doesn't know before it checks the key, so without a real alias the checks can't tell accepted keys
  from rejected keys.
- Permission to manage the gateway's keys, for example **Contributor** on its resource group. Reading a key
  value needs `Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/apiKeys/listSecrets/action`, which **Contributor** includes.
- Optional: an Azure Key Vault that uses Azure RBAC, where you have **Key Vault Secrets Officer**. You can create
  one below.
- Optional, for usage and cost per key: monitoring configured in
  [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md).
- Run the scripts and samples from the lab's folder, `~/ai-gateway/labs/10-api-keys`.


<details>
<summary>No Key Vault yet? Create one for this lab.</summary>

Key Vault names are globally unique, 3 to 24 characters. The vault uses Azure RBAC, and you get
**Key Vault Secrets Officer** so you can write and read secrets. A new role assignment can take a few minutes to
apply.

```bash title="Bash"
# Name the vault with a random number, because Key Vault names are globally unique
export KEY_VAULT="kv-aigw-$RANDOM"

# Create the vault with Azure RBAC authorization, so that roles decide who can read its secrets
az keyvault create -g "$RG" -n "$KEY_VAULT" --enable-rbac-authorization true -o none &&
  echo "✅ Key Vault is ready in $RG, and KEY_VAULT holds its name"

# Give yourself the Key Vault Secrets Officer role on the vault, so that you can write and read secrets
az role assignment create --role "Key Vault Secrets Officer" \
  --assignee "$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)" \
  --scope "$(az keyvault show -n "$KEY_VAULT" --query id -o tsv)" -o none &&
  echo "🛡️ You're a Key Vault Secrets Officer on the vault (it can take a few minutes to apply)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Name the vault with a random number, because Key Vault names are globally unique
$KEY_VAULT = "kv-aigw-$(Get-Random -Maximum 99999)"

# Create the vault with Azure RBAC authorization, so that roles decide who can read its secrets
az keyvault create -g $RG -n $KEY_VAULT --enable-rbac-authorization true -o none
if ($?) { Write-Host "✅ Key Vault is ready in $RG, and KEY_VAULT holds its name" }

# Give yourself the Key Vault Secrets Officer role on the vault, so that you can write and read secrets
az role assignment create --role "Key Vault Secrets Officer" `
  --assignee (az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv) `
  --scope (az keyvault show -n $KEY_VAULT --query id -o tsv) -o none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ You're a Key Vault Secrets Officer on the vault (it can take a few minutes to apply)" }
```

</details>

## How it works

A runtime API key is a gateway resource with a name and two values, **primary** and **secondary**.
Both values work at the same time, which is what makes rotation without downtime possible. Clients send either
value in the `api-key` header. The model endpoint also accepts it as a bearer token, which is how OpenAI SDKs
send their API key, but a request with both headers gets `400`. The gateway validates the key before it applies
policies or forwards the request, so a missing, wrong, rotated, or deleted value, or a suspended key, gets
`401 Unauthorized` and never reaches a model.

A key is gateway-scoped: it grants access to every published model and MCP server on the gateway. Each key is
also a separate caller identity, which token limits, cost limits, and Monitoring use to tell callers apart.
That's why every app, agent, or user should get its own key.

| Task | Portal (**Access** › **Keys**) | Azure CLI (`az aigateway api-key`) | Bicep (`aigateways/apiKeys`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Create a key | **Create API key** | `create` | Declare the key |
| Read a value | **View keys** (primary value) | `list-secrets` (primary and secondary values) | — (never an output) |
| Rotate | **Rotate key** (primary value) | `regenerate --key-type primary` or `--key-type secondary` | — |
| Block temporarily | — | `az rest` `PATCH` with `state` set to `suspended`, then back to `active` | — |
| Revoke | **Delete** | `delete` | — (removing the key from the template doesn't delete it) |

The gateway also has a built-in key named `master`. Don't hand it out; create named keys instead.

## Create a key for each app

Create three keys: `app-dev` for the web app, `support-bot` for the agent, and `old-notebook`, which stands in
for the key that leaked. Pick one track.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Create the first key

1. In the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com), open your gateway and select **Access** › **Keys**.
2. Select **Create API key**.
3. In **Key name**, enter `app-dev`, and select **Create**.
4. The **API key created successfully** dialog shows the value. Select **Copy & done**.

Store the value right away; the next section shows where. After you close the dialog, only people with the
`apiKeys/listSecrets/action` permission, such as Contributors, can display the value again, with **View keys**.

### Create the other two keys

Repeat the steps for `support-bot` and `old-notebook`. Names must be unique, ignoring case; a duplicate gets
`A key named "..." already exists.` The portal derives the key's resource name from **Key name**: lowercase, with
every character other than letters, digits, and hyphens replaced by `-`. Use that resource name with the CLI.

### Load a value in your shell

Select the **…** (**More actions**) button on the `app-dev` row, select **View keys**, and copy the value. Paste it
into your shell for the checks in this lab:

```bash title="Bash"
# Paste the key without showing it, and export it for the checks in this lab
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Paste the key without showing it, and keep it in an environment variable for the checks in this lab
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Create the keys

`create` needs a display name, but the service replaces it with its own, so identify keys by `name`.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create one runtime API key for each caller: the web app, the agent, and the notebook whose key leaks
for KEY in app-dev support-bot old-notebook; do
  az aigateway api-key create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$KEY" --display-name "$KEY" -o none &&
    echo "🔑 API key $KEY is ready"
done

# List the gateway's keys and their state, without their values
echo "🔑 API keys on $GATEWAY:"
az aigateway api-key list -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --query "[].{name:name, state:properties.state}" -o table
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Create one runtime API key for each caller: the web app, the agent, and the notebook whose key leaks
foreach ($key in "app-dev", "support-bot", "old-notebook") {
  az aigateway api-key create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $key --display-name $key -o none
  if ($?) { Write-Host "🔑 API key $key is ready" }
}

# List the gateway's keys and their state, without their values
Write-Host "🔑 API keys on ${GATEWAY}:"
az aigateway api-key list -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --query "[].{name:name, state:properties.state}" -o table
```

The list also shows the built-in `master` key, and every key is `active`. `create`, `list`, and `show` never
return key values.

### Load a value in your shell

`az aigateway api-key list-secrets` returns `primaryKey` and `secondaryKey`. Capture the value in a variable
instead of printing it:

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the primary value of the app-dev key into an environment variable, without showing it
export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n app-dev \
  --query primaryKey -o tsv)"
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the primary value of the app-dev key into an environment variable, without showing it
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n app-dev `
  --query primaryKey -o tsv
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

**What you need:** only the one-time setup from **Before you begin**. This track doesn't use your gateway from earlier
labs: `azd up` creates a new one, so it works on its own.

### Choose what to declare

A key is a child resource of the gateway, `Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/apiKeys`, so a template can declare
which keys exist. Their values aren't in the template: the gateway generates them, and a later deployment keeps
them. Rotating and revoking a key are operations, not declarations, so you run them with the Azure CLI in the next
sections.

### Review the templates

`infra/main.bicep` creates the resource group `rg-<environment name>` and calls the quick start's
[resources.bicep](../quickstart/infra/resources.bicep) for the gateway, the Foundry model, its default alias, and the
`app-first-call` key, so the checks have an alias to call. Then it calls `infra/api-keys.bicep` with the key names:

<!-- include: infra/main.bicep -->

`infra/api-keys.bicep` declares one key for each name. It only references the gateway, so you can also deploy it on
its own to a gateway you already have, with `az deployment group create`:

<!-- include: infra/api-keys.bicep -->

### Deploy with azd up

Move into the lab's folder, create an azd environment named `aigw-lab10` in your current subscription, then provision
everything. It takes about three minutes.

```bash title="Bash"

cd ~/ai-gateway/labs/10-api-keys &&
  echo "📂 Lab folder: $(pwd)"

  echo "📝 azd environment aigw-lab10 deploys to eastus2"

  echo "🚀 Gateway deployed: $(azd env get-value AI_GATEWAY_URL)"
```

### Read the outputs and the key

Set the variables that the next sections and **Verify** use from azd's environment values, and read the `app-dev`
key from the gateway, so that it never shows on screen.

```bash title="Bash"
# Read azd's outputs into the variables that the next sections use, and set the management URL for the az rest calls
export RG="$(azd env get-value AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP)"

```


> **Checkpoint**
> `azd up` ended with `SUCCESS`. The table lists the built-in `master` key, the quick start's `app-first-call`,
> and `app-dev`, `support-bot`, and `old-notebook`, all `active`.

### Change the keys

The key names come from the `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEYS` environment value, a JSON array, with the default in
`infra/main.parameters.json`. To add a key, set the whole list and provision again. Existing keys keep their values.

```bash title="Bash"
# Set the whole list of key names, with a new batch-job key at the end
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEYS '["app-dev","support-bot","old-notebook","batch-job"]' &&
  echo "📝 AI_GATEWAY_API_KEYS lists four keys, with batch-job"

# Provision again: azd creates batch-job, and the existing keys keep their values
azd provision &&
  echo "🔑 API key batch-job is ready, and the other keys keep their values"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Set the whole list of key names, with a new batch-job key at the end
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEYS '["app-dev","support-bot","old-notebook","batch-job"]'
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 AI_GATEWAY_API_KEYS lists four keys, with batch-job" }

# Provision again: azd creates batch-job, and the existing keys keep their values
azd provision
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔑 API key batch-job is ready, and the other keys keep their values" }
```

Removing a name from the list doesn't delete the key: the deployment only creates and updates what the template
declares. Delete a key with the CLI, as in [Revoke a leaked key](#revoke-a-leaked-key).

<!-- /tracks -->

From the lab folder, send one request with the `app-dev` key:

```bash title="Bash"
# Send one request with the app-dev key: the script prints the HTTP status, and only the key's last four characters
echo "🔑 Expect 200 OK for the app-dev key:"
./infra/check-key.sh app-dev
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Send one request with the app-dev key: the script prints the HTTP status, and only the key's last four characters
Write-Host "🔑 Expect 200 OK for the app-dev key:"
./infra/check-key.ps1 -Label app-dev
```

The script sends a tiny Chat Completions request and prints only the last four characters of the key. On GitHub,
open [check-key.sh](infra/check-key.sh) or [check-key.ps1](infra/check-key.ps1).

<!-- include: infra/check-key.sh -->

> **Checkpoint**
> **Access** › **Keys** lists `app-dev`, `support-bot`, and `old-notebook`, and the check prints
> `HTTP 200  accepted` for `app-dev`.

## Store the key outside your code

A runtime key opens every model and MCP server on the gateway, so treat it like a password:

- **Local development:** set an environment variable for the session, as in this lab, and read it in code, for
  example `os.environ["AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY"]` in Python. If you keep it in a `.env` file, add the file to
  `.gitignore`.
- **Hosted apps:** keep the value in Azure Key Vault. App Service and Azure Functions resolve
  [Key Vault references](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/app-service/app-service-key-vault-references) in app
  settings, and Azure Container Apps can
  [reference Key Vault secrets](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/container-apps/manage-secrets).
- **Pipelines:** use the secret store of your CI system, or read the value from Key Vault at run time.
- **Never** put the value in source code, a committed `.env` file, build logs, notebooks, chat, or tickets.

If you set `KEY_VAULT`, store the `app-dev` and `support-bot` values there. The commands print only the secret
IDs. Each secret is named `<key>-api-key`, which is the name the rotation script updates later.

```bash title="Bash"
# Copy the primary value of each key into a Key Vault secret named <key>-api-key, and print only the secret IDs
echo "🆔 Key Vault secret IDs:"
for KEY in app-dev support-bot; do
  az keyvault secret set --vault-name "$KEY_VAULT" -n "$KEY-api-key" \
    --value "$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$KEY" --query primaryKey -o tsv)" \
    --tags aigateway-key="$KEY" key-type=primary --query id -o tsv
done
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Copy the primary value of each key into a Key Vault secret named <key>-api-key, and print only the secret IDs
Write-Host "🆔 Key Vault secret IDs:"
foreach ($key in "app-dev", "support-bot") {
  $value = az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $key --query primaryKey -o tsv
  az keyvault secret set --vault-name $KEY_VAULT -n "$key-api-key" --value $value `
    --tags aigateway-key=$key key-type=primary --query id -o tsv
}

# Clear the last key value from your session
Remove-Variable value
```

An app, or you, then reads the value from the vault instead of from the gateway:

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the app-dev value from Key Vault instead of from the gateway, without showing it
export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az keyvault secret show --vault-name "$KEY_VAULT" -n app-dev-api-key --query value -o tsv)"
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the app-dev value from Key Vault instead of from the gateway, without showing it
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az keyvault secret show --vault-name $KEY_VAULT -n app-dev-api-key --query value -o tsv
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

> [!NOTE]
> The portal track can store the values the same way: run the commands above, or add the secrets to the vault in
> the Azure portal.

## Rotate a key without downtime

Rotate keys on a schedule, and whenever someone who had a value leaves the team. Regenerating a value invalidates
that value only, and right away. The trick is to regenerate the value that no client is using.

On the Bicep + azd track, follow the **Azure CLI** track. A later `azd provision` keeps the regenerated values.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Save the current value

You use the old value later to prove that it stopped working. On the `support-bot` row, select **…**
(**More actions**) › **View keys**, copy the value, and paste it into your shell:

```bash title="Bash"
# Paste the current support-bot value without showing it, to prove later that the rotation retired it
read -rsp "Current support-bot value: " OLD_SUPPORT_BOT && echo
echo "🔑 Current support-bot value: in OLD_SUPPORT_BOT (${#OLD_SUPPORT_BOT} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Paste the current support-bot value without showing it, to prove later that the rotation retired it
$OLD_SUPPORT_BOT = Read-Host "Current support-bot value" -MaskInput
Write-Host "🔑 Current support-bot value: in OLD_SUPPORT_BOT ($($OLD_SUPPORT_BOT.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

### Rotate the key

1. On the `support-bot` row, select **…** (**More actions**) › **Rotate key**.
2. The `Rotate "support-bot" key?` dialog warns that the current value stops working immediately and that the
   new value is displayed once. Select **Rotate**.
3. In **API key rotated successfully**, copy the new value and update the client, or the `support-bot-api-key`
   secret in Key Vault.

> [!NOTE]
> The portal rotates the **primary** value in place, so a client that still sends the old value gets `401` until
> you update it. To rotate without downtime from the portal, replace the key instead: create `support-bot-v2`,
> move the client to it, and then delete `support-bot`. The new key is a new caller identity, so move any
> cost-limit overrides to it, and expect Monitoring to report it separately. The CLI track avoids both trade-offs
> with the secondary value.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Save the current value

Clients use the primary value today. Keep it so you can prove later that it stopped working:

```bash title="Bash"
# Save the primary value that clients use today, without showing it, to prove later that it stopped working
OLD_SUPPORT_BOT="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n support-bot \
  --query primaryKey -o tsv)"
echo "🔑 Current primary value: in OLD_SUPPORT_BOT (${#OLD_SUPPORT_BOT} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Save the primary value that clients use today, without showing it, to prove later that it stopped working
$OLD_SUPPORT_BOT = az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n support-bot `
  --query primaryKey -o tsv
Write-Host "🔑 Current primary value: in OLD_SUPPORT_BOT ($($OLD_SUPPORT_BOT.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

### Regenerate the unused secondary value

No client uses the secondary value, so regenerating it breaks nothing:

```bash title="Bash"
# Regenerate the secondary value, which no client uses yet: the script shows only the last four characters of it
./infra/rotate-key.sh support-bot secondary &&
  echo "🔑 API key support-bot has a new secondary value, and clients on the primary keep working"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Regenerate the secondary value, which no client uses yet: the script shows only the last four characters of it
# To also update the support-bot-api-key secret, remove the # before -KeyVault
./infra/rotate-key.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY -KeyName support-bot -KeyType secondary # -KeyVault $KEY_VAULT
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔑 API key support-bot has a new secondary value, and clients on the primary keep working" }
```

The script runs `az aigateway api-key regenerate --key-type secondary`, which replaces only the secondary value,
and reads the new value with `az aigateway api-key list-secrets`. It prints only the last four characters of the
new value. If `KEY_VAULT` is set in Bash, or you pass `-KeyVault` in PowerShell, it also
writes the new value to the `support-bot-api-key` secret. On GitHub, open [rotate-key.sh](infra/rotate-key.sh) or
[rotate-key.ps1](infra/rotate-key.ps1).

<!-- include: infra/rotate-key.sh -->

### Move the client to the secondary value

Update the client's configuration to the new secondary value and restart it, or let it reload the Key Vault
secret. Both values are valid now, so no request fails during the switch. The old primary value still works:

```bash title="Bash"
# Check that the old primary value still works, so that clients can move over without failed requests
echo "🔑 Expect 200 OK for the old primary value, until you regenerate it:"
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$OLD_SUPPORT_BOT" ./infra/check-key.sh "old primary"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Check that the old primary value still works, so that clients can move over without failed requests
Write-Host "🔑 Expect 200 OK for the old primary value, until you regenerate it:"
./infra/check-key.ps1 -ApiKey $OLD_SUPPORT_BOT -Label "old primary"
```

### Regenerate the primary value

When every client uses the secondary value, regenerate the primary. This invalidates the old value, wherever it
might have been copied:

```bash title="Bash"
# Regenerate the primary value, so that the old value stops working wherever it was copied
./infra/rotate-key.sh support-bot primary &&
  echo "🔑 API key support-bot has a new primary value, and the old one stopped working"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Regenerate the primary value, so that the old value stops working wherever it was copied
# To also update the support-bot-api-key secret, remove the # before -KeyVault
./infra/rotate-key.ps1 -ResourceGroup $RG -Gateway $GATEWAY -KeyName support-bot -KeyType primary # -KeyVault $KEY_VAULT
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔑 API key support-bot has a new primary value, and the old one stopped working" }
```

Next time, rotate in the other direction: regenerate the primary, move clients to it, then regenerate the
secondary. With Key Vault, the secret always holds the newest value, so clients that reload it move along
automatically.

<!-- /tracks -->

> **Checkpoint**
> `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$OLD_SUPPORT_BOT" ./infra/check-key.sh "rotated value"` (or
> `./infra/check-key.ps1 -ApiKey $OLD_SUPPORT_BOT -Label "rotated value"`) prints `HTTP 401`.

## Revoke a leaked key

When a key leaks, revoke it first and investigate afterward. Deleting a key invalidates both of its values
immediately, and anyone who holds them gets `401`. Pick one track.

On the Bicep + azd track, follow the **Azure CLI** track. Then remove `old-notebook` from the template's list, and
keep any names you added, so that a later `azd provision` doesn't create it again, with new values:

```bash title="Bash"
# Keep only the keys you still need in the list, so that a later azd provision doesn't create old-notebook again
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEYS '["app-dev","support-bot"]' &&
  echo "📝 AI_GATEWAY_API_KEYS lists app-dev and support-bot"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Keep only the keys you still need in the list, so that a later azd provision doesn't create old-notebook again
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEYS '["app-dev","support-bot"]'
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 AI_GATEWAY_API_KEYS lists app-dev and support-bot" }
```

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Save the leaked value

You use it to prove that the key no longer works. On the `old-notebook` row, select **…** (**More actions**) ›
**View keys**, copy the value, and paste it into your shell:

```bash title="Bash"
# Paste the leaked value without showing it, to prove later that the gateway rejects it
read -rsp "Leaked value: " LEAKED_KEY && echo
echo "🔑 Leaked value: in LEAKED_KEY (${#LEAKED_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Paste the leaked value without showing it, to prove later that the gateway rejects it
$LEAKED_KEY = Read-Host "Leaked value" -MaskInput
Write-Host "🔑 Leaked value: in LEAKED_KEY ($($LEAKED_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

### Delete the key

Select the check box on the `old-notebook` row, and then select **Delete**. The `Delete "old-notebook" key?`
dialog warns that applications using the key will no longer authenticate to the gateway and that the action
can't be undone. Select **Delete**.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Save the leaked value and delete the key

```bash title="Bash"
# Save the leaked primary value without showing it, to prove later that the gateway rejects it
LEAKED_KEY="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n old-notebook \
  --query primaryKey -o tsv)"
echo "🔑 Leaked value: in LEAKED_KEY (${#LEAKED_KEY} characters, not shown)"

# Delete the key: both of its values stop working right away
az aigateway api-key delete -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n old-notebook --yes &&
  echo "🧹 API key old-notebook is deleted"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Save the leaked primary value without showing it, to prove later that the gateway rejects it
$LEAKED_KEY = az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n old-notebook `
  --query primaryKey -o tsv
Write-Host "🔑 Leaked value: in LEAKED_KEY ($($LEAKED_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"

# Delete the key: both of its values stop working right away
az aigateway api-key delete -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n old-notebook --yes
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 API key old-notebook is deleted" }
```

### Suspend a key instead

To block a key while you investigate, without deleting it, set its `state` to `suspended`. Calls with the key
get `401` until you set it back to `active`. The **Verify** section expects `support-bot` to work, so set it
back to `active` before you continue. The `aigateway` extension can't change a key's state yet, so call the Azure
Resource Manager REST API with `az rest`:

```bash title="Bash"
# Suspend the support-bot key: calls with it get 401 until you set it back to active
STATE="$(az rest --method patch --url "$GW/apiKeys/support-bot?$API" \
  --body '{"properties":{"state":"suspended"}}' --query properties.state -o tsv)" &&
  echo "🔑 API key support-bot is $STATE"

# Later, set the key back to active, so that it works again
STATE="$(az rest --method patch --url "$GW/apiKeys/support-bot?$API" \
  --body '{"properties":{"state":"active"}}' --query properties.state -o tsv)" &&
  echo "🔑 API key support-bot is $STATE"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Suspend the support-bot key: calls with it get 401 until you set it back to active
# The body goes in a file, so that PowerShell passes the JSON quotes to az intact
'{"properties":{"state":"suspended"}}' | Set-Content keystate.json
$STATE = az rest --method patch --url "$GW/apiKeys/support-bot?$API" --body "@keystate.json" --query properties.state -o tsv
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔑 API key support-bot is $STATE" }

# Later, set the key back to active, so that it works again
'{"properties":{"state":"active"}}' | Set-Content keystate.json
$STATE = az rest --method patch --url "$GW/apiKeys/support-bot?$API" --body "@keystate.json" --query properties.state -o tsv
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔑 API key support-bot is $STATE" }
Remove-Item keystate.json
```

The commands print the new state: `🔑 API key support-bot is suspended`, and then
`🔑 API key support-bot is active`.

<!-- /tracks -->

Then clean up after the leak: remove the value from the notebook and its history, and check
**Monitoring** for calls made with the key.

> [!NOTE]
> If the caller behind a leaked key must keep its identity, for example because a cost-limit override or
> Monitoring history is tied to it, regenerate **both** values instead of deleting the key. Run
> `./infra/rotate-key.sh <key> primary` and then `./infra/rotate-key.sh <key> secondary` (or the PowerShell
> script with `-KeyType`), and give the caller the new value.

## See usage and cost per key

Each key is a caller identity, so Monitoring can break usage down by key. This needs the monitoring setup from
[Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md) and a few requests with each key.

1. Select **Monitoring** › **Models**.
2. **Active caller identities** counts the API keys and Microsoft Entra identities with observed activity.
3. **Model usage by caller identity** compares caller identities by estimated model cost, tokens, and calls.
4. Use the **All caller identities** filter to scope the page to one key, for example `support-bot`. Keys appear
   by name, marked **API key**.

The same identity drives enforcement. A **Cost limit** counted by **Caller identity** gives each key its own
budget:

![A Cost limit policy with a $100 monthly budget counted by caller identity](../assets/screens/policy-cost-limit-details.png "A Cost limit counted by caller identity: each API key gets its own $100 monthly budget, and a caller that reaches it gets 403 LlmCostQuotaExceeded.")

To set budgets and limits per key, continue with
[Enforce cost budgets with per-caller overrides](../07-cost-budgets/README.md).

## When to move to Microsoft Entra ID

API keys are the fastest way to start, but the docs don't recommend them for production.

| | Runtime API key | Microsoft Entra ID with Azure RBAC |
|---|---|---|
| What the gateway sees | One named key | A user, agent, or workload identity in your tenant |
| What it can call | Every published model and MCP server | What its role grants: **AI Gateway User** (models and tools), **AI Gateway Models User**, or **AI Gateway Tools User**, at gateway, alias, or MCP server scope |
| Secret to protect | The key value | None with a managed identity; tokens are short-lived |
| Rotation | You rotate and redistribute values | Microsoft Entra ID issues new tokens |
| Good fit | Prototypes, labs, and tools that only accept a key | Production apps, agents, and per-user access |

Move to Microsoft Entra ID with
[Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md).

Run the checks from the lab folder. Only current values should get through; the rotated value, the deleted key,
and a request without a key should all get `401`.

## Go further

- **Prompt for the key in MCP clients.** VS Code can ask for the key when it starts an MCP server instead of
  storing it in `mcp.json`. See [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md).
- **Get a rotation reminder.** Set an expiry date on the Key Vault secret with
  `az keyvault secret set-attributes --expires`, and subscribe to the vault's `SecretNearExpiry` event.
- **Automate rotation.** Run the rotation script from a scheduled pipeline that signs in with a workload
  identity, with a pause between the secondary and primary steps for clients to reload.
- **Limit each key.** Give every key its own token allowance with
  [Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md).

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Delete the test keys

Delete any other keys you created for testing, such as `support-bot-v2`:

```bash
# Delete a test key, for example support-bot-v2 from the portal's rotation
az aigateway api-key delete -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n support-bot-v2 --yes &&
  echo "🧹 API key support-bot-v2 is deleted"
```

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Delete everything azd created

In the `ai-gateway/labs/10-api-keys` folder, delete the resource group with the gateway, the Foundry account, and the
keys. [`--purge`](../SETUP.md#delete-what-azd-created) also purges the soft-deleted Foundry account. It takes about
ten minutes.

```bash
# Delete everything that azd up created, and purge the Foundry account
azd down --purge --force &&
  echo "🧹 Everything that azd up created is deleted"
```

The Bicep + azd track of lab 07 creates its own `app-dev` and `support-bot` keys, so you don't need to keep these.

<!-- /tracks -->

If you created a Key Vault only for this lab, delete it. Key Vault keeps deleted vaults for a retention period
and reserves the name; purge it if you want to reuse the name right away:

```bash
# Delete the vault: Key Vault keeps it for a retention period, and reserves its name
az keyvault delete -n "$KEY_VAULT" &&
  echo "🧹 Key Vault is deleted, and its name stays reserved until you purge it"

# Purge the deleted vault, so that you can reuse its name right away
az keyvault purge -n "$KEY_VAULT" &&
  echo "🧹 Key Vault is purged"
```

Clear the key values from your shell with `unset AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY OLD_SUPPORT_BOT LEAKED_KEY SUPPORT_BOT`
(Bash) or `Remove-Variable OLD_SUPPORT_BOT, LEAKED_KEY, SUPPORT_BOT; Remove-Item Env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`
(PowerShell). Delete the gateway from earlier labs only when you finish all labs, as described in
[Provision your AI Gateway](../01-provision-gateway/README.md#clean-up). `azd down` doesn't touch it, because the
Bicep + azd track created its own gateway.

  `support-bot` different budgets.
- [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md): see usage and cost for each key.
- Docs: [Security and identity in AI Gateway](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/security-identity).

# Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC

A security review of your AI platform found runtime API keys in `.env` files, CI logs, and a shared notebook.
Every key grants every model and tool on the gateway, nobody can say which person is behind a key, and
rotation means chasing every team. The platform team wants callers to use **their own Microsoft Entra
identity** instead: access granted by Azure RBAC, scoped to one model alias or MCP server when needed, and
removed automatically when someone leaves a group. In this lab you grant a data-plane role, call a model with
an Entra token from the playground, the command line, and code, and see what the gateway answers when the role
is missing.

![Callers authenticate inbound to the gateway, and the gateway authenticates outbound to each backend](../assets/diagrams/identity-boundaries.svg "Inbound, callers present a Microsoft Entra token and Azure RBAC decides which models and tools they can use. Outbound, the gateway uses its own identity, which you configure in lab 12.")

<!-- widget: request-lifecycle -->

## Before you begin

<!-- setup: tools sign-in extension clone -->

> [!TIP]

> this section. You need only the one-time setup above.

- Complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md). You need a gateway with at least
  one model alias.
- Your Azure CLI sign-in in the tenant that holds the gateway.
- Permission to **create role assignments** on the gateway: **Owner**, **User Access Administrator**, or
  **Role Based Access Control Administrator**. **Contributor** can manage the gateway but can't grant roles.
  If you don't have one of these, ask an administrator to run the role assignment step for you.
- For the Code track, one of: Python 3.9 or later, Node.js 22.18 or later, or the .NET 8 SDK or later.
- Run the scripts and samples from the lab's folder, `~/ai-gateway/labs/11-entra-rbac`.

You don't need an API key in this lab. Set these variables once. Every track and the **Verify** section reuse
them.

```bash title="Bash"
# Name your gateway from lab 02, its model provider, and the backend model under that provider
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"
export PROVIDER="<provider-name>"          # for example foundry-models
export MODEL="<model-name>"                # the backend model name under that provider

# Read the gateway's resource ID, which role assignments use as their scope, and its runtime URL
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query id -o tsv)"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
echo "🆔 Gateway ID: $GATEWAY_ID"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Read the alias that apps send in the model field: for Foundry imports, it matches the deployment's model name
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(az aigateway model show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" \
  -n "$MODEL" --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv)"
echo "🏷️ Model alias: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Read your object ID in Microsoft Entra ID, so that you can grant yourself a role
export MY_OBJECT_ID="$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)"
echo "🪪 Your object ID: $MY_OBJECT_ID"

# Remove any API key from your shell, to prove that nothing in this lab uses one
unset AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY
echo "🔑 AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY is unset, so every call in this lab is keyless"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"

$GATEWAY  = "<gateway>"

$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = az aigateway model show -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER `
  -n $MODEL --query properties.deployment.modelName -o tsv
Write-Host "🏷️ Model alias: $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Read your object ID in Microsoft Entra ID, so that you can grant yourself a role

Write-Host "🪪 Your object ID: $MY_OBJECT_ID"
```
