## Go further

- **Query the token metrics.** Token and cost metrics land in the Azure Monitor workspace linked to Application
  Insights as `azure.ai_gateway.client.token.usage` and `azure.ai_gateway.client.token.cost`, with labels such as
  `gen_ai.request.model` and `gen_ai.token.type`. Docs show PromQL in its underscore form, for example
  `sum by (gen_ai_request_model) (gen_ai_client_token_usage)`. Check which names your backend received before you
  build on them. [Attribute tokens and cost with OpenTelemetry](../14-otel-chargeback/README.md) queries them.
- **Alert on what you can act on.** Start with token usage spikes, backend authentication failures, and telemetry
  export failures. Route each alert to an owner who can investigate the gateway, backend, policy, or destination.
- **Send telemetry somewhere else.** Use **Custom OpenTelemetry destination** to export to any OTLP endpoint. Store
  any credential headers as secrets.
- **Capture payloads carefully.** **Settings** › **Logging** has **Log request and response payloads**. It's off by
  default because prompts and responses can be sensitive and add volume.

# Attribute tokens and cost with OpenTelemetry

Three teams and a partner tenant share your gateway. Some call it with API keys, others with Microsoft Entra ID.
Finance wants a monthly report of who used which model and what it cost. In this lab you export the right token
claims with the gateway's telemetry, send traffic as both kinds of caller, and build that report from the data
Application Insights already collects.

![AI Gateway exports metrics, logs, and traces with caller attributes](../assets/diagrams/observability.svg "Token claims ride along with the telemetry the gateway already exports, so every log, root trace, and token metric can name its caller.")

## Before you begin

> assignment, so you can skip this section. You need only the one-time setup above, and permission to create role

  gateway exports all three signals to Application Insights with an OpenTelemetry exporter.

  user has **AI Gateway Models User** (or **AI Gateway User**) on the gateway or on the model alias.
- Permission to change the gateway, for example **Contributor** on its resource group, and **Log Analytics Reader**
  on the workspace behind Application Insights.
- Python 3.10 or later.
- Run the scripts and samples from the lab's folder, `~/ai-gateway/labs/14-otel-chargeback`.

## How it works

Every request already carries its caller. An API key call is attributed by the key's ID
(`azure.ai_gateway.api_key_id`). A Microsoft Entra call carries a validated JWT, and **token claim attributes**
copy the claims you pick into telemetry as `azure.ai_gateway.identity.claims.<claim>`. For each claim you choose the
signals independently: **logs**, **root traces**, and **observed token and cost metrics**.

Logs hold the per-request token usage the backend reported, so they're the best source for a detailed report.
Metrics are cheaper to query over long ranges, but every exported claim value becomes a label, so keep metrics to
claims with a bounded number of values.

Estimated cost is **observed tokens × public pricing**. Treat it as an allocation key and reconcile the total with
provider billing or Azure Cost Management.

| Claim | Identifies | Recommended preset | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tid` | The caller's tenant | Logs, Traces, Metrics | Tenant or customer totals. With `oid`, the dashboard's Entra caller. |
| `oid` | The user, service principal, or managed identity | Logs, Traces, Metrics | Per-caller totals |
| `appid` (v1 tokens), `azp` (v2 tokens) | The client application | Logs, Traces | Per-app chargeback. This lab adds Metrics. |
| A custom claim, such as `cost_center` | Whatever your tokens carry | You choose | Team chargeback, if the claim is in the token |

## Choose the claims to export

You keep the recommended preset and add **Metrics** for `appid` and `azp`, so token and cost metrics can also be
split by client app.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Open the token claim attributes

In the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com), select your gateway, then **Monitoring** › **Settings**.
On the **Logging** tab, find **Token claim attributes**: "Add selected JWT claims to exported logs, root traces, and
observed token and cost metrics." Each row is a claim with **Logs**, **Traces**, and **Metrics** checkboxes.

![Monitoring settings with token claim attributes for tid, oid, appid, and azp](../assets/screens/monitoring-token-claim-attributes.png "The recommended preset: tid and oid go to logs, traces, and metrics; appid and azp go to logs and traces.")

> [!NOTE]
> No **Token claim attributes** section? It's only shown for OpenTelemetry exporters. Reconfigure monitoring as
> in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md). If the table is empty ("No token claims are
> included in exported telemetry"), add `tid`, `oid`, `appid`, and `azp` with **Add claim**.

### Add metrics for the client app

Select **Metrics** for `appid` and for `azp`. Leave `tid` and `oid` on all three signals: the dashboard needs
both on metrics to attribute Entra callers. Changes save automatically while "Saving changes…" is shown. Every
claim needs at least one signal.

> [!TIP]
> **Add claim** adds a row (the placeholder suggests `cost_center`) that starts with **Logs** and **Traces**.
> Only add claims that your callers' tokens carry. The next section shows how to check.

<!-- track: rest | REST API -->

### Read the current configuration

The claim attributes live on the gateway's telemetry exporter. The `aigateway` extension doesn't manage telemetry
exporters yet, so call the Azure Resource Manager REST API with `az rest`. List the exporters and their claims:

```bash title="Bash"
# List the gateway's telemetry exporters, with the kind of each one and the token claims it exports
echo "📊 Telemetry exporters and their claims:"
az rest --method get --url "$WS/telemetryExporters?$API" \
  --query "value[].{name:name, kind:properties.kind, claims:properties.telemetry.attributes}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# List the gateway's telemetry exporters, with the kind of each one and the token claims it exports
Write-Host "📊 Telemetry exporters and their claims:"
az rest --method get --url "$WS/telemetryExporters?$API" `
  --query "value[].{name:name, kind:properties.kind, claims:properties.telemetry.attributes}"
```

Expected output: one exporter of kind `OpenTelemetry`, usually named `appinsights`, whose claims list `tid`, `oid`,
`appid`, and `azp`, each with its `signals`. A kind of `applicationInsights` is the legacy exporter. Reconfigure
monitoring as in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md) first.

### Change it in the portal

Make the change in the portal: open **Monitoring** › **Settings** › **Logging** › **Token claim attributes** and
select **Metrics** for `appid` and `azp`. To automate it, declare the claims in the exporter's
`telemetry.attributes` list, as the **Bicep + azd** track does. Then run the `GET` again. Both claims now list
`metrics` in their `signals`.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

**What you need:** only the one-time setup from **Before you begin**. This track doesn't use your gateway from the
earlier labs: `azd up` creates a new one, so it works on its own.

### Choose what to declare

The templates reuse lab 13's and lab 11's. Lab 13's
[monitoring.bicep](../13-monitoring/infra/monitoring.bicep) creates the Application Insights destination with OTLP
ingestion turned on, and its [otel-exporter.bicep](../13-monitoring/infra/otel-exporter.bicep) creates the gateway's
OpenTelemetry exporter. The claim attributes are part of that exporter, in its `telemetry.attributes` list. Each
entry names a claim in `source` (`kind` is `claims`, `value` is the claim name, such as `tid`) and lists the signals
that carry it in `signals`: `logs`, `traces`, and `metrics`.

`infra/main.bicep` passes the recommended preset and adds `metrics` for `appid` and `azp`. It also calls lab 11's
[role-assignment.bicep](../11-entra-rbac/infra/role-assignment.bicep) to grant you **AI Gateway Models User** on
the gateway, for the Entra calls in the next section. As in lab 13, `azure.yaml` grants the gateway's managed
identity **Monitoring Metrics Publisher** on the Data Collection Rule in a `postprovision` hook, because the rule's
managed resource group blocks deployments.

### Review the templates

[resources.bicep](../quickstart/infra/resources.bicep) for the gateway, the Foundry model, its default alias, and the
`app-first-call` key. Then it calls lab 13's templates with the claims to export, and lab 11's role assignment for
the identity that runs azd. `azd` passes your object ID in `AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID`:

### Deploy with azd up

Move into the lab's folder, create an azd environment named `aigw-lab14` in your current subscription, then provision

  echo "📂 Lab folder: $(pwd)"

### Change the claims

Each `azd provision` applies the claims in `infra/main.bicep` again. To go back to the recommended preset, without
metrics for the client app, set `CLIENT_APP_METRICS` to `false` and provision. Then run the `GET` again: `appid` and
`azp` list only `logs` and `traces`. If you try it now, set it back to `true` and provision again before you continue,
so that the PromQL section can split metrics by client app.

```bash title="Bash"
# Export the client app claims, appid and azp, to logs and traces only, as in the recommended preset
azd env set CLIENT_APP_METRICS false &&
  echo "📝 CLIENT_APP_METRICS is false"

# Apply the claims in infra/main.bicep to the gateway's exporter again
azd provision &&
  echo "🚀 Provisioned: appid and azp export to logs and traces only"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Export the client app claims, appid and azp, to logs and traces only, as in the recommended preset
azd env set CLIENT_APP_METRICS false
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 CLIENT_APP_METRICS is false" }

# Apply the claims in infra/main.bicep to the gateway's exporter again
azd provision
if ($?) { Write-Host "🚀 Provisioned: appid and azp export to logs and traces only" }
```

To export a custom claim, such as `cost_center`, add an entry to the `claimAttributes` list in `infra/main.bicep`
and run `azd provision`. Check that your callers' tokens carry it first, as the next section shows. For the chargeback
report, follow the **REST API** track: it uses the variables you set here.

## Send attributed traffic

<!-- steps -->

### Check what your token carries

A claim only appears in telemetry if the validated token has it. Decode your own token locally and look:

```bash title="Bash"
# Get a token for AI Gateway's audience, and decode its claims locally, including the custom cost_center claim
echo "🪪 Claims in your token for AI Gateway:"
az account get-access-token --resource https://azure-api.net/aigateway --query accessToken -o tsv \
  | python3 infra/show_claims.py cost_center
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Get a token for AI Gateway's audience, and decode its claims locally, including the custom cost_center claim
Write-Host "🪪 Claims in your token for AI Gateway:"
az account get-access-token --resource https://azure-api.net/aigateway --query accessToken -o tsv |
  python infra/show_claims.py cost_center
```

On GitHub, open [infra/show_claims.py](infra/show_claims.py). The script prints `aud`, `ver`, `tid`, `oid`, `appid`,
`azp`, and `idtyp`, plus any claim names you pass. Nothing leaves your machine.

Expected output: `aud` is `https://azure-api.net/aigateway`, `tid` and `oid` are GUIDs, and either `appid` (v1
token) or `azp` (v2 token) holds the Azure CLI's client ID. `cost_center` is `(not in token)`.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Tokens for AI Gateway are issued for its audience, `https://azure-api.net/aigateway`. Before you add a custom
> claim such as `cost_center` to **Token claim attributes**, decode a real token from that caller and confirm the
> claim is there. If it isn't, map client apps (`appid` or `azp`) to cost centers in your report instead.

### Call the gateway as two callers

Run the script for your shell. It sends five requests with your API key and five with your Entra token, each with an
`x-correlation-id` header.

```bash title="Bash"
# Send five requests with your API key and five with your Entra token, and print the status of each one
echo "📊 Requests by caller:"
./infra/send-attributed-traffic.sh "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" 5
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Send five requests with your API key and five with your Entra token, and print the status of each one
Write-Host "📊 Requests by caller:"
./infra/send-attributed-traffic.ps1 -Model $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL -Requests 5
```

On GitHub, open [send-attributed-traffic.sh](infra/send-attributed-traffic.sh) or
[send-attributed-traffic.ps1](infra/send-attributed-traffic.ps1).

Expected output: ten rows, all `200`, alternating between `api-key` and `entra`. A `401` or `403` on the `entra`
rows means your role assignment is missing or hasn't propagated yet.

### Find your callers in Monitoring

Wait a few minutes, then open **Monitoring** › **Models** with **1H** selected. In
**Model usage by caller identity**, your API key and your Entra identity appear as separate rows with their own
tokens and estimated cost. Entra callers are resolved from `tid` and `oid`. Callers with neither an API key nor
those claims show as **Unattributed**.

Then select **Traces**, open one of the Entra requests, and expand its log under **Correlated logs**. Look for
`azure.ai_gateway.identity.claims.tid`, `...oid`, and `...appid` or `...azp`. An API key request shows
`azure.ai_gateway.api_key_id` instead.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> Both callers appear on the **Models** tab, and an Entra request's correlated log shows its claims.

## Build a chargeback report

The report groups the token usage in request logs by owner and prices it with a price list you control. The query
is in [infra/chargeback.kql](infra/chargeback.kql):

<!-- include: infra/chargeback.kql kusto -->

On GitHub, open [infra/chargeback.kql](infra/chargeback.kql).

<!-- steps -->

### Prepare a price list

Copy [infra/prices.example.json](infra/prices.example.json) to `prices.json`. Replace `<model-name>` with each value
in the report's `Model` column, which is the model that answered (for example a versioned name), and copy current
prices per million tokens from your provider's pricing page or agreement. A versioned name such as
`my-model-2026-01-01` matches the key `my-model`.

> [!CAUTION]
> The example prices are placeholders. Don't publish a report until you've replaced them with real prices.

<!-- /steps -->

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Run the query

In the [Azure portal](https://portal.azure.com), open the Log Analytics workspace behind your Application Insights
resource and select **Logs**. Switch to **KQL mode**, paste the contents of `infra/chargeback.kql`, and select
**Run**. You get one row per tenant, object ID, client app, API key, alias, and model.

### Export it

Select **Export** and choose CSV with all columns. Save the file as `usage.csv` in the lab folder.

### Price it

```bash title="Bash"
# Price the exported usage with your price list, group it by tenant, client app, and API key, and save the report

```

```powershell title="PowerShell"

```

### Run the query

Send the query to the Log Analytics query API through Azure Resource Manager and save the response:

```bash title="Bash"
# Wrap the KQL query in a JSON request body, in a file because the query spans many lines
jq -n --rawfile q infra/chargeback.kql '{query: $q}' > query.json &&
  echo "📄 Query body written to query.json"

# Run the query on the Log Analytics workspace through Azure Resource Manager, and save the response
az rest --method post \
  --url "https://management.azure.com${LAW_ID}/query?api-version=2017-10-01" \
  --body @query.json > usage.json &&
  echo "📄 Usage by caller saved to usage.json"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"

@{ query = Get-Content infra/chargeback.kql -Raw } | ConvertTo-Json | Set-Content query.json
if ($?) { Write-Host "📄 Query body written to query.json" }

# Run the query on the Log Analytics workspace through Azure Resource Manager, and save the response

  --url "https://management.azure.com$LAW_ID/query?api-version=2017-10-01" `
  --body "@query.json" | Set-Content usage.json

```

The response holds a `tables` array with `columns` and `rows`, which the report script reads directly.

Expected output: a table with one row for your API key (`(none)` in `Tenant` and `ClientApp`) and one for your

## Query token and cost metrics with PromQL

Token and cost metrics land in the Azure Monitor workspace (managed Prometheus) linked to Application Insights, as
`azure.ai_gateway.client.token.usage` and `azure.ai_gateway.client.token.cost`. They're the same metrics the
dashboard reads, and they carry the claims you enabled for **Metrics** as labels.

<!-- steps -->

### Find the Prometheus endpoint

```bash title="Bash"
# Find the Azure Monitor workspace (managed Prometheus) linked to Application Insights, and its query endpoint
AMW_ID="$(az resource show --ids "$APPI_ID" --api-version 2020-02-02 --query properties.AzureMonitorWorkspaceResourceId -o tsv)"
PROM_URL="$(az resource show --ids "$AMW_ID" --api-version 2023-04-03 --query properties.metrics.prometheusQueryEndpoint -o tsv)"
echo "🌐 Prometheus endpoint: $PROM_URL"

# Get a Microsoft Entra token for the Prometheus query API
PROM_TOKEN="$(az account get-access-token --resource https://prometheus.monitor.azure.com --query accessToken -o tsv)"
echo "🪪 Token acquired: in PROM_TOKEN (${#PROM_TOKEN} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Find the Azure Monitor workspace (managed Prometheus) linked to Application Insights, and its query endpoint
$AMW_ID     = az resource show --ids $APPI_ID --api-version 2020-02-02 --query properties.AzureMonitorWorkspaceResourceId -o tsv
$PROM_URL   = az resource show --ids $AMW_ID --api-version 2023-04-03 --query properties.metrics.prometheusQueryEndpoint -o tsv
Write-Host "🌐 Prometheus endpoint: $PROM_URL"

# Get a Microsoft Entra token for the Prometheus query API
$PROM_TOKEN = az account get-access-token --resource https://prometheus.monitor.azure.com --query accessToken -o tsv
Write-Host "🪪 Token acquired: in PROM_TOKEN ($($PROM_TOKEN.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

### Query token usage for the last day

The metric names contain dots, so the selector uses quoted names. The `microsoft.appresourceid` label limits the
query to your Application Insights resource.

```bash title="Bash"
# Select the token usage metric of your Application Insights resource, with quoted names because they contain dots
SELECTOR="{__name__=\"azure.ai_gateway.client.token.usage\",\"microsoft.appresourceid\"=\"$(echo "$APPI_ID" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')\"}"

# Query the tokens of the last day, and print one row per model, token type, API key, tenant, and client app
echo "📊 Tokens in the last day, by model, token type, API key, tenant, and client app:"
curl -sS -G "${PROM_URL%/}/api/v1/query" -H "Authorization: Bearer $PROM_TOKEN" \
  --data-urlencode "query=increase(${SELECTOR}[1d])" \
  | jq -r '.data.result[] | [.metric["gen_ai.response.model"], .metric["gen_ai.token.type"],
      (.metric["azure.ai_gateway.api_key_id"] // "-"), (.metric["azure.ai_gateway.identity.claims.tid"] // "-"),
      (.metric["azure.ai_gateway.identity.claims.appid"] // .metric["azure.ai_gateway.identity.claims.azp"] // "-"),
      (.value[1] | tonumber | round)] | @tsv'
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Select the token usage metric of your Application Insights resource, with quoted names because they contain dots
$selector = '{__name__="azure.ai_gateway.client.token.usage","microsoft.appresourceid"="' + $APPI_ID.ToLower() + '"}'

# Query the tokens of the last day from the Prometheus query API
$result = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "$($PROM_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/api/v1/query" `
  -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $PROM_TOKEN" } -Body @{ query = 'increase(' + $selector + '[1d])' }

# Print one row per model, token type, API key, tenant, and client app
if ($?) { Write-Host "📊 Tokens in the last day, by model, token type, API key, tenant, and client app:" }
$result.data.result | ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{
  Model     = $_.metric.'gen_ai.response.model'
  TokenType = $_.metric.'gen_ai.token.type'
  ApiKeyId  = $_.metric.'azure.ai_gateway.api_key_id'
  Tenant    = $_.metric.'azure.ai_gateway.identity.claims.tid'
  ClientApp = $_.metric.'azure.ai_gateway.identity.claims.appid' ?? $_.metric.'azure.ai_gateway.identity.claims.azp'
  Tokens    = [math]::Round([double]$_.value[1]) } } | Format-Table
```

Expected output: rows per model, token type, and caller. Your Entra rows carry your tenant ID and the client app.

> [!WARNING]
> Don't add up every token type. A model reports totals and details (for example `total_tokens` and
> `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`) next to input and output, so a plain sum double counts. Use the total
> type if there is one, otherwise input plus output. Cached tokens are usually a subset of input tokens.

### Query estimated cost

Replace `azure.ai_gateway.client.token.usage` with `azure.ai_gateway.client.token.cost` and run the query again. Each
series carries `azure.ai_gateway.currency`. Series with `azure.ai_gateway.price_missing="true"` had no public price,
so their cost isn't counted.

<!-- /steps -->

> [!NOTE]
> Counters are cumulative, and `increase()` extrapolates and can miss the first sample of a brand new series, so
> treat short-range metric results as approximate. The docs show PromQL in its underscore form,
> `sum by (gen_ai_request_model) (gen_ai_client_token_usage)`, which is how some OTLP backends store these names.
> If a query returns nothing, list the names your backend stored with `count by (__name__) ({__name__=~".*token.*"})`.

<!-- steps -->

### Compare the report with the dashboard

Open **Monitoring** › **Models** with **24H** selected. The input and output tokens of your two callers in
**Model usage by caller identity** are in the same range as their rows in `chargeback.csv`.

### Confirm the client app label

Run the PromQL query again. Your Entra rows show a client app ID, which comes from the **Metrics** signal you
enabled for `appid` and `azp`.

## Go further

- **Enforce what you measure.** A cost limit can give a different budget to a specific Entra identity or to a
  **Custom token claim combination**, such as an `appid` value. See
  [Enforce cost budgets with per-caller overrides](../07-cost-budgets/README.md).
- **Send telemetry to another backend.** In the setup wizard, **Custom OpenTelemetry destination** takes a
  **Metrics endpoint**, **Logs endpoint**, and **Traces endpoint**, such as a collector, Grafana, Datadog, or any
  OTLP service. Authenticate with **Custom headers** (values are masked and never shown again after saving) or a
  **Managed identity** with a token audience. Claims are exported the same way. The built-in dashboard only reads
  Application Insights, so with a custom destination you build these views in that platform.
- **Fan out with a collector.** To keep claims in one place and send them to several backends, point the gateway at
  your own OpenTelemetry Collector and route from there.
- **Keep metric cardinality in check.** Every distinct claim value is a new series. Put high-cardinality claims such
  as `oid` on logs and traces for detail, and keep metrics to `tid`, client apps, and bounded custom claims.
- **Schedule the report.** Run the REST track monthly from a pipeline with a managed identity that has
  **Log Analytics Reader**, and store `chargeback.csv` with your finance data.

# Connect agent frameworks to models and tools

Your teams build agents with different frameworks, and each one wires its own model keys and tool servers. Nobody
can say which agent called what, and a policy change means touching every codebase. In this lab you point three
popular frameworks at one gateway: two URLs and one header, and every model and tool call the agent makes is
governed and observable in the same place.

![Agents call models and MCP tools through AI Gateway](../assets/diagrams/architecture.svg "Agents keep their framework. The gateway sits between them and every model and tool they call.")

<!-- widget: request-lifecycle -->

## Before you begin

<!-- setup: tools clone -->

- Complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md). You need the
  gateway URL, a callable alias, and a runtime key. Create a dedicated key for this agent under **Access** ›
  **Keys**, for example `docs-agent`, so its traffic is easy to find.
- Complete [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md). The samples use the
  `learn` MCP server from that lab. Any MCP server on your gateway works.
- Python 3.10 or later. The samples were tested together on Python 3.13 with the versions in
  [infra/requirements.txt](infra/requirements.txt).
- Optional: monitoring from [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), to see the agent's calls.
- Run the scripts and samples from the lab's folder, `~/ai-gateway/labs/15-agent-frameworks`.

## How it works

Agent frameworks talk to models through an OpenAI-compatible client and to tools through an MCP client. Point both at
the gateway. The model client takes the runtime key as its API key, which it sends as a bearer token that the
model endpoint accepts. The MCP client sends the same key in the `api-key` header, the only place the MCP endpoint
reads it.

The framework still owns orchestration, memory, and state. The gateway authenticates each call, applies the policies
on the alias, the MCP server, and the gateway, routes the alias to its provider, and records telemetry for every call
that leaves the agent. Changing a model, a policy, or a tool list then needs no agent code change.

| Framework | Model client | MCP tools | Model API |
|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft Agent Framework | `OpenAIChatClient` | `MCPStreamableHTTPTool` | Responses |
| OpenAI Agents SDK | `OpenAIChatCompletionsModel` with `AsyncOpenAI` | `MCPServerStreamableHttp` | Chat Completions |
| LangChain and LangGraph | `ChatOpenAI` | `MultiServerMCPClient` (langchain-mcp-adapters) | Chat Completions |

All three use the same two endpoints. The gateway serves both model APIs on the model endpoint:

- Model: `https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/models/openai/v1`
- MCP: `https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/toolservers/<server-name>/mcp`

## Point the model client at the gateway

Each framework takes the gateway's model endpoint as its base URL, the alias as the model name, and the runtime key
as its API key.

<!-- steps -->

### Configure the model client

```python title="Agent Framework"
# The model endpoint accepts the key as the SDK's bearer token. Adding an api-key header as well gets a 400.
client = OpenAIChatClient(
    model=model,
    base_url=f"{gateway_url}/default/models/openai/v1/",
    api_key=api_key,
)
```

```python title="OpenAI Agents SDK"
client = AsyncOpenAI(
    base_url=f"{gateway_url}/default/models/openai/v1",
    api_key=api_key,
)
# ...
model=OpenAIChatCompletionsModel(model=model, openai_client=client),
```

```python title="LangGraph"
model = ChatOpenAI(
    model=model_name,
    base_url=f"{gateway_url}/default/models/openai/v1",
    api_key=api_key,
)
```

Don't add an `api-key` default header to the model client as well: the gateway rejects a request that has both an
`api-key` and an `Authorization` header with `400`.

> [!NOTE]
> The OpenAI Agents SDK sample turns off the SDK's built-in tracing, which otherwise exports traces to OpenAI. The
> gateway already records each model and tool call.

<!-- /steps -->

## Add the gateway's MCP tools

The MCP client connects to one MCP server on the gateway and sends the same key. The agent only sees the tools that
the server publishes, after the gateway's tool controls.

<!-- steps -->

### Connect to the MCP endpoint

```python title="Agent Framework"
mcp_tool = MCPStreamableHTTPTool(
    name="gateway-tools",
    url=f"{gateway_url}/default/toolservers/{server}/mcp",
    static_headers={"api-key": api_key},
    approval_mode="never_require",
    request_timeout=60,
)
```

```python title="OpenAI Agents SDK"
async with MCPServerStreamableHttp(
    name="gateway-tools",
    params={
        "url": f"{gateway_url}/default/toolservers/{server}/mcp",
        "headers": {"api-key": api_key},
        "timeout": 60,
    },
    cache_tools_list=True,
    client_session_timeout_seconds=60,
) as mcp_server:
```

```python title="LangGraph"
mcp_client = MultiServerMCPClient(
    {
        "gateway-tools": {
            "transport": "streamable_http",
            "url": f"{gateway_url}/default/toolservers/{server}/mcp",
            "headers": {"api-key": api_key},
        }
    }
)
tools = await mcp_client.get_tools()
```

The `learn` tools only read documentation, so the Agent Framework sample runs them without asking for approval. For
tools that change data, set `approval_mode="always_require"` on the MCP tool and handle the approval requests in your
app. Also narrow the tool list on the gateway, as in
[Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md), so every agent gets the same limits.

### Build the agent

```python title="Agent Framework"
async with mcp_tool:
    agent = Agent(client=client, name="docs-agent", instructions=INSTRUCTIONS, tools=mcp_tool)
    result = await agent.run(question)
    print(result.text)
```

```python title="OpenAI Agents SDK"
agent = Agent(
    name="docs-agent",
    instructions=INSTRUCTIONS,
    model=OpenAIChatCompletionsModel(model=model, openai_client=client),
    mcp_servers=[mcp_server],
)
result = await Runner.run(agent, question)
print(result.final_output)
```

```python title="LangGraph"
agent = create_agent(model, tools, system_prompt=INSTRUCTIONS)
result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": question}]})
print(result["messages"][-1].content)
```

`create_agent` from LangChain builds a LangGraph graph that loops between the model and the tools. LangGraph keeps
orchestration and state, while AI Gateway applies policies and records telemetry for every call leaving the agent.

## Verify

### Prove the gateway is in the path

Run one sample with a wrong key. The gateway rejects the agent's first call with `401`, before any model or tool
runs.

```bash title="Bash"
# Run the LangGraph sample with a wrong key, for this command only, because your shell's value wins over .env
echo "🚦 Expect 401 Unauthorized: the gateway rejects the agent's first call"
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="not-a-key" python langgraph_agent.py
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Run the LangGraph sample with a wrong key, then remove it from your shell so that the samples read .env again
Write-Host "🚦 Expect 401 Unauthorized: the gateway rejects the agent's first call"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = "not-a-key"; python langgraph_agent.py; Remove-Item Env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY
```

Expected output: a traceback that ends with a `401 Unauthorized` error for the MCP endpoint, because each sample
connects to the MCP server before it calls the model. A key set in your shell takes precedence over `.env`.

### See the agent in Monitoring

If you set up monitoring in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), wait a few minutes and
open **Monitoring**. On **Overview**, **Model calls** and **Tool calls** both grew. On **Tools**, the `learn`
server shows up in **Usage by tool server**, and **Tool usage by caller identity** shows the agent's key. A run
usually makes at least two model calls: one that asks for a tool and one that writes the answer. Open
**Traces** to see each call with its gateway policies.

## Go further

- **Give each agent an identity.** Create one runtime key per agent, as in
  [Issue and rotate runtime API keys](../10-api-keys/README.md), so Monitoring and cost limits can tell agents apart.
  For production, drop keys: send a Microsoft Entra token for `https://azure-api.net/aigateway` from the agent's
  managed identity or agent identity, with the **AI Gateway User** role, as in
  [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md).
- **Govern the agent, not the code.** Add a token limit to the alias with
  [Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md), or a request rate limit to the MCP
  server. The agent gets `429` responses without any code change, so handle `Retry-After` in long-running agents.
- **Swap models behind the alias.** Retarget the alias to another model or provider, as in
  [Publish models from any provider behind stable aliases](../03-multi-provider-aliases/README.md). The agents keep
  working with the same `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL`.
- **Use .NET.** The [.NET hosted agent sample](https://github.com/Azure-Samples/simple-foundry-hosted-agent-dotnet-aigateway)
  connects Microsoft Agent Framework for .NET to a gateway. With the AI Gateway tier, pass the runtime key as the
  client's API key and don't add an `api-key` header to model calls.
- **Other SDKs.** For the GitHub Copilot SDK and other frameworks, use their model and MCP configuration points with
  the same endpoints, and confirm the endpoint formats and authentication they support.

## Clean up

- Delete `infra/.env`, because it holds a key, and `infra/.venv` if you don't need it.
- If you created a key just for this lab, revoke it under **Access** › **Keys**.

Keep the gateway, the alias, and the `learn` MCP server. Other labs reuse them.

For the errors you might hit in this lab, with their likely causes and fixes, see
[Troubleshooting](../TROUBLESHOOTING.md#lab-15-agent-frameworks).

# Deploy a Foundry hosted agent behind AI Gateway

Your team wants to run an agent in Microsoft Foundry, but the platform team needs every model call and every tool
call to be governed and visible in one place. In this lab you deploy a small Microsoft Agent Framework agent to
Foundry Hosted Agents. Its Foundry project has no model deployments and no tool connections: the agent reaches its
model and its tools only through AI Gateway, with a key of its own.

![A Foundry hosted agent calls a model alias and the Learn MCP server through AI Gateway](../assets/diagrams/hosted-agent.svg "Foundry runs the agent. AI Gateway governs its model calls and its MCP tool calls.")

## Before you begin

<!-- setup: tools sign-in extension clone -->

- Complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md) and
  [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md). The agent calls the alias from lab 02 and the `learn` MCP
  server from lab 04.
- An Azure subscription where you can create a resource group and a Foundry resource, and assign roles, for example
  **Owner**. azd gives the agent's identity access to its Foundry project.
- The [Azure Developer CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/developer/azure-developer-cli/install-azd) (azd) 1.34.2
  or later, and Python 3.13 or later. With [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) installed,
  azd uses it to create the agent's virtual environment.

> [!WARNING]
> `azd up` creates a Foundry resource, and the hosted agent and its model calls are billable. Run
> [Clean up](#clean-up) when you're done.

## How it works

The agent lives in [`infra/`](infra/), a complete azd project:

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`infra/azure.yaml`](infra/azure.yaml) | Declares a Foundry project with no model deployments, and the hosted agent `gateway-agent`: Python 3.13, code deploy, 0.5 CPU, 1 GiB, Responses protocol |
| [`infra/src/gateway-agent/main.py`](infra/src/gateway-agent/main.py) | The agent: one model client and one MCP tool, both pointing at the gateway |
| [`infra/src/gateway-agent/requirements.txt`](infra/src/gateway-agent/requirements.txt) | Pinned dependencies, compiled from `requirements.in`. Foundry builds the agent from this file. |

The agent has two outbound paths, and both end at AI Gateway:

- **Model.** An `OpenAIChatClient` points at the gateway's model endpoint, `/default/models/openai/v1/`, and sends
  your lab 02 alias as `model`. The runtime key is the SDK's API key, so it travels as `Authorization: Bearer`.
  The model endpoint accepts a runtime key either that way or in an `api-key` header.
- **Tools.** An `MCPStreamableHTTPTool` points at the gateway's `/default/toolservers/learn/mcp` endpoint with the
  same key in the `api-key` header. The MCP endpoint accepts keys only in that header: a bearer token there must be
  a Microsoft Entra token.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Send a key in one header only. If a request carries both `api-key` and `Authorization`, the gateway rejects it
> with `400` and "Specify either an API key or an Authorization header, not both". Older samples set a placeholder
> API key and add an `api-key` header, which the OpenAI SDK turns into exactly that request.

| Piece | Name in this lab | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Model alias | Your alias from lab 02, in `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL` | AI Gateway |
| MCP server | `learn`, at `/default/toolservers/learn/mcp` | AI Gateway |
| Runtime API key | `hosted-agent` | AI Gateway |
| Foundry resource and project | In resource group `rg-<env>`; the project is named after the azd environment | Foundry, created by azd |
| Hosted agent | `gateway-agent` | Foundry, created by azd |

Foundry runs the agent. AI Gateway decides what the agent may call, counts its tokens, and records every call.

## Give the agent its own key

A dedicated key makes the agent a separate caller identity: its token limits, cost limits, and Monitoring data
don't mix with other apps. Pick one track.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Create the key

1. In the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com), open your gateway and select **Access** › **Keys**.
2. Select **Create API key**.
3. In **Key name**, enter `hosted-agent`, and select **Create**.
4. The **API key created successfully** dialog shows the value. Select **Copy & done**.

### Load the values in your shell

Paste the key without echoing it, then set the gateway URL from the gateway's **Overview** page and the alias from
lab 02:

```bash title="Bash"
# Paste the hosted-agent key without showing it, and export it for azd
read -rsp "hosted-agent key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"

# Set the gateway's runtime URL from its Overview page, and the alias that the agent sends as its model
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://<gateway>.<region>-01.ai.gateway.azure.com"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="<model-alias>"    # the alias from lab 02
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"
echo "🏷️ Model alias: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Paste the hosted-agent key without showing it
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "hosted-agent key" -MaskInput
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"

# Set the gateway's runtime URL from its Overview page, and the alias that the agent sends as its model
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://<gateway>.<region>-01.ai.gateway.azure.com"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = "<model-alias>"    # the alias from lab 02
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"
Write-Host "🏷️ Model alias: $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Set your variables

```bash title="Bash"
# Set your resource group, your gateway, and the alias that the agent sends as its model
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="<model-alias>"    # the alias from lab 02
echo "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY in $RG, alias $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Read the gateway's runtime URL, which the agent calls for its model and its tools
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Set your resource group, your gateway, and the alias that the agent sends as its model
$RG                   = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY              = "<gateway>"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = "<model-alias>"    # the alias from lab 02
Write-Host "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY in $RG, alias $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Read the gateway's runtime URL, which the agent calls for its model and its tools
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"
```

### Create the key and load its value

`api-key create` returns metadata only. `list-secrets` reads the value straight into a variable, so it never
appears on screen.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create the hosted-agent key, which makes the agent a caller identity of its own
az aigateway api-key create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n hosted-agent --display-name hosted-agent -o none &&
  echo "🔑 API key hosted-agent is ready"

# Read the key's value straight into a variable, so that it never shows on screen
export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n hosted-agent \
  --query primaryKey -o tsv)"
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Create the hosted-agent key, which makes the agent a caller identity of its own
az aigateway api-key create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n hosted-agent --display-name hosted-agent -o none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔑 API key hosted-agent is ready" }

# Read the key's value straight into a variable, so that it never shows on screen
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n hosted-agent `
  --query primaryKey -o tsv
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

<!-- /tracks -->

> **Checkpoint**
> **Access** › **Keys** lists `hosted-agent` as active, and your shell has `AI_GATEWAY_URL`, `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL`,
> and `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`.

## Configure the azd project

<!-- steps -->

### Get the lab files

Move into the lab's `infra` folder and install the Foundry extensions for azd:

```bash
# Move into the lab's azd project
cd ~/ai-gateway/labs/16-foundry-hosted-agent/infra &&
  echo "📂 Lab folder: ~/ai-gateway/labs/16-foundry-hosted-agent/infra"

# Install the Foundry extensions for azd, which add the azd ai agent commands
azd ext install microsoft.foundry &&
  echo "🧩 The Foundry extensions for azd are installed"
```

`microsoft.foundry` installs the Foundry extensions for azd, including `azure.ai.agents`, which adds the
`azd ai agent` commands.

### Create an azd environment

The environment name also names the resource group, `rg-<env>`, and the Foundry project. Choose a region where
Foundry Hosted Agents are available, for example `eastus2`.

```bash
# Create the azd environment, which also names the resource group, rg-aigw-lab16, and the Foundry project
azd env new aigw-lab16 --location eastus2 &&
  echo "📝 azd environment aigw-lab16 deploys to eastus2"
```

### Pass the gateway settings to the agent

[`azure.yaml`](infra/azure.yaml) maps four azd environment values to the agent's environment variables:

```yaml
env:
  AI_GATEWAY_URL: ${AI_GATEWAY_URL}
  AI_GATEWAY_MODEL: ${AI_GATEWAY_MODEL}
  AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY: ${AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY}
  AI_GATEWAY_MCP_SERVER: ${AI_GATEWAY_MCP_SERVER}
```

Set them from your shell:

```bash title="Bash"
# Store the gateway's runtime URL and the alias in the azd environment
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_URL "$AI_GATEWAY_URL" &&
  echo "📝 AI_GATEWAY_URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_MODEL "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" &&
  echo "📝 AI_GATEWAY_MODEL: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Store the hosted-agent key, which azd passes to the agent as an environment variable
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY "$AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" &&
  echo "🔑 Key: in the azd environment as AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"

# Point the agent at the learn MCP server from lab 04
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_MCP_SERVER learn &&
  echo "📝 AI_GATEWAY_MCP_SERVER: learn"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Store the gateway's runtime URL and the alias in the azd environment
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_URL $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 AI_GATEWAY_URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL" }
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_MODEL $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 AI_GATEWAY_MODEL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" }

# Store the hosted-agent key, which azd passes to the agent as an environment variable
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔑 Key: in the azd environment as AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)" }

# Point the agent at the learn MCP server from lab 04
azd env set AI_GATEWAY_MCP_SERVER learn
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 AI_GATEWAY_MCP_SERVER: learn" }
```

azd keeps the values in `.azure/aigw-lab16/.env`, which Git ignores, and passes them to the agent locally and in
Foundry. Anyone who can read the agent's definition in Foundry can also read the key; see
[Go further](#go-further) for keyless options.

<!-- /steps -->

## Read the agent

[`main.py`](infra/src/gateway-agent/main.py) is the whole agent. The model client and the MCP tool are the only
places it talks to the network, and both point at the gateway:

```python
client = OpenAIChatClient(
    model=model,
    base_url=f"{gateway_url}/default/models/openai/v1/",
    api_key=api_key,
)

tools = MCPStreamableHTTPTool(
    name="gateway-tools",
    url=f"{gateway_url}/default/toolservers/{mcp_server}/mcp",
    static_headers={"api-key": api_key},
    approval_mode="never_require",
    load_prompts=False,
    request_timeout=60,
)
```

`ResponsesHostServer` serves the agent on the Responses protocol at port 8088, the same way locally and in Foundry.
The agent sets `store` to `false` on its model calls, because the hosting server already keeps the conversation
history. Tool approval is off because the Learn tools are read-only.

<!-- include: infra/src/gateway-agent/main.py -->

On GitHub, open [main.py](infra/src/gateway-agent/main.py) and [azure.yaml](infra/azure.yaml).

## Run the agent locally

<!-- steps -->

### Start the agent

From the `infra` folder:

```bash
# Start the agent locally: azd installs requirements.txt in a virtual environment and opens Agent Inspector
echo "🚀 Starting the agent on http://localhost:8088 (Ctrl+C to stop)"
azd ai agent run
```

azd creates a virtual environment, installs `requirements.txt`, starts the agent on `http://localhost:8088`, and
opens Agent Inspector, where you can chat with the agent and see its tool calls. Add `--no-client` to skip Agent
Inspector.

### Ask a question

In a second terminal, from the same folder:

```bash
# Ask the local agent a question: it calls the model and the Learn tools through the gateway
echo "🤖 The local agent's answer:"
azd ai agent invoke --local "Which Learn page explains Azure API Management key concepts? One sentence and the URL."
```

Expected output: an answer that cites a `learn.microsoft.com` URL, for example:

```text
🤖 The local agent's answer:
[local] The Learn page "What is Azure API Management?" explains its key concepts.
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/api-management/api-management-key-concepts
```

Behind that answer, the agent made a model call that asked for a tool, one or more Learn tool calls, and a model
call that wrote the answer, all through the gateway. Stop the agent with **Ctrl+C**.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The local agent answers with a Microsoft Learn URL.

## Deploy to Foundry

<!-- steps -->

### Provision and deploy

```bash
# Provision the Foundry resource and project, upload the agent's code, and create the hosted agent
azd up &&
  echo "🚀 The hosted agent gateway-agent is deployed to Foundry"
```

azd asks for a subscription if the environment doesn't have one. Then it creates `rg-aigw-lab16` with a Foundry
resource and a project that has hosted agents enabled, uploads `src/gateway-agent` as a code package, and creates the
hosted agent. Foundry builds it from `requirements.txt`. It takes about five minutes, and ends with:

```text
SUCCESS: Your application was deployed to Azure in 2 minutes 31 seconds.
🚀 The hosted agent gateway-agent is deployed to Foundry
```

### Invoke the hosted agent

```bash
# Ask the hosted agent the same question in Foundry, where its calls still go through the gateway
echo "🤖 The hosted agent's answer:"
azd ai agent invoke gateway-agent "Which Learn page explains Azure API Management key concepts? One sentence and the URL."
```

Expected output: the same kind of answer, now from Foundry. The first call can take 10 to 20 seconds while the
agent starts.

```text
🤖 The hosted agent's answer:
Agent:        gateway-agent (remote)
...
[gateway-agent] The Learn page titled "What is Azure API Management?" explains Azure API Management key concepts.
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/api-management/api-management-key-concepts
```

azd keeps the conversation, so a second `invoke`, such as `"Shorten that to ten words."`, continues it. Add
`--new-conversation` to start over.

### Find the agent in Foundry

```bash
# Show the hosted agent's status, its identity, its Responses endpoint, and its Playground URL
echo "📊 Hosted agent gateway-agent:"
azd ai agent show gateway-agent
```

The output shows **Status** `active`, the agent's own identity, its Responses endpoint, and a **Playground URL**.
Open that URL to chat with the agent in the Foundry portal.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> `azd ai agent show gateway-agent` reports `active`, and `azd ai agent invoke` returns an answer with a Learn URL.

## See the agent in Monitoring

The `hosted-agent` key is a caller identity of its own. With monitoring set up as in
[Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), invoke the agent a few times, wait a few minutes, then
open **Monitoring** in the portal:

- **Models**: use the **All caller identities** filter to select `hosted-agent`. You see the agent's calls, tokens,
  and estimated cost for your alias.
- **Tools**: the `learn` tool server under **Usage by tool server**, with the tools the agent called under
  **Top tools within tool servers**.
- **Traces**: one row per model or tool call, with the policies the gateway applied.

## Cap the agent's tokens

Give the agent's alias a strict token limit counted per caller identity, then watch the gateway enforce it without
any change to the agent. Pick one track.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Add the token limit

1. Select **Policies** › **Add policy**.
2. On **Type**, select **Token rate limit**.
3. On **Scope**, select **Individual assets** and pick your alias.
4. On **Configure**, set **Time period** to **Per minute**, **Allowed tokens** to `1000`, and
   **Counter dimensions** to **Caller identity**, then select **Create**.

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Add the token limit

Find the alias by the name that apps send, which works even when a portal-created alias contains `/`.
`az aigateway model-alias update --policies` replaces the alias's whole policy array, so these commands keep its
other policies:

```bash title="Bash"
# Find the alias's resource name from the name that apps send
ALIAS_NAME="$(az aigateway model-alias list -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" \
  --query "[?properties.aliasName=='$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL'].name | [0]" -o tsv)"
echo "🏷️ Alias resource name: $ALIAS_NAME"

# Write the alias's other policies, plus a limit of 1,000 tokens per minute counted per caller identity, to a file
az aigateway model-alias show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$ALIAS_NAME" -o json \
  | jq -c '[(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "tokenLimit") | del(.scope)] + [{type:"tokenLimit",period:"minute",count:1000,counterKey:["identity"]}]' > policies.json

# Replace the alias's whole policy array with the file's, and print the new array
az aigateway model-alias update -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$ALIAS_NAME" --policies @policies.json \
  --query properties.policies &&
  echo "🛡️ Token limit of 1,000 tokens per minute per caller identity is on $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Find the alias's resource name from the name that apps send
$ALIAS_NAME = az aigateway model-alias list -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY `
  --query "[?properties.aliasName=='$($env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL)'].name | [0]" -o tsv
Write-Host "🏷️ Alias resource name: $ALIAS_NAME"

# Write the alias's other policies, plus a limit of 1,000 tokens per minute counted per caller identity, to a file
$alias = az aigateway model-alias show -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $ALIAS_NAME -o json | ConvertFrom-Json
$p = @($alias.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'tokenLimit' } |
  Select-Object * -ExcludeProperty scope) +
  @(@{ type = 'tokenLimit'; period = 'minute'; count = 1000; counterKey = @('identity') })
ConvertTo-Json -InputObject $p -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content policies.json

# Replace the alias's whole policy array with the file's, and print the new array
az aigateway model-alias update -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $ALIAS_NAME --policies "@policies.json" `
  --query properties.policies
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Token limit of 1,000 tokens per minute per caller identity is on $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" }
```

<!-- /tracks -->

<!-- steps -->

### Trigger the limit

Wait about 30 seconds for the policy to apply, then invoke the hosted agent twice:

```bash
# Invoke the hosted agent twice, each time in a new conversation: the first invoke uses well over 1,000 tokens
echo "🚦 Expect the second invoke to fail with a 429 from the gateway's token limit"
azd ai agent invoke gateway-agent --new-conversation "Summarize Azure API Management in three sentences with Learn links."
azd ai agent invoke gateway-agent --new-conversation "Summarize Azure API Management in three sentences with Learn links."
```

The gateway counts tokens when a call completes, so the first invoke usually succeeds and uses well over 1,000
tokens, because Learn tool results are long. The second invoke fails, and the agent reports the gateway's `429`:

```text
ERROR: agent failed (server_error): (... Error code: 429 - {'statusCode': 429, 'message': 'Token limit is exceeded. Try again in <n> seconds.'} ...)
```

The counter belongs to the `hosted-agent` key. Your other apps, with their own keys, keep their full allowance on
the same alias. For more on limits, see
[Throttle tokens per caller with token limits](../06-token-limits/README.md).

### Remove the limit

In the portal, select **Policies**, open the **Token rate limit** you created for your alias, and delete it. With
the CLI, remove the `tokenLimit` policy the same way you added it:

```bash title="Bash"
# Write the alias's policies, without the token limit, to a file
az aigateway model-alias show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$ALIAS_NAME" -o json \
  | jq -c '[(.properties.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "tokenLimit") | del(.scope)]' > policies.json

# Replace the alias's whole policy array with the file's, then delete the file
az aigateway model-alias update -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$ALIAS_NAME" --policies @policies.json \
  --query properties.policies &&
  echo "🧹 The token limit is removed from $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
rm policies.json
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Write the alias's policies, without the token limit, to a file
$alias = az aigateway model-alias show -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $ALIAS_NAME -o json | ConvertFrom-Json
$p = @($alias.properties.policies | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'tokenLimit' } |
  Select-Object * -ExcludeProperty scope)
ConvertTo-Json -InputObject $p -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content policies.json

# Replace the alias's whole policy array with the file's, then delete the file
az aigateway model-alias update -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $ALIAS_NAME --policies "@policies.json" `
  --query properties.policies
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧹 The token limit is removed from $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" }
Remove-Item policies.json
```

If your alias had its own token limit before this lab, the CLI commands remove it too: add it back with the count
it had. When the alias has no policies left, the update prints no policies, only the 🧹 line.

<!-- /steps -->

## Verify

> **Verify**
> - `azd ai agent invoke --local` and `azd ai agent invoke` both return an answer with a Microsoft Learn URL.
> - The Foundry project has no model deployments, yet the agent answers: its model calls go through the gateway.
> - With the token limit in place, the agent got `429` from the gateway without any code change.
> - With monitoring set up, **Monitoring** › **Models** shows calls from the `hosted-agent` caller identity.

## Go further

- **Go keyless.** The hosted agent has its own Microsoft Entra identity, shown by `azd ai agent show gateway-agent`.
  Give it the **AI Gateway User** role, which covers models and MCP tools, as in
  [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md). Then send a Microsoft Entra token from
  `DefaultAzureCredential` to both endpoints instead of the key.
- **Keep the key out of the agent definition.** Store it in Azure Key Vault and read it at startup with the agent's
  identity, instead of passing it as an environment variable.
- **Lock down egress.** Foundry can restrict where a hosted agent may connect. Allow only your gateway's host name,
  so the gateway is the agent's only way out. See the
  [egress control sample](https://github.com/microsoft-foundry/foundry-samples/tree/main/samples/python/hosted-agents/agent-framework/responses/18-egress-control).
- **Use another framework.** Swap the agent's internals for the OpenAI Agents SDK or LangGraph, as in
  [Connect agent frameworks to models and tools](../15-agent-frameworks/README.md). The gateway settings stay the
  same.
- **Charge the agent back.** Attribute its tokens and estimated cost with
  [Attribute tokens and cost with OpenTelemetry](../14-otel-chargeback/README.md).

## Clean up

Delete the Foundry resource group and the hosted agent. `--purge` also purges the soft-deleted Foundry resource so
you can reuse its name:

```bash
# Delete the resource group with the Foundry resource and the hosted agent, and purge the soft-deleted resource
azd down --purge &&
  echo "🧹 The Foundry resource group and the hosted agent are deleted"
```

Then delete the `hosted-agent` key: in **Access** › **Keys**, select **…** (**More actions**) on its row and delete
it, or run `az aigateway api-key delete -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n hosted-agent --yes`. Delete the
`.azure` folder in `infra` if you no longer need the environment, because it holds the key value.

Your gateway, its alias, and the `learn` MCP server aren't affected.

For the errors you might hit in this lab, with their likely causes and fixes, see
[Troubleshooting](../TROUBLESHOOTING.md#lab-16-foundry-hosted-agent).

# Build on your gateway with coding agents

Your platform team publishes models and MCP tools behind AI Gateway, and product developers want to use them
without reading gateway settings or passing keys around in chat. The AI Gateway plugin teaches coding agents
such as GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI what your gateway offers. It then generates
code that uses the right endpoint, model name, and auth header. The plugin only reads from the gateway, so
developers build on top of your governance instead of around it.

![AI Gateway architecture with coding agents among the clients that call one gateway](../assets/diagrams/architecture.svg "Coding agents call the same gateway as apps and agents. The code they generate goes through the gateway's access checks, policies, and telemetry like any other client.")

## Before you begin

<!-- setup: tools sign-in extension -->

- Complete [Publish a Foundry model and make your first call](../02-first-model-call/README.md). You need the
  gateway, a model that answers, and its alias.
- Optional: complete [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md) so the gateway
  also has MCP tools to discover.
- One coding agent, installed and signed in: GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude Code, Cursor, or Gemini CLI. Each agent
  documents its plugin support: [GitHub Copilot CLI](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-cli/customize-copilot/plugins-finding-installing),
  [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins), [Cursor](https://cursor.com/docs/plugins), and
  [Gemini CLI](https://geminicli.com/docs/extensions/).
- Read access to the gateway: the plugin uses your Azure sign-in to read it.
- Python 3.10 or later to run the generated app. To scaffold a standalone agent, you also need the GitHub Copilot
  CLI, because the GitHub Copilot SDK uses it.

Set these variables in the shell that you'll start your coding agent from. Create a key for this app so you can
revoke it on its own later.

```bash title="Bash"
# Name your gateway and the alias that the generated app calls
export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="<model-name>"   # the alias from lab 02
echo "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY in $RG, alias $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Read the gateway's resource ID, which you pass to the plugin, and its runtime URL, which the app calls
export GATEWAY_ID="$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query id -o tsv)"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Create an API key for this app, so that you can revoke it on its own later
az aigateway api-key create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n app-coding-agent --display-name app-coding-agent -o none &&
  echo "🔑 API key app-coding-agent is ready"

# Read the key into an environment variable, so that it never shows on screen
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n app-coding-agent \
  --query primaryKey -o tsv)" && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Name your gateway and the alias that the generated app calls
$RG      = "<resource-group>"
$GATEWAY = "<gateway>"
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL = "<model-name>"   # the alias from lab 02
Write-Host "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY in $RG, alias $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Read the gateway's resource ID, which you pass to the plugin, and its runtime URL, which the app calls
$GATEWAY_ID = az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --query id -o tsv
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL = "https://$(az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Create an API key for this app, so that you can revoke it on its own later
az aigateway api-key create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n app-coding-agent --display-name app-coding-agent -o none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔑 API key app-coding-agent is ready" }

# Read the key into an environment variable, so that it never shows on screen
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n app-coding-agent `
  --query primaryKey -o tsv
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

Then print the gateway's Azure resource ID. You pass it to the plugin.

```bash title="Bash"
# Print the gateway's resource ID, to copy into the plugin's commands
echo "🆔 Gateway resource ID: $GATEWAY_ID"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Print the gateway's resource ID, to copy into the plugin's commands
Write-Host "🆔 Gateway resource ID: $GATEWAY_ID"
```

The ID looks like
`/subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<resource-group>/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/<gateway>`.

## How it works

The plugin bundles one skill and two commands. The skill holds the know-how: which endpoints to call, which
model name the gateway accepts, and how to send the key. The commands run that skill for a task.

Discovery goes through Azure Resource Manager, which is why the plugin needs the resource ID and your Azure
sign-in. Your app then calls the gateway's runtime URL with a runtime key, like any other client. The plugin is
read-only against the gateway: it never creates, updates, or deletes gateways, models, tools, or keys. Creating
those stays an administrator task in the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com).

| Piece | Invoked as | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Skill `use-ai-gateway` | `/ai-gateway:use-ai-gateway` | The full discover, select, credential, and integrate workflow. The commands use it too. |
| Command `discover` | `/ai-gateway:discover <resource ID>` | Lists the gateway's models and MCP tool servers and suggests the ones that fit your use case. Stops there. |
| Command `build` | `/ai-gateway:build <resource ID> <description>` | Discovers, gets a key, integrates the assets into your app, then runs the code once to check it. |

What the generated code relies on:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Model base URL (OpenAI-compatible) | `<gateway URL>/default/models/openai/v1` |
| MCP endpoint | `<gateway URL>/default/toolservers/<server-name>/mcp` |
| Auth header | `api-key: <runtime key>`. The plugin writes it as `Api-Key`; header names aren't case-sensitive. |
| Key source | The `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` environment variable, loaded from a git-ignored `.env` file |
| Model name | The model's deployment name as the gateway publishes it, for example `gpt-6-luna` |
| Agent scaffold | GitHub Copilot SDK, `github-copilot-sdk>=1.0.0`, Python unless you ask for TypeScript |

## Install the plugin

<!-- steps -->

### Create a project folder

Start in an empty folder with Git, so you can check later that no secret gets committed.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create the project folder, move into it, and start a Git repository quietly
mkdir ticket-summarizer && cd ticket-summarizer && git init -q &&
  echo "📂 Project folder with Git: $(pwd)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Create the project folder, move into it, and start a Git repository quietly
New-Item -ItemType Directory ticket-summarizer | Out-Null; Set-Location ticket-summarizer; git init -q
if ($?) { Write-Host "📂 Project folder with Git: $(Get-Location)" }
```

### Add the plugin to your agent

The plugin lives in the [Azure/ai-gateway](https://github.com/Azure/ai-gateway) repository and follows each
agent's plugin format. In GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code, start a session in the folder (`copilot` or
`claude`) and run the slash commands. In Gemini CLI, run the command in your shell, then start `gemini` in the
folder. In Cursor, use the dashboard, then open the folder.

```text title="GitHub Copilot CLI"
/plugin marketplace add Azure/ai-gateway
/plugin install ai-gateway@azure
```

```text title="Claude Code"
/plugin marketplace add Azure/ai-gateway
/plugin install ai-gateway@azure
```

```text title="Cursor"
In the Cursor dashboard, open Plugins and select Add Marketplace.
Import https://github.com/Azure/ai-gateway.
Install ai-gateway from Customize.
```

```bash title="Gemini CLI"
# Install the plugin as a Gemini CLI extension, straight from the GitHub repository
gemini extensions install https://github.com/Azure/ai-gateway
echo "🧩 The ai-gateway extension is installed in Gemini CLI"
```

The marketplace is named `azure` and the plugin `ai-gateway`.

### Check that the commands are available

In your agent, run the discover command without a resource ID:

```text
/ai-gateway:discover
```

The plugin asks you for the gateway's resource ID before it makes any call. That's how you know it's loaded.
Answer with the ID you printed, or continue with the next step.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> `/ai-gateway:discover` is recognized and asks for a gateway resource ID.

## Discover what the gateway offers

<!-- steps -->

### Run discover with your resource ID

Paste the gateway ID that you printed in [Before you begin](#before-you-begin):

```text
/ai-gateway:discover /subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<resource-group>/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/<gateway>
```

When your agent asks to run `az` or `curl` commands, approve the ones that read: getting a token, `GET` requests
to `management.azure.com`, and MCP calls to your gateway URL. Deny any `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE`. The plugin
never needs them.

### Read the summary

The plugin reads the gateway's runtime URL, lists the models with the exact name each one accepts, and lists the
MCP tool servers with their endpoints. It checks each tool server with a full MCP handshake and reports how many
tools it exposes. Then it highlights the best matches and asks which assets you want. Ask follow-up questions in
plain language, for example:

```text
Which model fits short summaries? Do any tool servers search Microsoft Learn?
```

Discover doesn't retrieve keys or write code. Stop here, or move on to `build`.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The summary lists the model you published in lab 02 and, if you did lab 04, the `learn` tool server.

## Build an app with the gateway

<!-- steps -->

### Describe what to build

Run `build` with the same resource ID and a short description. To use the key you created for this app instead of
letting the plugin pick one, say so in the description:

```text
/ai-gateway:build /subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<resource-group>/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways/<gateway> a Python command-line script that summarizes a support ticket from a text file. Use the <model-name> model and read the key from the AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY environment variable.
```

Other descriptions to try:

| You want | Describe it as |
|---|---|
| A model call in an app you already have | `add a /summarize endpoint to my FastAPI app that calls the gateway model` |
| Tools in your own MCP client | `connect my app to the learn MCP tools` |
| A ready-to-run agent | `a standalone agent that answers Azure questions with the learn tools` |

### Answer the plugin's questions

`build` runs the discovery again and asks you to confirm the model and tools. Then it gets a key and asks what
you're building, if your description didn't say:

- **Call a model**: code for the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, in your project's language.
- **Connect MCP tools**: configuration for an MCP-capable client or app.
- **Scaffold a standalone agent**: a complete GitHub Copilot SDK project with agent code, `.env`, `.env.example`,
  `.gitignore`, `requirements.txt` or `package.json`, and a `README.md`.

If you didn't name a key, the plugin lists the gateway's keys and reads the secret of an active one. That needs
permission to list key secrets on the gateway. When the plugin writes a key to `.env`, it's a live secret in
plain text, kept out of Git by `.gitignore`.

### Review the generated code

Read the code before you run it again or commit it. Check that:

- The base URL is your gateway URL followed by `/default/models/openai/v1`, or `/default/toolservers/<name>/mcp`
  for tools. Without `/default/`, calls return `404`.
- The `model` value is a name your gateway accepts. To retarget models later without a code change, ask the agent
  to use your alias, as explained in
  [Publish models from any provider behind stable aliases](../03-multi-provider-aliases/README.md).
- The key comes from `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` and goes in the `api-key` header. No key value appears in code,
  `README.md`, or config files, and `.env.example` holds only a placeholder.
- `.gitignore` lists `.env`.
- The app calls only the gateway's runtime URL, never `management.azure.com`.
- For a scaffolded agent: `requirements.txt` pins `github-copilot-sdk>=1.0.0`, each MCP server lists the selected
  tools by name instead of `"*"`, and tool permission requests wait for your approval.

### Run the app

`build` already ran the code once and reported the result. Run it yourself from the shell where you set
`AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`, using the command in the generated `README.md`. For a Python project, that's usually:

```bash title="Bash"
# Create a virtual environment in .venv and activate it, so that the packages stay out of your global Python
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate &&
  echo "🧩 Virtual environment .venv is active"

# Install the packages that the generated app lists in requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt &&
  echo "🧩 The packages in requirements.txt are installed"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Create a virtual environment in .venv and activate it, so that the packages stay out of your global Python
python -m venv .venv; .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧩 Virtual environment .venv is active" }

# Install the packages that the generated app lists in requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧩 The packages in requirements.txt are installed" }
```

Then start the entry point that the README names, for example `python summarize.py ticket.txt`.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The generated app prints a model response that came through your gateway.

## Verify

<!-- steps -->

### Confirm the key and model outside the generated code

If the app fails, this call tells you whether the problem is in the gateway setup or in the code.

```bash title="Bash"
# Call the model through the gateway with your key and alias, and print only the HTTP status code
echo "🤖 HTTP status of a model call through the gateway:"
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"ping\"}]}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Call the model through the gateway with your key and alias, and print only the HTTP status code
Write-Host "🤖 HTTP status of a model call through the gateway:"
$body = @{ model = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL; messages = @(@{ role = "user"; content = "ping" }) } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
(Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri "$($env:AI_GATEWAY_URL.TrimEnd('/'))/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
  -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body -SkipHttpErrorCheck).StatusCode
```

Expect `HTTP 200` (`200` in PowerShell).

### Check that no secret can be committed

Run this in the project folder. It checks that Git ignores `.env` and that your key appears in no other file.

```bash title="Bash"
# Check that Git ignores .env, the file that holds your key
git check-ignore -q .env && echo "✅ .env is ignored" || echo "⚠️ .env is not ignored"

# Search every other file for your key, skipping .git, .venv, and node_modules, and list any file that holds it
if grep -rIlF --exclude=.env --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=.venv --exclude-dir=node_modules -- "$AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" .; then
  echo "⚠️ The key appears in the files above"
else
  echo "✅ No key in project files"
fi
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Check that Git ignores .env, the file that holds your key
git check-ignore -q .env; if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) { Write-Host "✅ .env is ignored" } else { Write-Host "⚠️ .env is not ignored" }

# Search every other file for your key, skipping .git, .venv, and node_modules, and list any file that holds it
$hits = Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File -Force |
  Where-Object { $_.Name -ne ".env" -and $_.FullName -notmatch '[\\/](\.git|\.venv|node_modules)[\\/]' } |
  Select-String -SimpleMatch -Pattern $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY -List
if ($hits) { Write-Host "⚠️ The key appears in:"; $hits.Path } else { Write-Host "✅ No key in project files" }
```

Expect `✅ .env is ignored` and `✅ No key in project files`. If the plugin wrote a different key to `.env`, run the
check again with that key in `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The direct call returns `200`, the app works, and no key can reach Git.

# Use your gateway's models and tools in GitHub Copilot

GitHub Copilot can run on a model that you bring yourself: give it an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and a key, and it
sends every chat and agent request there. Make that endpoint your gateway, and Copilot's traffic gets the same
controls as your apps: a key that you can suspend, a token limit for each caller, and usage in Monitoring. Copilot
never sees a Foundry credential, because the gateway calls Foundry with its managed identity. In this lab you publish
`gpt-6-astra` for Copilot, then connect four Copilot surfaces to it: VS Code, the Copilot CLI, the Copilot SDK, and
the GitHub Copilot app. Then you publish the Microsoft Learn MCP server through the same gateway and give those
surfaces its tools, with the same key, so Copilot's tool calls get the same controls as its model calls.

![Four GitHub Copilot surfaces send requests with one runtime key to the gpt-6-astra alias and the learn MCP server on the gateway, which applies a token limit, records usage by key, calls the Foundry deployment with its managed identity, and calls the public Microsoft Learn MCP server](../assets/diagrams/github-copilot-byok.svg "Every Copilot surface uses the same four model settings: the gateway's base URL, the gpt-6-astra alias, the Responses API, and a runtime key. The same key in the api-key header opens the learn MCP server. The gateway limits and records the traffic, then calls Foundry with its managed identity and Microsoft Learn without credentials.")
