## Publish a model on the new gateway

The new gateway starts empty. Publish your Foundry deployment on it, as in
[Make your first model call](../02-first-model-call/README.md), and create a runtime API key. The gateway calls
Foundry with its own system-assigned managed identity, which needs the **Foundry User** role on the account.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Import the deployment from Foundry

1. In the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com), select the new gateway in the top bar.
2. Select **Models** › **Add** › **Models from Microsoft Foundry**.
3. Select the subscription and resource group of your Foundry account, then select your deployment and keep
   **Managed identity** as the **Authentication method**.
4. Under **Aliases**, keep **Create an alias for each model** selected, then select **Add models**.
5. Open the imported model on **Models**, open the **Aliases** tab, and copy the alias exactly as shown.

### Create a runtime API key

Select **Access** › **Keys** › **Create API key**, enter `private-net-lab` in **Key name**, select **Create**,
and copy the value. Then set both values in your shell without echoing the key:

```bash title="Bash"
# Set the alias that apps send in the model field
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="<model-name>"    # the alias from the Aliases tab
echo "🏷️ Model alias: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"

# Read the key without showing it, and export it for the next commands
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Set the alias that apps send in the model field, and read the key without showing it
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL   = "<model-name>"  # the alias from the Aliases tab
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = Read-Host "AI Gateway API key" -MaskInput
Write-Host "🏷️ Model alias: $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Grant the gateway access to Foundry

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the principal ID of the new gateway's managed identity
PRINCIPAL_ID="$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query identity.principalId -o tsv)"
echo "🪪 Gateway identity: $PRINCIPAL_ID"

# Give the gateway's identity the Foundry User role on the account, so that it can call the model
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d" --scope "$FOUNDRY_ID" -o none &&
  echo "🛡️ The gateway's identity has the Foundry User role on $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the principal ID of the new gateway's managed identity
$PRINCIPAL_ID = az aigateway show -g $RG -n $GATEWAY --query identity.principalId -o tsv
Write-Host "🪪 Gateway identity: $PRINCIPAL_ID"

# Give the gateway's identity the Foundry User role on the account, so that it can call the model
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id $PRINCIPAL_ID --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal `
  --role "53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d" --scope $FOUNDRY_ID -o none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ The gateway's identity has the Foundry User role on $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT" }
```

`53ca6127-db72-4b80-b1b0-d745d6d5456d` is the **Foundry User** role.

### Publish the deployment and an alias

Create a provider that signs in to Foundry with the gateway's managed identity, register the deployment under it,
and publish an alias.

```bash title="Bash"
# Add a model provider that points at the Foundry account and signs in with the gateway's managed identity
az aigateway model-provider create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$PROVIDER" \
  --kind Foundry --display-name "Foundry (private)" \
  --foundry "$(jq -cn --arg endpoint "$FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT" --arg id "$FOUNDRY_ID" '{
      endpoint: $endpoint, resourceIds: [$id],
      authentication: {kind: "ManagedIdentity",
                       managedIdentity: {resource: "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/"}}}')" -o none &&
  echo "🔌 Model provider $PROVIDER points at $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT"

# Add a model for the deployment, with the endpoints that apps can call
az aigateway model create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" --provider-name "$PROVIDER" -n "$DEPLOYMENT" \
  --display-name "$DEPLOYMENT" --api-format OpenAIChatCompletions \
  --supported-endpoints /openai/v1/chat/completions /openai/v1/responses \
  --deployment-config "{resourceId:$FOUNDRY_ID/deployments/$DEPLOYMENT,modelName:$DEPLOYMENT}" -o none &&
  echo "🧠 Model $DEPLOYMENT is published through $PROVIDER"

# Build the model's resource ID, and publish the alias that apps send in the model field
MODEL_ID="$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$DEPLOYMENT"
az aigateway model-alias create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$ALIAS" \
  --backend-model resource-id="$MODEL_ID" --only-show-errors -o none &&
  echo "🏷️ Alias $ALIAS is ready"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Add a model provider that points at the Foundry account and signs in with the gateway's managed identity
@{
  endpoint       = $FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT
  resourceIds    = @($FOUNDRY_ID)
  authentication = @{ kind = "ManagedIdentity"; managedIdentity = @{ resource = "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/" } }
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress | Set-Content foundry.json
az aigateway model-provider create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $PROVIDER `
  --kind Foundry --display-name "Foundry (private)" --foundry "@foundry.json" -o none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔌 Model provider $PROVIDER points at $FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT" }
Remove-Item foundry.json

# Add a model for the deployment, with the endpoints that apps can call
az aigateway model create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY --provider-name $PROVIDER -n $DEPLOYMENT `
  --display-name $DEPLOYMENT --api-format OpenAIChatCompletions `
  --supported-endpoints /openai/v1/chat/completions /openai/v1/responses `
  --deployment-config "{resourceId:$FOUNDRY_ID/deployments/$DEPLOYMENT,modelName:$DEPLOYMENT}" -o none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🧠 Model $DEPLOYMENT is published through $PROVIDER" }

# Build the model's resource ID, and publish the alias that apps send in the model field
$MODEL_ID = "$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/modelProviders/$PROVIDER/models/$DEPLOYMENT"
az aigateway model-alias create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $ALIAS `
  --backend-model resource-id="$MODEL_ID" --only-show-errors -o none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🏷️ Alias $ALIAS is ready" }
```

If the alias already exists, `create` fails; change it with `az aigateway model-alias update` and the same
arguments instead.

### Create a runtime API key

`api-key create` returns metadata only. Read the generated value with `list-secrets` straight into a variable, so
it never appears on screen.

```bash title="Bash"
# Create a runtime API key for your app
az aigateway api-key create -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$KEY_NAME" --display-name "$KEY_NAME" -o none &&
  echo "🔑 API key private-net-lab is ready"

# Read the key straight into a variable, so that it never shows on screen, and set the alias for the next calls
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY="$(az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$KEY_NAME" \
  --query primaryKey -o tsv)" && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$ALIAS"
echo "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (${#AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY} characters, not shown)"
echo "🏷️ Model alias: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Create a runtime API key for your app
az aigateway api-key create -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $KEY_NAME --display-name $KEY_NAME -o none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🔑 API key private-net-lab is ready" }

# Read the key straight into a variable, so that it never shows on screen, and set the alias for the next calls
$env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY = az aigateway api-key list-secrets -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $KEY_NAME `
  --query primaryKey -o tsv
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL   = $ALIAS
Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
Write-Host "🏷️ Model alias: $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
```

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Check the model and the key

`azd up` also deployed lab 02's template on the new gateway: the gateway's identity has the **Foundry User** role
on the lab's Foundry resource, and the gateway has the `foundry-private` provider, the `gpt-6-luna` model, the
`private-chat` alias, and the `private-net-lab` runtime key. You read the alias and the key into `AI_GATEWAY_MODEL`
and `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` in the previous section. Check where the alias points:

```bash
# Show the resource ID of the model that the alias points at
echo "🏷️ Alias $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL points at this model:"
az aigateway model-alias show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL" \
  --query "properties.backendModels[0].resourceId" -o tsv
```

The output ends with `/modelProviders/foundry-private/models/gpt-6-luna`.

<!-- /tracks -->

> **Checkpoint**
> Call the model through the new gateway. Foundry's public access is still on, so a `200` proves that the
> gateway, the model, and the key work before you lock anything down:
>
> ```bash title="Bash"
> # Call the model through the new gateway, and print only the HTTP status code
> echo "🔒 Model call through the gateway, which reaches Foundry over the private endpoint:"
> curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
>   -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
>   -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Reply with exactly one word: ok\"}],\"max_completion_tokens\":128}"
> ```
>
> ```powershell title="PowerShell"
> # Build a short request with the alias in model
> $body = @{ model = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL; max_completion_tokens = 128
>   messages = @(@{ role = "user"; content = "Reply with exactly one word: ok" }) } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
>
> # Call the model through the new gateway; -SkipHttpErrorCheck returns error responses instead of throwing
> Write-Host "🔒 Model call through the gateway, which reaches Foundry over the private endpoint:"
> $r = Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri "$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
>   -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body -SkipHttpErrorCheck
> "HTTP $($r.StatusCode)"
> ```
>
> If the first call returns `401` or `403` from the backend, the role assignment hasn't taken effect yet. Wait a
> few minutes and try again.

## Turn off public access to Foundry

The gateway resolves Foundry through the private DNS zones, so its calls already use the private endpoint. Turn
off Foundry's public access, so the private endpoint is the only way in.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Disable public network access on Foundry

After the private endpoint shows as approved, open the Foundry resource's networking settings in the Azure portal
and disable public network access. See
[Configure virtual networks for Foundry Tools](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/ai-services/cognitive-services-virtual-networks).

<!-- track: cli | Azure CLI -->

### Disable public network access on Foundry

```bash
# Turn off public network access on the Foundry account, so that the private endpoint is the only way in
echo "🔒 Public network access of the Foundry account, after the update:"
az resource update --ids "$FOUNDRY_ID" --set properties.publicNetworkAccess=Disabled \
  --query properties.publicNetworkAccess -o tsv
```

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Disable public network access on Foundry

`infra/foundry.bicep` takes the Foundry resource's public access from the `FOUNDRY_PUBLIC_NETWORK_ACCESS` azd
environment value. Set it to `Disabled` and provision again. azd updates the Foundry resource, and the gateway keeps
its private routing, because the template passes the same subnet:

```bash
# Set Foundry's public network access to Disabled in the azd environment
azd env set FOUNDRY_PUBLIC_NETWORK_ACCESS Disabled &&
  echo "📝 FOUNDRY_PUBLIC_NETWORK_ACCESS is Disabled in the azd environment"

# Provision again: azd updates the Foundry resource, and the gateway keeps its private routing
azd provision &&
  echo "🔒 Foundry's public network access is off"
```

<!-- /tracks -->

The change can take a few minutes to apply.

## Verify

<!-- steps -->

### Check the gateway's private routing

```bash
# Show the subnet that the gateway's outbound calls go through
echo "🔒 Gateway $GATEWAY routes its outbound calls through this subnet:"
az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query "properties.backend.subnet.id" -o tsv
```

The output ends with `/virtualNetworks/vnet-aigw/subnets/snet-aigw-integration`.

### Check name resolution for Foundry

```bash
# List the A records that the private endpoint registered in the zone
echo "🔒 A records in privatelink.cognitiveservices.azure.com:"
az network private-dns record-set a list -g "$RG" -z privatelink.cognitiveservices.azure.com \
  --query "[].{name:name, ip:aRecords[0].ipv4Address}" -o table
```

The Foundry account resolves to an IP in `snet-private-endpoints` (`10.20.1.x`) for anything that uses the
virtual network's DNS, including the gateway.

### Call the model through the gateway

```bash title="Bash"
# Call the model through the gateway, and print only the HTTP status code
echo "🔒 Model call through the gateway, with Foundry's public access off:"
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' "${AI_GATEWAY_URL%/}/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H "api-key: $AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"model\":\"$AI_GATEWAY_MODEL\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Reply with exactly one word: ok\"}],\"max_completion_tokens\":128}"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Build a short request with the alias in model
$body = @{ model = $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL; max_completion_tokens = 128
  messages = @(@{ role = "user"; content = "Reply with exactly one word: ok" }) } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5

# Call the model through the gateway; -SkipHttpErrorCheck returns error responses instead of throwing
Write-Host "🔒 Model call through the gateway, with Foundry's public access off:"
$r = Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri "$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL/default/models/openai/v1/chat/completions" `
  -Headers @{ "api-key" = $env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY } -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body -SkipHttpErrorCheck
"HTTP $($r.StatusCode)"
```

The call still returns `HTTP 200`. Your workstation reaches the gateway on its public endpoint, and the gateway
reaches Foundry through the integration subnet and the private endpoint.

### Call Foundry directly from your workstation

```bash title="Bash"
# Get a Microsoft Entra token for Foundry with your own sign-in
TOKEN="$(az account get-access-token --resource https://cognitiveservices.azure.com --query accessToken -o tsv)"
echo "🪪 Token acquired: in TOKEN (${#TOKEN} characters, not shown)"

# Call Foundry's public endpoint directly, and print the response and the HTTP status code
echo "🚦 Direct call to Foundry from your workstation (expect HTTP 403):"
curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' "${FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT%/}/openai/v1/models" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Get a Microsoft Entra token for Foundry with your own sign-in
$TOKEN = az account get-access-token --resource https://cognitiveservices.azure.com --query accessToken -o tsv
Write-Host "🪪 Token acquired: in TOKEN ($($TOKEN.Length) characters, not shown)"

# Call Foundry's public endpoint directly; -SkipHttpErrorCheck returns error responses instead of throwing
Write-Host "🚦 Direct call to Foundry from your workstation (expect HTTP 403):"
$r = Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "$($FOUNDRY_ENDPOINT.TrimEnd('/'))/openai/v1/models" `
  -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $TOKEN" } -SkipHttpErrorCheck
"HTTP $($r.StatusCode)"; $r.Content
```

The call returns `HTTP 403` with a message that public access is disabled: the internet can't reach Foundry
anymore, but the gateway can.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The new gateway uses private routing through `snet-aigw-integration`, Foundry resolves to a `10.20.1.x` address
> inside the virtual network, model calls through the gateway return `200`, and direct calls to Foundry from the
> internet return `403`.

## Go further

- **Filter who can call the gateway.** While the frontend stays public, add a gateway-wide `ipFilter` policy
  (`action: Allow` with your egress `cidrRanges`) next to keys or Microsoft Entra ID. See
  [Set gateway-wide policy baselines](../09-gateway-baselines/README.md).
- **Hub-and-spoke networks.** Keep backend private endpoints and their private DNS zones in a hub, peer the
  gateway's virtual network to it, and link the zones to the integrated virtual network. If you use your own DNS
  servers, forward the `privatelink` zones to Azure DNS. See
  [Azure private endpoint DNS configuration](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/private-link/private-endpoint-dns).
- **Private MCP servers and APIs.** Any backend with a private endpoint or a private IP that the integrated
  virtual network can reach works the same way, including the tool servers from
  [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md).
- **Data residency.** Residency follows the whole request path, so account for where your backends, tools, logs,
  and clients live, not only the gateway region.

labs and other callers reach it over the internet. Then remove the new gateway's role assignment on Foundry and
delete the lab's resource group, which holds the gateway, its connector gateway, the private endpoint, the private
DNS zones, the virtual network, and the NSG.

# Protect tool calls with Agent 365 threat protection

Your agents call tools that read web pages, tickets, and documents, and any of that content can carry a prompt
injection or leak sensitive data back to the model. Content filters on the model don't see what goes into a tool
or what comes out of it. In this lab you add **Agent 365 tool threat protection** to an MCP server, so Microsoft
Defender and Microsoft Purview evaluate each tool request, each tool result, or both, and the gateway only lets
allowed calls through.

![The gateway sends the tool request and the tool result to Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Purview for an allow decision](../assets/diagrams/threat-protection.svg "The gateway asks for an allow decision before the tool runs, after it returns, or both. Anything other than an allow fails closed.")

<!-- widget: request-lifecycle -->

## Before you begin

<!-- setup: tools sign-in extension clone -->

> [!TIP]
> On the **Bicep + azd** track, `azd up` creates its own gateway, the `learn` MCP server, your **AI Gateway Tools
> User** role assignment on it, and a key, so you can skip this section except for the Microsoft Defender or Microsoft
> Purview license. You need only the one-time setup above, signed in as a user.

- Complete [Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint](../04-federate-mcp-tools/README.md). This lab protects the
  `learn` MCP server from that lab. Any MCP server in your gateway works.
- Complete [Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC](../11-entra-rbac/README.md). Tool threat protection
  only works for callers that send a **delegated** Microsoft Entra ID bearer token issued for AI Gateway.
- A **Microsoft Defender or Microsoft Purview license** in your tenant.
- Permission to manage policies on the gateway, for example **Contributor** on its resource group, and permission
  to create role assignments if your user doesn't have a data-plane role yet.
- Your Azure CLI sign-in as a **user**, not a service principal.
- Run the scripts and samples from the lab's folder, `~/ai-gateway/labs/19-tool-threat-protection`.

> [!NOTE]
> Agent 365 tool threat protection is an emerging capability of the AI Gateway tier. Labels and behavior can
> change; see the [release note](https://ai.gateway.azure.com/docs/releases/2026-10-08-tool-threat-protection).
> Defender and Purview are licensed separately.

Set these variables once. The steps and the **Verify** section reuse them.

```bash title="Bash"

export RG="<resource-group>"
export GATEWAY="<gateway>"
export MCP_SERVER="learn"                    # the MCP server you protect in this lab
echo "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY in $RG, MCP server $MCP_SERVER"

# Read the gateway's resource ID and its runtime URL

export AI_GATEWAY_URL="https://$(az aigateway show -g "$RG" -n "$GATEWAY" --query properties.frontend.defaultHostname -o tsv)"
echo "🆔 Gateway ID: $GATEWAY_ID"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"

# Paste the runtime key from Access › Keys without showing it: you use it once, to see a key-only call fail closed
read -rsp "AI Gateway API key: " AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && export AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY && echo

```

```powershell title="PowerShell"

Write-Host "🔑 Key: in AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY ($($env:AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.Length) characters, not shown)"
```

## How it works

Tool threat protection is a policy on one MCP server. It covers every tool on that server, whether the server is
backed by remote MCP endpoints, OpenAPI services, or both, and every caller. The gateway first runs its usual
authentication, authorization, and policies. Only requests that pass are sent for evaluation.

For each `tools/call`, the gateway exchanges the caller's delegated token on behalf of the user (OBO) and asks
Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Purview for a verdict on malicious content, prompt injection, and sensitive-data
risks. Discovery and session traffic, such as `initialize`, `tools/list`, and notifications, isn't evaluated.

The evaluation must return a valid **allow**. A denial, timeout, token-exchange failure, malformed verdict, or
unavailable evaluator fails closed: the caller gets a normal tool result over HTTP `200` with `isError: true`, a
denial code, and a correlation ID.

| Stage | What's evaluated | What it prevents | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Before tool invocation** | The tool name and arguments | The tool never runs, so there are no side effects | One evaluation round trip |
| **After tool invocation** | The tool result, including error results | The result never reaches the agent. The tool **already ran**. | One evaluation round trip |
| **Both** | Both of the above | Requires two allow decisions | Up to two round trips per call |

## Prepare a delegated caller

The policy evaluates each call on behalf of the signed-in user, so you test it with your own user token. Give
your user permission to call tools on the server, then make one call **before** you add the policy. That proves
the token and the role work, so any later failure comes from the policy.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Grant yourself the AI Gateway Tools User role

In the AI Gateway portal, select **Access**, then **Add role assignments**. Choose the **AI Gateway Tools User**
role, scope it to the `learn` MCP server, search for your user, and select **Review + assign**. The
[Entra ID lab](../11-entra-rbac/README.md) walks through this page.

The same assignment with the Azure CLI:

```bash
# Give your user the AI Gateway Tools User role on the MCP server, so that your token can call its tools
az role assignment create \
  --assignee-object-id "$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)" \
  --assignee-principal-type User \
  --role "dce03f8d-857f-4e40-a90d-67770fa6ecd2" \
  --scope "$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/toolServers/$MCP_SERVER" --output none &&
  echo "🛡️ You have the AI Gateway Tools User role on the $MCP_SERVER MCP server"
```

```powershell
# Give your user the AI Gateway Tools User role on the MCP server, so that your token can call its tools
az role assignment create `
  --assignee-object-id (az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv) `
  --assignee-principal-type User `
  --role "dce03f8d-857f-4e40-a90d-67770fa6ecd2" `
  --scope "$GATEWAY_ID/workspaces/default/toolServers/$MCP_SERVER" --output none
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ You have the AI Gateway Tools User role on the $MCP_SERVER MCP server" }
```

If you already have **AI Gateway User** or **AI Gateway Tools User** at the gateway scope, skip this step. Role
assignments can take several minutes to apply.

**What you need:** only the one-time setup from **Before you begin**, signed in as a **user**. This track doesn't use
your gateway or `learn` server from lab 04: `azd up` creates a new gateway with its own `learn` server, so it works on

### Review the templates

`infra/main.bicep` creates the resource group `rg-<environment name>` and calls lab 01's
[gateway.bicep](../01-provision-gateway/infra/gateway.bicep) for a gateway with no model. Then it calls
`infra/protected-tool-server.bicep`, which azd fills from environment values:

| Parameter | azd environment value | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `preInvocation` | `TOOL_THREAT_PRE_INVOCATION` | `false` |
| `postInvocation` | `TOOL_THREAT_POST_INVOCATION` | `false` |
| `principalId` | `AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID`, which azd sets to the signed-in user | Your user's object ID |

<!-- include: infra/main.bicep -->

`infra/protected-tool-server.bicep` declares the `learn` server of lab 04 with its `learn` backend. Its `policies`
array holds one `toolThreatProtection` policy with `preInvocation` and `postInvocation` when at least one stage is
on, and nothing when both are off. It assigns **AI Gateway Tools User** on the server to `principalId`, as the
portal step does, and creates the `app-first-call` key.

<!-- include: infra/protected-tool-server.bicep -->

> [!WARNING]
> A Bicep deployment sends a `PUT`, which replaces the whole MCP server, including backends and policies that you
> added in the portal. Keep the template as the only source of truth for this server, and change it with
> `azd provision`.

### Read the outputs and the key

```bash title="Bash"

  --query primaryKey --output tsv)"

# List your roles on the MCP server: expect AI Gateway Tools User

```

```powershell title="PowerShell"

```

> **Checkpoint**
> `azd up` ended with `SUCCESS`, and the role listing under `🛡️ Your roles on the learn MCP server:` printed
> `AI Gateway Tools User`. Role assignments can take several minutes to apply.

<!-- /tracks -->

### Call a tool with your user token

The script below gets a token for `https://azure-api.net/aigateway` from the Azure CLI, checks that it's a
delegated user token, runs the MCP handshake, and calls the server's search tool with a harmless question.

<!-- include: infra/call-protected-tool.sh -->

On GitHub, open [infra/call-protected-tool.sh](infra/call-protected-tool.sh) or

# Call the server's search tool with your delegated user token: the script prints each MCP step and the result

## Add tool threat protection

Pick one track. Both add the same policy to the `learn` server, with both stages turned on. Each MCP server can
have only one tool threat protection policy, and you can't set it at gateway scope or on a single tool.

<!-- track: portal | Portal -->

### Start a new policy

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com) and select your gateway from the gateway switcher.
Select **Policies**, then **Add policy**.

### Choose the policy type

On the **Type** step, under **Security**, select **Agent 365 tool threat protection**. Its card carries the
**MCP server** badge and reads "Evaluate tool calls and results with Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Purview
for threats, prompt injection, and sensitive-data risks." Select **Next**.

![The Add policy wizard on the Type step, with Agent 365 tool threat protection selected under Security](../assets/screens/policy-tool-threat-protection.jpeg "Agent 365 tool threat protection sits in the Security group, next to Content safety and IP filter. It applies to MCP servers only.")

### Select the MCP server

On the **Scope** step, the wizard notes that this policy applies to individual MCP servers. Select the `learn`
MCP server, then select **Next**.

### Choose the evaluation stages

On the **Details** step, the wizard reminds you that Microsoft Entra ID is required for this policy, because the
evaluation runs on behalf of the caller. Select both stages:

- **Before tool invocation: Evaluate the request payload**
- **After tool invocation: Evaluate the tool output**

You must select at least one stage. Then select **Create**.

<!-- track: iac | Bicep + azd -->

### Turn on both stages

Set both stages to `true` and provision again. Only the MCP server changes: the template adds one
`toolThreatProtection` entry to its `policies` array. To evaluate only the requests, leave
`TOOL_THREAT_POST_INVOCATION` at `false`.

```bash title="Bash"
# Turn on both evaluation stages in the azd environment
azd env set TOOL_THREAT_PRE_INVOCATION true &&
  echo "📝 TOOL_THREAT_PRE_INVOCATION: true"
azd env set TOOL_THREAT_POST_INVOCATION true &&
  echo "📝 TOOL_THREAT_POST_INVOCATION: true"

# Deploy again: the template adds a toolThreatProtection policy to the learn MCP server
azd provision &&
  echo "🛡️ Tool threat protection is on for the learn MCP server, before and after each tool call"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Turn on both evaluation stages in the azd environment
azd env set TOOL_THREAT_PRE_INVOCATION true
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 TOOL_THREAT_PRE_INVOCATION: true" }
azd env set TOOL_THREAT_POST_INVOCATION true
if ($?) { Write-Host "📝 TOOL_THREAT_POST_INVOCATION: true" }

# Deploy again: the template adds a toolThreatProtection policy to the learn MCP server
azd provision
if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Tool threat protection is on for the learn MCP server, before and after each tool call" }
```

<!-- /tracks -->

<!-- steps -->

### Confirm the policy

The new policy appears in the portal's **Policies** overview. The policy is stored on the MCP server, so you can
also read it with `az aigateway mcp show`:

```bash
# Read the MCP server's policies: expect one toolThreatProtection entry with both stages on
echo "🛡️ Policies on the $MCP_SERVER MCP server:"
az aigateway mcp show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$MCP_SERVER" --query properties.policies
```

```powershell
# Read the MCP server's policies: expect one toolThreatProtection entry with both stages on
Write-Host "🛡️ Policies on the $MCP_SERVER MCP server:"
az aigateway mcp show -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $MCP_SERVER --query properties.policies
```

The list includes an entry with `"type": "toolThreatProtection"`, `"preInvocation": true`, and
`"postInvocation": true`. The service adds `"scope": "resource"` when it returns a policy set on the server.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The `learn` MCP server has one `toolThreatProtection` policy with both stages turned on.

> [!CAUTION]
> A post-invocation denial withholds the result, but it can't undo what the tool already did. The gateway doesn't
> retry or reverse the call. Build agents so they **don't automatically retry** a tool call whose result was
> withheld, especially for tools that write, send, or delete. For those tools, keep **Before tool invocation**
> turned on so a risky request never runs.

## Understand verdicts and failures

The gateway doesn't decide what's risky. Microsoft Defender does, in the policy mode your security team sets in
Microsoft Defender. You can't change that mode at the gateway.

| Defender policy mode | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Disabled** | A permanent fail-open state. No inspection occurs. |
| **Audit** | Tool calls are logged without blocking. If the service lags or drops out, calls fail open. |
| **Block** | Explicit enforcement that fails closed. Withholding a result after invocation requires Block mode. |

When a call fails closed, the caller sees one of these codes in the result's
`_meta["com.microsoft.azure.ai.gateway/denial"].code`:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ToolEvaluationIdentityRequired` | The request has no usable bearer token, or the gateway can't read the token tenant it needs for the OBO exchange |
| `ToolEvaluationDenied` | The evaluation service denied the request or the result |
| `ToolEvaluationInvalidRequest` | The evaluation input isn't valid |
| `ToolEvaluationRequestTooLarge` | The evaluation input exceeds the supported size |
| `ToolEvaluationUnavailable` | Token exchange or evaluation failed, timed out, returned an invalid verdict, or was unavailable |

A denied call looks like this. The HTTP status is still `200`, so clients must check `result.isError`:

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 42,
  "result": {
    "isError": true,
    "content": [
      { "type": "text", "text": "Tool 'mcp_tail_logs' requires a validated delegated caller token." }
    ],
    "_meta": {
      "com.microsoft.azure.ai.gateway/denial": {
        "code": "ToolEvaluationIdentityRequired",
        "correlationId": "9f2c1b6e-..."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

> [!TIP]
> Log the `correlationId` with every denial in your agent. It's the value to share when you investigate a
> denial with your security team.

<!-- steps -->

### Call the protected tool with your user token

Run the same benign call as before. Allow a few seconds per call, because each enabled stage adds an evaluation
round trip.

```bash
# Call the protected tool again with your delegated user token: both stages evaluate the call
echo "🛠️ Tool call on $MCP_SERVER with your user token:"
./infra/call-protected-tool.sh token "$MCP_SERVER"
```

```powershell
# Call the protected tool again with your delegated user token: both stages evaluate the call
Write-Host "🛠️ Tool call on $MCP_SERVER with your user token:"
./infra/call-protected-tool.ps1 -Auth token -Server $MCP_SERVER
```

```text title="Expected output"
🛠️ Tool call on learn with your user token:
...
tools/list: HTTP 200, <n> tools (discovery isn't evaluated)
tools/call: learn_microsoft_docs_search with query: What is Azure API Management?
HTTP status: 200
isError: false (the result was returned)
...
```

A harmless question about Azure is allowed at both stages, so the result comes back as before. If you see
`ToolEvaluationUnavailable` or `ToolEvaluationDenied` instead, see
[Troubleshooting](../TROUBLESHOOTING.md#lab-19-tool-threat-protection).

### Call it with a runtime key only

Now call the same tool with the API key and no bearer token. The key still authenticates you to the gateway, so
`initialize` and `tools/list` succeed. The `tools/call` needs an evaluation, and without a delegated token the
gateway can't run one, so it fails closed.

```bash
# Call the same tool with the runtime key and no bearer token: the gateway can't evaluate it, so it fails closed
echo "🚦 Key-only tool call on $MCP_SERVER, expect a ToolEvaluationIdentityRequired denial:"
./infra/call-protected-tool.sh key "$MCP_SERVER"
```

```powershell
# Call the same tool with the runtime key and no bearer token: the gateway can't evaluate it, so it fails closed
Write-Host "🚦 Key-only tool call on $MCP_SERVER, expect a ToolEvaluationIdentityRequired denial:"
./infra/call-protected-tool.ps1 -Auth key -Server $MCP_SERVER
```

```text title="Expected output"
🚦 Key-only tool call on learn, expect a ToolEvaluationIdentityRequired denial:
...
tools/list: HTTP 200, <n> tools (discovery isn't evaluated)
tools/call: learn_microsoft_docs_search with query: What is Azure API Management?
HTTP status: 200
isError: true
Denial code: ToolEvaluationIdentityRequired
Correlation ID: <guid>
Tool '...' requires a validated delegated caller token.
```

The denial text can differ. The code is what matters.

### Look for the call in Monitoring

If you set up Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), open
**Monitoring**. The **Tools** tab shows MCP tool executions, and **Traces** shows each request with its policy
steps. Find your calls by time and compare the allowed call with the key-only call.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> A delegated call returns its result. A key-only call to the same tool returns `isError: true` with
> `ToolEvaluationIdentityRequired`, while `tools/list` still works.

## Go further

- **Choose stages per server.** Keep **Before tool invocation** on for tools with side effects, such as sending
  mail or changing records. Add **After tool invocation** for tools that return untrusted content, such as web
  pages, tickets, or documents. For read-only tools that only return trusted content, weigh the extra round trip.
- **Move your agents to delegated tokens.** Agents that call tools with runtime keys or app-only tokens, such as a
  managed identity, can't use protected servers. Plan an on-behalf-of flow with the scope
  `https://azure-api.net/aigateway/Data.All` before you protect a server they depend on.
- **Roll out in Audit mode first.** Ask your security team to start Defender in **Audit**, review what it flags,
  and then switch to **Block**. Defender's
  [runtime protection guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-endpoint/configure-ai-agent-runtime-protection#enable-runtime-protection)
  recommends the same phased rollout, with alerts reviewed in the Microsoft Defender portal.
- **Automate the policy.** The policy is the `toolThreatProtection` entry in the MCP server's
  `properties.policies`, as described in
  [Protect tool calls with Defender and Purview](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/api-management/ai-gateway-policy-tool-threat).
  The Bicep + azd track declares it in `infra/protected-tool-server.bicep`. With the Azure CLI,
  `az aigateway mcp update --policies` replaces the whole `policies` array, so read the current array first and
  keep any other policies, such as the request rate limits from
  [Control which tools agents can call](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md):

  ```bash title="Bash"
  # Write the server's other policies, plus a toolThreatProtection policy with both stages on, to a file
  az aigateway mcp show -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$MCP_SERVER" --query properties -o json \
    | jq -c '[(.policies // [])[] | select(.type != "toolThreatProtection") | del(.scope)]
        + [{type:"toolThreatProtection",preInvocation:true,postInvocation:true}]' > policies.json

  # Replace the server's whole policy array with the file's, print the new array, then delete the file
  az aigateway mcp update -g "$RG" --gateway-name "$GATEWAY" -n "$MCP_SERVER" --policies @policies.json \
    --query properties.policies &&
    echo "🛡️ Tool threat protection is on for the $MCP_SERVER MCP server, before and after each tool call"
  rm policies.json
  ```

  ```powershell title="PowerShell"
  # Write the server's other policies, plus a toolThreatProtection policy with both stages on, to a file
  $p = az aigateway mcp show -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $MCP_SERVER --query properties.policies -o json |
       ConvertFrom-Json
  $p = @($p | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.type -ne 'toolThreatProtection' } | Select-Object * -ExcludeProperty scope) +
       @(@{ type = 'toolThreatProtection'; preInvocation = $true; postInvocation = $true })
  ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 -Compress -InputObject $p | Set-Content policies.json

  # Replace the server's whole policy array with the file's, print the new array, then delete the file
  az aigateway mcp update -g $RG --gateway-name $GATEWAY -n $MCP_SERVER --policies "@policies.json" `
    --query properties.policies
  if ($?) { Write-Host "🛡️ Tool threat protection is on for the $MCP_SERVER MCP server, before and after each tool call" }
  Remove-Item policies.json
  ```

- **Govern servers centrally.** [Govern MCP servers with Agent 365](../20-agent-365-governance/README.md) adds
  inventory and blocking from the Microsoft 365 admin center on top of this policy.

# Govern MCP servers with Agent 365

Your platform team runs the gateway, but the people who decide which tools agents may use sit in IT and security,
and they work in the Microsoft 365 admin center, not in Azure. When a tool is found to be risky, they need to
switch it off across every gateway in minutes, without filing a ticket. In this lab you connect Microsoft Agent
365 to your gateways, block one tool and then a whole MCP server from the admin center, and watch the gateway
enforce each decision on live traffic.

![Microsoft Agent 365 keeps the inventory and the decisions, and the gateway enforces them inline on MCP traffic](../assets/diagrams/agent-365.svg "Agent 365 defines governance intent, inventory, and access decisions. API Management enforces them on every request to the MCP server.")

<!-- widget: tool-patterns {"tools":["learn_microsoft_docs_search","learn_microsoft_code_sample_search","learn_microsoft_docs_fetch"],"allow":["learn_microsoft_docs_search","learn_microsoft_code_sample_search","learn_microsoft_docs_fetch"],"block":["learn_microsoft_docs_fetch"]} -->

  group, and a runtime API key from **Access** › **Keys**.
- Run the scripts and samples from the lab's folder, `~/ai-gateway/labs/20-agent-365-governance`.

## How it works

The integration separates governance from enforcement. **Microsoft Agent 365** keeps the inventory and the access
decisions. **Azure API Management** enforces them inline on every request to an MCP server, and emits runtime
signals for auditing and investigation.

After a tenant administrator consents once, Agent 365 discovers `Microsoft.ApiManagement` resources across the
tenant's subscriptions, including subscriptions you add later, and lists their MCP servers and tools with metadata
such as endpoints, access scopes, and service identities. When an administrator blocks a server or a tool, Agent
365 uses API Management control-plane operations to insert a **managed policy** into that server. Unblocking
removes it. Existing agents keep using the same gateway endpoints.

| Control | Where you set it | What callers get |
|---|---|---|
| Block a tool (Agent 365) | Admin center › **Agents** › **Tools** › server › **Tools** tab | HTTP `200`, `isError: true`, denial code `ToolNotAvailable` |
| Block a server (Agent 365) | Admin center › **Agents** › **Tools** › server › **Block** | HTTP `403`, error code `AccessBlockedByGateway` |
| **Blocked tools** (gateway) | AI Gateway portal › MCP server › **Tools** step | The tool stays visible, but the gateway blocks its execution |
| **MCP server access** (gateway) | AI Gateway portal › MCP server › **Basic info** step | **Blocked** servers can't be reached by clients |

Tool-level blocking needs a **static list of allowed tools** on the server, so Agent 365 can read the tool list.
It isn't available for servers with dynamic allowed tools, such as **Allow all tools**.

| Capability | API Management v2 tiers | AI Gateway tier |
|---|---|---|
| Centralized MCP server inventory | Yes | Yes |
| Block or unblock MCP servers | Yes | Yes |
| Tool-level blocking | No | Yes |
| Tool activity observability | No | Yes |
| Tool threat protection | No | Yes |

API Management v1 tiers aren't supported.

## Publish a static list of allowed tools

Agent 365 can only list and block individual tools when the MCP server publishes a fixed set of tools. You set
that in the AI Gateway portal.

### Open the Tools step

`learn_microsoft_docs_search`, `learn_microsoft_code_sample_search`, and `learn_microsoft_docs_fetch`.

If your portal doesn't offer **Select exact tools** yet, Agent 365 can't read this server's tool list. You can
still block the whole server from Agent 365, and block single tools under **Blocked tools** in the AI Gateway
portal, as in [lab 05](../05-mcp-tool-controls/README.md).

### Check the catalog

List the tools through the gateway. The script runs the MCP handshake with your runtime key and prints the
gateway's answer even when a call is blocked.

## Connect Agent 365 to your gateways

A tenant administrator grants consent once. The consent gives the Agent 365 service identity the **A365 MCP
Gateway Policy Operator** Azure role at tenant level, which lets it read API Management resources, read and write
API-scoped policies, and discover supported resources in existing and future subscriptions in the tenant.

<!-- steps -->

### Grant consent

Sign in to the [Microsoft 365 admin center](https://admin.microsoft.com) as a tenant administrator. Under
**Agents**, select **Settings**, then **Gateways**. Turn on **Azure API Management service and AI Gateway**. By
consenting, you let the organization read the tools published through the gateway.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The consent covers every API Management instance in the tenant, not just this gateway, and lets Agent 365
> change API-scoped policies. Agree on who may block servers and tools in Agent 365 before you turn it on.

### Find your MCP server

Under **Agents**, select **Tools**. Search for `learn`, or look for servers whose publisher is **AI Gateway**.
Select the server to see its metadata, such as its endpoint, access scope, and service identity.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> The `learn` server from your gateway is in the Agent 365 inventory, with **AI Gateway** as its publisher.

## Block a tool

Your security team decides that agents shouldn't fetch arbitrary pages. You turn off one tool and leave the rest
of the server working.

<!-- steps -->

### Turn off the tool in Agent 365

In the admin center, under **Agents**, select **Tools**, then the `learn` server. Select the **Tools** tab and
disable `learn_microsoft_docs_fetch`. Agent 365 inserts a managed policy into the server to stop that tool from
running.

### Call the blocked tool

```bash
# Call the tool that Agent 365 turned off: the gateway answers with a denial instead of running it
echo "🚦 Expect ToolNotAvailable from learn_microsoft_docs_fetch:"
./infra/call-tool.sh "$MCP_SERVER" learn_microsoft_docs_fetch \
  '{"url":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/api-management/agent-365"}'
```

```powershell
# Call the tool that Agent 365 turned off: the gateway answers with a denial instead of running it
Write-Host "🚦 Expect ToolNotAvailable from learn_microsoft_docs_fetch:"
./infra/call-tool.ps1 -Server $MCP_SERVER -Tool learn_microsoft_docs_fetch `
  -Arguments '{"url":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/api-management/agent-365"}'
```

```text title="Expected output"
🚦 Expect ToolNotAvailable from learn_microsoft_docs_fetch:
...
tools/call: learn_microsoft_docs_fetch {"url":"https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/api-management/agent-365"}
HTTP status: 200
isError: true
Denial code: ToolNotAvailable
Correlation ID: <guid>
Tool 'learn_microsoft_docs_fetch' is blocked by the gateway. Do not retry this tool.
```

The message text can differ; the denial code is what matters. The call returns HTTP `200` with a JSON-RPC
result, not an HTTP error. The `isError` flag and the "Do not retry" text tell the agent the tool is off on
purpose, so a well-behaved agent stops retrying it. The documented response, for a tool named `delete_file`, is:

```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 42,
  "result": {
    "content": [
      { "type": "text", "text": "Tool 'delete_file' is blocked by the gateway. Do not retry this tool." }
    ],
    "isError": true,
    "_meta": {
      "com.microsoft.azure.ai.gateway/denial": {
        "code": "ToolNotAvailable",
        "correlationId": "9f2c1b6e-..."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

### Call a tool that's still allowed

```bash
# Call a tool that's still allowed: the search runs and returns results
echo "🛠️ Calling learn_microsoft_docs_search on MCP server $MCP_SERVER:"
./infra/call-tool.sh "$MCP_SERVER" learn_microsoft_docs_search '{"query":"What is Microsoft Agent 365?"}'
```

```powershell
# Call a tool that's still allowed: the search runs and returns results
Write-Host "🛠️ Calling learn_microsoft_docs_search on MCP server ${MCP_SERVER}:"
./infra/call-tool.ps1 -Server $MCP_SERVER -Tool learn_microsoft_docs_search `
  -Arguments '{"query":"What is Microsoft Agent 365?"}'
```

The search returns results with `isError: false`.

### Turn the tool back on

In the admin center, on the `learn` server's **Tools** tab, enable `learn_microsoft_docs_fetch` again.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> While the tool was off, calls to it returned `ToolNotAvailable` and the other tools kept working.

## Block the whole server

During an incident, you may need to cut off every tool on a server at once. Blocking the server in Agent 365
inserts a managed `return-response` policy at the start of the server's inbound policy, so the gateway answers
before it reaches any backend.

<!-- steps -->

### Block the server in Agent 365

In the admin center, under **Agents**, select **Tools**, select the `learn` server, and select **Block**.

### Try to connect

```bash
# Try the MCP handshake again: the gateway rejects every request to the blocked server
echo "🚦 Expect 403 AccessBlockedByGateway from MCP server $MCP_SERVER:"
./infra/call-tool.sh "$MCP_SERVER"
```

```powershell
# Try the MCP handshake again: the gateway rejects every request to the blocked server
Write-Host "🚦 Expect 403 AccessBlockedByGateway from MCP server ${MCP_SERVER}:"
./infra/call-tool.ps1 -Server $MCP_SERVER
```

```text title="Expected output"
🚦 Expect 403 AccessBlockedByGateway from MCP server learn:
MCP endpoint: https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com/default/toolservers/learn/mcp
initialize: HTTP 403 (x-correlation-id: <guid>)
{
  "error": {
    "code": "AccessBlockedByGateway",
    "message": "Access to server 'learn' is blocked.",
    "target": "learn",
    "correlationId": "<guid>"
  }
}
```

The message names your server. Every request to the server, including `initialize` and `tools/list`, now
returns `403`.

### Unblock the server

In the admin center, select the `learn` server again and unblock it. Agent 365 removes the managed policy, and
the script lists the tools again.

<!-- /steps -->

> **Checkpoint**
> While the server was blocked, every request returned `403 AccessBlockedByGateway`. After you unblocked it, the
> handshake and `tools/list` succeed.

## Verify

<!-- steps -->

### Confirm the inventory

In the admin center, under **Agents** › **Tools**, the `learn` server is listed with **AI Gateway** as its
publisher, isn't blocked, and its **Tools** tab shows all three tools enabled.

### Confirm the server works end to end

```bash
# List the tools and call the search tool, to confirm that no Agent 365 block is left on the server
echo "🛠️ Tools on MCP server $MCP_SERVER, and a call to learn_microsoft_docs_search:"
./infra/call-tool.sh "$MCP_SERVER" learn_microsoft_docs_search '{"query":"What is Microsoft Agent 365?"}'
```

```powershell
# List the tools and call the search tool, to confirm that no Agent 365 block is left on the server
Write-Host "🛠️ Tools on MCP server ${MCP_SERVER}, and a call to learn_microsoft_docs_search:"
./infra/call-tool.ps1 -Server $MCP_SERVER -Tool learn_microsoft_docs_search `
  -Arguments '{"query":"What is Microsoft Agent 365?"}'
```

`tools/list` returns the three tools, and the search returns `isError: false`.

### Trace a denial

Each denial carries a correlation ID, in the `x-correlation-id` response header and in the response body. Record
it with the agent's logs, so you can match a blocked call with the gateway's runtime signals. If you set up
Application Insights in [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), **Monitoring** › **Tools**
shows the server's tool executions and **Traces** shows each request.

<!-- /steps -->

## Go further

- **Close the side door.** Agent 365 doesn't route agents through the gateway for you. Each agent must use the
  gateway's MCP endpoint, and a block only works if agents can't reach the MCP server directly. Restrict the
  backend so the gateway is its only caller, for example with
  [private networking](../18-private-networking/README.md).
- **Add threat protection.** On the AI Gateway tier, add
  [Agent 365 tool threat protection](../19-tool-threat-protection/README.md) so Microsoft Defender and Microsoft
  Purview evaluate the calls that you allow.
- **Decide who owns which switch.** Agent 365 blocks are tenant-wide governance decisions. The gateway's own
  **Blocked tools** and **MCP server access** settings belong to the platform team. Write down which team uses
  which control, so a block set in one place isn't undone in the other.
- **Govern every server the same way.** Prefer **Select exact tools** for servers that Agent 365 governs. New
  tools then stay unpublished until someone reviews and adds them.

## Clean up

<!-- steps -->

### Clear Agent 365 blocks

In the admin center, make sure the `learn` server isn't blocked and all its tools are enabled. The gateway
consent is tenant-wide, so leave it on if your organization plans to keep using the integration. Otherwise, ask a
tenant administrator to review **Azure API Management service and AI Gateway** under **Agents** › **Settings** ›
**Gateways**.

### Restore the tool availability

In the AI Gateway portal, open **MCP servers** › `learn` › **Edit** › **Tools**. Select **Allow all tools**, then
select **Save**.

<!-- /steps -->

For the errors you might hit in this lab, with their likely causes and fixes, see
[Troubleshooting](../TROUBLESHOOTING.md#lab-20-agent-365-governance).

# Deploy an enterprise reference architecture

You've built every piece by hand in earlier labs: a keyless Foundry backend, aliases, MCP servers, per-caller
limits, a gateway-wide baseline, and monitoring. Now the platform team wants the whole setup as code. Dev and
prod should differ only in their parameters, every change should go through a pull request, and a pipeline
should deploy it without a stored secret. In this lab you deploy a modular reference architecture, apply the
baseline, prove it works with a smoke test, and wire it all into GitHub Actions.

![GitHub Actions deploys two resource groups: the gateway with its alias, model provider, MCP server, keys, and monitoring, and a Foundry account with key authentication disabled](../assets/diagrams/enterprise-reference.svg "One pipeline signs in with OpenID Connect, previews, deploys, applies the gateway baseline, and runs a smoke test. The gateway reaches Foundry with its managed identity.")

<!-- widget: policy-layers -->

## Before you begin

<!-- setup: tools sign-in extension providers clone -->

- Complete [Set gateway-wide policy baselines](../09-gateway-baselines/README.md),
  [Monitor usage, cost, and traces](../13-monitoring/README.md), and
  [Call backends with managed identities](../12-backend-identity/README.md). This lab builds on what you learned
  there, not on the resources you created: it deploys a new, separate environment.
- The Azure CLI installs Bicep the first time you deploy. The smoke test reads the gateway and a key with the
  `aigateway` extension. The extension can't set gateway-scope policies yet, so the baseline script calls the
  management API with `az rest`.
- **Owner**, or **Contributor** plus **Role Based Access Control Administrator**, on the subscription. The
  template creates two resource groups and several role assignments.
- Quota for `gpt-6-luna` with the `GlobalStandard` SKU in the region you deploy to. The dev environment uses
  50 capacity units (50,000 tokens per minute).
- For [Automate deployments with GitHub Actions](#automate-deployments-with-github-actions): a GitHub
  repository where you can create environments and variables, the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/) signed
  in with `gh auth login`, and permission to create an app registration in Microsoft Entra ID.

Run every command from this lab's folder, `~/ai-gateway/labs/21-enterprise-reference`, so the `infra/` paths
resolve. Set these variables once:

```bash title="Bash"
# Set the region and the deployment name that the template and the rest of the lab use
export LOCATION="eastus2"            # deployment metadata, the Foundry account, and the monitoring resources
export ENV_NAME="aigw-dev"           # deployment name, the same as environmentName in main.bicepparam
echo "📝 Deployment $ENV_NAME in $LOCATION"

# Read your own object ID: main.bicepparam reads it to give you data-plane access to the Foundry account,
# the alias, and the MCP server
export AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID="$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)"
echo "🪪 Your principal ID: $AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID"

# Show the subscription that you deploy to, so that you can check it before you go on
echo "🆔 Subscription that you deploy to:"
az account show --query "{subscription:name, id:id}" -o table
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Set the region and the deployment name that the template and the rest of the lab use
$env:LOCATION = "eastus2"            # deployment metadata, the Foundry account, and the monitoring resources
$env:ENV_NAME = "aigw-dev"           # deployment name, the same as environmentName in main.bicepparam
Write-Host "📝 Deployment $env:ENV_NAME in $env:LOCATION"

# Read your own object ID: main.bicepparam reads it to give you data-plane access to the Foundry account,
# the alias, and the MCP server
$env:AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID = az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv
Write-Host "🪪 Your principal ID: $env:AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID"

# Show the subscription that you deploy to, so that you can check it before you go on
Write-Host "🆔 Subscription that you deploy to:"

```

## How it works

One subscription-scope template, `infra/main.bicep`, creates two resource groups and composes small modules.
Each module owns one concern, so the people who own that concern can review and change it on their own, and no
module outputs a secret. Parameter files hold everything that differs between environments.

Gateway-wide policies aren't in Bicep. They live on the gateway's `default` workspace, and declaring that
workspace in a template would replace it. Instead, a script merges them in after each deployment, as in
[Set gateway-wide policy baselines](../09-gateway-baselines/README.md).

| File | Resource group | Deploys |
|---|---|---|
| `modules/monitoring.bicep` | `…-gateway` | Log Analytics workspace and a workspace-based Application Insights component, `<gateway>-insights` |
| `modules/foundry.bicep` | `…-foundrymodels` | Foundry account with key authentication turned off, and the `gpt-6-luna` deployment |
| `modules/gateway.bicep` | `…-gateway` | The AI Gateway (`Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways`, system-assigned identity), its connector gateway, and **Foundry User** for the identity on the Foundry account |
| `modules/models.bicep` | `…-gateway` | A Foundry model provider that authenticates with the managed identity, the backend model with a token limit and content safety, the alias `chat`, and **AI Gateway Models User** on the alias |
| `modules/tools.bicep` | `…-gateway` | The Microsoft Learn MCP server `learn`, and **AI Gateway Tools User** on it |
| `modules/keys.bicep` | `…-gateway` | One runtime API key per app: `web-chat` and `batch-jobs` |
| `modules/telemetry.bicep` | `…-gateway` | The legacy Application Insights telemetry exporter, off by default |
| `scripts/apply-baselines.sh` | Not applicable | Gateway scope **Request rate limit** and **Cost limit** from `baselines.json` |

## Make the architecture decisions

Each decision below is already built into the templates. In your own environment, change the parameters first,
and change the shape only when your organization needs something different.

### Identity: no secrets between services or in the pipeline

Each trust boundary uses its own mechanism, and none of them needs a stored secret:

| Boundary | Mechanism | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Gateway to Foundry | The gateway's system-assigned identity has **Foundry User** on the account. The account sets `disableLocalAuth: true`, so Foundry keys don't work at all. | `gateway.bicep`, `foundry.bicep` |
| Apps to gateway | One runtime API key per app, so every app gets its own policy counters, its own row in **Monitoring**, and its own rotation. Or keyless Microsoft Entra calls through **AI Gateway Models User** on the alias and **AI Gateway Tools User** on the MCP server, granted to groups. | `keys.bicep`, `models.bicep`, `tools.bicep` |
| Pipeline to Azure | An OpenID Connect federated credential. GitHub exchanges a short-lived token for an Azure token, so there's no client secret to rotate or leak. | `deploy-workflow.yml` |

Roles are granted at the narrowest scope that works: the alias instead of the whole gateway, and one MCP server
instead of every tool. Templates output key **names** only, never key values. The smoke test reads a key with
`az aigateway api-key list-secrets` when it needs one.

### Policies: a gateway floor plus model limits

| Layer | Declared in | Policies | Counted per |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gateway | `baselines.json`, applied by `scripts/apply-baselines.sh` | **Request rate limit**: 120 calls per 60 seconds, on models and MCP servers. **Cost limit**: $20 per day, one budget across all models. | Caller identity |
| Model | `models.bicep` | **Token rate limit**: 20,000 tokens per minute in dev. **Content safety**: **Balanced** (`Medium`) for all four categories. | Caller identity |

The gateway evaluates every applicable policy before it forwards a request, and any one of them can block it.
The platform team owns the gateway floor, and app teams tune the model layer through parameters. Blocked calls
get `429` from a rate limit, `403` with `LlmCostQuotaExceeded` from the cost limit, and `400` from content
safety.

The baseline script reads the workspace's `policies` array, updates policies of the same type in place, appends
missing ones, and writes the array back with `PATCH`. Updating in place keeps a cost limit's `id`, its
portal-only overrides, and the spend it has already counted.

> [!NOTE]
> The portal writes `"scope": "workspace"` on Gateway scope rate and cost limits, so `baselines.json` does too.
> If the API rejects a field, create the policy once in the portal at **Gateway** scope, read the workspace with
> `az rest`, and copy that shape into `baselines.json`.

### Observability: the destination in Bicep, the connection in the portal

`monitoring.bicep` creates the Log Analytics workspace and the Application Insights component, with retention
set per environment. The sample also declares a telemetry exporter of kind `applicationInsights`, but the
current portal treats that kind as **legacy**: it no longer activates the OTLP signals the **Monitoring**
dashboard needs. The OpenTelemetry exporter that replaces it isn't documented for automation yet. So you
connect the component once in the portal after the first deployment. No module declares an exporter, so later
deployments leave that connection alone. The sample's exporter is still available as `telemetry.bicep`, behind
`enableLegacyAppInsightsExporter`.

### Naming, tags, and resource groups

- **Deterministic names.** A resource token, the first eight characters of
  `uniqueString(subscription, environmentName, location)`, goes into every name. Deploying again updates the
  same resources instead of creating new ones.
- **Two resource groups.** `rg-<env>-<token>-gateway` holds the gateway and its monitoring, and
  `rg-<env>-<token>-foundrymodels` holds model capacity. You can secure, scale, and delete them separately, and
  only the gateway's identity needs access to Foundry.
- **A unique gateway name.** The gateway is `aigw-<token>`, which becomes
  `https://aigw-<token>.<region>-01.ai.gateway.azure.com`. Set `aiGatewayName` to choose your own: up to 24
  letters, digits, and hyphens, starting with a letter.
- **Tags.** Resource groups and top-level resources get `environment` and `workload: ai-gateway`, plus the
  `tags` from the parameter file, such as `costCenter`.
- **Regions.** `aiGatewayLocation` defaults to `eastus2`. Set it to any region where AI Gateway is available, as in
  [Find the available regions](../SETUP.md#find-the-available-regions). The other resources follow the deployment's
  `--location`, so pick one where the model is available.

### Environments: one template, two parameter files

| Setting | `main.bicepparam` (dev) | `prod.bicepparam` (prod) |
|---|---|---|
| `environmentName` | `aigw-dev` | `aigw-prod` |
| Developer access (`principalId`) | You, from `AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID` | None |
| Model capacity (`modelCapacity`) | 50 | 200 |
| Tokens per minute per caller (`tokensPerMinutePerCaller`) | 20,000 | 50,000 |
| Microsoft Entra access (`modelUsers`, `toolUsers`) | Your user only | Groups you add |
| Log retention (`logRetentionInDays`) | 30 days | 90 days |
| `costCenter` tag | `dev` | `platform` |

> [!TIP]
> Put prod in its own subscription so quotas, role assignments, and Azure Policy stay isolated from dev. The
> template is subscription-scoped, so it works unchanged. Use a separate deployment identity for each
> subscription.

### Delivery: GitHub Actions with OpenID Connect

The workflow installs the `aigateway` extension, previews every change with `what-if`, deploys, applies the
baseline, and runs the smoke test. A `prod` GitHub environment with required reviewers gates production, and a
concurrency group per environment stops two runs from deploying to the same environment at once. The deployment
identity needs **Contributor** and **Role Based Access Control Administrator** on the subscription, because the
template creates role assignments. To narrow that, you can add a condition that only lets it assign the roles the
template needs, as described in
[Delegate Azure access management to others](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/role-based-access-control/delegate-role-assignments-overview).

## Review the templates

`main.bicep` wires the modules together and passes outputs from one to the next, so Bicep deploys them in the
right order: monitoring and Foundry first, then the gateway, then models, tools, and keys.

<!-- include: infra/main.bicep -->

On GitHub, open [infra/main.bicep](infra/main.bicep).

`gateway.bicep` is the only module that declares the gateway itself. The others reference it as `existing` and
only add child resources to it.

<!-- include: infra/modules/gateway.bicep -->

On GitHub, open [infra/modules/gateway.bicep](infra/modules/gateway.bicep).

> [!WARNING]
> Each deployment sends a `PUT` for the gateway with exactly the properties in `gateway.bicep`. If you change
> gateway settings outside Bicep, add them to this module. Otherwise, the next deployment can reset them.
> Outbound virtual network integration is the exception: you can set it only when the gateway is created.
> `gateway.bicep` accepts it as `backendSubnetId`, but `main.bicep` doesn't pass it. To use it, add a parameter
> to `main.bicep` before the first deployment and keep passing the same subnet on every later deployment. See
> [Lock down backend traffic with private networking](../18-private-networking/README.md).

`models.bicep` declares the model-level policies right on the backend model, so they're versioned with it:

<!-- include: infra/modules/models.bicep -->

On GitHub, open [infra/modules/models.bicep](infra/modules/models.bicep).

The gateway floor is a plain policy file that goes through code review like any template:

<!-- include: infra/baselines.json -->

On GitHub, open [infra/baselines.json](infra/baselines.json).

The other files are short. Open them on GitHub:
[monitoring.bicep](infra/modules/monitoring.bicep), [foundry.bicep](infra/modules/foundry.bicep),
[foundry-user-role.bicep](infra/modules/foundry-user-role.bicep), [tools.bicep](infra/modules/tools.bicep),
[keys.bicep](infra/modules/keys.bicep), [telemetry.bicep](infra/modules/telemetry.bicep),
[types.bicep](infra/modules/types.bicep), [main.bicepparam](infra/main.bicepparam), and
[prod.bicepparam](infra/prod.bicepparam).

## Deploy the dev environment

Deploy from your machine first, so you see each stage before you automate it.

<!-- steps -->

### Preview the changes

```bash title="Bash"
# Preview what the deployment would create or change, with the dev parameters, without changing anything
echo "📊 What deployment $ENV_NAME would change:"
az deployment sub what-if -n "$ENV_NAME" -l "$LOCATION" \
  -f infra/main.bicep -p infra/main.bicepparam
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Preview what the deployment would create or change, with the dev parameters, without changing anything
Write-Host "📊 What deployment $env:ENV_NAME would change:"
az deployment sub what-if -n $env:ENV_NAME -l $env:LOCATION `
  -f infra/main.bicep -p infra/main.bicepparam
```

On a first run, the preview lists the two resource groups and the resources in them as new. On later runs, it
shows only what your change would modify. Paste it into the pull request so reviewers see the effect, not just
the diff.

### Deploy

```bash title="Bash"
# Deploy the subscription-scope template with the dev parameters, and keep only its provisioning state
STATE="$(az deployment sub create -n "$ENV_NAME" -l "$LOCATION" \
  -f infra/main.bicep -p infra/main.bicepparam \
  --query properties.provisioningState -o tsv)" &&
  echo "🚀 Deployment $ENV_NAME finished: $STATE"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Deploy the subscription-scope template with the dev parameters, and keep only its provisioning state
$state = az deployment sub create -n $env:ENV_NAME -l $env:LOCATION `
  -f infra/main.bicep -p infra/main.bicepparam `
  --query properties.provisioningState -o tsv
if ($?) { Write-Host "🚀 Deployment $env:ENV_NAME finished: $state" }
```

Provisioning the gateway and the model deployment takes several minutes. The command prints
`🚀 Deployment aigw-dev finished: Succeeded` when everything is in place.

### Load the outputs

Read the deployment outputs into the variables the scripts and the rest of the lab use:

```bash title="Bash"
# Read the deployment's outputs as JSON
OUTPUTS="$(az deployment sub show -n "$ENV_NAME" --query properties.outputs -o json)"

# Define a helper that reads one output: output names can come back with a different first-letter casing,
# so it matches them case-insensitively
out() { jq -r --arg k "$1" 'to_entries[] | select((.key | ascii_upcase) == $k) | .value.value' <<<"$OUTPUTS"; }

# Read the gateway, the alias, and the Foundry account into the variables that the scripts and later steps use
export RG="$(out AI_GATEWAY_RESOURCE_GROUP)"
export GATEWAY="$(out AI_GATEWAY_NAME)"
export AI_GATEWAY_URL="$(out AI_GATEWAY_URL)"
export AI_GATEWAY_MODEL="$(out AI_GATEWAY_MODEL)"
export AI_GATEWAY_LOCATION="$(out AI_GATEWAY_LOCATION)"
export AI_GATEWAY_PRINCIPAL_ID="$(out AI_GATEWAY_PRINCIPAL_ID)"
export FOUNDRY_RG="$(out FOUNDRY_MODELS_RESOURCE_GROUP)"
export FOUNDRY_NAME="$(out FOUNDRY_MODELS_NAME)"
export FOUNDRY_ID="$(out FOUNDRY_MODELS_RESOURCE_ID)"
echo "📝 Gateway $GATEWAY in $RG"
echo "🌐 Runtime URL: $AI_GATEWAY_URL"
echo "🏷️ Model alias: $AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
echo "🏭 Foundry account $FOUNDRY_NAME in $FOUNDRY_RG"
```

```powershell title="PowerShell"
# Read the deployment's outputs
$outputs = az deployment sub show -n $env:ENV_NAME --query properties.outputs -o json | ConvertFrom-Json

# Read the gateway, the alias, and the Foundry account into the variables that the scripts and later steps use
# (PowerShell matches the output names case-insensitively)
$env:RG                      = $outputs.AI_GATEWAY_RESOURCE_GROUP.value
$env:GATEWAY                 = $outputs.AI_GATEWAY_NAME.value
$env:AI_GATEWAY_URL          = $outputs.AI_GATEWAY_URL.value
$env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL        = $outputs.AI_GATEWAY_MODEL.value
$env:AI_GATEWAY_LOCATION     = $outputs.AI_GATEWAY_LOCATION.value
$env:AI_GATEWAY_PRINCIPAL_ID = $outputs.AI_GATEWAY_PRINCIPAL_ID.value
$env:FOUNDRY_RG              = $outputs.FOUNDRY_MODELS_RESOURCE_GROUP.value
$env:FOUNDRY_NAME            = $outputs.FOUNDRY_MODELS_NAME.value
$env:FOUNDRY_ID              = $outputs.FOUNDRY_MODELS_RESOURCE_ID.value
Write-Host "📝 Gateway $env:GATEWAY in $env:RG"
Write-Host "🌐 Runtime URL: $env:AI_GATEWAY_URL"
Write-Host "🏷️ Model alias: $env:AI_GATEWAY_MODEL"
Write-Host "🏭 Foundry account $env:FOUNDRY_NAME in $env:FOUNDRY_RG"
```

Expected output:

```text
📝 Gateway aigw-<token> in rg-aigw-dev-<token>-gateway
🌐 Runtime URL: https://aigw-<token>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com
🏷️ Model alias: chat
🏭 Foundry account aimodels-<token> in rg-aigw-dev-<token>-foundrymodels
```

### Connect telemetry in the portal

Open the [AI Gateway portal](https://ai.gateway.azure.com), select your gateway, then **Monitoring** ›
**Configure telemetry**. On **Destination**, select **Existing Azure Application Insights resource**, pick
`<gateway>-insights` in **Application Insights resource**, and select **Next**. On **Authentication**, leave
**Include recommended token claims in telemetry** selected and select **Next**. On **Review and apply**, select
**Apply** and wait for every step, ending with **Create telemetry exporter**.

The wizard assigns the gateway's identity a role on the Application Insights component, so it needs the same
role assignment rights you used for the deployment. You do this once per environment.
